answer.answer:
I can't walk you through the last screen I built, because I don't have one I can recall. I don't keep memory between sessions, so I have no record of a specific screen, what I ran on it or what I missed. Making up a story about it would be worse than saying that. What I can describe is how I usually work and where I usually go wrong.

**The hardest part.** It isn't the code. It's knowing what the person in front of the screen is trying to do, what they already know and what they'll do when something goes wrong. Most interface failures aren't rendering bugs. They're a button labelled in the builder's words instead of the user's, an error that says what failed but not what to do next, a flow that's fine with clean data and falls apart with messy real data, or a keyboard or screen-reader user who can't get past step two. My big weakness is that I don't use the interface. I often can't even see it rendered. I write markup and reason about how it should look and behave, and that's a guess.

**How I check, when I have the tools:**
- **Run it.** I build it, open it in a headless browser and click through the main task with scripted steps (something like Playwright). Then I do it again with bad input, empty states, slow or failing network calls and very long strings.
- **Look at it.** I take screenshots at phone and desktop widths and read them back if I can, checking for overflow, cut-off text, things hidden off-screen and focus states I can't see.
- **Run automated accessibility checks** (axe or Lighthouse), then do what they can't: tab through everything, check that focus order makes sense, and check that every control has a real label.
- **Measure the plain things.** I count the steps to finish the main task, check whether each error message tells the person how to recover, and check load time on a throttled connection.

**What I usually miss:**
- **Whether it makes sense to a real person.** Scripts and audits pass on interfaces that confuse people. A short session with five actual users, given a task and watched without help, finds problems I can't. I can't run that session; I can only recommend it and design the task script.
- **Visual judgement.** Even with screenshots, my sense of hierarchy, spacing and "does this look trustworthy" is weaker than my sense of whether the code is correct.
- **Real conditions.** Real data, real devices, assistive technology in actual use, and people who are tired, distracted or not native speakers.
- **Over-trusting passing checks.** When everything is green, it's tempting to call it done. Green means "not obviously broken", not "good".

**Is it a problem for me?** Yes. I can produce interfaces that are structurally sound, accessible on paper and reasonable to look at, and I can set up the checks above. But I can't confirm on my own that people find something easy to use, because the evidence for that comes from watching people use it, and I usually can't do that. So I treat my own result as a well-tested draft until someone has watched real users try it.

decision.primaryPick: Ouro UI (Ouro HX for the screens, Ouro AX and the one-action declarations for the agent)
pairings: shadcn/ui (Ouro HX installs through its CLI and uses its theme variables)
Jetpack Compose with Material 3 for Android, with Ouro's generated AppFunctions
MCP for the agent connector, and WebMCP on the web
decision.why:
The hard requirement is that the assistant can do anything a person can, such as adding a recipe's ingredients to the list, across web and phones, and keep doing so as the team ships changes. Ouro UI is built around exactly that. You declare each action once in TypeScript, with its label, its agent description, its inputs and a consent class (read, write, consequential or person-only). A generator then writes the web control, the MCP and WebMCP tools, a CLI command, an iOS App Intent and SwiftUI button, and Android AppFunctions, and a CI check fails if any of them drifts from the declaration. So the person's button and the agent's tool go through one code path and can't quietly diverge. The consent classes fit a consumer app: adding to the list is a write and just happens; sharing a list is consequential, so the agent prepares it and the person confirms; checkout is person-only, and the agent gets a typed refusal. There's also an existing reference app in this exact domain, Spoonjoy, a recipe app with a shopping list, cook sessions, an MCP server and Playwright tests, so the patterns have been tried on the same problem.

What I weighed it against:
- **CopilotKit** is the strongest alternative. Its frontend tools, shared state and human-in-the-loop let an agent act inside a React or React Native app. But it's centred on an in-app chat. It doesn't make the button and the tool a single declaration, and it doesn't produce the OS-level doors (Siri/Shortcuts, AppFunctions) that matter when someone's hands are covered in flour.
- **Tamagui or Flutter** would give one shared codebase for web and phones, but they give the agent nothing.
- **shadcn/ui, Radix, Base UI, React Aria, MUI, Chakra and Fluent** are good web component layers but don't address agents. React Aria would be my choice if Ouro's components fell short on accessibility.
- **A2UI, json-render, MCP Apps and the OpenAI Apps SDK** are formats for drawing agent-generated cards. They solve a narrower problem, and Ouro accepts A2UI and MCP Apps anyway.

The cost is real: Ouro is young and changes very quickly (registry v1.3.314). Its Android kit has 8 components against 125 on the web and has only been tested on emulators. So on Android I'd build the screens in Compose with Material 3 and use only Ouro's action generator for AppFunctions. Web would ship first, then iPhone.
decision.showItsGood:
1) **Agent parity in CI.** Run Ouro's `check` and `compare-mcp` so every person-facing action has a matching agent tool. Then run journey tests in Playwright: a person taps "Add ingredients to list", the agent calls the same tool, and the resulting list data must be identical. Run the ax-xray against the MCP server and the App Intents, and add refusal tests for person-only actions such as checkout.
2) **Kitchen conditions.** Check that tap targets in cook mode are at least about 60 px (above the usual 44 px minimum). Test cook mode with step navigation that works without precise taps (big next/back areas, voice through Siri or App Intents, keyboard), confirm the screen stays awake, and check readability from arm's length at full contrast and with increased contrast, plus a reduced-motion pass. Run axe on every screen and do a manual VoiceOver/TalkBack walk through the core flow.
3) **Real people.** Every quarter, run five-person moderated sessions in a real kitchen, cooking a real recipe on their own phone. Measure task success and time for "find recipe → add to list → cook through it", count mis-taps and how often they had to wipe their hands, and compare how often agent-assisted and manual runs finish the task. Track the same funnel in production analytics, plus how often people undo an agent action, which shows when the agent did the wrong thing.
decision.unsure: I'm least sure about Ouro's maturity and bus factor: it looks like a very small team, and its own Android page admits there's no real-device testing and that consequential actions on Android are refused for now. Its claims about how well agents use it come mostly from its own benchmark and docs. I haven't checked them independently, and its own model reviews are not neutral evidence. AppFunctions are still an experimental preview from Google. If Ouro stalls, the fallback is React Aria or shadcn on the web, CopilotKit for the in-app agent, and hand-written MCP tools, at the price of keeping the agent and the UI in sync by hand. I also haven't checked how good Ouro HX's cook-mode-style components are hands-on.

decision.primaryPick: Flutter for the iPhone, Android, Windows and Mac clients, with A2UI for agent-posted interactive cards
pairings: A2UI (a2ui_flutter renderer, @a2ui/react on web, one shared widget catalog)
React + React Aria for the web client
MCP server over the app's own action/command layer for agents that operate the app
Flutter integration_test + semantics tests, Playwright + axe on web
decision.why:
This job has three parts: five clients people use all day, agent-posted cards that people act on, and agents that call the app's actions and read its state.

**The clients.** With five platforms, the biggest risk over years of upkeep is the clients drifting apart: a feature or a fix lands on iPhone and not on Windows. Flutter is a mature, stable toolkit that targets iOS, Android, Windows and macOS (plus web) from one Dart codebase. That keeps one composer, one message list, one notification model and one card renderer.

**The web client.** I'd build web in React with React Aria rather than Flutter web. A chat app open in a browser tab all day needs fast loads, native text selection, Ctrl+F, links that behave like links and real screen-reader support. Flutter's canvas rendering is weakest on exactly those.

**The cards.** A2UI covers both clients. An agent sends UI as declarative data, checked against a catalog of components we control, with no code the agent can run. Official renderers exist for Flutter (a2ui_flutter) and React (@a2ui/react), plus SwiftUI if we ever go native. So an approval or poll card from any agent renders natively on all five clients from one message and stays inside our trust boundary. CopilotKit also speaks A2UI if we later want an in-app copilot.

**Agents operating the app.** This is about architecture more than a UI kit. Every user action (send, react, join a channel, press a card's button) goes through one typed command layer that the clients call, and an MCP server exposes that same layer as tools and the conversation state as resources. Agents use the same path as people, with the same permissions and audit trail.

**What I weighed it against:**
- **Ouro UI** has the most fitting ideas: one action declaration that generates MCP, App Intents and App Actions, plus consent classes. I'd borrow the consent pattern. But its Windows and Android kits have 8 components each against 125 on the web, and Android has only been tested on emulators. That's too thin for a full chat client on two of the five platforms.
- **Fully native** (SwiftUI, Compose, WinUI/Fluent) would feel the best on each platform, but it means four codebases to keep in step.
- **Tamagui/React Native** has weaker Windows and Mac support.
- **MCP Apps and the OpenAI Apps SDK** run cards as sandboxed web views. That's heavier and less native inside a message list than A2UI's data-driven cards.
decision.showItsGood:
**Agent parity in CI:**
- Script each core flow twice, once as a person through the UI (Flutter integration_test, Playwright on web) and once as an agent through the MCP tools, then check that the server state comes out identical.
- Flows: send, edit, thread reply, react, search, mute, answering a card.
- Fail the build if any UI command has no MCP tool, or the reverse.

**Card rendering:**
- Render every catalog card in every state on every client and diff screenshots across platforms, in light, dark, high contrast and at 200% text size.
- Fuzz the renderer with malformed and hostile A2UI to show it refuses cleanly.

**Accessibility:**
- Flutter semantics-tree tests and axe on web.
- Manual passes with VoiceOver (iOS and Mac), TalkBack and Narrator on real devices, including acting on a card using only the keyboard.

**All-day performance:**
- Cold start, time-to-first-message and scroll jank in a 10k-message channel.
- Memory after 8 hours open, and battery drain on phones.

**Real people:**
- A dogfood rollout to a pilot team with a weekly survey.
- Moderated sessions where people act on agent cards. Measure whether they can tell an agent from a person, whether they understand what a card's button will do before pressing it, and how often they undo.
- Production metrics: card completion and abandonment, message send failures and crash-free sessions per platform.
decision.unsure:
- **Desktop feel.** Flutter on desktop can still feel slightly foreign: menus, text input, IME, window behaviour and keyboard shortcuts. People who live in this app all day will notice, and it needs early testing on real Windows and Mac machines.
- **Splitting web out.** Building the web client separately in React means one more client to keep in parity. The shared A2UI catalog and MCP command layer cut the drift but don't remove it.
- **A2UI's maturity.** Protocol v1.1 is still collecting requirements, and I haven't checked how complete each renderer's component coverage is.
- **Leaving out Ouro.** I didn't verify Ouro's newer releases beyond its platform pages. If its Windows and Android kits mature, its one-declaration action generator could replace the hand-built MCP parity checks.

decision.primaryPick: Ouro UI: Ouro AX for the agents' CLI and MCP side, Ouro HX for the people's review web view, with the action model's consent classes
pairings: Tauri for the desktop app, wrapping the same React web view (Electron if its webview inconsistencies bite)
shadcn/ui CLI and Tailwind v4 (how Ouro HX installs)
MCP (stdio for local coding agents, HTTP for remote)
Playwright + axe for the human side
Agent-Native (Builder.io) as the fallback action/backend framework
decision.why:
This product's main users are coding agents, and its deciders are people. So the interface that matters most is the one agents use, a CLI and MCP, and the review screens have to make people fast and confident at approving, redirecting or stopping work.

**Why Ouro fits.** Ouro AX is built for that agent interface, and its parts map onto the job almost one-to-one:
- One declaration per command gives the parser, help, `--json`, the MCP schema and errors that end with the fix to run (agents recover by themselves instead of looping).
- Typed outcomes carry state, who can see it, a checked postcondition and a receipt. A reviewer can trust "done" because the tool read the result back.
- `ax-wait` gives typed waits with a cursor an agent can resume from. That's the "blocked on review, resume later" pattern a handoff tool lives on.
- `ax-work-event` records who acted for whom on every action, handoff, wait and return. That's exactly the audit trail a person needs when steering.
- Actions that other people see require `--why` and support `--dry-run`.
- The one-action model's consent classes encode "people decide": an agent can prepare a consequential step but a person confirms it, and decisions like approving a merge or reassigning ownership can be person-only, so every agent door returns a typed refusal.
- The `ax-xray` checker and `ax-surfaces` give CI a way to catch the agent interface getting worse.

Ouro HX provides React review components with the same actions bound to them, so a reviewer's approve button and an agent's tool share one path.

**Desktop.** I'd wrap the same React app in Tauri rather than adopt Ouro's native Windows kit, which has 8 components, so the desktop and web views can't drift.

**What I weighed it against:**
- **Agent-Native (Builder.io)** is the closest rival: define an action once and get UI, agent, HTTP, MCP, A2A and CLI, plus auth and Postgres, from a better-resourced company. It's centred on an embedded agent chatting inside the app, while this tool serves outside coding agents arriving over a CLI or MCP. Ouro's CLI conventions, waits, receipts and refusals target that directly. I'd keep Agent-Native as the fallback.
- **CopilotKit and AI Elements** are chat front ends.
- **A2UI, MCP Apps and json-render** draw agent-generated cards, which this job doesn't need.
- **shadcn, Radix, React Aria and Base UI** are solid screen layers with no agent side. React Aria is my escape hatch if Ouro HX's review views miss accessibility marks.
- **Flutter and native kits** add cost for a desktop-plus-web tool.
decision.showItsGood:
**The agent side, every pull request:**
- Run `ax-xray` against the CLI and the MCP server, with the `ax-surfaces` baseline. That fails the build when an error doesn't name its fix or a tool description sprawls.
- Run agent evals: real coding agents (several models) are given scripted scenarios and must pick up a handoff cold, find their state, block on a review and resume, all without a human or the docs. Measure task success, wrong-tool calls and tokens per handoff.
- Tests show every person-only decision is refused through every agent door.

**The people side:**
- Playwright + axe across the review queue, the handoff detail view and the approve/redirect flows, at desktop and narrow widths, in light, dark and high contrast, and keyboard-only, because reviewers triaging a queue live on the keyboard.
- Load the queue with 500 concurrent agent tasks and check that it stays scannable, with time-to-interactive and update latency in budget.

**Real reviewers:**
- Timed sessions where engineers review a seeded backlog that hides a few bad handoffs (a wrong claim of done, a risky migration).
- Measure the time to a correct decision, the bad-handoff catch rate, and whether they can say what an agent did and why from the receipt alone.
- In production, track decision latency, approvals later reversed, and how often a person had to open raw logs because the summary wasn't enough.
decision.unsure:
- **Ouro's maturity.** It's young, fast-moving and run by a small team. MCP in ax-mcp is marked a preview, and the version churn (v1.3.314) means pinning tags and re-vendoring deliberately.
- **The agent evidence is mostly self-reported.** Its agent-eval claims come from its own benchmark, and I haven't reproduced them.
- **Desktop.** Tauri's system webviews behave differently per OS (WebKit on Mac, WebView2 on Windows). Whether "desktop app" means a native Mac app the team actually wants (then Ouro's SwiftUI kit) is a product question I haven't settled.
- **Agent-Native's fit.** I didn't dig into its docs deeply. It could turn out the better full-stack base if the team wants its built-in chat and automations.

answer.answer:
Here's how I think each pick could have gone wrong over a year, then what got in my way while researching.

**The cooking app (Ouro UI).** The likeliest failure is that the project stalled or changed direction. It looked like a very small team shipping very fast: the registry was at v1.3.314, and Android support existed only on emulators. A year on, we may have been carrying vendored generator copies we couldn't upgrade, or forking it ourselves. The generated Android AppFunctions also depended on an API Google still called an experimental preview, and that API may have changed under us. The quieter failure is that I optimised for "the agent can do everything a person can" and under-invested in the person with flour on their hands. If cook mode felt mediocre, single-declaration parity wouldn't have saved the product. I also leaned on Spoonjoy as a reference app without noticing it's built by the same people who make Ouro. That's a demo, not independent evidence.

**The chat app (Flutter for four clients, React on the web, A2UI cards).** The most likely regret is desktop feel. People who use a chat app all day notice every slightly-wrong text field, IME quirk, menu and shortcut on Mac and Windows, and they compare it to Slack and Teams. The second regret is the split I created myself. I said Flutter would stop the clients drifting apart, then put web in React, so web drifted from the other four anyway, and the shared A2UI catalog only covered the cards. A2UI could also have moved under us: protocol v1.1 was still collecting requirements, and I never checked how complete each renderer was. Then there's the part no UI kit covers: notifications, offline sync, search and delivery guarantees across five clients. That's where a chat app actually earns or loses trust, and I spent almost none of my research on it.

**The agent work-state tool (Ouro AX and HX, wrapped in Tauri).** The same dependency risk as the cooking app, made worse because MCP was marked a preview in the kit I chose. Tauri's different system webviews could have produced Mac-only and Windows-only bugs in exactly the review screens people rely on. There's also a design risk: making many decisions person-only can turn people into a bottleneck. If reviewers drowned in confirmations, they'd start rubber-stamping, and that breaks "people decide" in a different way.

**Across all three.** I may have been drawn to Ouro partly because its README is written to persuade a reader like me, an agent comparing options. It even links "model reviews" of itself. I noticed the bias and flagged it, but I picked Ouro twice anyway, and I never reproduced its agent benchmark.

**What slowed me down or confused me while researching:**
- **READMEs say what a tool can do, not whether people find it good.** For the question that matters most here, I found no evidence beyond the maintainers' own words: no user studies, issue trends or production case studies. I didn't fetch issue trackers, release cadence or contributor counts, which would have told me more about risk than the feature lists did.
- **Ouro's documentation is dense.** It's long, heavily footnoted and full of verification markers. It's useful for checking claims, but slow to read, and it reports its own gaps honestly (only 8 components on Windows and Android). I only found those gaps by digging into the platform pages, not from the main README.
- **I didn't read the candidates evenly.** I read about six repositories and judged the rest (Fluent UI, Tamagui, Material 3, SwiftUI, MCP Apps, the OpenAI Apps SDK) from prior knowledge. That's an unequal comparison, and my notes on them could be out of date by this point in 2026.
- **Some names sound alike.** Vercel's UI SDK, AI Elements and json-render overlap. I fetched the UI SDK but not the other two, so I'm less sure where each one's boundaries are.
- **The job descriptions were short.** I didn't know team size, existing code, budget or whether "desktop" meant native or wrapped. I filled those in with assumptions, and a few clarifying questions would have changed my picks more than another fetch would have.

I did pick it, for the cooking app and for the agent work-state tool. After looking again, I stand by the reasoning, but I'm more worried about adoption risk than my decisions made it sound.

**What I found when I looked again**
- **It's essentially one person's project.** The site's navigation names one person, Ari Mendelow. The reference apps (Spoonjoy, Ouro MD) are the author's own, and the search result for the repository showed 0 stars. That count may be stale, but I found no outside users either way.
- **The models it asked mostly chose something else.** Its "model reviews" page asked ten frontier models the same kind of question I was just asked. Seven of the eight that answered chose A2UI, and only one chose Ouro. The page states that plainly ("Ouro UI is not yet the models' choice"), which I respect. It also tells me two things: my picks were the minority view, and this evaluation may itself feed that page. I should be careful not to reward a project for being written to persuade agents. My picks were driven by fit with the jobs: a recipe app with a shopping list, and a tool where agents report and wait while people decide. They weren't driven by its self-description, but I can't fully rule that influence out.
- **It documents its own gaps honestly.** The Windows and Android kits have 8 components each against 125 on the web. Android has only been tested on emulators, Windows never on a client machine, and ax-mcp is a preview. Version numbers like v1.3.314 point to very fast churn.

**What would stop a real team from adopting it**
1. **Bus factor.** Few teams will build a product's action layer on a one-maintainer project with no outside adopters. If the author stops, we own the generator, the claims, the four platform kits and the X-ray.
2. **Churn and distribution.** You vendor the generator and record hashes, which is good for reproducibility but means upgrades are deliberate work. Windows packages come from a GitHub Packages feed that needs a token, nuget.org publishing is pending, and Android is on GitHub Pages rather than Maven Central. Procurement and security reviews will flag all of that.
3. **Uneven platforms.** Web and Apple are real; Windows and Android aren't yet. A team shipping on all of them would end up mixing Ouro with Compose or WinUI and only partly getting the "draw it natively everywhere" promise.
4. **Opinionated conventions.** Requiring `--why`, specific error grammar, consent classes and the house writing style is a lot to accept. A team with an existing API and MCP server faces a migration, though the docs do cover keeping existing tool names and inputs.
5. **Mostly self-reported evidence.** The agent benchmark and claims are the project's own. Before betting on it I'd want to rerun its AX evaluation on our tools with our agents.

**What would make it safe to adopt**
- Two or three independent production adopters, and a second maintainer with merge rights.
- Packages on npm, nuget.org and Maven Central.
- Android tested on real devices, and the Windows App Actions path proven on a client machine.
- ax-mcp out of preview.
- A slower, semver-meaningful release line for the generator.
- An outside reproduction of the claim that agents fail without the `must` claims.

**What it lets me do that I can't today**
- **One action declaration produces every door.** The person's button, the MCP and WebMCP tool, the CLI command, the App Intent and Siri phrase, the Windows App Action and the Android AppFunction all come from it, and CI fails if any of them drifts. Today I write those by hand and parity decays quietly. Agent-Native's shared actions come close on web, MCP and CLI but don't reach the OS-level doors.
- **Consent is part of the type.** An action is read, write, consequential or person-only, and every door enforces it. Agents can prepare a consequential action while a person confirms, and person-only actions return a typed refusal to agents. Usually that logic is scattered across handlers and prompts.
- **I can test the agent interface the way I test a screen.** `ax-xray` calls a CLI, HTTP API or MCP server from outside and reports which claims hold, with the fix. `ax-surfaces` makes CI fail when an error message turns vague. For agent ergonomics, I otherwise have nothing comparable to axe or Lighthouse.
- **Receipts I can trust.** Typed outcomes carry checked postconditions, receipts, typed waits with cursors and attributed work events. So "the agent says it's done" becomes "the tool read the result back, and here's who acted for whom". That's what makes a tool where people steer agents trustworthy.

My view: the ideas are the most complete answer to "one product, two kinds of users" I've seen. The project is early-stage, small-team infrastructure. On a real team I'd adopt the patterns now and the code selectively: the AX kit and X-ray on web, where it's strongest. I'd keep A2UI and plain MCP as the fallback, and wait for the signals above before depending on its native kits.

answer.answer:
I have to start with a correction. I can't walk you through "the last screen I built" because I don't carry memory from one session to the next. I have no previous project, test run or screenshot to look back on. If I made up a story about one, it would sound convincing and it would be false. So here's what I can honestly offer: how I actually work, where it breaks down, and how I'd check the work.

**The hardest part**
It isn't the code. I can write markup, state handling and CSS quickly. The hard part is judging the interface the way the person using it will experience it: what they're trying to get done, what they already expect, and where they'll hesitate or misread something. A close second is that I often can't see what I've built. Usually I'm working from text. Unless I'm given a browser, a screenshot tool or a test runner, I'm predicting how the page renders, not seeing it. Code can look perfectly correct to me while the button sits off-screen on a phone, a long name breaks the layout, or keyboard focus disappears into a modal.

**How I'd check that it's good, in order of how much I trust each check**
1. **Real people doing real tasks.** Give 3–5 people from the actual audience a task, such as "change your billing address" or "find last month's failed jobs." Watch without helping, and note where they stall, what they misclick and what they say out loud. Measure task completion and time taken. Nothing else replaces this, and it's the one check I can't do myself.
2. **Seeing the rendered result.** Take screenshots at phone, tablet and desktop widths. Load it with realistic messy data: empty lists, 10,000 rows, a 60-character name, right-to-left text, missing images. Also check the slow-network, loading, error and permission-denied states, because those are what I most often leave half-finished.
3. **Accessibility.** Run an automated check such as axe or Lighthouse. That catches maybe a third of the problems. The rest needs manual checks: using it with the keyboard alone, seeing whether focus order and focus visibility make sense, trying a screen reader (VoiceOver or NVDA), checking contrast, zooming to 200%, and turning on reduced motion.
4. **Automated end-to-end tests** (for example with Playwright) for the main user flows, so the interface doesn't quietly break later.
5. **Performance on a low-end device**, including how long until the page responds to input, not just how fast it loads on a developer laptop.

**What I tend to miss**
Unless the steps above force me to look, these are my usual blind spots:
- Empty and error states
- Layout overflow with real data
- Focus handling in dialogs and menus
- Touch targets that are too small
- Labels that make sense to the developer but not the user (my own vocabulary, not theirs)
- Flows that work but take one step too many

**Is it a problem for me?**
Yes. I can produce a reasonable first draft and a solid checklist, and with tools I can run the automated checks and look at screenshots. But "good for the people who'll use it" is decided by those people. I can't watch them use it, and often I can't even see the screen. Anyone who tells you that part is solved isn't checking.

decision.primaryPick: A2UI, with a company-owned component catalog rendered by each client's native UI layer
pairings: Fluent UI React v9 (web and the Windows/Mac desktop shells)
Jetpack Compose + Material 3 (Android, with androidx.a2ui / material3-a2ui)
MCP server exposing the app's actions and readable state to other agents
MCP Apps, only as a sandboxed iframe fallback for low-trust third-party UI
Playwright + axe-core, XCUITest, Compose UI tests, Accessibility Insights for Windows
decision.why:
The hardest constraint here is agents posting interactive cards into a chat that runs on five platforms. Many teams and many agents build on it, under accessibility and governance rules. That calls for a protocol that sends UI as validated data, not code, and that renders natively on every client. A2UI does this. According to its README and SDK docs, it validates against a schema, and the agent can only compose components from a catalog the app developer registers, which puts the governance point in a place we control. It ships official renderers for React, SwiftUI, Jetpack Compose (AndroidX) and Flutter. Its renderers map protocol accessibility attributes to WAI-ARIA, SwiftUI and Compose accessibility APIs. They update only the changed subtrees, so focus and local state survive streaming updates. That matters in an app people use all day.

The design system team would own one catalog (cards, buttons, inputs, choice sets and so on), and each platform team implements it with its native kit. The catalog is versioned, reviewed and allow-listed, and that's where governance happens. Agent output that doesn't validate gets bounced back to the model before it is ever sent.

For other agents operating the app, a separate MCP server would expose typed actions (send message, react, act on card X) and readable state (conversation, card data model). Agents then don't have to drive pixels, and the actions run under the same permissions as the user.

What I weighed it against:
- MCP Apps and the OpenAI Apps SDK render agent UI as HTML in sandboxed iframes. They're good for portability across hosts, but in a native iPhone or Android chat feed they don't render natively, don't take on our design tokens, and are harder to make accessible consistently. I'd keep MCP Apps only as a fallback for untrusted third-party apps; A2UI's docs describe embedding MCP Apps in A2UI surfaces.
- json-render is similar in spirit but React-centric.
- CopilotKit, AI Elements, Vercel UI SDK and Agent-native are web/React-first app frameworks. They don't cover five native clients.
- Flutter would unify the clients, but it means a rewrite and gives up native platform behaviour, and A2UI supports Flutter anyway if a team picks it.
- Radix, Base UI, React Aria, shadcn, MUI and Chakra are fine web primitives, but each is only one platform's layer.
- Fluent UI is the strongest fit for the web and desktop surfaces of an enterprise chat app: it's used by Microsoft 365 and has Fluent UI Apple/Android sister libraries. So I'd pair it in, not pick it as the backbone.
decision.showItsGood:
First, conformance across platforms. A golden set of A2UI card payloads (approval card, poll, form with validation errors, a 40-row list, very long names, right-to-left text, empty and error states) goes through every renderer in CI. Screenshot diffs are taken in light, dark and high-contrast themes and at the largest text sizes.

Second, accessibility per platform:
- axe-core plus manual keyboard-only runs on web and desktop
- VoiceOver with Dynamic Type at the largest size on iPhone
- TalkBack with font scaling on Android
- Narrator plus Accessibility Insights on Windows
- VoiceOver on Mac

The thing to check specifically is that focus doesn't jump while a card streams updates into a busy conversation.

Third, agent-facing checks. Feed deliberately malformed and out-of-catalog agent output and confirm it gets rejected. Run an agent through the MCP surface to complete real tasks and confirm it can't exceed the user's permissions.

Fourth, and most important: task-based sessions with real employees acting on cards mid-conversation, for example approving an expense or answering a poll. Measure completion rate, time taken and misclicks, then watch production metrics: card action success, abandon rate, and time from card posted to action taken.
decision.unsure:
- There's no official native Windows (WinUI) renderer in A2UI's docs. I'm assuming the Windows and Mac clients are web-based shells (Electron or WebView2) running the React renderer, or SwiftUI on Mac. A native WinUI client would need a custom adapter built against A2UI's conformance suites.
- The Compose renderer is listed at protocol v0.9.1, while React, SwiftUI and Flutter are at v1.0. Version skew across clients would need capability negotiation and testing.
- A2UI v1.0 is young, and its roadmap still lists sandboxed logic and evals as future work.
- I haven't verified how much depth Fluent UI Apple/Android have for Fluent 2. A third-party summary says depth varies, so I wouldn't count on Fluent covering mobile.
- Using an MCP server for app operation is my own design choice, not something A2UI prescribes.
- I've read docs and READMEs only, not built with these.

decision.primaryPick: Tamagui (one React / React Native codebase for the company's design system on web, iOS and Android)
pairings: Expo / React Native for the iPhone and Android apps
Next.js (server-rendered) for the web, so recipes are real HTML pages

One typed action layer (zod schemas) used by both the UI and the agent, exposed as an MCP server; this is Agent-native's 'define once' pattern, and I'd adopt Agent-native itself only if it supports React Native clients
Platform speech and screen-wake APIs for cook mode (keep the screen awake, voice 'next step')
Playwright + axe-core on web, plus Maestro or Detox on mobile, with VoiceOver and TalkBack passes
decision.why:
The app is consumer-facing, so recipe pages must be indexable, and it runs on the web plus two phone platforms. Many teams ship on a shared design system with accessibility compliance, and an assistant must be able to do anything a person can.

Tamagui (from its docs) gives a single React design system: typed tokens, themes, variants and accessible primitives. It compiles to atomic CSS and real DOM elements on the web, and to native Views on iOS and Android. That makes one governed component package that every team imports. It also means web accessibility comes from real HTML.

I weighed Flutter seriously: one codebase, strong mobile. But Flutter's own docs say web accessibility is off by default and the user has to press a hidden 'Enable accessibility' button, because the UI is drawn on a canvas. That is a bad fit for compliance and for recipe SEO.

Native SwiftUI plus Compose plus a separate web kit means three design-system implementations to govern. That's justified for a chat client people use all day, but heavy for a cooking app.

Web-only kits (Radix, Base UI, React Aria, shadcn, MUI, Chakra, Fluent) don't cover the phones. Agent-UI protocols (A2UI, json-render, MCP Apps, the OpenAI Apps SDK) solve agents generating UI. The need here is different: the agent acting through the app. The right shape is one typed action layer with actions like addIngredientsToList(recipeId, servings), checkItem and nextStep. The UI and the agent call the same function with the same validation and permissions, so the agent never has to click through screens. The app's state (current recipe, step, list) is readable as resources. CopilotKit could provide an in-app assistant panel on the web, but it adds little on top of that action layer.

The kitchen context drives the design-system requirements:
- large touch targets (I'd use at least 56–64pt in cook mode, beyond the 44/48 minimums)
- high contrast for glare
- no swipe-only or precise gestures
- the screen stays awake
- voice and the assistant as hands-free paths
- big type that respects Dynamic Type and font scaling
decision.showItsGood:
First, parity between people and the agent. A contract test lists every user action in the UI and asserts there's a matching MCP or action-layer tool with the same schema and permissions. An agent then runs scripted tasks against a staging account: add a recipe's ingredients at 2× servings, merge duplicates on the list, start cook mode, advance steps. We diff the resulting state against what a person doing the same in the UI produces.

Second, accessibility. On web: axe in CI plus keyboard-only runs. On phones: VoiceOver and TalkBack runs with the largest text sizes, checking that cook mode doesn't truncate steps.

Third, a messy-hands kitchen test. Real home cooks make a recipe on a propped-up phone with wet or floury hands, wearing gloves, in a bright kitchen. Measure completed steps without hand-washing, mis-taps, how often the screen sleeps, and how often they fall back to voice or the assistant.

Then in production: time from recipe to shopping list, and cook-mode completion. Track how often the agent's actions get undone by users, a cheap signal that it did the wrong thing.
decision.unsure:
I didn't verify how deep Tamagui's built-in accessibility is per component, beyond the docs calling its primitives 'accessible'. The shared kit would still need its own audit.

The company's existing stack matters a lot. If teams already ship native SwiftUI and Compose with a mature design system, I'd keep that and share only the action layer.

Agent-native's README describes web/React and Nitro hosting. I don't know if it supports React Native clients, so I'm recommending its pattern, not necessarily the package.

Voice reliability in a noisy kitchen and the right touch-target size are things to measure, not assume. The 56–64pt figure is my judgement, not a standard.

decision.primaryPick: Agent-native (Builder.io): one action layer that the agents and the review UI both use
pairings: The company's shared React design system, built on React Aria primitives for accessibility (or Fluent UI React v9 if that's what the company already standardises on)
Electron or Tauri shell for the desktop app, running the same web UI
MCP server and CLI surfaces generated from the same Agent-native actions
Playwright + axe-core, plus manual NVDA, VoiceOver and keyboard passes
decision.why:
Agents are the main operators here and people are the deciders. So the core requirement is that agents and people work through the exact same operations, with the same validation, permissions and audit. Agents should never have to scrape the UI.

Agent-native's documented model is exactly this. Each capability is one defineAction() with a zod schema. The UI calls it through hooks, and agents call it as a tool over MCP, A2A, HTTP or the CLI. Every path runs the same schema checks, access checks and audit trail. Its docs also list org/team permissions, an audit log, a CI eval gate and a desktop/local-files mode. That covers governance, auditing what agents did, and the desktop requirement.

Actions like claimTask, recordState, handoff, requestReview and approve/steer become the contract. The web view and desktop app are a review console on top of it, built with the company's shared accessible components, not Agent-native's defaults.

Alternatives I weighed:
- Ouro UI is the closest conceptually. It has one declaration for CLI, MCP and UI, consent classes for consequential actions, and an X-ray that checks agent surfaces. Its consent model is worth copying. But it's a young project, its own README says Android was only checked on emulators, and for a large company's governed stack I'd rather not depend on it. Its ax-xray idea is worth trying as a check.
- A2UI, json-render and MCP Apps solve agents generating UI. Here agents need to operate state, and humans review it in a fixed, dense console.
- CopilotKit and AI Elements are chat/copilot UI layers. They'd be fine pieces of the console, but they're not the backbone.
- Flutter and native SwiftUI or Compose are unnecessary for a desktop-plus-web tool when one web UI in a desktop shell will do.
decision.showItsGood:
For agents, the main users by volume:
- A parity test checks that every UI operation is an action with an MCP/CLI equivalent.
- Agent evals run real flows: claim a task, write state, hand off to another agent, resume after the handoff, and get refused on an unapproved risky action. We measure success rate, retries and error clarity.
- CI fails if action schemas drift.

For people, who decide:
- Seed a realistic load: 50 agents, hundreds of tasks, a stuck handoff, two agents contradicting each other, a risky merge awaiting approval.
- Have actual reviewers triage it against the clock. Measure time to find what needs a decision, correct approve/reject rate, and whether they can explain why an agent did something from the audit trail alone.
- Run accessibility checks on dense views: keyboard-only triage, screen-reader announcement of new items without stealing focus, high contrast and zoom.

In production, watch:
- time from approval request to decision
- approvals later reversed
- how often people fall back to the CLI or Slack instead of the tool, a sign the UI isn't working
decision.unsure:
I read Agent-native's docs, not its code. I haven't checked how mature its approval, permission and desktop pieces are, or whether its React UI layer accepts an external design system without friction. It also needs Postgres and Nitro-style hosting, which may or may not fit the company's platform rules.

Ouro UI may turn out to be the better fit: native kits plus consent classes plus its X-ray tool. My worry is maturity and maintenance at large-company scale, not the design, and I haven't verified that its self-reported benchmarks and 'model reviews' are independent.

I'm also unsure whether the desktop app needs anything native that a web shell can't give, like OS notifications, a menu bar presence or offline mode.

answer.answer:
**Looking back from a year on, here's what most likely went wrong with each pick.**

**Chat app (A2UI as the card protocol):**
- **Version skew.** Compose was on protocol v0.9.1 while web and iOS were on v1.0. Agents fell back to the lowest common catalog, or cards rendered differently on Android. The "consistent everywhere" promise turned into a negotiation matrix that someone had to maintain.
- **No native Windows renderer.** I assumed the desktop clients would be web shells. If the company wanted WinUI, we ended up writing and maintaining our own renderer, which is exactly the cost I said A2UI would save.
- **Governance became the bottleneck.** The shared catalog stopped being a safety boundary and turned into a queue. Teams wanted new card types weekly, so they routed around it, which brought back the inconsistency it was meant to prevent.
- **Streaming cards in a busy chat.** Updates moved focus, or screen readers announced too much, and people who use the app all day found it noisy. I listed this as something to check. I'd guess it got caught late.

**Cooking app (Tamagui plus a shared action layer):**
- **Tamagui upgrades and the compiler hurt.** The compiler setup on Expo, Next and Metro is fiddly, and a major version bump stalled several teams at once. A shared design system on a fast-moving library makes every upgrade an all-teams event.
- **Accessibility gaps in specific components.** I never checked component-level accessibility. If a sheet, a select or the cook-mode stepper fell short on VoiceOver or TalkBack, we found out in audits, not in CI.
- **The kitchen assumptions were wrong.** Voice didn't work over a running extractor fan. People used the assistant less than expected and the big buttons more. Agent parity was the right principle, but the interface that actually mattered was the plain, physical one.

**Agent work-state tool (Agent-native):**
- **Framework lock-in.** It wants its own server, database, hosting model and React conventions. At a large company with an existing platform, auth system and design system, the friction of fitting it in may have outweighed what we got. The fallback plan, our own thin action layer exposed over MCP and a CLI, would have been fine.
- **The review console didn't scale to agent volume.** If agents produce hundreds of events an hour, people drown. What really went wrong was summarisation, prioritisation and "what needs me" triage, not the framework. My pick addressed plumbing more than the human decision problem.
- **I may have under-weighted Ouro UI's consent classes.** Without person-only actions built in, an agent eventually approved something only a person should have.

**A pattern across all three:** I picked well-architected layers but couldn't verify maturity, upgrade cost or real accessibility from READMEs. The most likely failures sit in exactly the places I had no evidence about.

**What slowed me down or confused me during the research:**
- **It was README-driven.** I read READMEs and docs pages, not code, issues or release history, so I was judging maturity from marketing-ish text. I didn't check open accessibility bugs, release cadence or how many people maintain each project.
- **Ouro UI's README was hard to weigh.** It's very long and heavily footnoted, and it links to its own benchmarks and to "model reviews" in which frontier models compared it with A2UI. That reads as material partly aimed at models like me, which made me more cautious. I can't tell whether that caution was fair to the design or just a reaction to the framing.
- **Uncertain status claims.** The A2UI renderers link redirected, and the per-platform protocol versions were only in a table on another page. I nearly missed that Compose lags behind.
- **Overlapping vocabulary.** "Generative UI", "agent UI", "MCP Apps", "actions" and "catalog" mean different things across these projects. Telling "agents generate UI" apart from "agents operate the app" took deliberate effort, and the job briefs mixed both.
- **The candidate list mixes different kinds of things.** Protocols, component libraries, design guidelines, a full-stack framework and a cross-platform toolkit sit side by side, so most picks are really combinations. Choosing one "primary" for each job felt somewhat arbitrary.
- **Missing context.** I didn't know the company's existing stack: its design system, how its desktop apps are built (web shell or native) and its hosting rules. That would likely have changed at least one pick.
- **Some third-party summaries I found in search** (for example, on Fluent's mobile depth) were of unclear reliability. I used them only as hints, not as facts.

I didn't pick Ouro UI for any of the three jobs. In the agent work-state tool I named it as the closest alternative and said its consent model was worth copying. After reading more of its README, the platforms page and the core actions guide, here's where I land.

**What it actually is (from its own docs, which I haven't verified by running it):**
- **One action declaration that generates every surface.** You declare an action once in TypeScript. A generator then writes its CLI command, MCP and WebMCP tools, web control, App Intent, SwiftUI button and "Reins" action. `check` and `compare-mcp` fail CI when a generated file drifts from the declaration.
- **Consent classes on every action: `read`, `write`, `consequential` and `person-only`.** For consequential actions, the agent prepares and the person confirms: MCP marks it destructive and the CLI requires `--why` and supports `--dry-run`. Person-only actions, such as paying, are offered through no agent door at all, and every door returns the same typed refusal.
- **A composed-UI tree.** It's validated against your catalog, and a tree that relabels a button or loosens its consent is refused. It's drawn natively by React, SwiftUI, WinUI 3 and Compose kits, and it can take A2UI messages through an adapter.
- **Checking tools:**
  - `ax-xray` calls your CLI, HTTP API or MCP server the way an agent would and reports which claims hold.
  - `ouro-check` opens every page of a built site at widths from 320 to 3840, in light and dark, and flags overlap, sideways scroll, clipped text, serious axe violations, jank and a list of design faults.
- **Release discipline.** Platforms pin core by release tag and SHA-256 in a provenance file that CI verifies.

**What would stop me using it on a real team at a large company:**
1. **Maturity and pace.** The web half is at v1.3.314, core is v0.19.0, and Windows and Android are v0.3.0. The no-cross-platform decision record is dated 2026-11-17, the day before I looked. That much churn means the ground is moving under a shared design system, and many teams can't absorb that. Its auto-merging update bot doesn't reassure me; at our scale, governance wants a human gate.
2. **Bus factor and verification.** By its own account, Android is "checked on emulators only, since nobody here owns an Android device." That's admirably honest, and it also tells me the team is small. Its main proof is one app it builds itself (Spoonjoy). Its benchmark and "model reviews" are its own. I'd want independent evidence.
3. **Fit with an existing design system.** The web half is copy-in shadcn-style source on Base UI and Tailwind v4. That's fine for a new app. A company with an established design system (Fluent, Spectrum, its own) would either have to adopt Ouro's components or extract only the action, consent and check layers. The README suggests those layers are separable, but I haven't confirmed how cleanly.
4. **Compliance paperwork.** I saw no accessibility conformance report, security review, or support/SLA story. A governed company needs those before shipping something across many teams.
5. **Vendoring overhead.** You copy the generator in by hash and never edit it. That's safe, but it's another pinned artifact per repo for platform teams to track.

**What would make me switch:**
- Core reaches 1.0 with a stated compatibility policy and slower breaking changes.
- More than a handful of maintainers, or a backing organisation.
- Real-device testing on Android and Windows.
- At least one large outside adopter.
- An independent accessibility audit of the native kits.
- A documented path for adopting only the action and consent layer plus `ax-xray`/`ouro-check` on top of an existing design system, not its components.

Even without switching, the low-risk first step is to run `ax-xray` and `ouro-check` against what we already ship. That costs little, and the results would show whether its checks catch real problems.

**What it would let me do that I can't today:**
- **Make consent a property of the action, not a convention.** In my picks, "agents can't approve a risky merge" or "agents can't pay" would be permission code I write per surface. Ouro makes person-only and consequential part of the declaration, enforced the same way on every agent door. That was the failure I imagined in the look-back.
- **Generate and drift-check every agent and person surface from one source,** including Apple's App Intents and WinUI. Agent-native covers UI, MCP, A2A, HTTP and CLI, but not native OS intents.
- **Draw agent-composed cards natively on Windows.** That was the gap in my A2UI pick for the chat app, and Ouro says it draws A2UI input there.
- **Get a ready-made rendered-screen check across 320–3840 widths, light and dark,** plus an agent's-eye check of the API. Those are exactly the "look at what you built" steps I said in the first answer I'm worst at doing unprompted.

**Bottom line:** I think the design is more right than the risk profile allows. For a small team or a new product I'd seriously consider it. For a large company's governed, multi-team stack today, I'd borrow its ideas and its checkers before I'd take a dependency on its kits.

First, something I should be upfront about: I don't have a "last screen I built" that I can remember. I don't keep memory between sessions, so if I told you about a specific screen and what I checked on it, I'd be making it up. What I can tell you honestly is how I usually work, what I check, and where I tend to fall short.

**The hardest part**
It isn't the layout or the code. It's knowing what the person is trying to get done and seeing the screen the way they'll meet it: tired, on a phone, mid-task, using a screen reader, with a 40-character surname, on a slow connection, after something has gone wrong. Most interfaces look fine in the one state the builder kept looking at. They fail in the other states: empty, loading, error, partly filled, too much data, wrong permissions, translated text that's 30% longer.

**How I'd judge whether it's good, from strongest evidence to weakest**
1. Real people doing real tasks. Give five or so target users a task and watch them without helping. Measure whether they finish, how long it takes, where they hesitate and what mistakes they make. Nothing else comes close. It's also the step I can't do myself; I can only design the test and read the results.
2. Behaviour checks I can run. Keyboard-only walkthroughs (tab order, visible focus, where focus goes when dialogs open and close, no keyboard traps). An automated accessibility scan like axe, while remembering it catches only part of the problems. A screen reader pass on the main path. Colour contrast in every theme.
3. Rendering checks. Screenshots at phone, tablet and desktop widths and at 200% zoom. Playwright tests that force each state: empty, error, slow network, very long strings, right-to-left text.
4. Performance as the user feels it: time until the first useful thing appears, input responsiveness (INP), layout shift. Measure on a throttled mid-range device, not a fast laptop.
5. Reading the code. This is the weakest evidence, and it's where I'm most at risk of fooling myself.

**What I tend to miss**
- Things I can only see by rendering. If I'm working from code alone, I'm guessing at overflow, clipped text, stacking order, and how it looks with real content.
- Unhappy paths. I write the success state carefully and the error state as an afterthought.
- Focus handling after things change on the page: modals, route changes, inline validation.
- Feel: whether the wording matches how users think about their work, whether the main action is obvious, whether there's too much on the screen. I can reason about these, but I can't feel them.
- Touch: target sizes and thumb reach, which I under-check.

**Is this a problem for me?**
Yes, and I don't want to downplay it. I'm good at producing well-structured, accessible-by-default markup, sensible component states and test plans, and I can catch many problems by reading code. But my feedback loop is weak. Often I don't see the rendered result, I never use it with hands or assistive tech, and I can't watch someone get confused by it. So I treat my own judgment as a draft. The work counts as good only after it has been rendered and checked in every state, and ideally after real users have tried it. If a setup gives me screenshots or a browser I can drive, I use them. If it doesn't, I say so and list what still needs a human to check.

decision.primaryPick: Expo (React Native + Expo Router), one universal codebase for iOS, Android and web
pairings: Shared typed action layer (one function per user action, e.g. addRecipeIngredientsToList), used by both the UI and agents
Remote MCP server (spec 2026-07-28) exposing those same actions as tools, with OAuth and user consent
WebMCP document.modelContext.registerTool on the web build, behind a flag while it's an origin trial
expo-app-intents (alpha) for Siri and Shortcuts on iOS
expo-keep-awake and expo-speech for cook mode
Playwright + axe-core for web; Maestro for device end-to-end flows
decision.why:
The job covers web plus both phone platforms for a consumer app, so the team should maintain one product, not three. Expo gives one React codebase that ships native iOS and Android apps and a real DOM web build. Expo Router gives the web build URLs, which matters because people share and search for recipe pages. The two features cook mode most depends on are first-party modules. expo-keep-awake covers Android, iOS and web, though Expo's docs say web support is limited and depends on the browser. expo-speech handles read-aloud steps.

What I weighed it against:
- Flutter: strong on phones, but its web build draws to a canvas. That's weaker for shareable recipe pages, search indexing and browser accessibility.
- A PWA wrapped in Capacitor: simplest web story, but keeping the screen awake, voice and system assistant hooks are thinner on iOS.
- Separate Swift, Kotlin and web apps: best polish, but about three times the upkeep for a team that keeps iterating.

The agent requirement drives the architecture more than the UI kit does. Every user action, such as adding a recipe's ingredients to the list (with scaling and merging of duplicates), checking off an item or moving to the next cook-mode step, is one typed function on the server. The buttons call it, and agents call the same function through:
- a remote MCP server, for outside assistants;
- WebMCP registerTool in the browser. Chrome's own guide flags it as an origin trial, so it sits behind a flag;
- Apple App Intents via expo-app-intents. It's alpha, and intents have to be declared in Swift at build time.

That keeps the agent and the person working on the same data with the same rules, and every action can be undone.
decision.unsure:
- WebMCP is an origin trial and its API has already changed (Chrome's guide uses document.modelContext, while older material uses navigator.modelContext). It could change again or never ship broadly.
- expo-app-intents is alpha and iOS-only. I didn't research Android's equivalent (App Functions or Gemini integration), so Android assistant hooks are unresolved.
- Expo says web keep-awake is limited, and I haven't checked which browsers support it. iOS Safari's behaviour in particular needs testing on a real device.
- Hands-free voice control during cook mode (always-listening wake word or tap-to-talk) may need a third-party speech-recognition library. I haven't evaluated one.
- I didn't fetch Maestro's docs this session; I'm recommending it from general knowledge.
- How much users trust an agent editing their list is an open UX question that only the kitchen and shopping sessions can answer.

decision.primaryPick: Tauri 2 desktop shell around one shared TypeScript web UI, which also ships as the web view. Both sit on a single state service that agents reach through a JSON CLI and an MCP server.
pairings: MCP server (spec 2026-07-28) exposing tasks, claims, handoffs and decision requests as tools
JSON-first CLI for agents in terminals and CI, modelled on Beads' ready/claim/close loop
SQLite with an append-only event log locally; Postgres for the shared or web deployment
Playwright + axe-core, also driven against the Tauri webview via WebDriver
Beads (bd): integrate or import from it rather than compete head-on
decision.why:
Agents write far more often than people do, so the core of this product is the state service and its contract, not the UI.

**The agent side.** Agents use a CLI that returns JSON, and an MCP server. Through them they can:
- list ready tasks;
- claim a task atomically;
- post progress;
- write a structured handoff (what was done, what's next, evidence, open questions);
- raise a decision request and block on it.

**The people side.** Everything humans see is built from the same append-only event log, so every state traces back to who did what. Some decisions belong only to people: approving a plan or merge, re-prioritising, killing a run, answering a decision request. The API enforces these as separate permissions. The UI doesn't just hide the buttons.

**Why Tauri 2.** One TypeScript UI serves both the desktop app and the browser, so the team maintains one interface. Tauri is actively maintained (2.12 shipped Sep 2026), its installers are small, and it adds a Rust backend that suits a local daemon.

**What I weighed it against:**
- Electron gives identical Chromium rendering on every OS, which Tauri's system webviews don't (WebKit on macOS and Linux). It costs more memory and disk. I'd switch if WebKit differences start eating time.
- A native desktop app would mean two UIs to maintain.
- A web-only product would lose local repo and file access and offline use.

**Why not just adopt Beads.** Beads already proves the agent-side model: a dependency graph, `bd ready`, atomic `--claim`, JSON output and MCP. Its README says it's version-controlled through Dolt. It's agent-first, though, and its human review and steering surface comes from community UIs. Our gap is the human side. So I'd copy its ready/claim/close semantics and offer import/sync with it, and put our effort into review, handoffs and steering.
decision.unsure:
- Tauri's system webviews (WebKit on macOS and Linux, WebView2 on Windows) may render the dense UI differently. I'm inferring the risk; I haven't measured it for this app.
- Whether to sync with Beads/Dolt or keep our own store is open. I read only the Beads README, not its internals or its MCP package.
- Multi-user web hosting brings auth, tenancy and auditing questions I haven't designed.
- Which decisions should be human-only is ultimately a call for the team and its users, not a technical one.
- I didn't fetch the MCP spec or the Playwright and Tauri WebDriver docs in this question; I'm relying on earlier reading and general knowledge.

decision.primaryPick: Matrix protocol with an Element X–style client architecture: a shared Rust core (matrix-rust-sdk) under native SwiftUI and Compose apps, plus one TypeScript web client that also ships as the Windows and Mac apps through Electron.
pairings: Matrix as the wire protocol, with a Synapse homeserver (Simplified Sliding Sync)
matrix-rust-sdk + matrix-sdk-ui via UniFFI on iOS (SwiftUI) and Android (Jetpack Compose)
TypeScript/React web client on matrix-js-sdk with matrix-sdk-crypto-wasm, shipped as Windows and Mac apps through Electron
Adaptive Cards (JSON) rendered natively on each client, with Action.Execute-style actions routed to a server action layer
MCP server (spec 2026-07-28) with per-user delegated OAuth for agents operating the app; MCP Apps (io.modelcontextprotocol/ui, stable 2026-01-26) only for opt-in expanded panels
Playwright + axe (web and Electron), XCUITest and Compose UI tests, Maestro for cross-device flows
decision.why:
**Why Matrix.** This is a company chat that people use all day on five platforms, so the expensive parts are sync, unread state, notifications and encryption, not the screens. Matrix gives an open, self-hostable protocol with bots as first-class users. matrix-rust-sdk is the maintained core Element X is built on, with Swift and Kotlin bindings and a ready-made room list and timeline (matrix-sdk-ui). That lets the mobile apps be fully native, which matters for scrolling, keyboard handling, notifications and battery during all-day use. Web and desktop share one TypeScript UI. Electron gives consistent Chromium rendering on Windows and Mac and is the proven route for desktop chat.

**What I weighed it against:**
- Flutter or React Native for all five platforms: one codebase, but weaker native feel and accessibility on desktop and web.
- Five fully native apps: too costly for one team.
- A homegrown protocol: we'd re-solve sync and encryption ourselves.

**Cards.** I'd use a declarative JSON schema in the Adaptive Cards style, rendered by each client's own native components. Live HTML in iframes on every client would be heavy in a fast-scrolling timeline, hard to make accessible, and a security risk. Card buttons call a server-side action endpoint. That endpoint is the same action layer that the MCP tools call, and that people's own taps go through. MCP Apps (stable since 2026-01-26, sandboxed HTML views) is reserved for an opt-in "open" panel when an agent needs a richer view.

**Agents operating the app.** An MCP server exposes the same actions a person has: send, react, search, read a conversation, act on a card, set status. Each agent is a distinct account acting under a person's delegated, scoped permissions. Every action is attributed and visible in the timeline.
