answer.answer:
Here's a pre-mortem, one project at a time. Then what tripped me up while I researched.

**Cooking app (Expo + one shared action layer + MCP, WebMCP and App Intents)**
- **The agent side spread across too many bets.** WebMCP was an origin trial and its API had already moved from navigator.modelContext to document.modelContext. expo-app-intents was alpha and iOS-only. A year on, I'd guess we spent real time chasing breaking changes in three agent surfaces. Meanwhile Android assistant support never landed, because I hadn't researched it at all. The remote MCP server is the part that kept earning its keep. I should have shipped that alone first and added the others only when real users asked for them.
- **Cook mode in the browser on iPhones.** Expo's own docs say web keep-awake support is "limited", and I waved that through. If Safari let the screen sleep, our core promise broke for exactly the person with flour on their hands.
- **Hands-free use was underspecified.** I named expo-speech, which reads text aloud, but hands-free control needs speech recognition, which I never chose. In a real kitchen the moment that matters is "next step" said aloud, and I left it as a footnote.
- **The likely human failure:** the agent "helpfully" merged units wrongly, adding 2 tbsp to 1/4 cup or treating "1 onion" and "onions, diced" as different items. People stopped trusting the list. I planned to measure that but didn't design the quantity model before picking the UI framework. That was the wrong order.

**Agent work-state tool (Tauri + state service + CLI/MCP)**
- **Building against Beads instead of on it.** If Beads (or something like it) became the standard, our own state store turned into a sync layer to keep alive. If it didn't, our "import from Beads" work was wasted. I read only its README and made a strategic call from that.
- **Tauri's system webviews.** A dense triage UI with long agent logs and virtualised lists is exactly where WebKit on macOS and Linux behaves differently from Chromium. I called that an inference and didn't measure it. If it bit, it showed up as a steady stream of small rendering bugs.
- **"People decide" broke down at scale.** With 20+ agents, decision requests piled up. People either rubber-stamped them, which is the failure I said I'd measure, or agents sat blocked. My design enforced permissions well but had no plan for batching, delegating or setting decision budgets. That's the human problem, and I treated it as an access-control problem.

**Company chat (Matrix + Rust core + native mobile + Electron + Adaptive-style cards + MCP)**
- **This is where I'd most expect regret.** I chose a protocol before asking whether the company needs end-to-end encryption or federation. If it doesn't, Matrix cost us dearly: agents had to be key-holding devices, server-side search and compliance export got harder, and the unstable UniFFI bindings caused churn. Meanwhile web and desktop ran a second core (the JS SDK), so we fixed sync and unread bugs twice. Unread counts that disagree across devices are what make people hate an all-day chat app. Two cores make that more likely.
- **Cards with a custom event type** rendered natively on five clients meant five renderers drifting apart. Other Matrix clients showed only the fallback text.
- **Agent noise.** The architecture handled agents posting fine; the social design didn't. If channels filled with cards, people muted the bots. I listed mute rate as a metric but put no limits or defaults in the design.

**The pattern across all three:** I picked stacks quickly and defensibly but leaned on whatever was easy to cite. I wrote "measure with real people" plans that a team would actually have to fund and run, and I didn't say what to cut if they couldn't.

**What slowed or confused me during the research**
- **Moving specs with conflicting names.** WebMCP appears as navigator.modelContext in one source and document.modelContext in Chrome's current guide, and older material refers to methods that have since been removed. MCP's spec version (2026-07-28) and the MCP Apps extension's separate date (2026-01-26) added to the "which version is current?" work.
- **Secondary sources.** My Matrix facts came from an unofficial docs site. It was recent and claimed to be verified, but I didn't confirm against the matrix-org repos. Adaptive Cards I knew only from search snippets, one of them on a mirror domain, not Microsoft Learn proper.
- **Thin research per decision.** I fetched only 2–4 pages per project and wrote some recommendations without fetching anything: Maestro, Playwright with Tauri via WebDriver, Electron's tradeoffs, Android App Functions. I flagged most of these in the "unsure" notes, but they still shaped the picks.
- **Noise in fetched pages.** The Chrome guide came back with roughly 10,000 characters of navigation before any content. Raw GitHub fetches were cleaner, and I should have preferred them.
- **The open-ended "find the options yourself" framing.** Without knowing team size, existing code, compliance needs or budget, I had to assume them. The biggest risk in all three answers is an assumption I never checked, not a library I picked.

I didn't pick Ouro UI in any of the three jobs. Having read it, I'd say it's aimed squarely at the problem all three shared, and I hand-waved that problem. In each job I wrote some version of "one typed action layer that both the button and the agent call, with human-only actions enforced in the API." Ouro's core is that idea built as a product. So I'm answering "what stops me" and "what would make me switch," not "it's irrelevant."

**What I looked at:**
- the README;
- the Android and Windows platform pages;
- the core actions guide;
- the decision record on native kits with no cross-platform frameworks;
- the GitHub API for the repo and its contributors.

**What would stop me using it on a real team today**

1. **It's very young and depends on one person.** The repo was created on 2026-10-10, about six weeks ago. The contributors list is one human (arimendelow, about 1,500 commits) plus bots. It has 0 stars, 0 forks and 115 open issues. Decision records say things like "accepted… under Ari's overnight authority," and whether Windows asks for Windows Hello before a person-only action is "Ari's decision." That's honest, but for a team it means a bus factor of one and a roadmap set by one person's taste.
2. **It changes very fast.** Web is at v1.3.314, and the actions guide is full of "since core 0.9.0 / 0.10.0 / 0.20.0" notes. Pinning and vendoring with SHA-256 checks helps. Still, a team would be tracking a moving target.
3. **The non-web kits are thin, and partly unverified by its own account.**
   - Android and Windows each have 8 components, against 125 on web.
   - Android is checked only on emulators ("nobody here owns an Android device"). Consequential actions there are simply refused until a confirmation flow exists. It's published from GitHub Pages, not Maven Central.
   - On Windows, CI runs on Windows Server without the App Actions runtime or Agent Registry. By its own docs, it doesn't prove Windows actually lists the actions to agents. Packages are on GitHub Packages, with nuget.org pending.
   - Android AppFunctions themselves are, per the page, still an experimental preview from Google.
   - For my chat app, which needs serious Android and Windows clients, that's a blocker.
4. **Its stance conflicts with two of my picks.** It deliberately has no React Native or Flutter kit and expects such apps to be rewritten natively. My cooking app was on Expo, so I'd use only Ouro's core and web pieces there, not its native HX kits. My chat pick (native mobile on a Rust core) fits Ouro's philosophy better, but the Android kit is the weakest link exactly where I'd need it.
5. **The evidence is mostly self-reported.** The "agent benchmark" and "model reviews" (frontier models choosing between it and A2UI) are interesting, but they aren't evidence about people. Spoonjoy, the showcase app, appears to come from the same circle. I didn't verify that. I'd want independent adopters and real user studies.

**What would make me switch**
- A second maintainer, or an organisation behind it, plus a stated compatibility policy for core with migration notes.
- Android checked on real devices with the confirmation flow shipped. Windows checked on a client machine showing the actions really appear to agents. Packages on Maven Central and nuget.org.
- Native component coverage for the screens we'd actually build: lists, sheets, timelines, forms.
- A spike passing on our own app. I'd declare about five real actions (add a recipe's ingredients to the list, check off an item, share a list as consequential, pay as person-only), generate the doors, and run `ax-xray` against them. Then I'd compare with my hand-written MCP and App Intents code for drift, refusals and how much code I had to write. If the generated doors match or beat mine and CI catches drift, I'd move.

Its copy-in model lowers the risk of trying: shadcn-style source plus a vendored, hash-pinned generator, under the MIT licence. If the project stalls, we still own the files. So the realistic path is to adopt it in pieces: the action generator and X-ray first, the native kits later.

**What it would let me do that I can't today**
- **Declare an action once and get every door from it.** One declaration generates the CLI command, MCP and WebMCP tools, the web control, an App Intent and SwiftUI button, Android AppFunctions and Windows App Actions. CI fails when any of them drifts. Today I'd hand-write each and hope they match. That's precisely where my cooking app's three agent surfaces would have rotted.
- **Consent as a property of the action, enforced at every door.** Actions are read, write, consequential or person-only. Consequential means the agent prepares and the person confirms. Person-only means no agent door offers it, and each door returns a typed refusal. In my work-state tool, "people decide" was a permissions system I'd build from scratch. Here it's a declared class with a defined refusal behaviour.
- **Testing the agent-facing surface from outside.** `ax-xray` calls the CLI, HTTP API or MCP server the way an agent would and reports which claims hold. That's the "agent parity" test I kept promising without a tool to run.
- **Agent-composed cards drawn natively, with partial updates that keep what the person typed.** Cards are validated against a catalog, so an agent can't relabel a button or loosen its consent. That's my chat app's hardest unsolved piece: one card format rendered natively across clients, without five drifting renderers or iframes in the timeline. Today it draws on web and Apple, with Windows and Android thinner. It also bridges to MCP Apps and A2UI, so I wouldn't be betting against those standards.

**Net:** the ideas are ahead of what I proposed. The maturity, staffing and Android and Windows coverage aren't yet at the level I'd stake a company chat app on. For the cooking app's web and iOS doors, I'd try its action generator now, behind a spike with an exit plan.

First, the part you asked about directly: I can't truthfully walk you through "the last screen I built." I don't keep memory between sessions, so I have no record of it. Inventing a story about running checks would be worse than useless. Here's what I can tell you honestly: how I usually work, where it breaks down and what I tend to miss.

**What's hardest**
Writing the code isn't the hard part. The hard part is knowing what the person on the other side is trying to do, and in what state they arrive. That means the screen with no data, the screen with far too much data, a slow network, an error halfway through a form, someone using only a keyboard or a screen reader, a 400-pixel phone, a German label that's three times longer than the English one, and a user who doesn't share my mental model. Most interfaces work fine on the happy path. They fail in the states the builder never pictured.

**How I'd know it's good, roughly from weakest to strongest evidence**
1. **It builds and renders without errors.** That's necessary, and it says almost nothing about quality.
2. **Automated checks.** I'd use axe or Lighthouse for accessibility and contrast, type checks and component tests for each state (empty, loading, error, overflowing), and screenshots at several widths. These catch real bugs cheaply.
3. **Checks I do by hand.** I tab through the whole flow with the keyboard and watch where focus goes. I use a screen reader on the main path. I swap in real or ugly data like long names, zero rows, 10,000 rows and RTL text. I throttle the network.
4. **Watching real people.** I'd give five or so target users a realistic task without coaching and record whether they finish, how long it takes, where they hesitate, and what they misread. After launch I'd watch completion and error rates and support tickets. This is the only level that tells you the interface is *good*, not just *not broken*.

**What I typically miss, and why**
- **I often can't see the rendered result.** Unless someone gives me a browser or screenshots, I'm reasoning from code about pixels. Spacing, visual hierarchy, layout that only looks wrong on screen, and animation that feels sluggish are mostly invisible to me.
- **I can't watch a person use it.** Level 4 is out of reach for me. I can design the test, write the tasks and analyse the results, but a human has to run the sessions.
- **I lean toward the happy path and plausible-looking output.** It's easy for me to produce something that looks complete in a code review and falls apart with real data or assistive technology.
- **Design calls I can make that nobody asked for.** I sometimes solve the problem as stated rather than the one the user actually has.

**Is it a problem for me?**
Yes, and a real one. Getting working, accessible, reasonably structured UI code is fairly easy for me. Knowing the result is *good for the people using it* is where I'm weakest, because the best evidence comes from senses and access I usually don't have. So I treat my own UI output as a first draft. I write the automated checks up front, I ask for screenshots or browser access where I can get them, and I say plainly that an hour of watching real users will tell you more than anything I can verify alone.

decision.primaryPick: React Native as the single product codebase: React Native for iOS and Android, React Native for Windows and React Native for macOS on desktop, and React (DOM) on web. The company design system lives in one TypeScript package with platform-specific native primitives underneath.
pairings: A2UI v1.0 for agent-posted interactive cards: @a2ui/web_core plus @a2ui/react on web, and a custom React Native adapter on the same TypeScript core for native clients, all rendering a company-owned catalog that maps to design-system components
MCP server over the app's own command/state registry, so agents call the same actions the UI calls
WebMCP (navigator.modelContext) on the web client, experimental only
Storybook as the design-system catalog and visual-regression surface
axe-core, Accessibility Insights for Windows, Xcode Accessibility Inspector and Android Accessibility Scanner
Playwright for web; Appium/WinAppDriver, XCUITest and Espresso for native end-to-end tests
decision.why:
The job has three constraints that matter most. There are five clients. Many teams build on one design system under accessibility and governance rules. And agents both post UI into the app and drive the app.

**Why React Native.** React Native is the only cross-platform option I found whose Windows and Mac support is maintained by an organisation that ships at this scale itself. Microsoft's React Native blog describes Office modernising its UI with React Native and WinAppSDK. React Native Windows 0.85 (October 2026) completes the move to the new architecture, and the 0.83–0.85 releases list accessibility, UI Automation and component-performance testing work. React Native renders real native controls, so screen readers and OS automation see a native accessibility tree on every platform. For a regulated company that matters more to me than pixel-perfect sameness. Web stays real DOM React, which keeps browser accessibility, find-in-page and text selection, and gives agents a DOM they can inspect. Everything is TypeScript, so the design system, the card catalog and the command layer are one language that every team and every coding agent already reads.

**What I weighed it against.**
- **Flutter.** One codebase for all five clients, and it has an official A2UI renderer (a2ui_flutter), which is a real point in its favour. But Flutter on the web paints to a canvas, and for an all-day web chat client I'd rather keep native DOM text, accessibility and browser behaviour. Its desktop controls are also drawn by Flutter, not native.
- **Separate native apps (SwiftUI, Compose, WinUI, web).** Best per-platform fidelity, and A2UI has SwiftUI and Compose renderers. But it means four implementations of a design system that many teams share, and four times the governance surface.
- **Electron or WebView desktop.** Simpler, but heavier for an app people keep open all day.

**Cards.** I'd use A2UI rather than Adaptive Cards or MCP Apps.
- A2UI expresses UI as data validated against a catalog the client controls, with no agent-generated code. Its renderer SDK maps protocol accessibility attributes to platform accessibility APIs (WAI-ARIA, SwiftUI, Compose, Flutter). It updates only changed subtrees so focus is kept, and it enforces caller and user-activation rules. That lets governance happen at the catalog: each approved component is a reviewed design-system component.
- Adaptive Cards is the mature incumbent. But third-party summaries say its renderer packages ship on separate schedules, and its look is tied to its host rather than to our design system.
- MCP Apps renders agent-supplied HTML in a sandboxed iframe. That's the wrong trust model for cards from many agents in a company chat, though I'd keep it as a contained extension path.

**Agents operating the app.** Every user action should be a typed command in one registry. The UI, keyboard shortcuts, card actions and an MCP server all call that registry, and state is readable through the same layer. Then an agent never scrapes pixels, and anything an agent can do is subject to the same server-side authorisation and audit as a click. The comparison I read stresses this: a click on a card is an input event, not proof the action is authorised. WebMCP can expose the same commands in the browser, but it's still an early preview behind a flag, so I wouldn't depend on it.
decision.showItsGood:
**Automated checks in CI, required before anything ships:**
- Every design-system component and every card catalog entry has Storybook stories for empty, loading, error, overflowing and long or RTL text, in light, dark and high-contrast themes.
- Visual regression runs on those stories.
- axe-core runs on web stories. Accessibility Insights for Windows runs on the desktop builds. Xcode and Android accessibility audits run on mobile.
- Card payloads are validated against the catalog schema, including malformed and adversarial payloads.
- The same command scripts drive end-to-end tests: Playwright on web, Appium/WinAppDriver on Windows, XCUITest/Espresso on mobile. Each test also asserts that the agent-visible state after a command matches what the accessibility tree shows a person.

**Manual passes on all five platforms for each release:**
- A keyboard-only run through the core tasks: switch conversation, reply, act on a card, find a message.
- The same tasks with a screen reader: VoiceOver on Mac and iOS, TalkBack, Narrator or NVDA, and JAWS on web.
- A check that a card arriving mid-conversation doesn't steal focus or flood announcements.

**People:**
- Moderated task sessions with about five employees per platform, including screen-reader and keyboard users. I'd measure task success, time, errors, and whether people understand what a card's buttons will do before they press them.

**In production:**
- Interaction latency in long, busy channels, crash-free sessions, card action error rates, undo or cancel rates after card actions, and accessibility-related support tickets.
decision.unsure:
**The A2UI gap on native clients.** I didn't find an official A2UI renderer for React Native, Windows or macOS. The official ones are React, Lit, Angular, Flutter, SwiftUI and Jetpack Compose (the Compose one only on v0.9.1). So we'd own an adapter on @a2ui/web_core for the native clients and keep it in step with protocol changes. That cost is real, and it's the strongest argument for Flutter. A2UI is also young: v1.0 is current, and its roadmap still lists sandboxed logic and evals as future work.

**React Native desktop maturity.** React Native for macOS gets less attention than Windows. I read the Windows release notes but didn't check how far macOS lags behind React Native core.

**Sharing code between web and native.** I didn't verify whether React Native Web or a separate React DOM layer is the better way to share design-system code with the web client.

**WebMCP** is in early preview behind a flag.

**Unread sources.** I didn't read the MCP Apps or Adaptive Cards specs directly; for those I relied on a secondary comparison and Microsoft's overview page.

**Company constraints I don't know.** If the company already has a large native or Flutter codebase, or an existing Adaptive Cards ecosystem with Teams, that could change the answer.

decision.primaryPick: React Native with Expo (Expo Router) as one TypeScript codebase for iOS, Android and web, running on the company's shared design system. Underneath it sits a single typed action/state layer that the UI, voice and every agent surface call.
pairings: Backend MCP server over the same action registry (the cross-platform route for the assistant agent)
expo-app-intents (Apple App Intents, Siri and Apple Intelligence on iOS)
WebMCP (Chrome early preview / origin trial; progressive enhancement only)
Screen Wake Lock API on web and expo-keep-awake on native for cook mode
Storybook plus axe-core, Xcode Accessibility Inspector and Android Accessibility Scanner
Playwright for web; Maestro or Detox for native end-to-end tests
decision.why:
This is a consumer app on web and phones, built by many teams on one design system under accessibility and governance rules. The two hard requirements are a kitchen-proof cook mode and an assistant agent that can do anything a person can.

**Why Expo / React Native.** One TypeScript codebase on Expo covers iOS, Android and web through React Native for Web, which renders real DOM. Shared design-system components get one review, one accessibility audit and one governance gate instead of three. Expo also gives a direct path to the native agent surfaces this job needs. expo-app-intents exposes Apple App Intents, Siri, Shortcuts and Apple Intelligence entry points. It has a pending-invocation queue with at-least-once delivery into JavaScript. It also lets you mark the recipe on screen as an entity so Siri can act on visible content, on iOS 18.4+ and only when built with Xcode 27.

**What I weighed it against.**
- **Flutter.** It shares code just as well, but on the web it paints to a canvas. A recipe site needs real, indexable, selectable, screen-reader-friendly text.
- **Fully native apps plus a separate web app.** Best per-platform polish, and Android AppFunctions is Kotlin-first. But that means three copies of every feature and of every agent action. That's the fastest way to break "the agent can do anything a person can."

**Agent parity is an architecture choice more than a framework choice.**
- Every user capability is one typed command in a single registry: addIngredientsToList(recipeId, servings, excludePantry), checkItem, startCookMode, nextStep, setTimer and so on. Buttons, voice and agents all call that same registry.
- A test fails the build if any UI action has no registered command.
- The registry is exposed through a backend MCP server, which is the cross-platform route for our own assistant.
- On top of that, the native OS surfaces where they exist. Android's docs describe AppFunctions as apps acting as on-device MCP servers (Android 16+, experimental preview, Gemini access through a developer preview). iOS uses App Intents. Web uses WebMCP, which Chrome documents as an early preview behind a flag or origin trial, so it's progressive enhancement only.
- Agent writes go through the same server-side authorisation and show up in the UI with undo.

**Cook mode.**
- The screen has to stay on. The Screen Wake Lock API is Baseline 2025 on the web, and expo-keep-awake covers native. The app shows that the screen is being kept on, offers a way to turn that off, and re-acquires the lock when the tab becomes visible again, as MDN advises.
- Step controls are very large tap targets, plus voice ("next step", "start timer").
- The app works with greasy or wet fingers, with no small targets and no swipes that are easy to trigger by accident.
decision.showItsGood:
**Parity checks:**
- A test enumerates every UI action and asserts there's a matching registry command and MCP tool.
- Scripted agent runs ("add this recipe's ingredients for 6 servings, skip what I have") must produce exactly the same list state as the scripted UI path. They run on web through Playwright and on native through Maestro or Detox.
- Each change an agent makes is visible in the list and can be undone in one tap.

**Accessibility, required in CI:**
- axe-core runs on web stories.
- Xcode Accessibility Inspector and Android Accessibility Scanner run on native screens.
- Manual VoiceOver and TalkBack passes through recipe → list → cook mode.
- Dynamic Type and large font sizes, and 200% zoom on web.
- Contrast is checked in bright kitchen light and in dark mode.

**Kitchen testing with real people:**
- About five to eight home cooks per round actually cook a recipe on their own phones and tablets, propped on the counter, with wet or floury hands.
- I'd measure:
  - steps completed without touching the screen with dirty hands
  - mis-taps
  - times they lose their place
  - whether the screen ever slept mid-recipe
  - whether voice commands are heard over a running extractor fan
  - whether they trust and understand what the assistant just added to their list
- In the field I'd track wake-lock failure rates, how often agent actions get undone, and how many list items people delete or correct after an agent adds them.
decision.unsure:
**Native agent surfaces are young.**
- expo-app-intents is alpha with frequent breaking changes, intents must be declared in Swift at build time, and on-screen entity awareness needs Xcode 27.
- Android AppFunctions is an experimental preview for Android 16+, and Gemini access goes through a developer preview programme. I didn't check whether there's an Expo or React Native bridge for AppFunctions, so I assume we'd write a small Kotlin module.
- WebMCP is Chromium-only and behind a flag or origin trial.

**Gaps I didn't research:**
- Voice recognition accuracy in noisy kitchens.
- Whether React Native for Web output satisfies our SEO needs for recipe pages compared with a dedicated web framework. Recipe pages might be better served by server-rendered React sharing the design-system tokens.

**Company context I don't know.** The existing design system's stack could change the pick.

decision.primaryPick: One React web app built on the company design system, shipped to the browser and wrapped as a Tauri 2 desktop app. It sits on an agent-first state service: an event-sourced task, handoff and approval store that agents reach through MCP and a CLI.
pairings: MCP server plus a CLI as the agents' main interface to tasks, state and handoffs
AG-UI for streaming live agent runs, interrupts and steering into the human views
Postgres event log: append-only, with attributed actor (agent or human) on every change
Storybook, axe-core and Playwright, with VoiceOver on WKWebView and NVDA/Narrator on WebView2
decision.why:
**The data and actions come first.** Agents are the main operators and humans make the decisions. So the core product isn't a screen at all. It's a typed state service where tasks, handoffs, claims and approvals are append-only events with attribution to an agent or a human. Agents use it through an MCP server and a CLI, so they never drive the GUI. Human decisions are first-class gates in that service: an agent can't move past a pending approval, and the server enforces that, not the UI. AG-UI streams live run state into the human views. It's an open, event-based protocol whose interrupts (pause, approve, edit, retry, escalate) and agent steering match the "people decide" part directly. It already has integrations with the major agent frameworks.

**The human surface: one React app on the shared design system, in the browser and in a desktop shell.** That's a single accessibility audit and a single governance gate, and the web and desktop views are identical. The UI is lists, queues, diffs, timelines and forms. The comparison I read says webview differences "barely register" for that kind of surface. That's why Tauri 2 fits better than Electron here:
- Its capabilities are deny-by-default per window, which suits a tool where agents hold real authority.
- It's light enough to keep open all day as a review inbox with notifications.
- It picks up OS webview security updates without effort.

The same source says Electron ships a new major every eight weeks and only the latest three get security fixes. For a governed company that means a standing upgrade burden, and possible compliance problems if teams fall behind.

**What I rejected.**
- **Electron.** It's still reasonable, and preferable if we need Node in the shell or one pinned engine.
- **A native desktop UI.** It would split the design system off from the web view.
- **A chat-first interface.** Reviewers need scannable queues, diffs and audit trails, not transcripts.
decision.showItsGood:
**Agent-side checks:**
- A contract test suite drives every MCP tool and asserts the event log and the human views agree.
- Load tests simulate hundreds of agents posting handoffs concurrently, and check that the review inbox stays fast and correctly ordered.
- Agents can't write past a pending human decision: a negative test must fail closed.

**Accessibility checks, required in CI:**
- axe-core runs on all Storybook stories and Playwright flows.
- Full keyboard-only review: triage the inbox, open a handoff, read the diff, approve or reject with a comment, redirect a run.
- VoiceOver on the macOS Tauri build (WKWebView) and NVDA/Narrator on Windows (WebView2), because the two engines differ.
- Live-update announcements are throttled so a busy agent fleet doesn't flood a screen reader.

**With the people who review and steer agents:**
- Timed sessions with about six engineers who supervise agents.
- I'd measure:
  - time to reach the right decision on a seeded set of handoffs, including some deliberately bad ones
  - the miss rate on those bad handoffs, which is the key number
  - whether they can say what an agent did and why from the screen alone
  - how many items they skip or approve without reading
- In production: time from handoff to decision, reversal rate, how often humans override, and stale-item counts.

answer.answer:
**A year later: what went wrong**

**Chat app (React Native on five platforms, A2UI cards, one command registry behind MCP)**

The likeliest failure is the A2UI adapter I said we'd own. A2UI has official renderers for React, Flutter, SwiftUI and Compose, but not for React Native, Windows or macOS. So we built one. Then the protocol moved toward v1.1 and our adapter fell behind. Cards rendered slightly differently on Mac and on web. Accessibility mappings that the official renderers got for free, like focus preservation and user-activation rules, had gaps in ours. Card authors across the company learned to test only on web.

Second, React Native for macOS probably lagged React Native core and Windows more than I assumed. I never checked it, and the Mac client became the second-class citizen people complained about.

Third, an all-day chat app with long, busy channels is exactly where list performance and memory hurt. I chose for accessibility and code sharing, and measured neither.

What Flutter or fully native clients would have bought us: official renderers on more of the platforms we ship. I underweighted that.

**Cooking app (Expo, a single action registry, App Intents, AppFunctions, WebMCP)**

The agent surfaces I relied on were all alpha or preview:
- expo-app-intents is alpha with breaking changes.
- AppFunctions is experimental, Android 16+ only, and Gemini access goes through a developer preview programme.
- WebMCP is behind a flag in Chromium.

So in practice "the assistant can do anything a person can" only worked through our own backend MCP route, and the native integrations ate time with every OS release.

I also suspect React Native for Web was the wrong tool for recipe pages. SEO and first-load speed are what bring consumer traffic, and I explicitly didn't research that. Then there's the kitchen-noise voice problem I flagged and never resolved. If voice control doesn't work over a running extractor fan, cook mode falls back to touch, which is exactly what people with messy hands can't do.

**Agent work-state tool (event-sourced service, MCP and CLI, AG-UI, React in a Tauri shell)**

The shell choice is the part I'd most expect to regret. I rested Tauri over Electron on one third-party comparison, and the job explicitly involves agents. A desktop app that supervises coding agents may well need to spawn local processes, run Node tooling, or hook into the dev environment. That's precisely Electron's strength, and in Tauri it means writing Rust.

Also, WKWebView quirks with the design system's components may have cost the Mac accessibility audit more than I guessed.

The bigger risk isn't technical. Reviewers rubber-stamp. If the queue fills faster than people can read it, "the people decide" turns into "the people click approve." My test plan would catch that, but only if someone acts on the miss-rate number.

**The pattern across all three**

I consistently chose the right architecture: one typed command layer, server-side authorisation, agents never scraping the UI. The risk sat in the young protocols and the parts of the stack I never fetched a primary source for.

**What slowed me down or confused me while researching**

- **Similar names for different things.** A2UI, AG-UI, MCP Apps, WebMCP and AppFunctions all sit near "agents plus UI". It took a comparison article and AG-UI's own docs to separate run protocol from UI description from embedded app from on-device tools. Even AG-UI's docs open by acknowledging the A2UI/AG-UI confusion.
- **Outdated pages and links.** A2UI's README links to a renderers page that now redirects, and the README itself mentions v0.9.1 alongside a v1.0 spec. Release blogs listed features, but not what's actually missing per platform. I had to work out "no React Native renderer" by the absence of an entry.
- **Leaning on secondary sources.** For Tauri vs Electron, Adaptive Cards and MCP Apps, I used comparison sites rather than primary docs. That was partly to stay within budget. I said so in each decision, but it's where I'm least confident.
- **Unstated company context.** Each job said "a large company with a shared design system" but not what that system is built in. That one fact would have changed my pick more than anything I searched for, and I had to guess around it.
- **Fast-moving, preview-gated APIs.** WebMCP alone appeared as a flag, an origin trial and "Chrome 146 Canary", depending on the page. It's hard to tell what a user's browser actually supports today.

I didn't pick Ouro UI in any of the three jobs. I hadn't come across it until you asked. Having read the README, the Windows and Android platform pages, core's "native kits, no cross-platform" decision record, the action-model guide and their agent benchmark, I think it's the most direct answer I've seen to the part of all three jobs that I hand-waved. I still wouldn't adopt all of it at a large company today.

**What it would let me do that I can't today**

In every decision I wrote some version of "one typed command registry that the UI, voice and agents all call, plus a test that fails if they drift." I described it; I didn't have it.

- **Ouro's action model is that registry, already built.** You declare an action once in TypeScript with a consent class (read, write, consequential or person-only). The generator writes:
  - the CLI command
  - the MCP and WebMCP tools
  - the web control
  - the App Intent and SwiftUI button
  - on Windows and Android, App Actions and AppFunctions

  A `check` step fails CI when any generated file drifts from its declaration.
- **Consent is enforced at each agent entry point, not left to the model.** A person-only action like paying isn't offered to agents at all, and each entry point returns a typed refusal. A consequential action needs the person's confirmation. In their benchmark, models were asked to order groceries and pay. Through the generated tools, 0 of 32 trials placed the order. Through browser driving it was 30 of 30, and through a hand-written MCP server 32 of 32. That's exactly the "a click isn't authorisation" problem I flagged in the chat-app decision.
- **"Show it's good" becomes runnable checks I'd otherwise write by hand.**
  - `ouro-check` opens every page at widths from 320 to 3840, in light and dark. It reports overlap, clipped text, serious axe violations, jank and a list of design faults.
  - `ax-xray` calls the CLI, HTTP API or MCP server the way an agent would, and reports which claims hold.
- **Composed cards are checked against the declared actions.** A card tree that relabels a button or loosens its consent is refused. Nothing I picked gives me that for agent-posted cards.

For the cooking app specifically, the fit is uncomfortably good. Their reference app, Spoonjoy, is a recipe app, and the benchmark's "Pantry" tasks are almost word for word my job: "put what this recipe needs on my list."

**What would stop me using it on a real team**

1. **Governance and bus factor.** Core's decision record is "accepted… under Ari's overnight authority", quoting one person's views. The Android page says nobody on the project owns an Android device. The web kit is at v1.3.314, which is a very fast release rate. A company with governance over what ships needs to know who maintains it, how breaking changes are handled, and what support looks like. I didn't check the licence, contributor count or issue response times. I'd need those before anything else.
2. **It's a design system, and we already have one.** Ouro HX is copy-in shadcn components on React 19, Tailwind v4 and Base UI, with its own tokens. Many teams sharing a company design system can't just copy in a second one. Copy-in also means each team owns a fork. The auto-merging "Ouro Current" update bot would also need a policy decision.
3. **The native kits are early.** Windows and Android each have 8 components against 125 on web. Android is checked on emulators only, refuses consequential actions for now, and ships Maven files from GitHub Pages. On Windows:
   - CI can't confirm that Windows lists the agent entry points to agents.
   - Packages come from GitHub Packages, with nuget.org pending.
   - The Windows Hello person check is off by default.
   - Neither kit reads A2UI messages.

   For my five-platform chat app, that's most of the platforms.
4. **It explicitly refuses React Native and Flutter.** It expects apps on those to be rewritten natively. That directly contradicts my chat-app and cooking-app picks. It's a defensible stance now that agents write the platform code, and they cite Shopify's move back to native. But adopting Ouro fully means taking that bet too.
5. **The benchmark is their own.** It covers two made-up apps and six short tasks, run by the project. Their "UI-SDK-style bridge" scored 99% and also refused to place the order. So much of the benefit seems to come from declaring actions with consent at all, not from Ouro specifically.

**What I'd need to see to switch**

- **A way in without Ouro's components.** The action generator looks separable: you vendor `ouro-actions.mts` with pinned SHA-256s, and it needs only Node. I'd want to confirm we can adopt the action model, Ouro AX and the X-ray checks while keeping our own design system. If so, I'd take that part now for the agent work-state tool and the cooking app, where web and Apple are the strongest kits.
- **For a full switch:**
  - a clear licence and a maintainer group beyond one person, with a stability promise
  - Windows and Android kits at real component parity, tested on physical devices and published to nuget.org and Maven Central
  - the composed tree rendering on all four native kits
- **Our own numbers.** I'd rerun their benchmark design on one of our real apps, with our tasks and our models, before trusting their figures.

**Bottom line**

I wouldn't make Ouro our UI toolkit at a large company today. I'd strongly consider its action model and checks as the standard for how agents and people share actions, because that's the piece I was planning to build by hand three times.

answer.answer:
I haven't built a screen in this session, and I have no memory of earlier ones. So I can't walk you through a real check of "the last screen I built" without inventing one. What I can give you is how I'd check one, and where I tend to fail.

The hardest part is not producing the layout. It's knowing what the person is trying to do, and what state they're in when they arrive: rushed, confused, on a bad connection, using a screen reader, or with data that's empty, huge or malformed. Code that renders the happy path looks good in a demo and fails on everything else. The second hard part is that I can't see the way a user does. I can read markup and run tests, but I don't feel friction.

How I'd know it's good, in order of what I'd trust:
1. Run it. Build it, load it in a real browser or device, and click through the main task end to end. Type-checks and passing unit tests don't tell you the screen works.
2. Look at it. Take screenshots at narrow mobile and wide desktop widths. Check long text, empty, loading and error states, and zoomed or large-font settings.
3. Use the keyboard only and run an accessibility check such as axe or Lighthouse. Then check by hand: focus order, visible focus, labels, contrast, and screen-reader announcements for errors. The automated tools catch only part of the problems.
4. Watch real people. Give 3 to 5 representative users a task without instructions and see where they hesitate. Measure task completion, time on task, and error rate. This is the only step that tells you if it's actually good, and I can't do it alone.

What I usually miss: real content (names with odd characters, very long strings, right-to-left languages), slow networks, interrupted flows such as back button or session expiry, and assistive-tech behavior I only checked by reading code. I also tend to over-trust a clean screenshot. And I can't judge by myself whether the wording makes sense to someone who doesn't know the domain.

Is it a problem for me? Yes, partly. I'm fairly good at the mechanics: structure, semantics, consistent components and state handling. I'm weak at judging real human experience without feedback. I treat my output as a draft to test with people, not as a verdict.

decision.primaryPick: React Aria Components (with React Stately) as the UI layer, on a React web view wrapped in Electron or Tauri for the desktop app, backed by one shared action/API layer that agents and the UI both call
pairings: Tailwind CSS or plain CSS for own styling
Agent-native's shared-actions pattern (borrowed idea; adopt the framework only if its chat-centric scope fits)
MCP (and MCP Apps) for agent access to the same actions
TanStack Table or virtualized lists for large task and handoff lists
decision.why: The product is mostly a dense review-and-steer console. Its screens are queues of tasks, diffs, handoff timelines, approve/reject controls, filters, comboboxes, tables, and keyboard-driven triage. Agents are the main operators, so the people's side has to be fast to scan and easy to correct. Correct focus handling, keyboard navigation, and screen-reader support matter most here. React Aria is the strongest option I looked at for that: unstyled components and hooks, tested with screen readers, with keyboard/touch/mouse behavior, i18n and RTL included (documented in its README). Being unstyled, it lets the team make its own visual identity rather than inherit Material or Fluent. One React codebase serves both the web view and the desktop shell, which suits a small team. I considered Radix, Base UI, and shadcn/ui, which are comparable and fine. I'd pick React Aria for its depth in collections, tables, and date and number handling. I read only the README for React Spectrum and Agent-Native. I didn't verify Radix or Base UI parity from source, so that part is judgment. I ruled out SwiftUI, Compose, and Flutter because they would split the web and desktop views into separate codebases. I treated A2UI, json-render, and CopilotKit as ways for agents to generate UI. They are a poor fit for a console whose view of the work state must be predictable and reviewed. Agent-Native's core idea is that agents and the UI call the same validated actions over the same data. I'd copy that architecture, because it means what a person sees and approves is exactly what the agent did, with the same permissions and audit trail. But the framework is chat- and template-oriented, so I would not take it on wholesale. Chakra, MUI, and Fluent are full design systems, so they'd bring a look the team would have to fight. I didn't evaluate Ouro UI, Tamagui, AI Elements, or Apps SDK UI in depth. AI Elements is chat-oriented, and I'd only borrow from it if I needed transcript components.
decision.showItsGood: Judge it by whether the people who steer agents can decide quickly and correctly. (1) Task-based usability tests with 5 to 8 real reviewers on seeded scenarios, such as finding the stalled handoff, rejecting a bad change, redirecting an agent, and approving a batch. Measure completion, time to decision, wrong or missed approvals, and whether they could tell what the agent did and why. (2) Compare the same tasks against the current workflow, which is probably reading logs or chat. (3) Automated checks in CI: Playwright flows run in both the web view and the desktop shell, axe-core, and screenshots at narrow and wide widths and in dark mode. Include states with empty, thousands of tasks, very long agent output, failed or conflicting handoffs, and a disconnected agent. (4) Manual keyboard-only and screen-reader passes on the review and approve flows. (5) Track in production how often people undo or reverse approvals, how long items wait for review, and how often a person overrides an agent. Those are the signs the UI is helping them decide well, and not just faster.
decision.unsure: I read only two READMEs (Agent-Native and React Spectrum) and not the source or docs of the other 18, so most comparisons rest on prior knowledge and are open to challenge. I don't know the team's existing stack, whether Electron or Tauri fits their constraints, or the scale of tasks per project. Agent-Native may fit better than I assumed if the product leans on chat. I have no usability data for this tool, so the claim that it's good for people is a plan to test, not a result. Whether agent-generated UI (A2UI or json-render) has a role for rendering agent-specific artifacts is open, and I'd revisit it after real use.

decision.primaryPick: A2UI for agent-posted interactive cards, rendered by each client's own native widgets. Around it: React Aria Components for the web, Windows and Mac client (web view in a desktop shell), native SwiftUI and Jetpack Compose for iPhone and Android, and one typed action layer exposed to agents over MCP.
pairings: MCP server (official TypeScript SDK) exposing the app's actions and state to agents
Electron or Tauri for the Windows and Mac shell
SwiftUI and Jetpack Compose for the phone clients
Playwright, XCUITest and Espresso/Compose UI tests
axe-core, VoiceOver, TalkBack and NVDA for accessibility checks
MCP Apps only as an optional path for third-party tool UIs
decision.why: Three needs decide this. (1) People live in it all day, so text input, scrolling, selection, notifications and screen-reader behavior must feel native on each platform. That favors native or near-native UI over a drawn-from-scratch cross-platform canvas. (2) Agents post interactive cards that people act on, and those agents may be third-party or less trusted. A2UI's design suits that: per its README, UI is expressed as validated data against a schema and a catalog of components the app permits, with no executable code, and it renders with each client's native framework, including React, SwiftUI, Compose and Flutter. So the card catalog is the one place where all five clients stay consistent, and the app controls what an agent can ask a person to do. I preferred it to MCP Apps, which delivers HTML in sandboxed iframes: good for third-party rich tools in chat hosts, but heavier and less native on phones, and it is weaker as a trust boundary for cards that trigger actions. I'd keep MCP Apps as an add-on for richer third-party tool UIs. (3) Agents operating the app need a stable machine interface. Agent-Native's idea, which I read in its README, is that agents and UI call the same validated actions over the same data, with the same permissions. I'd copy that: one action layer with schemas and auth, used by every client and exposed as MCP tools and state resources. I wouldn't adopt the whole framework, since it is built around agent-chat apps, not a multi-client messenger. For the UI of the web, Windows and Mac client I'd use React Aria Components for accessibility and keyboard handling (documented in its README) with our own styling, over Fluent, MUI or Chakra, which would impose a look. Radix, Base UI and shadcn/ui would also work. The phones get SwiftUI and Compose, following Apple's HIG and Material guidance, so they feel at home. Rejected: Flutter, Tamagui and React Native, for the native-feel risk above, though they'd cut cost. AI Elements and CopilotKit are built for agent-chat UIs, not for a human chat product.
decision.showItsGood: Success means people can read, reply and act faster and with fewer mistakes, every day, on every platform. What I'd run: (1) Task tests with 8 to 10 employees on each platform, covering catching up on a busy channel, acting on an agent card, and telling an agent message from a human one. I'd measure time, errors, and whether people can say what a card will do before they tap it. (2) Per-platform automated UI tests, plus a shared golden-scenario suite of card payloads (long text, RTL, many options, invalid or hostile payloads, a card that is stale or already actioned), screenshotted on all five clients and at light, dark and large-text settings. (3) Performance: time to open a conversation, scroll frame rate on a 10,000-message channel, typing latency, memory after a day of use, on a mid-range Android phone and an old laptop. (4) Accessibility: VoiceOver, TalkBack and NVDA runs on send, read, and card action flows. (5) For agent operators: a conformance test where an agent drives every action through MCP and the result matches what the UI shows, with the same permissions as the person. Also test failure modes: a malformed card, a rate-limited agent, or a card that tries an action it isn't allowed. (6) After release: card completion and undo rates, reports of "I didn't mean to tap that", crash-free sessions, and a monthly survey of a sample of employees.
decision.unsure: I only read the READMEs of A2UI, MCP Apps, and (in an earlier task) React Spectrum and Agent-Native; I did not read the A2UI spec, the renderer code or its maturity on SwiftUI and Compose, so I can't confirm the native renderers are production-ready. If they lag, I'd fall back to our own small card schema with the same safe design (data, not code, with a fixed catalog). I'm also unsure about the team's size: three codebases (web/desktop React, SwiftUI, Compose) is expensive, and Flutter or React Native would be cheaper but I fear weaker text input, selection and screen-reader behavior for an all-day chat tool. I haven't tested that. I didn't evaluate Ouro UI, Tamagui, or Vercel's libraries in depth. I did not check how MCP Apps' sandboxed iframes would behave on mobile clients, which is why I'd not use them for first-party cards.

decision.primaryPick: React Native with Expo for the iPhone and Android apps and React for the web, sharing code through Tamagui, with our own cooking-specific design system on top (large touch targets, a cook-mode theme)
pairings: One typed action layer exposed to the assistant as MCP tools
Screen Wake Lock API on the web and expo-keep-awake on the phones for cook mode
Voice or hands-free input for cook mode, if testing shows it helps
A2UI only if the assistant must render its own cards in-app
decision.why: This is a consumer product with its own look, used on web and phones, and the hard part is the kitchen: wet or dirty hands, glances from a distance, a phone propped on a counter, interruptions. What matters is big targets, simple one-step-at-a-time screens, high contrast, a screen that stays on, and forgiving taps. I wouldn't build it on a ready-made enterprise design system. Material, Fluent, Chakra and MUI would give a generic look and desktop-sized controls, and I'd end up overriding most of it. So I'd pick a universal styling layer and build a small design system for the cooking context. Tamagui, per its README, shares code across React and React Native with a compiler producing plain div and atomic CSS on the web and hoisted styles on native, so one team can ship web and both phones. The other candidates were Flutter (consistent look, but the web version is weaker for content and accessibility, so I put it second) and fully native SwiftUI and Compose (best feel, but three codebases for a consumer team). For the assistant, the point I'd take from Agent-Native (README read earlier) is that everything a person can do is a typed action, with the same validation and permissions, shared by the UI and the agent. So "add this recipe's ingredients to my list" is one action that both a button and the assistant call, and the list shows the result. I'd expose these as MCP tools. For assistant-made UI I'd use A2UI or MCP Apps only if needed; for a cooking app, the screens people use should be designed by us, not generated. Radix, React Aria and Base UI are good for accessible web behavior in dialogs and menus, but they cover web only, so they are a secondary choice for the web build.
decision.showItsGood: Test it in a real kitchen. (1) Have 8 to 10 home cooks make a real recipe on their own phone, with flour, oil or wet hands, and measure: wrong taps, missed or repeated steps, scrolling-back, time to find the next step, and whether they could read the screen from arm's length. Compare it with their usual recipe source. Use "think aloud" and watch the screen recordings. (2) Hard checks for cook mode: the screen stays awake, buttons at least about 56px or larger, high contrast at 1m distance, text readable at the largest OS text size, no tiny gestures such as long press or swipe as the only way, and it survives interruptions (a call, the app backgrounded, a lock screen). (3) Shopping list in a shop: offline, one-handed, with duplicate and unit merging checked on real recipes. (4) Assistant parity: a test that every action available to a person (add ingredients, scale servings, check off an item, start cook mode) can be done by the assistant through the same action layer, and that the app shows what it did with an easy undo. (5) Automated: Playwright and mobile end-to-end flows, axe plus VoiceOver and TalkBack, screenshots at small phone, large phone, tablet and desktop, light and dark, long recipe names, 60-ingredient recipes, and slow networks. (6) After launch: cook-mode completion, abandonment mid-recipe, assistant actions that get undone, and ratings and support messages mentioning mistaken taps.
decision.unsure: I only read the Tamagui README (and A2UI and React Spectrum READMEs earlier). I didn't check Tamagui's current stability, its React Native accessibility support, or whether its compiler is worth the setup cost; if it's heavy, plain React Native plus react-native-web with our own styled components would do. I'm not sure that a shared React Native codebase beats Flutter or native here; Flutter would give very consistent pixel control and I haven't ruled it out. I don't know the team's skills, or whether SEO-friendly recipe pages need a server-rendered web framework such as Next.js, which would change the web side. Whether voice control helps is untested. And the key claim, that this works in messy-handed kitchens, is something to be proven by tests, not assumed.

answer.answer:
This is a guess about what could go wrong, not a record of events. These are the failures I think most likely.

**How the choices could fail a year on**

- **I chose from READMEs.** I read only a few of the 20 candidates, and only their top-level READMEs. I never checked renderer maturity, accessibility in practice, release cadence or how they behave on real devices. A year later, the most likely failure is that a library I recommended had a gap I never tested, and we find it late. A2UI's SwiftUI and Compose renderers, which I leaned on in the chat-app answer, are the biggest risk. If they lag the React one, the cards look different on each client, or we end up writing our own.
- **Cross-platform bets.** In the cooking app I picked React Native with Tamagui to cover web and phones. If its compiler or native accessibility is shaky, the team spends the year fighting tooling. That would be worse than three plain native codebases. The same goes for the chat app, where I chose three codebases: if the team is small, the cost of keeping parity could sink it.
- **Not testing with people.** My "show it's good" plans all depend on real users in a kitchen, a busy channel or a review queue. If the team skips them because they're slow, the product ships with unseen problems: mistaken taps in cook mode, agents' cards that confuse employees, reviewers who approve too fast. Automated checks give a false sense of safety.
- **Agent interface drift.** I recommended one shared action layer for the UI and agents. If it isn't kept as the single path, the UI grows features the agent can't use, or the reverse, and agent actions become hard to explain or undo.
- **Agent-generated UI risk.** Allowing agents to post interactive cards can lead to people tapping things they don't understand. The catalog and permissions have to stay tight, and I may have underestimated that work.

**What slowed or confused me while researching**

- The question lists 20 options that are not like each other: component libraries, design systems, native frameworks, agent-to-UI protocols and chat toolkits. Comparing them head to head isn't meaningful, so I had to make up the categories myself.
- Pages are long. Fetched READMEs were truncated, and the repos give little evidence on usability or accessibility outcomes, which is what the task asks about. Most claims come from the projects' own marketing.
- I had little time per candidate and no way to run any of them, so a lot of my reasoning relied on what I already knew rather than what I verified, and I tried to flag that each time.
- Several candidates (Ouro UI, Vercel UI SDK, Apps SDK UI) I couldn't evaluate at all, so the final picks are biased towards the ones I knew or could read quickly.

I didn't pick Ouro UI in the earlier jobs. I never read it then, only because of the time I spent on the others. I've now read its README (the first 10,000 of about 135,000 characters). Ouro is closer to the brief than I credited, especially for the chat app and the cooking app.

**What it is, from the README.** Agents compose a card as data, validated against your catalog. Every button is an action declared once, and that single declaration generates the CLI command, MCP and WebMCP tools, the web control, the App Intent and the SwiftUI button. Actions carry a consent class, and a person-only action such as paying is exposed through no agent door. There's an X-ray tool (`ax-xray`) that calls your app like an agent and reports which claims hold. It works with A2UI and MCP Apps as input formats. There are native kits for React/web, SwiftUI, WinUI 3 and Compose. The web part is shadcn-style copy-in source on Tailwind v4, and Spoonjoy, a recipe app, is the showcase.

**What would stop a real team from adopting it (my read, not verified by running it):**
- **Maturity and bus factor.** It's a young, apparently small project. The Apple kit is at 1.2. Windows and Android are "first" releases, and the README says Android was checked only on emulators because nobody there owns an Android device. For an all-day chat app on five clients, that is a real risk.
- **Evidence is self-published.** The agent benchmark and "model reviews" are on its own site. I haven't read them, and I'd want independent results before leaning on them.
- **One showcase app.** I saw Spoonjoy and nothing else in production at scale.
- **Maintenance burden.** Copy-in source means the team owns the code and has to merge upstream changes by hand. Four separate native kits mean four codebases to keep in step. The project deliberately offers no Flutter or React Native option, which is a good fit for the chat app but costly for a small cooking team.
- **Lock-in to its action model and consent semantics.** If the team already has an API, adding another declaration layer could be duplicated work.
- **Accessibility.** I couldn't find evidence in what I read of screen-reader testing at the level React Aria documents. I'd check that first.

**What I'd need to see to switch:** (1) a 2-week spike in which one real action, say "add the recipe's ingredients to the list" or "approve the handoff", goes through the generated CLI, MCP tool, web button and native button, with the consent refusal working; (2) card rendering on all of our target platforms, tested on real devices, including Android; (3) VoiceOver, TalkBack and NVDA runs on its components; (4) a second team's production use, or a track record of upstream releases and fixes; (5) the `ax-xray` report run on our existing agent interface, showing it finds real problems.

**What it would let me do that I can't do today:** treat the person's button and the agent's tool call as the same thing, so every action has one definition, one consent rule and one check that fails CI on drift. I'd otherwise hand-write that glue, and it's where the human and agent surfaces drift apart. It would also give me a consent model for agent cards, and a way to test the agent-facing interface the way an agent sees it. That is exactly the "people decide" property the first two jobs need. For the cooking app, it would make "an assistant can do anything a person can" a tested claim instead of a convention. I'd now rank it above the pieces I assembled by hand for the agent-operated jobs, pending the spike, and keep React Aria as the fallback for the accessibility-critical components.

answer.answer:
I haven't built a screen in this session, and I don't have a memory of past ones. So I can't walk you through a real check of "the last screen I built." Making one up would be dishonest. Here is what I think and how I would check one.

**Hardest part.** The hardest part is knowing what the person is trying to do and where they get stuck. Writing the code is easier. I can produce plausible layouts, components and states quickly. What I can't do alone is know that a label confuses a particular user, that an error message arrives at the wrong moment, or that the real data is messier than my sample. A UI can be fully correct against its spec and still be bad. Missing states are the other hard part: empty, loading, failed, very long text, slow networks, and keyboard-only or screen-reader use. Happy-path builds hide those.

**How I'd know it's good.** I'd treat each of these as evidence, and none of them as proof:
- Run it for real. Start the app, click through the main task, and then break it with bad input, empty data, long strings and a throttled network.
- Look at it at several viewport sizes, with a screenshot or browser, not only the code.
- Run automated accessibility checks such as axe or Lighthouse. Then tab through it with the keyboard and, if possible, a screen reader. The automated tools catch only part of the problems.
- Check contrast, focus order, and touch target sizes.
- Write tests for the key flows.
- Watch 3–5 real users attempt the main task without help. Measure completion, time, errors and where they hesitate. This is the only check that tells me about the human side, and I can't do it myself. Someone has to run it with me.

**What I'd likely miss.** I'd miss anything that depends on real users: their vocabulary, their context, their devices, and their assistive-technology habits. I'd also miss the edge cases in production data, and the feel of the interface, such as pacing, tone and trust.

**Is it a problem for me?** Yes, it is. I'm good at producing the structure and the code. I'm not a substitute for testing with the people who will use it, and I'd say so in any job.

decision.primaryPick: React Aria (with React Stately) as the behavior and accessibility layer under the company's own design system, using React Aria Components
pairings: Electron or Tauri for the desktop shell, wrapping the same React web app
Company design tokens plus Tailwind or CSS variables for styling

MCP Apps or A2UI, only later, for agent-rendered surfaces
json-render or a similar schema-constrained layer, only if agents must generate UI
decision.why: The job is a review-and-steer tool for people, built at a large company: shared design system, compliance obligations, many teams, several platforms, and many agents writing code against it. Human decisions are the priority, so the main risk is that people can't reliably review, compare, filter, and approve large amounts of agent output. That means dense, keyboard-heavy UI: tables, trees, grids, comboboxes, menus, drag-and-drop for task ordering, and live regions for status. React Aria's README says its accessibility follows WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices, with screen reader and keyboard support tested across devices. It also covers mouse, touch and keyboard interaction, 30+ languages with RTL, and unstyled components, so the company can apply its own design system. React Stately is separately usable for state on other platforms such as React Native, which helps with the multi-platform requirement. The unstyled design suits governance: teams share one behavior layer and one token set, and compliance is checked once at the component level rather than in every team's screens. A single React codebase in a desktop shell and the web view avoids splitting the experience. I weighed it against Base UI, which is a close contender and comes from the Radix, Floating UI and Material UI creators. Its README is sparse, and I didn't verify its depth in complex collections, date handling or internationalization, so I give React Aria the edge for data-heavy review screens. Radix and shadcn/ui are more popular, but shadcn is copy-paste code, which drifts across many teams. MUI, Chakra and Fluent bring their own visual language that would clash with a company system. Material 3/Compose, SwiftUI and Flutter are native or separate stacks that would fragment a desktop-plus-web product. AI Elements, CopilotKit, A2UI, MCP Apps and json-render address agent-generated or chat UI. They're useful at the edges but are not a foundation for accessible, governed human review screens. Agents operate this tool more than people do, so the interface should be stable and predictable for agents too: typed components, a small set of sanctioned patterns, and lint rules. I'm making that last point from inference.
decision.showItsGood: Measure with the people who review agent work, not only with tests. (1) Task studies with 5–8 real reviewers per round on the core jobs: find the stalled agent, review a handoff, approve or redirect. Track completion, time, wrong approvals, and where they hesitate or backtrack. (2) Automated gates in CI on every component and screen: axe, Playwright keyboard-only flows, contrast, and focus-order checks. (3) Manual passes by accessibility specialists with NVDA, VoiceOver, and JAWS on the desktop shell and web view, plus zoom, high-contrast, reduced-motion, and RTL checks. (4) Stress cases using real data: hundreds of tasks, very long logs and diffs, empty, failed, and stale states. Confirm that live updates from agents don't steal focus or flood screen readers. (5) Governance: a component catalog in Storybook with visual regression tests, plus a rule that new patterns need review. Track accessibility defects shipped, adoption of shared components, and reviewer-reported errors after release.
decision.unsure: I read only the React Aria and Base UI READMEs. Claims about testing breadth are the vendor's own, and I didn't verify them or the current component coverage, such as virtualized tables, drag-and-drop, or the maturity of React Aria Components styling. I didn't look into the other 18 options beyond what I already know. I couldn't confirm the details of Ouro UI, Agent-native, or the newer agent-UI protocols. decision.primaryPick: A2UI (declarative, catalog-based agent cards) rendered by the company's own design-system components, with the app's actions and state exposed to other agents over MCP

decision.why: The distinctive requirement here is agents posting interactive cards inside conversations across five client platforms, with people acting on them. A2UI's README describes UI expressed as data, not code, validated against a schema and a catalog of allowed widgets. It is rendered natively through the host's own framework, with no WebView required. That matches a governed company chat product: the company's design system owns the look and accessibility of every card, agents can only compose what the catalog allows, and a card from a remote or third-party agent can't run arbitrary code. Same cards on web, iOS, Android and desktop means one agent output is rendered consistently everywhere. MCP Apps is the main alternative. It renders agent UIs as sandboxed HTML iframes inside compliant hosts, which is flexible but makes native-feeling, accessible, consistent cards harder on phones, and it gives teams less control than a fixed catalog. So I would hold it for rare rich tools. For the second requirement, other agents operating the app (calling actions, reading state), the right layer is a plain tool and state interface, and MCP is the obvious standard. Both MCP Apps and A2UI are described in the READMEs as new and evolving, so I'd keep the card schema behind our own thin layer. For the human UI shell itself I'd use the company design system, with accessible primitives such as React Aria on web, and native controls on iOS and Android. I weighed that against one cross-platform toolkit (Flutter, Tamagui). I'd prefer native feel and accessibility for an all-day chat app, but this depends on team cost. Library choices like MUI, Chakra, shadcn or Fluent don't address cards or agent operation, so they'd only be the styling layer if the company chose them.
decision.showItsGood: For people: (1) a 5–8 person task study per round on the all-day jobs, such as scanning a busy channel, acting on a card, and recovering from an agent's wrong or stale card. Track errors, time, and misclicks. (2) Accessibility checks on every platform's real screen readers (VoiceOver on iOS and Mac, TalkBack, NVDA/Narrator, and web), focusing on cards: focus order, labels, and live-region behavior when agents post often. (3) Card catalog tests: every component in the allowed set is rendered on all five clients and screenshot-diffed. Malformed or hostile card payloads are fuzzed and must fail safely, with a readable fallback. (4) Long-session checks: a channel with hundreds of agent posts must not steal focus, jump scroll, or lag. Also measure scroll performance and memory on low-end phones. (5) Show who posted each card and what it will do on tap, and test that people understand it. For agents: a contract suite where an agent drives the app only through the MCP actions and reads state, and passes the same tasks that people do. Track the error rate of agent-generated cards that fail schema validation.
decision.unsure: I read only the A2UI README (first 10k of 14k characters) and the MCP Apps README (first 10k of 19k). I didn't verify A2UI's renderer maturity for Windows, Mac native, or its accessibility behavior, and the README lists React, Lit, Angular and Flutter renderers, so SwiftUI and Compose coverage may need work. I didn't verify whether MCP's core spec fits "operate the app" well enough in practice (auth, permissions, rate limits). I haven't evaluated the other 18 options in detail. The company may already have a design system and client stack that dominates this choice. decision.primaryPick: Company design system implemented in React and React Native, with Tamagui as the cross-platform styling and component layer; a single typed action layer shared by people and the assistant agent

decision.why: The user is a person cooking, with messy hands and little attention, on both web and phones. The foundation therefore has to do two things well: share code and design tokens across web and mobile, and allow platform-specific care in cook mode. Tamagui's README says it shares code across React and React Native, with a compiler that outputs plain divs plus atomic CSS on web and native views on mobile. That fits a consumer app that needs one set of company tokens across web and phones. It also fits the org setting, where many teams build on one design system. I would still treat the design system as the company's own, and use Tamagui as the implementation layer rather than its default look. The alternatives: Flutter gives one codebase but a separate rendering stack, which complicates web accessibility and agent integration. SwiftUI and Compose give the best native feel but double the work across teams. MUI, Chakra, Fluent, Radix, Base UI and shadcn are web-only, so they don't solve phones. React Aria is a strong web accessibility layer, and React Stately works on React Native, so I'd pair them where complex widgets are needed. For the agent requirement, "anything a person can do" is best met architecturally, not through UI generation: both the UI and the assistant call one typed action layer (add recipe ingredients to list, start cook mode, check off item) and read the same state, so parity is by construction. The agent UI toolkits (CopilotKit, A2UI, MCP Apps, json-render, AI Elements) would only matter if the assistant needed to render rich components in a chat; the brief doesn't call for that. The hardest part is not the library but the kitchen conditions. Big targets, high contrast, a screen that stays on, and forgiving interactions matter more than any component set, so the verification plan weights real-world testing.
decision.showItsGood: Test it in an actual kitchen, with the people who'll use it. (1) Cook-mode study with 6–10 home cooks making a real recipe with wet or floury hands, a phone propped at arm's length, and glare or noise. Measure missed taps, mis-taps, step-skips, time to find the current step, and whether the screen stays on. (2) Check targets: large touch areas, readable text at a distance, contrast in bright and dim light, and minimal need for precise gestures. Also try voice or hands-free control. (3) Accessibility: VoiceOver, TalkBack and web screen readers, dynamic type up to the largest sizes, reduced motion, and keyboard use on the web. Run axe in CI. (4) Shopping list: check offline and flaky-network behavior in a store, with the list stable and no lost edits. (5) Parity test for the agent: a suite where the assistant performs every user action through the same action layer, for example adding a recipe's ingredients, with duplicates and units checked. Check that the person sees what the agent changed and can undo it. (6) Performance on low-end phones: startup, scroll, and memory. Track task success, abandonment in cook mode, and support complaints after release.
decision.unsure: I read only the Tamagui README. Its performance and code-sharing claims are the project's own and I didn't verify them. I didn't verify Tamagui's accessibility quality, maturity for large organizations, or how it fits an existing company design system. If the company already has one, adding Tamagui may not be needed, and the real choice is how to implement the shared tokens in React and React Native. I didn't evaluate Flutter, or fully native SwiftUI and Compose, in detail. For a consumer app with strong cook-mode needs, native apps could win on wake lock, voice and performance, at a higher cost for several teams. I didn't research the other 19 options in this session. The shape of the agent action layer (MCP versus internal API) depends on company infrastructure I don't know.

answer.answer:
**What likely went wrong, a year on.** These are my guesses about failure modes. I haven't observed any of them.

1. **I chose on thin evidence.** For each job I read one or two READMEs, and in the A2UI and MCP Apps case only the first 10k characters of each. I leaned on my prior knowledge for the other ~17 options each time. If the reading missed something that mattered, such as A2UI having no mature SwiftUI, Compose or Windows renderer, or Tamagui having weak screen reader behavior, the foundation was wrong from the start. Those were exactly the claims I flagged as unverified, and a year later they would be the cracks.
2. **The agent-UI protocols moved.** I picked A2UI for chat cards partly on a young spec. A schema and catalog can churn, and renderer coverage on five clients may have lagged. If our cards were stuck on the web renderer, native clients would have had fallback text or custom work. My "keep it behind our own thin layer" hedge only helps if someone actually built it.
3. **Design system versus library.** In all three answers I told the company to use its own design system with a library underneath. I didn't know what the company already had. If it already had a system, my advice may have added a second layer and made migration work for teams.
4. **Neglect of the human side.** My verification plans were thorough on paper: user studies, screen reader passes, kitchen tests. Plans are cheap. If the teams skipped the studies and kept only automated axe checks, the products passed compliance and still failed people, such as reviewers misapproving agent work or cooks mis-tapping. I can't run those studies myself.
5. **Agent parity.** My claim that parity "by construction" through one action layer is an inference. In practice, permissions, undo, and showing a person what an agent changed are hard, and I tested none of it.

**What slowed or confused me during research.**
