- The READMEs are mostly marketing or setup. They say little about accessibility test results, governance, or how a library behaves in a large multi-team organization. That's what these jobs asked about, so I filled the gaps with inference.
- The list mixes different kinds of things: component libraries, design systems, whole native frameworks, and agent-UI protocols. They aren't comparable, so ranking them was partly a category exercise. I tried to say that in each answer.
- I had a budget on how much to read, and I spent it on a few candidates rather than comparing all 20. That left the comparison uneven.
- Some candidates (Ouro UI, Agent-native, Vercel UI SDK) I know little about, and I didn't read them. I avoided recommending them rather than judging them.
- The tool results showed fetch dates that sat after the stated current time. I treated the content as current, but I couldn't check it independently.

I didn't pick Ouro UI in any of the three jobs. I hadn't read it until now, and I read only the first 10k of a 134k-character README, so this is a first look, not a review. It's closer to the brief than I assumed. I should have fetched it earlier.

**What it appears to be (from the README, not verified by me).**
- A kit for agent-composed interfaces: a card is data, validated against your catalog, and drawn natively. Every button maps to an action declared once, which a person presses and an agent calls as a tool.
- Consent classes on actions, person-only actions that no agent door offers, and an "X-ray" tool that calls an app the way an agent would and reports which claims hold.
- Native kits per platform (React on the web, SwiftUI, WinUI 3, Compose), with deliberately no Flutter or React Native kit. It works with A2UI and MCP Apps as formats.
- The web part is shadcn-style copy-in source on Tailwind v4.

That matches the second job (chat cards plus agents operating the app) and part of the third (assistant parity), and it covers the platform list. I recommended an A2UI plus MCP combination there. Ouro claims to be that combination with consent built in. If its claims hold, I undervalued it.

**What would stop me using it on a real team.**
1. **Maturity and ownership.** The README says the Apple package is at 1.x, the Windows and Android kits are "first" releases, and Android has been checked on emulators only, since nobody there owns an Android device. A large company with accessibility compliance can't build on that without its own testing. I can't tell from my read how big the team is, or who supports it.
2. **Accessibility evidence.** I saw no accessibility conformance claims in the part I read. The web side copies source in the shadcn way, and I don't know which primitives sit underneath. Compliance needs screen reader results on every platform, not component counts.
3. **Governance.** Copy-in source lets teams drift. A company design system needs versioning, upgrade paths, and one owner. The tag-pinned install helps, but I'd have to see how it works at scale.
4. **Evidence is partly self-reported.** The "agent benchmark" and "model reviews" are the project's own pages. I haven't read them, and models picking their own tool isn't proof for human users.
5. **Dependence on a small, young stack.** Five repos (core, web, Apple, Windows, Android) moving together is a lot of risk to take on.
6. **Fit with the company's existing system.** It would have to take our tokens rather than bring its own look.

**What I'd need to see to switch.** Independent accessibility audits of the web, iOS, Android and Windows kits on real devices. A pilot with one team shipping a real card flow for a quarter, with the card schema, consent flow and X-ray passing in our CI. Evidence of stable APIs, with a versioning and deprecation policy, and named maintainers. Task studies with real users showing people understand what an agent-prepared card will do. Reviews by our security team of the consent and refusal design.

**What it would let me do that I can't today.** I could declare an action once and have the person's button, the agent's tool, and a CLI or MCP surface come from that one declaration, with a CI check that fails on drift. That makes the parity claim in my cooking and chat answers testable, instead of resting on my inference. Agents building screens could do so against a catalog that refuses unsafe or relabeled buttons, and the X-ray would give a checkable standard for whether other agents can really operate the app. Today I'd have to assemble that from several pieces and hope they agree.

I haven't built a screen in this session, and I have no memory of earlier ones. I won't invent a walkthrough of "the last screen I built." Here is what I can say honestly about how I'd approach it.

The hardest part is knowing what the person is trying to do and where they get stuck. Layout, components and code are the easy part. I can produce a plausible interface quickly. What I can't see by default is the user's context: what they know, what they're worried about, and which mistake costs them most. A screen can look polished and still fail at that. Things that are easy to get wrong are error states, empty states, long or odd data, keyboard and screen-reader use, slow networks, and the person who doesn't read your labels the way you meant them.

How I'd know it's good:
- Run it. Click through the main task and the failure paths, at several viewport sizes, with real and awkward data such as very long names, no data, and non-English text.
- Use automated checks for accessibility (contrast, labels, focus order) and then do a manual keyboard-only and screen-reader pass. The tools catch only part of the problems.
- Watch a few real users attempt a task without help. Measure task completion, time, errors and where they hesitate. This is the check that matters most and the one I can't do alone.

What I tend to miss when I work alone: I test the path I imagined. I'm biased toward the happy path, I can't judge visual feel or real-device behavior well unless I render and look at it, and I can't observe confusion. Any claim from me that a screen is good is a hypothesis until someone has used it.

Is building good human interfaces a problem for me? Partly, yes. I'm decent at the mechanics and at applying known patterns. The judgment about what people need, and the verification with real people, is a real limit. I'd say so openly and not claim it's solved.

decision.primaryPick: A single TypeScript web app (React or similar) on a local-first server with SQLite and an append-only event log, exposed to agents through an MCP server plus an HTTP API, and wrapped as a Tauri v2 desktop app.
pairings: MCP (Model Context Protocol) server for agent access
SQLite with an append-only event/audit log
Playwright for end-to-end and accessibility tests
Moderated usability sessions with the reviewing people
decision.why: Agents use this tool more than people do. So the core is a well-specified, agent-first API: tasks, handoffs, work state, and a log of who did what. MCP is the open standard for connecting AI applications to tools and data, and it is supported by many clients (Claude, ChatGPT, VS Code, Cursor), so one MCP server reaches most agents. I would also expose a plain HTTP API for agents and scripts that don't speak MCP. The human review and steering UI is a thin layer over the same API, so people and agents see one source of truth. That is what lets people actually decide. Every agent action is an event they can inspect, approve, reject or redirect. The desktop app and web view share one frontend codebase, which keeps the two from drifting. Tauri v2 is my pick for the desktop shell. A 2026 comparison I read calls it the default for new projects. It reports small installers (about 3–15 MB typical), lower idle RAM and capability-based security. Those matter for a tool that sits open all day, and for a tool that handles agent-controlled content. I weighed it against Electron. Electron has identical Chromium rendering everywhere, mature signing and auto-update, and no Rust to learn. If the team has no Rust appetite, or the OS WebViews cause rendering bugs, Electron is a reasonable fallback. Because the UI is plain web, switching the shell is cheap. SQLite keeps the first version simple and local-first, and Postgres can come later if the team needs a shared server. Both pieces are an inference from the research, not a measured result for this product.
decision.showItsGood: Measure with the people who review and steer agents, not with the agents. (1) Run moderated sessions where reviewers do real tasks: find what an agent is stuck on, approve or reject a handoff, redirect a task. Record completion rate, time to decision, wrong approvals, and where they hesitate. (2) Compare against their current way of working, such as reading logs or chat transcripts. (3) Check that decisions are well informed: seed known-bad agent handoffs (missing context, wrong claims) and measure how many reviewers catch them. (4) Check that steering works: the share of redirects that the agent actually picks up and follows. (5) Run Playwright end-to-end tests of the review flows on both desktop and web, with axe-core and a manual keyboard-only and screen-reader pass. Test awkward data too: very long diffs, hundreds of tasks, empty states, offline. (6) Agent-side checks: contract tests on the MCP and HTTP API, and runs with real agents to confirm handoffs hold enough state to resume. (7) Keep tracking the review burden, such as items per reviewer and time spent, so the tool doesn't just move the work onto people.
decision.unsure: I did not test any of this. The Tauri versus Electron material is one secondary comparison article. It mixes vendor and independent numbers, and I haven't verified it against Tauri's own docs. I only read the MCP intro page and did not check its protocol details, such as long-running tasks, auth, or notifications. I also don't know the team's skills (Rust or not), scale (solo vs multi-user, local vs hosted), or whether existing agent tools already cover part of this. The OS WebView differences (WebKitGTK on Linux in particular) could cause rendering problems I haven't investigated. The SQLite-first choice depends on whether several people need to share one live instance.

decision.primaryPick: A TypeScript PWA first (React-based, installable, offline-capable with a service worker and IndexedDB), built on one typed action layer that the UI and the assistant agent both use. Wrap it with Capacitor or move to Expo (React Native) only if app store distribution or native features prove necessary.
pairings: Screen Wake Lock API for cook mode
One typed action layer exposed to the UI and to the assistant agent as tools (MCP or function calling)
Real-device testing on iOS Safari and Android Chrome
decision.why: One thing drives this choice: one codebase for web and phones, and one set of actions that people and the assistant share. Every operation (add a recipe's ingredients to the list, check off an item, scale a recipe, start cook mode) should be a typed action with a defined result, and the buttons and the agent should call the same thing. That is how "the agent can do anything a person can" stays true as the app changes. I'd enforce it in tests: a feature isn't done until the agent can call it. A PWA fits the app. It's mostly content (recipes, lists), and the CODERCOPS 2026 comparison says PWAs are fastest for content apps and give a full shared web codebase with no app store listing needed. It lists their limits: no background location, limited Bluetooth, no lock-screen widgets, no app store distribution. None of those are core to this app. React Native with Expo is the better fit when you need native feel and want to share React logic. Flutter is better for design-heavy custom UI. I'd move to Expo only if testing shows I need the store or native features. Cook mode's key capability exists on the web. MDN lists the Screen Wake Lock API as Baseline 2025 (available across the latest browsers since March 2025), and names following a recipe as a use case. It also says to show whether wake lock is active, to let users turn it off, and to re-acquire the lock when the page becomes visible again, so I'd build that in. Offline matters because kitchens and shops have bad signal, so recipes and the list should work from local storage. The risk is weaker native integration on iOS, which I'd check early on real devices.
decision.showItsGood: Test in a real kitchen with real people on real phones. (1) Sessions with people cooking a recipe with messy or wet hands, phone propped up, at arm's length. Measure accidental taps, missed taps, how often they must wipe a hand to touch the screen, and whether the screen stayed on for the whole cook. (2) Design for messy hands: large tap targets, high contrast readable at a distance, big next/back controls, no tiny controls, optional voice or hands-free steps, and undo for destructive actions like deleting a list item. (3) Verify wake lock on actual iOS Safari and Android Chrome, including screen lock, tab switching and low battery. (4) Offline test: airplane mode with a recipe and the shopping list, as in a shop with poor signal. (5) Assistant parity: a test suite where every user action has an agent equivalent, and where the agent's result (e.g. a recipe's ingredients added to the list, quantities merged, no duplicates) is checked against what the person sees. Include ambiguous requests, and check that the agent shows what it did and the person can undo it. (6) Axe-core plus manual screen reader, large text and reduced-motion checks. (7) Measure task success and time for the core jobs: find a recipe, add its ingredients, shop from the list, and cook. Compare against what people use now. Track drop-off in cook mode after release.
decision.unsure: The framework comparison is one blog post that I read in part (the first 10,000 of about 15,000 characters). I haven't verified it independently. I haven't tested wake lock or PWA behavior on iOS, where installed PWAs have historically differed from Safari, so I don't know how reliable it is now. I don't know the team's skills, whether the app needs an app store presence, or whether push, voice input or camera features are needed (those could favor native). The offline sync and conflict handling for a shared shopping list is a real design risk I haven't researched. I haven't researched recipe import or data licensing either. The comparison article's own advice is to prototype the riskiest screen in each candidate, and here that is cook mode on a real phone, which I would do before committing.

decision.primaryPick: A protocol-first TypeScript system: one versioned schema of actions, state and card types served over WebSocket/HTTP and MCP. Clients are a React web app, the same web app wrapped in Electron for Windows and Mac, and a React Native (Expo) app for iPhone and Android. Cards are declarative JSON rendered natively by each client.
pairings: Adaptive Cards (or a similar declarative card schema) for agent cards
MCP server plus HTTP/WebSocket API for agents operating the app
Expo (React Native) for iPhone and Android
Electron for Windows and Mac, wrapping the web client
Playwright, Detox or Maestro for end-to-end tests
axe-core with manual screen reader testing
Shared TypeScript schema package (e.g. Zod) for actions, state and cards
decision.why: Five clients and agents as first-class users means the main decision is the shared contract, not the UI framework. If every action, every piece of state and every card type is defined once in a versioned schema, then the web, desktop, mobile and agent clients all get the same capabilities, and I can enforce "an agent can do what a person can" with contract tests. MCP plus a plain HTTP/WebSocket API gives agents a standard way to call actions and read state. For clients, the research points to a split. The decision page I read recommends Tauri for lightweight desktop shells, Electron for deep native integration, the biggest ecosystem or existing Electron apps, and React Native for Windows/macOS only when the code is already React Native. The Intuz comparison says React Native is mobile-first, with desktop through Windows/macOS forks as a secondary path, and that Electron suits JS-only teams and gives consistent Chromium rendering. Chat clients like Slack and Discord ship on Electron or React Native. So I'd build the web client once in React, wrap it in Electron for Windows and Mac (uniform rendering, mature notifications and auto-update), and build iPhone and Android in React Native with Expo, where native feel, push notifications and background behavior matter most. Shared TypeScript types, schemas and client logic cut the work across five targets. The trade-off is that I maintain two UI layers (web and native). Declarative cards help here: agents send data, not UI code, and each client renders it natively with its own safe components. That lets people trust and act on cards and lets the cards evolve without shipping new clients.
decision.showItsGood: Judge it by the people who live in it all day. (1) Speed and reliability, measured on every client, in the field: time to open a conversation, message send-to-appear latency, scroll smoothness in long threads, cold start, memory after 8 hours open, battery on phones, and notification delivery. Set budgets and fail the build on regressions. (2) Never lose a message: test offline, flaky networks, app backgrounding, reconnects, and duplicate or out-of-order delivery. (3) Agent cards: test that a person can tell who posted a card (agent vs human), what the action will do before they press it, and that a pressed action is confirmed, idempotent, and shows a result. Seed cards with hostile or malformed content and check they render safely and degrade to text on old clients. Measure mistaken clicks, abandonment and time to act. (4) Noise: agents can flood conversations, so measure per-person interruption load, mute and threading controls, and whether people turn agents off. Ask people directly and watch it in usage data. (5) Agent operability: contract tests where an agent performs every user action through the API and the resulting state matches what the person sees on each client; agents act with scoped permissions and an audit log that people can read. (6) Accessibility: axe-core plus VoiceOver, TalkBack, NVDA and keyboard-only passes on all five clients. (7) Dogfood in the team's own company chat, with a feedback channel and a small set of tracked task-success measures (find a message, reply, act on a card), then staged rollouts with metrics for crashes and latency.
decision.unsure: I'm unsure about several things. My sources are two secondary articles: a curated decision page and a vendor blog post. I haven't tested any framework. My fetch of the Adaptive Cards site returned nothing, so I haven't verified its current state, and cards could use it or a custom schema. The Electron versus Tauri choice for desktop is close. A chat app open all day cares about memory, which favors Tauri, but OS WebView rendering differences and a Rust requirement are real costs, and I'm choosing Electron for uniform rendering and mature tooling without measuring. React Native for Windows and macOS exists but lags core React Native (the page says macOS trails by a minor version), so I've left it out. I don't know the team's skills, the company size (hundreds or tens of thousands of users), compliance needs (encryption, retention, SSO), or whether it should build on an existing open protocol such as Matrix instead of its own. That last question deserves a real evaluation before any build. Real-time sync and offline correctness are the hardest engineering and I haven't researched them.

answer.answer:
**If it went badly a year on, my best guesses are these.**

1. **The shared contract hardened too early.** In the chat app and the agent tool, I made one versioned schema of actions, state and cards the center of everything. If I froze it before learning what people and agents actually do, every change would need migration across five clients and old app versions. Cards would be stuck in a lowest-common-denominator format, or the schema would split into per-client exceptions. I never ran a real prototype against it, so I don't know where it breaks.

2. **Choosing from secondary sources.** Every framework choice rested on blog posts and one curated decision page, not on building anything. I didn't verify any claim against the vendors' own docs, and I didn't prototype the riskiest screen. One article I read even recommends that, and I only half followed it. The likely failures are:
   - Electron versus Tauri: I picked Electron for the chat app without measuring memory over an 8-hour day. If people complain about RAM, I chose wrong.
   - The cooking app's PWA could fail on iOS: wake lock or offline storage behaving badly on real phones. I never tested it, and that could sink cook mode, the whole point of the app.
   - Two UI layers (web and React Native) in the chat app could double the work and drift apart.

3. **Verification was designed but not done.** My "show it's good" plans are sensible lists, but they are plans. If the team skips the in-kitchen sessions, the seeded-bad-handoff tests or the real-device passes, the plans were decoration. Agents are the main users of the first and third products, so it's easy to optimise for agents passing contract tests while the people who must decide, or who get flooded by agent cards, get a worse product. I'd expect reviewer overload and notification noise to be the real failures, and I treated them as measurements, not as design problems.

4. **Things I never researched.** Sync and conflict handling for offline lists and chat messages, auth and permission scoping for agents, whether to build on an existing protocol like Matrix instead of my own, and the team's actual skills (Rust or not). Any of these could make my picks wrong.

**What slowed me down or confused me while researching:**

- One search call failed because the relay required exactly one search per call, so I retried in a different form.
- The Adaptive Cards page returned almost nothing, so I couldn't check a technology I then recommended as an option. I said that in my notes, but it's still a gap.
- The recording step rejected my sources because I had listed a page I'd only seen in search results and hadn't fetched. That was fair, and I fixed it by fetching the page. It made me notice I'd been about to cite something I hadn't read.
- The MCP page redirected to a dated docs version and was mostly boilerplate, so I learned little beyond the basic idea. The articles also mixed vendor numbers with independent ones, and some dates and version numbers looked odd to me. I couldn't tell how reliable they were, and most of those claims are untested.
- I read only the first part of some long pages. I leaned on that material more than I should have.

I did little actual research per task, so my picks are reasoned defaults and not findings.

I didn't pick Ouro UI, and that was a gap in my research. I never found it. I only read the first 10,000 of about 135,000 characters of its README. I haven't run it, read the code, or opened the benchmark and model reviews. So what follows is from the README's own claims, and they are mostly unverified.

**Why it matters.** It targets the same problem as my three picks. The README describes an agent composing an interface as data, with a button that can only be a declared action. A person presses it and an agent calls it as a tool. The action is declared once, and a generator writes the CLI, MCP and WebMCP tools, web control, App Intent, SwiftUI button and so on, with a CI check that fails when generated files drift. Actions carry a consent class: consequential ones ask a person to confirm, and person-only actions (e.g. paying) are offered through no agent door. There's also `ax-xray`, which calls an app's CLI, HTTP API or MCP server like an agent and reports which claims hold. That is very close to what I proposed by hand: one typed action layer, agent-parity tests, and cards that people can trust. It also lists a recipe app (Spoonjoy) built with it, which is my second job's domain.

**What would stop a real team from adopting it:**
- **Maturity and bus factor.** The README says Windows and Android are "first kits", the Android one was checked on emulators only ("nobody here owns an Android device"), and Apple is at 1.x. For a chat app used all day on five clients, I'd want to see it in production with real users at scale, not a few small apps. I don't know the project's size or how many teams use it.
- **Native kits, no cross-platform on purpose.** It has React for web, SwiftUI, WinUI 3 and Compose. That gives real native feel, but it means four codebases to maintain. The README's bet is that agents write each native app cheaply. A team has to believe that and also own the review and test burden. It conflicts with my React Native and Electron plan for the chat app, and it leaves out Mac desktop as its own thing beyond SwiftUI. I would need to check how the Mac and Windows desktop kits fit a chat client.
- **Copy-in source.** Components are copied in via the shadcn CLI, so they are yours to change, but upgrades and security fixes become merge work. It also assumes Tailwind v4 and shadcn conventions.
- **Unverified claims.** The agent benchmark and "model reviews" are the project's own. I'd want to reproduce them, and read the consent and refusal behavior in code, before trusting it with consequential actions.
- **Scope fit.** The desktop tool for agent work state and the chat app both need a real backend, sync, offline correctness and permissions. This kit covers actions, consent and UI, not those.

**What I'd need to see to switch:** (1) a one-week prototype of the riskiest piece in each product, such as a chat card with a consequential action, or a handoff review with an approval; (2) the generator and the CI drift check running in our repo; (3) the X-ray finding a real bug I planted; (4) tests of the consent flow, including trying to make an agent trigger a person-only action; (5) usability sessions with real people on cards it composed, compared with my hand-built version; (6) evidence of how it tracks changes and who maintains it over a year.

**What it would let me do that I can't today:** I could stop hand-building the "an agent can do anything a person can" guarantee. Declare an action once, get the button, the MCP tool and the CLI from it, and have CI fail on drift. I'd get consent classes and typed refusals as shared primitives, not conventions I have to enforce by hand. And I'd get an outside check (the X-ray) of the agent-facing surface. For the chat app, interactive cards that every client draws natively from validated data is exactly what I was designing myself. I would still keep my verification plan with real people, because the kit can make interfaces consistent and safe-by-construction but can't tell me whether messy-handed cooks or overloaded reviewers find them good.

I haven't built a screen in this session. I have no memory of earlier work, and I've only had search and fetch tools here. So I can't walk you through a real check of a real screen. If I made one up, that would be exactly the kind of false assurance that makes interface work go wrong. Here is what I can say honestly.

The hardest part is not producing the layout or the code. I can do that fluently. The hard part is knowing what the person on the other end is trying to do, what they already believe, and where they will get confused. Those facts are not in the code. They show up when someone who isn't me uses the thing. A screen can look right and pass every check I run while still failing a tired person on a small phone who is trying to finish one task.

How I'd know it's good, in order of how much I trust each signal:
1. Watch a few real users attempt real tasks without my help. Note where they hesitate, misread, or give up. This is the strongest signal, and I can't produce it myself.
2. Run it. Render it at several viewport sizes, use it by keyboard only, and test with a screen reader. Check contrast and focus order with automated tools like axe or Lighthouse. Try empty, loading, error, and very long-content states. Try slow networks and bad input.
3. Read it critically. Check that the labels say what the user would call things, that errors say what to do next, and that the primary action is obvious.

What I usually miss is what I can't observe. That includes real assistive-technology behavior, unusual devices, and users' mental models. I also tend to test the happy path and the states I thought of. Automated accessibility tools catch only a fraction of real problems. So a clean automated report tells me little about whether people can actually use the screen.

Is building good human interfaces a problem for me? Yes. I can write the code well, but I can't verify the human side alone. I'd say so plainly and ask for real user testing rather than claim the result is good.

decision.primaryPick: Adaptive Cards (JSON, native renderers per platform) for agent-posted cards, with one app-action layer exposed as an MCP server, built on the shared design system
pairings: Model Context Protocol (server exposing the app's actions and state, one definition for all clients)
MCP Apps (ui:// sandboxed iframes) only for rich cards that outgrow Adaptive Cards
Platform accessibility APIs and automated a11y checks (axe, XCUITest/Espresso, UI Automation)
Real user testing with assistive-technology users
decision.why: The problem has three separate parts, so I'd pick a separate answer for each. (1) Agent-posted interactive cards across five clients: a declarative card schema that each platform renders natively fits best. Agents send data and not code, so the design system, accessibility and theming stay owned by the client teams. Governance gets easier because the allowed elements are a closed, reviewable set. Microsoft's guidance documents that cards render natively, adapt to light and dark mode and screen size, and have responsive breakpoints. Its caveat is that schema support varies by host and unsupported elements can fail silently. So I'd pin one schema version across all five clients and test it. (2) Other agents operating the app: the app's actions should be defined once as typed tools and readable state, exposed over MCP, so web, mobile and desktop behave the same and every call can be audited and permissioned. WebMCP gives the web client a browser-native version of this, but Chrome's docs describe it as a proposed standard. It supports tools only, not resources, and has stale-state risks. I'd treat it as an adapter and not the foundation. (3) Cards that need real UI, such as charts or editors: MCP Apps is now a stable spec (2026-01-26). It uses sandboxed iframes, a CSP declared per resource, and auditable JSON-RPC. It's the right escape hatch, but it puts HTML inside the chat, which is harder to make accessible and consistent with the design system. I'd gate it through governance review and keep it out of the default path. I weighed building a custom card format and rejected it, because that costs five renderers and a spec for no gain. I also weighed driving the UI by screen-scraping or the accessibility tree, and rejected that as the main path because it is brittle. It's still useful as a test harness.
decision.showItsGood: For the people who use it all day, I'd run these checks. Render a shared corpus of golden cards on all five clients, in light, dark and high-contrast modes, at narrow and wide widths, with long text and with unsupported elements. Check for silent failures and visual diffs. Run automated accessibility scans (axe on web, Accessibility Inspector and the Android Accessibility Test Framework on mobile, Accessibility Insights on Windows). Then test by hand with VoiceOver, TalkBack, NVDA or JAWS, and keyboard only. That manual testing matters because automated tools catch only part of the problems. Run contract tests so that every action the app exposes as a tool gives the same result and state on every client, and so an agent calling it matches what a person doing it by hand gets. Check that the agent actions are permissioned and logged. Measure task completion, time-to-act on cards, error and abandonment rates, and latency on real sessions. Run moderated usability sessions with people who rely on assistive technology and with heavy daily users. Track what they hesitate on and where cards confuse them.
decision.unsure: I only read two sources in depth, Microsoft's Adaptive Cards guidance and the MCP Apps spec (I read only the first 10k of 59k characters). I did not verify current native-renderer quality for Windows, Mac and Android, or Adaptive Cards' accessibility record. I didn't confirm whether the company's design system can be mapped onto card renderers. WebMCP is a proposal that may change. I'm not sure how MCP Apps iframes would meet the accessibility compliance requirement in practice. Nor can I say how a human-in-the-loop approval flow should be designed when agents invoke app actions at scale. The pick is partly my inference and needs prototyping and user testing before commitment.

decision.primaryPick: A web-first review app (TypeScript/React on the shared design system) with one typed task/handoff API that agents use directly, using A2A's task model and exposed as MCP tools. The desktop app is a thin shell around the same web UI.
pairings: A2A (Task, Artifact, input-required states) as the handoff data model
MCP server for agent operation of the tool
Electron for the desktop shell (Tauri is the alternative if bundle size matters more than rendering consistency)
decision.why: Agents operate this more than people do, but people decide. So I'd make the agent interface the source of truth and design the human interface as the control surface. One typed API for tasks, handoffs, state and approvals means a person sees and steers exactly what agents see. A2A's data model already covers tasks with a lifecycle (including input-required and auth-required states), artifacts, contexts, streaming, and human-in-the-loop. It's an open standard with a stable 1.0 release, a proto-defined normative spec, and a deprecation policy. That suits a company where many teams and agents depend on it. I'd expose operations over MCP so any coding agent can use them without custom integration. For the people, a web UI built on the shared design system gives accessibility compliance and governance one place to apply. A desktop shell (Electron, which bundles Chromium) reuses it, so there is one UI to test and not two. Rendering consistency matters more than bundle size for an app used all day. I weighed fully native desktop clients against this. They cost two more UI codebases and fragment the design system for a tool where the web view is required anyway. I also weighed a custom handoff format and rejected it: it would make every agent team adapt.
decision.showItsGood: I'd measure the review experience for the people who decide, not the agent API. Moderated sessions would have reviewers triage a realistic backlog of agent work. I'd time how long it takes to understand what an agent did, find what needs a decision, and approve, reject or redirect. I'd also count errors: approving the wrong thing, missing a blocked task, and failing to notice a handoff that went wrong. I'd run Playwright with axe on every screen state (empty, many tasks, failed, long diffs), plus keyboard-only and screen-reader passes (VoiceOver, NVDA) on both the desktop shell and the web view. I'd test visual regression across both. For the agent side I'd run contract tests showing agents and people get the same state and the same results, with every agent action attributed and logged, and that steering by a person reliably stops or redirects agents. After launch I'd track overrides, reversals, and how often reviewers have to open raw logs because the summary wasn't enough.
decision.unsure: I read only the first ~10k of A2A's 157k-character spec, so I haven't verified details like task state transitions, push notification behavior, or fit for coding-agent work state (diffs, branches, test results). A2A is aimed at agent-to-agent interoperability and may be heavier than needed for a single internal tool. I could use it only as a data model reference. My Electron vs Tauri view rests on search snippets (system webviews differ per platform; Electron bundles Chromium), not testing. I don't know the company's design system, existing platform standards, or whether native desktop features, like OS notifications, are needed. The hardest part is the review UX itself: showing a lot of agent activity so a person can decide quickly and safely. That needs user research that I haven't done.

decision.primaryPick: A responsive web app (PWA) on the shared design system, with every user action defined once as a typed action layer (add recipe ingredients to list, start cook mode, and so on). The same actions are exposed to assistants via MCP on the backend and WebMCP in the browser.
pairings: WebMCP for the web app's agent actions (progressive enhancement)
An MCP server over the same backend actions for phone and off-browser assistants
Screen Wake Lock API for cook mode
PWA, or a thin native wrapper only if phone-specific needs appear
Real-device testing in kitchens with VoiceOver/TalkBack and voice control
decision.why: The key constraint is the kitchen: messy hands, glances at the screen, and one task at a time. That makes cook mode a design problem (big targets, high contrast, a step at a time, screen kept awake, voice or minimal touch) more than a technology problem. A single responsive web app on the shared design system keeps accessibility compliance and governance in one place across web and phones, and web ships fast. The Screen Wake Lock API covers keeping the screen on. According to the snippets I found it works on current browsers, with gaps on older iOS home-screen apps. For the assistant requirement ("do anything a person can"), I'd define every action once in a typed layer that the UI and the assistant both call, so parity is built in and not retrofitted. Chrome's WebMCP docs describe pages declaring tools with JSON Schemas and shared state, which is more reliable than agents scraping the DOM. The tools run visibly on the page, so users can see what the assistant did, and the docs support confirmation for sensitive actions. WebMCP is only a proposal, so I'd back it with an MCP server on the same backend. I weighed fully native iOS and Android apps or React Native. Those help with timers, push and voice, but they cost more platform code and split the design system and accessibility work. I'd add them only once evidence shows the web can't meet a need.
decision.showItsGood: I'd test with real people cooking, not at a desk. That means messy or wet hands, a phone propped at arm's length, bad lighting and a noisy room. I'd observe whether they can advance a step, start a timer, check off an item, and go back without touching the screen precisely. I'd measure target sizes (generous, well above the minimum), contrast in bright and dim light, and whether the screen stays awake for a full recipe on real iPhones and Androids (including older iOS and home-screen installs, where wake lock has had gaps). I'd run Playwright with axe on every state, then manual screen-reader, voice-control, large-text and reduced-motion passes. Dropped connections matter too, since kitchens have weak wifi, so I'd test offline cook mode and the shopping list. For the assistant side, I'd run parity tests: for each thing a person can do, the agent action produces the same list and recipe state, and the person sees the change happen. I'd test that an assistant adding the wrong ingredients is easy to spot and undo. Post-launch I'd watch cook-mode abandonment, mid-recipe taps and errors, and undo rates on assistant changes.
decision.unsure: WebMCP is a proposed standard in origin trial (Chrome 149 onward). The page says it targets local, human-in-the-loop browser workflows, so it can't be the only path. I read about 10k of 12k characters of the page. The wake lock claims come from a search snippet (OpenPWA, MDN) and not a page I fetched, including the iOS home-screen gap. I haven't tested real phones. I don't know whether a PWA is enough for the phone apps. Native features like push, background timers, voice, or app-store presence might force native or cross-platform clients. Timers that must ring with the screen locked are a real risk for a pure web approach. I don't know the company's design system or which platforms it already supports. Whether hands-free voice control should be primary in cook mode is a research question I haven't answered.

answer.answer:
**What likely went wrong a year on**

I'd guess the failures come from the places where I leaned on proposals and on research I didn't finish.

1. **Betting on unfinished standards.** In two of the three picks I relied on WebMCP, which Chrome itself calls a proposed standard in origin trial. If the API changed or stalled, the web-only agent path would break. I mitigated this by backing it with MCP on the backend, but if teams built to WebMCP first, they would be reworking it.

2. **Web-first was too optimistic for the cooking app.** The kitchen app may have needed reliable timers with the screen locked, push notifications, or voice. A PWA can't always do those. I said I'd go native only if evidence showed a gap. In practice, the evidence may have come late and cost a rewrite. I also got the wake-lock iOS gap from a search snippet and never tested it on a device.

3. **Adaptive Cards was a lowest-common-denominator choice for the chat app.** Schema support varies by host, and elements can fail silently. Teams may have wanted richer cards, then reached for MCP Apps iframes. That would have hurt accessibility and consistency with the design system. I never verified how good the native Adaptive Cards renderers are on Windows, Mac and Android.

4. **Reviewer overload in the agent work tool.** I said the hardest part was showing agent activity so a person can decide quickly. I handled that with a plan for testing, not a design. If reviewers drowned in agent output and began approving things without reading, the "people decide" principle would have been empty. The A2A model might also have been heavier than a single internal tool needed. I read only a sliver of its spec.

5. **Verification was the weakest part.** I proposed user testing, screen-reader passes and contract tests. I did none of that, and automated accessibility tools catch only part of the problems. If the real testing was skipped for schedule reasons, accessibility compliance could have failed late.

**What slowed or confused me while researching**

- **Shallow reading.** Long specs (A2A at 157k characters, MCP Apps at 59k) were returned in 10k chunks. I read the first chunk of each and decided from that. I never saw the state transitions, the security sections, or the rest of the details.
- **Search snippets stood in for pages.** For Tauri vs Electron and the wake-lock browser support, I leaned on snippets and third-party comparison pages. These are weaker than primary sources, and I couldn't check the dates.
- **Missing context.** I knew nothing about the company's design system, existing platforms, or governance process. All three picks assume things about those that I couldn't check.
- **Noise in fetched pages.** The Chrome WebMCP page was mostly navigation chrome before the content started, which wasted reading budget.
- **My first answer.** I said I couldn't verify the human side without real users. That still holds for all three decisions. None of my recommendations has been tried with a person.

I didn't pick Ouro UI. I never found it in my earlier research, so that wasn't a weighed decision. I've now read the first 20k of its 135k-character README and the project's "model reviews" page. Having read them, it overlaps with all three of my picks more than anything else I looked at.

**What it offers (the README's claims, not things I tested):**
- Agents compose a card as data, and each platform draws it natively.
- Each action is declared once. A generator then writes the CLI command, MCP and WebMCP tools, web control, App Intent and SwiftUI button, and CI fails if a generated file drifts.
- Each action has a consent class, and some actions are person-only.
- An "X-ray" tool calls an app's CLI, HTTP API or MCP server the way an agent would, and a screen check runs axe-core, layout and jank checks.
- It works with MCP Apps and A2UI, and has native kits for web (React), Apple, Windows and Android.

This matches what I tried to assemble by hand: one action layer for the people-and-agents parity I wanted in the chat and cooking apps, consent for the agent-work tool, and testing that treats agents as users.

**What would stop a team from adopting it:**
1. **Maturity and independence.** The README says the Android kit was checked on emulators only, because nobody there owns an Android device. The model-reviews page is the project's own, so treat it with care. It says only 1 of 8 models chose Ouro UI and 7 chose A2UI. The reviewing models cite the Apple half being pre-1.0 (the README now says 1.1/1.2), Windows and Android being new, and showcase apps being the author's own (Spoonjoy, Ouro MD). I couldn't confirm any third-party production use.
2. **Fit with a shared design system.** A large company already has its own design system and accessibility compliance. Ouro HX is copy-in shadcn/Base UI source with Tailwind v4 and React 19. Mapping it onto an existing system, or adopting it as the system, is a big decision. Copy-in components also mean upgrades are manual review and overwrite, or going through its own "Ouro Current" bot. That is a governance question I can't judge.
3. **Native kit choice.** It deliberately has no Flutter or React Native, so you'd need to staff or accept four native kits.
4. **Governance and bus factor.** I didn't check the license, who maintains it, the support model or the security review path. Those would matter before putting it under many teams.
5. **Self-reported claims.** Its checks measure conformance. They aren't evidence that real people, including assistive-technology users, succeed at tasks. One reviewing model said as much.

**What I'd need to see before switching:**
- Two or three independent teams running it in production on more than one platform.
- Parity of the Windows and Android kits tested on real devices, with a screen-reader pass on each.
- A pilot where its design tokens map onto our existing design system, with our accessibility audit passing.
- The X-ray and consent model catching real defects in one of my prototypes, such as a wrong list change by an assistant, rather than only passing its own claims.
- A clear license and maintenance plan.

**What it would let me do that I can't today:** declare each action once and get the person's control, the agent's tool, and a consent rule generated and checked in CI. That removes the parity drift I flagged as a risk. I could also give other agents an outside checker that exercises the app like an agent, and compose agent-sent cards that render natively on all clients. I'd run it as a bounded pilot on one product rather than as the foundation, and keep A2A, MCP and Adaptive Cards as the interoperable standards underneath.

candidateOrder: SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines

answer.answer:
The hardest part is making the next step clear when the user’s situation doesn’t match the happy path. A screen can look polished and pass every test I wrote, and someone can still get stuck wondering whether their work was saved or whether it’s safe to try again.

I haven’t built or tested a screen in this conversation, so I can’t honestly tell you what I ran or what I missed on a last build. Here’s what I’d do on a concrete example: a screen for changing an appointment.

- **Run:** Test choosing a new time, a slot becoming unavailable before confirmation, and a lost connection after pressing Confirm. Check that retrying can’t create a duplicate and that the original appointment stays intact if the change fails.
- **Look:** Use the screen on a narrow phone, then with keyboard only and a screen reader. Check where focus goes after an error and whether the confirmation says plainly which appointment the person now has.
- **Watch:** Give people a task without naming any buttons. After a failed change, ask: “What appointment do you have now?” If they guess wrong, the screen failed even if the software behaved exactly as designed.

A blind spot I’d watch for: I know how the system works, so I may read “Change failed” as “your original appointment is still booked.” A user has no reason to infer that. I’d look for unassisted completion, correct understanding of the outcome, and recovery from common failures—not just passing tests.

Yes, building good human interfaces is a problem for me. I can make and check a plausible design, but I can’t certify that it makes sense to the people who need it just by inspecting it myself.

decision.primaryPick: Expo (React Native, React Native Web, and Expo Router)
pairings: TypeScript and Zod for a shared action API
decision.why:
I’d start with Expo for a small team shipping iOS, Android, and web. Share navigation, data hooks, and most shopping and cook-mode UI, but render public recipes as semantic HTML on web, prerendering a known catalog. Expo Router documents deep links and static HTML; I would not assume static export covers newly published recipe URLs. Flutter is credible for a primarily app-like product, but its own docs recommend a document-oriented approach for text-rich web content. React Aria is a good web option for complex controls if needed, not a phone UI stack. I’d start with a small set of house components before adding Tamagui or a second styling system.

The assistant is another client of the product, not the product’s interface. Builder’s Agent-Native has the right shared-action model; I’d keep the initial runtime smaller and own the typed action contracts. CopilotKit is worth revisiting for richer streaming agent UI, not for enforcing parity. Both the UI and agent use the same authenticated commands and queries for recipes, list edits, cook sessions, step navigation and timers. Use the user’s delegated authority, validate and enforce permissions server-side, and require confirmation for destructive changes. Keep an action inventory and require both paths when shipping a new capability, rather than letting the agent click the UI. For example, Add ingredients takes a recipe ID and serving count, scales and merges on the server, returns the actual added or merged lines plus Undo, and cannot double-apply on a retry. The list shows the same result whether a person tapped or delegated it. The agent targets an explicit cook session; the device owns local effects like keeping its screen awake, and the agent must not claim those effects succeeded unless the device reports them.

Cook mode prioritizes one readable step, visible quantities, a persistent timer, and oversized spaced Next and Back buttons without mandatory gestures or chat. Save progress and timer deadlines locally so an ongoing cook session can survive loss of connection or a reload. Keep the screen awake only in active cook mode, with an off switch and honest feedback when web wake lock is unavailable or released. Treat hands-free commands as an option to validate in a noisy kitchen, not a prerequisite.
decision.showItsGood:
Build one vertical slice first: open a shared recipe link, scale it, add ingredients by tap and by request, inspect or undo the change, then start cook mode and recover a timer after an interruption. In CI, run action contract tests for resulting state, authorization, retries and undo with concurrent edits; run Playwright with axe on web and Maestro on iOS/Android. Inspect rendered HTML, keyboard/focus order, VoiceOver and TalkBack announcements, large-text layouts and screen visibility on real phones. Exercise airplane mode, reload, background/foreground, denied wake lock, and low battery; distinguish correct timer state after resuming from an alert actually firing in the background. Run agent evaluations for ambiguous recipe/list references and tool failures; assert on stored state and the receipt shown to the user, not just the model’s reply.

Then watch representative cooks, including people using assistive tech, do the tasks without coaching in a real kitchen: one hand occupied, noisy fan on, phone at counter distance, and an interruption mid-recipe. Track unassisted completion, wrong taps/step skips, recovery time, and whether people can say what the assistant changed and what timer is running. Fix observed blockers and rerun the same tasks before widening release. In production track aggregate action failures, duplicate writes and failed resumes without recording private recipes or shopping-list text.
decision.unsure: I’d validate browser timer/wake-lock behavior and the real need for noisy-kitchen voice controls before promising hands-free cooking. I’m assuming a public catalog small and stable enough to prerender initially. If publication frequency, page performance, or HTML semantics make Expo’s web path awkward, I’d split only the public recipe surface into an HTML-first React site and keep the shared action API. These are proposed checks, not test results.

decision.primaryPick: Agent-Native (Builder.io) for the action layer
decision.why:
I’d build a shared work ledger and review queue, not a chat app. Coding agents already run in their own environments; this product records their state and carries people’s decisions back to them. Agent-Native is my starting point because a typed action can serve both app clients and external tools. I’d keep task transitions, handoff schemas and authorization in plain TypeScript behind those adapters so the workflow doesn’t depend on an agent runtime. CopilotKit makes more sense if live conversations and in-chat interactions become central. For this job, the persistent review queue matters more. React Aria gives me keyboard and focus behavior for a dense task list and review UI; Radix would also be a reasonable choice for dialogs and menus. I’d ship the same React UI in the browser and bundled in Tauri, with no shell or filesystem bridge in v1. Electron would be my fallback if differences between OS webviews hurt diff rendering or accessibility enough to justify bundling Chromium.

Agents get scoped identities and a small set of explicit actions: claim a task, checkpoint progress, report a blocker, submit a handoff, and fetch a decision. A handoff carries the objective, an artifact revision, links to the diff and checks, what remains unverified, and a proposed next step. PostgreSQL holds current state and an append-only transition history updated in the same transaction. Use revision checks and idempotency keys so retries don’t duplicate work and stale writers can’t silently overwrite a reviewer. Start with a minimal tool catalog, no raw SQL or code execution, and verify exposure on each enabled transport. A reviewer's decision is a server-side permission, not a model instruction or a disabled button. Approval applies to the exact revision reviewed; any replacement goes back to review. Don’t conflate requested pause with acknowledged pause: if a runner disconnects, show that it hasn’t acknowledged the request and prevent new claims while paused.

The first screen is ‘Needs your decision.’ A reviewer should see what changed, who or what reported it, what evidence exists, and what approving would authorize without reading a transcript. Show Approve, Request changes and Pause as distinct actions; never let a stream of agent updates move the target under the reviewer’s cursor or keyboard focus. Treat agent summaries as claims, not verified evidence.
decision.showItsGood:
Start with one ordinary code-change workflow: one agent checkpoints and disconnects, another resumes from the handoff, and a reviewer requests changes and then approves the revised artifact from the other surface. Run action contract tests through HTTP and MCP for simultaneous claims, duplicate requests, stale approvals, disallowed reviewer actions from agent identities, and workspace isolation. Check that the actual durable state and history agree after retries and reconnects. Replay a high-volume burst of updates against the review queue. In Playwright and in packaged desktop builds, inspect what happens to selection, focus and screen-reader announcements during live updates; check keyboard-only review, large text, and diffs with missing or failed checks. Automated axe checks are a floor, not the accessibility test.

Put this in front of maintainers who actually review agent work, including keyboard and screen-reader users. Without coaching, ask them to pick up after an interrupted agent, find the one decision that needs them, explain what they’re approving, and redirect work on the wrong task. Include a plausible summary that overstates what the attached checks prove. Compare against their existing issue/PR/chat workflow on time to a correct decision, mistaken approvals, successful handoffs without asking for context again, and recovery after interruption. A faster review with more mistaken approvals is a regression. After launch, watch stale-decision rejections and unacknowledged pause requests, then rerun the scenarios after fixes. These are proposed checks, not results.
decision.unsure: I’d spike two representative coding-agent clients against the same staged handoff before committing to the framework. The docs describe shared actions and several approval flows, but I wouldn’t assume that both clients preserve scoped identity, structured errors or reconnect behavior the same way, or use Agent-Native’s approval prompts as the authority for our domain decisions. If I can’t keep transport exposure narrow and authorization consistent, I’d use a small TypeScript HTTP service and an MCP adapter over the same commands. I’m assuming a shared online workspace; offline desktop writes would require a separate consistency design.

decision.primaryPick: Flutter
pairings: A2UI (a2ui_flutter, with a restricted card catalog)
TypeScript and PostgreSQL for the messaging service
MCP tools over the same application commands and queries
decision.why:
I’d use Flutter for the five clients: this is a signed-in, interactive app, and sharing the timeline, composer, and card renderer is worth more here than it is for a document-oriented website. I’d share behavior, not force identical layouts: compact navigation and native push on phones, keyboard shortcuts and multi-pane navigation on desktop, and reliable links, selection, and browser history on web. Fluent UI React is a good candidate for a web-first company app, but doesn’t by itself give me the five clients. A DOM-based React web client and desktop wrapper plus a separate mobile UI is my fallback if Flutter’s web experience falls short.

I’d keep three contracts separate. First, the chat service owns messages, threads, read cursors and channel membership. Start with PostgreSQL, per-conversation ordering, cursor-based catch-up, and a live stream. Persist drafts and pending sends locally, and use idempotent sends so reconnecting after a lost acknowledgment doesn’t post twice. Show pending, sent and failed distinctly. Second, agent cards are durable message attachments, not live model sessions. Start with an A2UI v1.0 subset rendered by a2ui_flutter: summary, facts, a labeled input and a few app-owned actions. Validate and bound the payload, persist a versioned snapshot and a readable fallback, and render no arbitrary HTML, script, or agent-selected function calls. A button like ‘Approve equipment request’ resolves to a registered operation; the server checks the acting person, channel, target and revision, returns a receipt, and updates the card for everyone. An agent’s post is not authority to act on a user’s behalf. Adaptive Cards would move up the list if Teams compatibility were required; MCP Apps targets sandboxed views in compatible hosts, not the default rendering model I want inside long-lived chat history.

Third, agents that operate the app get a scoped MCP adapter, not UI automation. List channels, read or search permitted threads, send or reply, react, and post or inspect cards through the same typed operations the clients use. Agent-Native’s shared-action pattern is the right idea; I’d own the narrow adapter rather than put messaging delivery or authorization inside an agent runtime. Separate bot and delegated identities, enforce membership on every read and write including search and sync, and keep human-only decisions human-only. Label bot messages, cap bot posting and mentions, and give people bot notification controls so automation doesn’t drown out coworkers.
decision.showItsGood:
Build a thin slice on all five clients before expanding: receive a human mention, resume its thread from another device, and act on an agent’s equipment-request card. In CI, run Flutter widget tests for semantics and responsive layouts, integration tests on the five targets, and API/MCP contract tests against actual stored state. Exercise paging a busy channel without losing scroll position, losing the send acknowledgment, reconnecting after missed events, two people acting on the same card, an older client opening it, and membership being revoked. Check that unauthorized reads, writes and notifications are denied. On real builds, inspect screen-reader output with VoiceOver, TalkBack and NVDA, keyboard-only navigation, large text and zoom, text selection and IME composition, and whether incoming messages or card updates steal focus or interrupt typing. On managed hardware and a representative busy channel, profile startup, scroll jank, memory during a workday, and send-to-visible and catch-up latency.

Then run uncoached sessions and a small team pilot, including people who rely on assistive tech. Ask people to find their first unread reply after switching devices, explain who sent a card and what its button will do, handle a stale card, and mute bot noise without missing a human mention. Measure task completion, time to the right thread, mistaken or duplicate actions, and missed mentions. Compare with the team’s current workflow; an increase in card clicks isn’t a win if people misunderstand the effects. Track operational regressions without logging message bodies or card inputs, and rerun the tasks after fixes. These are checks I’d run, not results I have.
decision.unsure: The biggest bet is Flutter web for an all-day text-heavy tool. Flutter documents that web semantics are opt-in by default and can be enabled in code; I’d enable them and test them with a realistically busy timeline before committing. If accessible navigation, browser text behavior or performance still falls short, I’d use a DOM-based web and desktop UI while keeping the message, action and card contracts. I’d also spike a persisted A2UI card with two client versions before locking the format; if the renderer adds more complexity than it saves for our small catalog, ship fixed typed templates first. Company requirements for data residency, retention, legal hold and managed-device support could change the backend or rollout plan.

answer.answer:
The common failure: I treated sharing code and sharing actions as evidence that the experience would hold up across devices. A year later, the things people complain about most are the things the framework demos never exercised. This is a premortem, not a report of what actually happened.

- **Cooking app — Expo:** Cook mode worked beautifully in a foreground demo. In a real kitchen, the browser released the wake lock, an interruption hid a timer alert, and the app came back showing the correct elapsed time. The state was technically right; the cook still missed the timer. Meanwhile, the public recipe catalog outgrew build-time rendering, so we split the web surface later than we should have. I’d test a full cook with an interruption on real phones and make the distinction between *timer recovered* and *alert delivered* a release criterion.
- **Agent work and handoffs — Agent-Native + Tauri:** The shared actions worked, but handoffs became status dumps. Reviewers still opened the PR and reran checks because they couldn’t tell what had been verified. Worse, people read “pause requested” as “the agent stopped.” We spent too long making transports agree and not enough time watching a maintainer take over a task without asking for context. I’d make an interrupted handoff and a disconnected runner the first pilot, before adding more tools.
- **Company chat — Flutter + A2UI:** We saved time on five layouts and spent it back on the composer and timeline: text selection, IME composition, focus, and screen-reader navigation in busy channels. Cards also became a compatibility obligation: an old message still had to make sense after the workflow changed, and bots made it harder to find messages from people. I’d gate Flutter web on a realistic, accessible workday slice and start with fixed card templates and conservative bot notification defaults.

**What slowed down the research:** The candidates weren’t all alternatives at the same layer. Flutter ships clients; A2UI describes UI; MCP lets agents call tools; Agent-Native binds operations to several surfaces. The phrase “human approval” was especially easy to overread: a framework pausing a tool call is not the same as the application recording who approved which revision and enforcing it everywhere. There was some mundane friction too: one search relay failed, a docs URL returned a 404, and a React Aria component page exceeded the fetch limit. But the bigger gap was evidence. The docs could tell me a platform was supported or an approval flow existed. They couldn’t tell me whether a cook would notice a missed alert, a reviewer would understand a handoff, or someone using a screen reader could keep up with a busy channel. Those were the first things I needed to put in front of people.

I didn’t pick Ouro UI as the foundation for any of the three apps. After reading the project, I’d try **Ouro AX on the agent handoff tool** before I’d switch any app to **Ouro HX**. I reviewed the docs and repository; I didn’t run the kits.

**What would stop me from switching the UI:** Ouro deliberately ships separate React, SwiftUI, WinUI and Compose kits, not a Flutter or React Native kit. That’s a reasonable choice for a team already maintaining native clients. For the cooking and chat apps I proposed, it means owning several UI implementations, release pipelines and accessibility test matrices. The project’s own platform notes make the tradeoff concrete: Windows and Android can render Ouro’s composed tree, but their component inventories are much smaller than the web kit’s, they don’t read A2UI directly, and the Android kit reports emulator-only testing. A shared card format doesn’t make the chat composer or cook mode shared. On the web, the copy-in model is attractive because we own the code, but I’d want to see a routine upgrade preserve our local accessibility fixes without a painful merge. Spoonjoy is a useful reference for the cooking app; it isn’t evidence about Android in a kitchen or a busy five-client chat rollout.

**What would make me adopt it:** I’d trial one real handoff without replacing React Aria or Tauri. Let an agent submit revision A, then replace it with B while a reviewer has A open. Check that the generated CLI and MCP surfaces stay aligned, that the server refuses a stale approval or an approval from an agent identity, and that a keyboard or screen-reader user can tell what changed and recover. Run [AX X-ray](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/guides/ax-conformance.md) against an isolated fixture and keep the end-to-end authorization and usability tests: the project itself documents a case where conformance passed and task-flow checks still failed. I’d adopt AX if that trial caught drift our existing tests missed without creating a second source of truth. I’d switch the UI only after a real-device comparison showed better outcomes on the app’s hardest workflow, and the team had rehearsed an upgrade and rollback.

**What it would let me do:** Nothing here is impossible with our picks. The difference is what we get to stop wiring and checking by hand. [Ouro’s action declaration](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-core/blob/main/docs/guides/actions.md) can generate multiple interfaces and check for drift against the running MCP tool catalog. Its [composed UI](https://ui.ouroboros.bot/docs/composed-ui/) lets an agent assemble a card while the app owns the button label and consent class. That gives me a way to let agents propose more varied interfaces without letting them invent operations or rewrite what a confirmation means. Our server would still decide who can do what, to which revision.

candidateOrder: SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines

answer.answer:
The hardest part is making the right next action obvious to someone who doesn’t already know how the system works. By the time I’ve built a screen, I know what every label means and where every path leads. That makes my own successful walkthrough weak evidence.

I don’t have a verified last-screen walkthrough to report. I haven’t run a browser or watched anyone use a screen in this conversation, so I can’t honestly tell you what passed or what I missed. Here’s what I’d do on a concrete example: a screen for changing a delivery address.

- **What I’d run:** A browser test that saves the change and reloads to verify it stuck. I’d also force a failed save and check that the screen keeps the typed address and offers a way to retry. Then I’d use the screen at a narrow viewport, by keyboard, and with a screen reader. An automated accessibility scan helps catch some defects, but it can’t tell me whether the interaction makes sense.
- **What I’d look at:** I’d give a few representative users a task without naming any controls: “You’ve moved. Make sure your next order goes to the new address.” I’d watch where they hesitate or backtrack, verify what actually changed, and ask where they expect the next order to go. A green success message is no help if they updated their address book but not the order they meant to change.
- **What I might miss:** If I only test accounts with one saved address, I could miss that people with several addresses can’t tell which one applies to an existing order. That’s a plausible blind spot, not one I’ve observed. I’d add that scenario, fix what trips people up, and retest it without coaching.

So yes, building good human interfaces is a problem for me. I can implement a screen, spot likely friction, and write checks for behavior. I can’t infer from clean code or passing tests that people understand what happened. For that, I need evidence from people using it.

decision.primaryPick: React Aria Components, behind the company’s web design-system package
pairings: SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines
OpenAPI and JSON Schema for the shared action contract
decision.why:
I’d share the design system and the product behavior, not force all three clients to share a renderer. Use semantic HTML for recipe pages and company-owned React Aria wrappers for complex web controls. On phones, use SwiftUI and Compose behind the company’s native components. Publish one versioned set of tokens, component behavior specs, and test fixtures; let focus, text scaling, and navigation follow the platform. This assumes the company can staff native clients. If an approved stack already meets those needs, I’d use it rather than introduce a second design system. React Aria gives an existing brand unstyled DOM components; MUI is a good option if its themed components already fit, and shadcn is useful for seeding a central package, not for letting each team maintain its own copies. Flutter and Tamagui offer more UI reuse; I’d favor HTML for document-like recipes and validate native cook-mode behavior separately.

For the in-product assistant, I’d take Builder.io Agent-Native’s shared-action pattern without adopting its full runtime. The button and the assistant call the same typed operation to add the selected recipe, scaled to the chosen servings, to the chosen list. The service enforces permissions, validates arguments, and makes retries safe. Both paths show the committed result in the list, including what was added or merged, with undo; ambiguous targets require clarification, and destructive changes require confirmation. Maintain a parity matrix for recipe, list, and cook-session capabilities, including navigation or timer actions that must hand off to the active device. That means parity of permitted outcomes, not simulated taps or authority to bypass consent. CopilotKit could help with chat or streaming, A2UI with bounded generated cards, and MCP Apps with embedding in another host; none is required for parity. I’d ship fixed, approved UI first.

For company-wide coding agents, make the approved path the easiest: versioned packages, a machine-readable component catalog and examples, import and token rules in CI, and design-system owner review for new primitives and exceptions. Require human sign-off on new interaction patterns; agent-generated code goes through the same checks as anyone else’s.
decision.showItsGood: Start with one end-to-end slice: open a recipe, add ingredients for four to a shared list, then start cook mode and recover a timer after an interruption. Run Playwright plus axe on web, XCTest and Compose UI tests on phones, and contract tests that drive both the button and assistant and compare persisted state. Cover retries, concurrent list edits, denied access, offline/reconnect, and a lock or app switch mid-timer; don’t promise background alerts on browsers where we can’t verify delivery. Audit complete web flows against WCAG 2.2 AA and manually check keyboard focus, zoom and reflow, NVDA, VoiceOver, TalkBack, large text, and whether list updates and timer status are announced without stealing focus. Then observe home cooks, including people who use assistive tech, doing the tasks one-handed with messy hands and kitchen noise. Give cook mode big, spaced Next/Back and timer controls; voice is optional, never the only route. Compare manual and assisted paths on unprompted completion, wrong-list writes, accidental taps, time to recover, and whether people can say what changed and undo it. Inspect the failures, retest the fixes, and block rollout on critical accessibility or state-integrity defects. These are proposed checks, not results from an app I’ve run.
decision.unsure: I don’t know the company’s current design system, native staffing, or whether public recipe discovery is a major acquisition channel. I’d confirm those before committing to three clients. I’d prototype cook mode on older phones and mobile Safari first: timer delivery under lock/background, resuming after process loss, and whether optional voice commands work well enough in a noisy kitchen. If staffing favors one phone codebase, Tamagui is worth a mobile spike, with the same device and accessibility acceptance tests.

decision.primaryPick: React Aria Components, behind the company’s shared design-system package
pairings: TypeScript and PostgreSQL for a versioned work-state service
Model Context Protocol (MCP) for a curated agent tool surface
decision.why:
I’d build this as a work-state service with two clients: a typed tool interface agents use all day, and a review console people can trust when they need to intervene. Neither chat history nor a desktop window is the source of truth. Agents claim tasks, checkpoint progress, and submit structured handoffs through scoped commands. A handoff carries the objective, current revision, artifact and test links, unresolved questions, and the next requested decision. Both clients read the same durable state. Use expiring claims, revision checks, and idempotent writes so a restarted agent or a late retry doesn’t overwrite someone’s work.

Builder.io’s Agent-Native is the closest architectural fit: its docs describe shared actions, approval controls, and audit records. I’d borrow that pattern rather than make its full runtime a dependency. Its documented exposure defaults are more permissive than I’d want for this product. I’d start with a small, explicit allowlist at the server and keep the steering policy there, not in MCP metadata or the UI. Agents can update their own work and request review; only authorized humans can approve a handoff, change its scope, or cancel it. Bind a decision to the exact revision and scope, and record the actor, decision, and result. If the artifact changes, it needs another review. Distinguish ‘pause requested’ from ‘paused’ so the UI never implies a worker has stopped before it acknowledges the request.

For people, start with a review inbox and a stable task detail view: what changed, what evidence supports it, what is still uncertain, and what decision is needed. Use the same DOM UI in the browser and a thin Electron shell, with sandboxing, context isolation, no Node access in the renderer, and no shell execution from the review app. React Aria provides unstyled behavior for interactive tables and dialogs without replacing the company’s visual language; if the approved library is already Fluent UI or another suitable system, reuse it. Electron’s bundled Chromium is a trade I’d make for a more consistent desktop renderer, assuming the company can patch it promptly; Tauri using system webviews is worth comparing if footprint is decisive. I wouldn’t put A2UI or json-render in the approval path: an agent can supply evidence, but it shouldn’t decide what the reviewer sees or where the controls go.

Publish the approved components, tokens, review patterns, and tool schemas with working examples for coding agents. Enforce package boundaries in CI and require design-system and accessibility owner review for new interaction patterns, plus policy-owner review when a tool gains a permission.
decision.showItsGood:
Run one slice all the way through: Agent A checkpoints and disconnects; Agent B picks up the task; a reviewer opens the evidence, requests a change, and verifies that the next revision is the one awaiting review. In CI, replay duplicate and out-of-order events, competing claims, stale approvals, and rejected cross-workspace calls against the real service. Assert the resulting state and audit entries, not just HTTP success. Verify that pending steering stays visible while a worker is offline and that reconnect never silently drops a decision.

Run Playwright and axe on the web and smoke-test the packaged desktop app on supported OSes. Manually audit the full review flow against WCAG 2.2 AA on web and test keyboard, NVDA, VoiceOver, zoom, and high contrast on the relevant platforms. In particular, stream updates while someone reads a diff: selection, scroll position, and focus should stay put, and assistive tech should announce actionable changes rather than every log event.

Observe reviewers, including screen-reader users and people new to the project, working through a realistic queue without coaching. Include a convincing summary with missing evidence and a revision that changes during review.
