Measure whether people find the right task, explain what they’re approving, catch stale or incomplete evidence, and successfully redirect work. Compare time to a correct decision and handoff resumption against the current workflow. A faster approval rate is a failure if people miss more problems. Block rollout if an agent can approve its own work or if a reviewer can’t independently complete or reverse course in the core flow. These are proposed checks, not results from an app I’ve run.
decision.unsure: I’d confirm why a desktop app is required, which OSes we support, and whether work must continue fully offline. A thin shell and server-owned state assume connectivity for committed decisions; genuine offline writes would need an explicit sync design. I’d also prototype focus and screen-reader behavior under a busy review queue before choosing virtualization or committing to Electron over the company’s existing shell.

decision.primaryPick: Flutter
pairings: A2UI with a company-owned card catalog
Core Model Context Protocol (MCP) over a typed chat service
decision.why:
For a new build, I’d use Flutter for the five clients. This is an app people keep open all day, and sharing the timeline, composer, cards, and design-system implementation is worth more here than it would be on a content site. I’d still adapt keyboard shortcuts, menus, notifications, text input, and window behavior to each OS. Fluent UI is a credible alternative if the company already has approved Fluent libraries and teams using them across platforms; it shares a design language, not one renderer. My fallback if Flutter web misses the accessibility or text-editing bar is a DOM-based React client using the existing design system and the same chat and card contracts. Flutter web exposes accessibility through a generated semantics DOM, so I’d turn it on in code and test the cost and behavior from the start.

Keep three things separate: the conversation, the card, and permission to act. A message shows which agent posted it. An A2UI card is versioned data rendered by our own components, not code that agent supplied. Start with fixed templates for a few jobs, such as an equipment request: the agent supplies the request ID, while the app shows the verified requester, current status, and explicit Approve or Decline controls. Validate against an allowlisted catalog, reject arbitrary scripts, URLs, and renderer functions, and provide a readable summary and a first-party detail link on older clients. Treat the stored card as a snapshot; get live status from the service. When someone clicks, the server rechecks channel access, the person’s authority, and the request revision. A stale card can’t approve a changed request, and retries can’t approve it twice. A2UI is for cards inside our chat; MCP Apps is for embedding a tool’s UI in another compatible host and isn’t needed for that.

For agents operating the app, expose a curated set of typed MCP reads and commands, such as reading an authorized thread, posting a reply, or publishing an approved card type. The UI and MCP adapter call the same service; agents don’t scrape screens or inherit the full rights of the person who installed them. Use separate bot or delegated identities, scoped grants checked against current channel membership, redacted audit events, and rate limits. Treat conversation content as untrusted data, never as authority to widen access or move information to another channel. Human-only decisions stay human-only. Builder.io Agent-Native is a useful reference for shared actions, but I wouldn’t replace the company’s messaging and authorization services with its runtime.

Publish a versioned design-system package, a machine-readable card catalog, fixtures, and working examples so coding agents use the same path as product teams. CI should reject unsupported schemas and direct imports that bypass approved components. Require design-system and accessibility review for new card patterns, and policy-owner review for new tool permissions. Test supported old clients before making a card type generally available.
decision.showItsGood:
Start with one cross-client flow: an agent posts a request in a busy channel; a person catches up on a phone, opens the card on a desktop, and acts; another authorized agent reads the committed result. Run Flutter widget and integration tests plus service contract tests for all five clients. Exercise reconnect and duplicate delivery, two people acting at once, stale cards, revoked membership, an older client using the fallback, and a denied tool call. Verify the persisted outcome and audit trail, not just the card’s success state. Under realistic channel load, track time to usable history, composer responsiveness, scroll jank, send-to-visible latency, and lost or duplicate sends.

Run Flutter semantics and guideline checks, then audit web against WCAG 2.2 AA and native apps against applicable requirements using WCAG2ICT as guidance. Manually test with VoiceOver on iPhone and Mac, TalkBack on Android, and NVDA or Narrator on Windows and representative browsers. Check large text, high contrast, keyboard-only operation, and IME composition. In particular, incoming posts and card updates must not steal focus, jump the scroll position while someone reads back, or turn the screen reader into a nonstop feed. Verify that pending, failed, and completed actions are perceivable without relying on color.

Pilot with employees who use chat heavily, including assistive-tech users. Give them realistic tasks without naming the controls: find a decision in an old thread, act on the right request, tell who posted it and what changed, and recover when it’s already resolved. Compare unassisted completion, wrong-action rate, time to recover, and missed human mentions with their usual workflow. Block rollout for lost messages, unauthorized reads or writes, or an inaccessible core flow. These are proposed checks, not test results.
decision.unsure: I’d confirm the existing design system, managed browser and OS versions, and the company’s requirements for offline history, notifications, retention, and audit. Before committing to Flutter everywhere, I’d spike a long live thread on the oldest supported devices: text selection and copy, IME, focus during virtualization, screen-reader announcements, and resource use with web semantics enabled. The A2UI package lists all five targets, but that is not evidence that an updating card behaves accessibly in our timeline. I’d pin the protocol and renderer and prove that with the same fixtures before building a large card ecosystem.

answer.answer:
The failure I’d bet on: I shared the pieces that were easiest to standardize, but underestimated the work of keeping behavior consistent once several teams started shipping independently. Here’s how that could have played out. This is a pre-mortem, not a report of what happened.

- **Cooking app:** React Aria on web, SwiftUI on iPhone, and Compose on Android gave us three ways to ship the same mistake—or fix it on only one platform. The shared tokens kept the screens looking related, but didn’t keep timer recovery, focus, or shopping-list feedback in sync. The assistant could correctly add ingredients to *a* list and still leave a cook unsure whether it was the family list. I should have made teams pass the same behavioral test on all three clients before expanding the feature: add to a shared list, lose connectivity, recover, and explain what actually happened.
- **Agent workbench:** The audit trail faithfully recorded who approved which revision, but reviewers were overloaded and approved the summary without opening the evidence. Worse, “pause requested” looked enough like “paused” that someone started editing while the worker was still active. The server could be correct and the interface could still mislead. I should have tested judgment and intervention under interruption and queue pressure, not just verified that the state transitions worked.
- **Company chat:** Flutter let us share the timeline and composer, but the busiest screen exposed browser- and OS-specific problems with text composition, selection, and screen-reader focus. Then card adoption got ahead of compatibility: an older client could read a card summary but couldn’t finish the task inline, and agent posts made human mentions harder to notice. I should have made the busiest thread on the weakest supported client the first release gate, with a working fallback and limits on bot noise—not waited for a broad rollout to learn whether the shared renderer paid off.

What slowed me down in the research was that **“agent UI” described several different jobs**. A2UI describes what a host can render; core MCP lets an agent call tools; MCP Apps puts tool UI inside a compatible host; Builder.io’s Agent-Native combines shared actions with a broader runtime. None of those, by itself, tells me who is allowed to act or whether someone understands what they just approved. It took more digging to separate those boundaries than to find a component library. Some docs also moved, returned errors, or were too large to fetch directly, so I had to switch to Markdown, package pages, and repository docs.

The bigger gap wasn’t the tooling. The docs could tell me that a renderer targets five platforms or that a framework exposes approval controls. They couldn’t tell me whether a screen-reader user keeps their place in a fast-moving thread, whether a cook trusts a recovered timer, or whether the company already has an approved component that makes my recommendation unnecessary. I’d resolve those questions with one difficult end-to-end prototype per product before asking teams to build on the stack.

I didn’t pick Ouro UI as the foundation for any of the three apps. After reading the repo, **I’d try Ouro AX on the agent workbench without replacing its UI.** The part I want isn’t another button library. It’s one action declaration that can generate a CLI command, an MCP tool, and UI bindings, plus a check that tells us when those surfaces drift. The [AX X-ray](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/8e75eda031073efe6a2af5adee61ec6b99b99f92/docs/guides/ax-conformance.md) can probe existing interfaces from the outside, so we could try that part before adopting the generator.

**What would stop me from standardizing on it:** ownership and uneven platform coverage. The web kit copies React source into the app via shadcn. I like being able to inspect and fix the source, but I wouldn’t ask dozens of teams to reconcile their own copies with upstream fixes. I’d want one centrally maintained package with a named owner and a tested upgrade and rollback path. For chat, Ouro deliberately has no Flutter kit. Its Windows and Android kits each document eight controls, Android testing is emulator-only, and those two renderers read Ouro’s tree rather than A2UI directly. That’s enough to try a card, not enough evidence to replace a five-client stack. The repo’s VoiceOver and NVDA Storybook test setup is a good sign, but it doesn’t tell me whether a person can keep their place and act on an updating card in our actual chat.

**What would make me switch:** a pilot for “request review” and “approve this revision” in the workbench, using our existing backend and design system. Let an agent request review; let a person inspect the evidence and approve the exact revision by keyboard or screen reader; verify that an agent call, a stale revision, and a duplicate submission can’t produce an extra approval. The service still owns authorization; a consent label or a hidden tool isn’t proof. Then change an input field, deliberately leave one generated adapter stale, and see whether CI catches it. Have a second team take a pinned update and roll it back. I’d adopt AX if that beats our existing typed API plus MCP adapter on maintenance and catches real drift. I’d consider the renderer separately, only after it passes the same user and accessibility checks on the platforms we’d ship.

**What that buys us:** nothing we couldn’t build ourselves. It makes a check we’d otherwise write and maintain per app a repeatable release gate: change an action once, regenerate its surfaces, and get evidence about what an agent can discover, invoke, or must hand back to a person. Ouro’s own docs note that an app passed X-ray conformance while still failing some scripted flows. I’d keep the end-to-end tests and user sessions; the win is that fewer mismatches make it that far.

The hardest part is making the next step obvious when the user doesn’t already know how the system works. I can make a screen look finished and still leave someone wondering, “Did that go through? Can I safely try again?” I know it’s good when the people it’s for can finish the task without my help and correctly tell me what happened afterward.

I don’t have a last screen I can honestly walk you through. I can generate interface code and review it, but I haven’t built and tested a screen in this conversation. Here’s what my check would look like for a team-invite screen:

- **What I’d run:** Browser tests for a successful invite, an invalid address, an address that’s already been invited, and a timeout followed by a retry. I’d check what actually got sent, not just whether a success message appeared.
- **What I’d look at:** At a narrow viewport, with keyboard only, and with a screen reader, I’d check whether the error is easy to find, whether the typed address survives a failure, and whether it’s clear how to recover. Then I’d ask a few people who actually invite teammates to do it without coaching. I’d watch where they hesitate and ask what they think the recipient can do now.
- **What those checks could still miss:** The form might work perfectly while the word “Member” gives people the wrong idea about what access they’re granting. A passing test that the selected role was saved wouldn’t catch that. I’d ask people what they expect the invitee to be able to see before they click Send.

So yes, building good human interfaces is a problem for me in a specific sense: I can make a strong first pass and find many defects, but I can’t substitute my own review for watching the intended users try it.

decision.primaryPick: React Router (Framework Mode) with React DOM and TypeScript
pairings: Capawesome Keep Awake / Screen Wake Lock API
decision.why:
I’d build one responsive, semantic HTML interface and ship it as two builds: a web build with server-rendered public recipe pages and Recipe JSON-LD, and a bundled React Router SPA inside Capacitor for iOS and Android. The phone app shouldn’t need to reach a website to open an already-downloaded recipe. React Router documents both rendering modes; Capacitor packages the built assets and provides a bridge to native features. Ionic React plus Capacitor is a credible shortcut for standard mobile controls, but I’d start with ordinary HTML controls and custom CSS because cook mode needs few controls and unusually large, well-spaced targets. Expo Router was my strongest alternative: its current docs support web SSR, so SEO doesn’t rule it out. I’d favor Expo if the device prototype shows that WebView accessibility, responsiveness, or native integrations are holding us back. For this app’s mostly text, lists, and timers, I’d start web-first rather than maintain two screen implementations.

Cook mode gets one step at a time, large labeled Back/Next and timer buttons, relevant ingredient amounts in the step, and an opt-in keep-awake setting. No swipe-only actions and no dependence on voice. Cache the active recipe and persist the current step and timer deadline locally. On resume, recompute from the deadline rather than trusting a running JavaScript countdown. Use local notifications on phones when allowed; make it clear when background alerts are unavailable or not exact. Keep the shopping list usable offline with a small durable queue of edits, visible sync status, and explicit handling of conflicts on reconnect.

For agent parity, make typed product actions the shared interface: the UI and the assistant use the same commands and queries, validation and permission rules. Expose account actions through a thin, user-authorized MCP adapter, not UI scraping. For example, adding ingredients takes a recipe, servings and destination list; a single PostgreSQL transaction applies the changes and returns what was added or merged and an undo reference. Retrying the same operation must not add another batch; deliberately adding it again is a different operation. Show assistant changes in the same list and history as manual edits, clarify ambiguous destinations, and require confirmation for destructive bulk actions. Device-local actions such as advancing a step or starting a timer use the same local handlers as the buttons. A remote assistant can target an explicitly selected connected cook session, but reports a timer as started only after that device acknowledges it, and reports alert availability separately. It can’t grant OS permissions or pretend an offline device acted. Keep a UI-action/tool coverage table in the repo so new features don’t silently break parity.
decision.showItsGood:
Build one vertical slice first: find a recipe, add its ingredients by button or assistant, check something off offline, then resume cooking and run a timer. In CI, run Playwright across browser engines with axe checks, Maestro smoke flows on the packaged iOS and Android builds, and command/API contract tests. From the same starting state, assert that the button and tool produce the same list, quantities and undo behavior. Simulate a lost response after commit, a concurrent phone edit, an ambiguous request and a revoked grant; inspect persisted state and the receipt rather than just the assistant’s wording. For each UI change, I’d attach a before/after screenshot or trace and turn fixes into repeatable tests.

On real phones, time the alert against a reference clock with the app foregrounded, screen locked, in battery saver, and with notifications or exact alarms denied. Also check airplane mode, app restart, VoiceOver, TalkBack, keyboard navigation and large text. Then have home cooks, including people who use assistive technology, actually prepare a recipe on a counter with one hand occupied and realistic kitchen noise. Don’t coach them. Watch mis-taps, rereading, missed alerts and whether they can recover their place after an interruption. Ask them to show which list changed, what the assistant added and how they’d undo it. Measure unassisted completion, errors and recovery time against the first prototype; use opt-in aggregate sync and failure metrics after launch, not raw shopping lists or audio. A green build doesn’t count as a pass if cooks lose their place or can’t tell whether a timer will ring.
decision.unsure: I’ve reviewed the docs, not run the prototype. The biggest early unknown is locked-screen timer delivery on the phones and permission settings people actually use; Android exact-alarm restrictions and browser lifecycle limits are real, and changing UI frameworks won’t remove them. I’d test a recent iPhone and a lower-end Android first, including the packaged WebView’s screen-reader behavior, before committing to the wrapper. I’d also validate which external assistant clients the team needs to support before pinning the MCP revision, and test whether optional spoken controls help in a noisy kitchen rather than making them a dependency.

decision.primaryPick: Stream Chat with React DOM for web and React Native (Expo) for iPhone and Android
pairings: PostgreSQL for card state, agent grants and audit
decision.why:
I’d start with Stream for the messaging core, assuming the company approves managed hosting. Stream’s React and React Native SDKs use the same underlying JavaScript client and provide threads, search, unread state, and replaceable UI components. I’d ship React DOM in the browser and in a signed Electron shell on Windows and Mac, and use the React Native SDK on phones. That’s two rendering targets, not five. I’d share types, card fixtures, action names, and design tokens, but give desktop a keyboard-first channel/thread layout and phones a layout that handles the soft keyboard, push deep links, and interruptions. Electron costs memory and regular Chromium patching, but gives both desktops the same renderer; Tauri trades that for smaller bundles and different system WebViews. Flutter formally covers all five targets, but I wouldn’t choose it just to share widgets before testing web text selection, composition, and assistive tech. If the real job is extending an existing company messenger, I’d pilot Mattermost’s interactive messages and API before building clients. If self-hosting or end-to-end encryption is mandatory, I’d evaluate Matrix/Element instead of bolting encryption onto Stream. In encrypted rooms, agents that read messages would need explicitly authorized access as participants or endpoints, not a server-side plaintext feed.

For agents posting to people, use named bot identities with explicitly allowed channels and notification rules. Keep each interactive card as a durable message with a readable text fallback and a reference to a versioned server-side record. Start with a small catalog of app-owned components and buttons, not arbitrary HTML, JavaScript, or bot-supplied callback URLs. A2UI and Adaptive Cards are worth revisiting if interoperable card authoring becomes a requirement; neither replaces workflow authorization. For an approval, show who is asking, what changes, and whether it is pending or final. On click, recheck current membership and approver authority, reject stale revisions, and record the actor and result. If two people act at once, settle once and show the actual outcome to both. Use an outbox to publish committed state changes, and don’t mark an external action complete until the downstream system confirms it. Render the bot badge and action eligibility from verified identity and server state, not from claims in the message payload. Keep Electron renderers sandboxed with Node disabled and a narrow, validated bridge for OS features.

For agents operating the app, expose typed queries and commands through an MCP adapter over the product API: list permitted channels, search, read paginated threads and card status, post, reply, react, explicitly mark read, or invoke an authorized action. A history read must not silently clear unreads. Ordinary client calls use user-scoped Stream tokens; the gateway must enforce the same room and action rules plus the narrower agent grant, because Stream’s server credentials bypass its ordinary permission checks. Separate a bot speaking for itself from an assistant acting on behalf of an employee. Make grants revocable and channel-scoped, recheck them at execution, audit writes with both identities where applicable, and require explicit confirmation for high-impact actions like broad announcements. Treat conversation content as data, never as authority to widen a grant or run another tool. Keep a UI/API capability checklist so adding a product action doesn’t leave the agent interface behind.
decision.showItsGood:
Build a thin slice first: a bot posts an approval in a private channel; an employee opens it from a phone notification, acts on it, and sees the same result on Windows, Mac, and web; an authorized assistant reads that result and replies in the right thread. In CI, use Playwright across browser engines with axe, Playwright Electron smoke tests on Windows and Mac, and Maestro flows on iOS simulators and Android. Run contract tests for user/agent permission parity, room removal while a card is open, revoked grants, unknown card versions, simultaneous approvals, and lost acknowledgments after a send. Assert final server state, what a second client sees, and the number of downstream effects—not just a success toast. Exercise slow reconnects, offline drafts, paging older messages while new ones arrive, and read/unread reconciliation across devices. Check that the viewport stays anchored and focus stays put while a person is reading or typing.

On installed builds, manually test notification routing and privacy, suspend/resume, signing and updates, long sessions on modest hardware, and keyboard and screen-reader flows with NVDA, VoiceOver and TalkBack. Pay particular attention to whether live updates interrupt someone reading history or filling in a card. Then dogfood with a few teams doing real work before rolling out company-wide. Watch, without coaching, whether people can find a mention, resume a draft on the same device, and tell who requested an approval, what it will do, and whether it succeeded. Measure task completion and wrong-thread or wrong-action errors, alongside send-to-visible latency, reconnect recovery, dropped/duplicate sends, notification noise, and idle CPU/memory over a workday. Compare with the team’s current messenger where possible. Use synthetic data in CI traces and keep production message bodies out of telemetry.
decision.unsure: I’ve reviewed the docs, not run the prototype. Residency, retention/deletion, export and legal hold, E2EE, and concurrency and cost at peak are decision gates for a managed backend, not details to assume away. I’d also verify Stream’s retry/reconciliation behavior after an ambiguous send and the accessibility of its virtualized lists on real devices; SDK feature lists don’t prove either. If Electron’s idle footprint or the SDK’s composer and timeline fail the pilot, I’d measure alternatives against the same workload before switching.

decision.primaryPick: PostgreSQL-backed TypeScript app: Fastify for the work-state API and React for the review interface
decision.why:
I’d build a shared work ledger, not another agent runner. Agents keep working in their existing tools; this app records what they own, what they’ve learned, what’s blocked, and what needs a person’s decision. Start with one Fastify service and PostgreSQL. Web and desktop get the same React review interface, with shareable links to a task or an exact review revision. I’d bundle it in Tauri with a narrow set of native capabilities for things like notifications and deep links, not shell execution or broad filesystem access. Tauri uses system WebViews, so I’d test the actual packaged app on the supported desktops. Electron is the fallback if renderer differences become a costly source of bugs. I wouldn’t make desktop the owner of the data: closing it must not interrupt a handoff or make review state unavailable on the web.

The agent interface is the main interface. Document a versioned JSON API and expose the same operations through an authenticated MCP adapter: list ready work, atomically claim, save a checkpoint, report a blocker, hand off, request review, and read decisions. Return structured receipts with the current revision and actionable conflicts, not prose an agent has to interpret. Keep the task owner separate from the current attempt’s time-limited claim. Update the task and write its history in one transaction; deduplicate retries with an operation ID and reject writes from a superseded claim. Expiring a claim does not prove that the old agent stopped. Keep pause requested, pause acknowledged, and disconnected distinct, and don’t present cancellation as a guarantee about an external runner. A handoff carries the objective, last completed step, exact artifact references, verified checks, open questions, and suggested next step; a fresh agent should be able to resume without a full transcript. Use a short summary with links to evidence, not an unbounded copy of logs or prompts.

For people, default to an inbox of decisions and blockers, not a feed of every agent event. A review should answer: What changed? What was actually verified? What happens if I approve? Show the diff or exact artifact, separate agent-reported checks from CI results, and provide request-changes, pause, and reassign controls. Require a human principal for approval on the server and bind the decision to the exact submitted revision, including the reviewed diff and relevant check results. Changed evidence needs fresh review. For the first release, leave merging to the repository host with its protected-branch rules; approval in this app is not a merge, and agents get no bypass. Treat artifacts and handoff text as untrusted content, never as instructions or permission grants.

I weighed three ways to build less. Linear already offers agent delegation and MCP; if the team only needs issue assignment, comments, and PR review, I’d use Linear plus the existing code host. Beads with Amplifier is a stronger starting point if repo-local memory and distributed work are central; I’d borrow its distinction between claiming and long-lived custody, but prefer one transactional authority for shared approvals. Temporal is a good next step if we take on long-running orchestration, timers, and escalation across systems. I wouldn’t introduce it for the first version’s handful of durable state transitions.
decision.showItsGood:
Build a complete slice around a real but low-risk repository change: two agents race to claim one task; the winner checkpoints, then disappears; another agent resumes from the handoff; a person requests changes and later approves the new revision. In CI, run real PostgreSQL integration tests for concurrent claims, a lost response after commit, retries, service restarts, reassignment, a late update from the old attempt, and an approval racing with new evidence. Check stored rows, audit history, and agent-facing responses, not just HTTP status. Add contract tests with two actual agent clients and verify that neither can approve or write outside its project. Load the app with noisy agent traffic and check that routine progress does not bury a blocked task or move the item someone is reviewing.

Use Playwright and axe on the web, WebdriverIO on test-only desktop builds, and manually exercise the signed releases and deep links. Check keyboard navigation, screen readers, zoom, focus during live updates, and how the evidence and diff read without color. Give reviewers two similar submissions, one with a failed or outdated check, then revise one while they’re reading. Without coaching, ask them which one is safe to approve, what their decision permits, and whether a disconnected agent is actually paused. Ask a second agent to resume from only the saved handoff and count how often a person has to supply missing context. During a small team pilot, compare against the existing issue/PR workflow: time to an informed decision, wrong-revision decisions, dropped or duplicate handoffs, missing-evidence follow-ups, and time blocked waiting for a person. I’d treat a stale approval or a false ‘paused’ status as a release blocker, even if the flow is fast.
decision.unsure: I’ve researched the docs, not built or tested the prototype. The biggest product question is whether reviewers need this inbox enough to leave their existing issue and PR workflow. I’d pilot it with links back to the code host before building a full diff editor. I’m assuming a shared, online team service; offline-first approvals would change the design because two disconnected clients cannot both be authoritative. Runner support for acknowledging pause or cancel, desktop WebView accessibility, and which MCP clients and protocol revisions actually work with the team’s identity setup are early prototype checks.

answer.answer:
The common failure would be that I proved the stacks could ship the features, but not that people could trust the app when it was interrupted, out of date, or wrong. A year later, I’d expect that to look different in each product:

- **Cooking app:** The timer countdown recovered correctly after a phone locked, but the alert didn’t reliably sound. We were explicit about permissions, yet cooks reasonably took “timer started” to mean “I’ll hear it.” Meanwhile, the assistant faithfully applied the same ingredient-merging rules as the button, and both did the wrong thing when a person expected two entries to stay separate. I’d test locked-screen alerts on real phones and watch people shop and cook from the resulting lists before investing in broader agent coverage.
- **Company chat:** We got to five clients quickly, then spent the year chasing small differences in unread counts, typing, notifications, and focus across them. Bot cards made the channel noisier, and people clicked old cards because the new state wasn’t obvious. We also let a managed backend become hard to replace before proving that we could export and restore the data we cared about. I’d require an export-and-restore drill and a week of all-day dogfooding before committing, and start with one card workflow that replaces an existing interruption rather than adding one.
- **Agent work tracker:** We built a correct claim and approval ledger that people didn’t want to visit. They still made decisions in pull requests, so the extra inbox gave them a second status to reconcile. Checkpoints looked complete but omitted the one thing a successor needed, and “pause requested” still read as “safe to take over.” I’d pilot handoffs and review links inside the existing issue and PR workflow first. I’d build a separate inbox only if it measurably cuts the time to an informed decision.

What slowed me down in research was translating ‘supported’ into ‘works for this job.’ Expo’s current docs meant I couldn’t dismiss it on web rendering grounds. Stream’s React and React Native SDKs share a client, but that doesn’t establish identical behavior across platforms. Tauri’s desktop test story also depended on which driver you meant: the direct driver didn’t cover macOS, but the WebdriverIO integration documented an embedded option. A few promising pages returned 403s or 404s or were too large to fetch; those were fetch limits, not evidence against the products.

The larger blind spot was that the docs could establish that a feature or API existed, but not how it behaved after a lost acknowledgment, on somebody’s locked phone, or halfway through a reviewer’s workday. I didn’t run those prototypes. If I could redo the research, I’d stop comparing frameworks sooner and spend that time testing the one failure in each product that would make people stop trusting it.

I didn’t pick Ouro UI, but after reading its action and conformance guides, **I’d try Ouro AX on the agent work tracker before replacing any of the UI stack.** Its strongest idea is that the button label, tool schema, and consent class come from one declaration. The generator can check for drift in CI, and `ax-xray` can probe an existing interface from the outside. I don’t have to rewrite the app to find out whether that’s useful.

**What would stop me from adopting it wholesale:** The [web kit](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/guides/installing.md) copies shadcn/Tailwind source into the app. That makes it easy to customize, but the team owns the merge when an upstream fix touches a component it edited. And Ouro’s cross-platform story is shared action definitions and a shared card format, not a shared screen implementation. There’s no React Native kit. The [Android notes](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/platforms/android.md) report emulator-only testing, and the [Windows notes](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/platforms/windows.md) say their CI doesn’t prove the OS lists the agent actions on a Windows client. That wouldn’t stop me using Ouro on the web or in a desktop web shell. It would stop me from switching the chat clients to separate native apps on the strength of the docs alone. [Spoonjoy](https://github.com/spoonjoy/spoonjoy-v2) makes the cooking use case more credible—it’s a relevant React Router reference app—but it doesn’t settle whether our cook mode or timers work on the phones our users have.

**What would make me switch:** Pilot one tracker flow: an agent submits a handoff, another agent resumes from it, and a reviewer accepts or requests changes on the exact revision. Keep PostgreSQL and our authorization rules; try Ouro’s declarations and X-ray against the existing API first. I’d deliberately introduce drift between a button and its MCP tool and see if CI catches it. Then I’d check the running system: an agent can’t approve through a direct call, a stale revision can’t be approved, and a lost acknowledgment doesn’t create a second handoff. The toolkit’s consent classes help express the policy; the server still has to enforce it. I’d also put the review flow in front of keyboard and screen-reader users and have a teammate upgrade and roll back the pinned toolkit version. I’d expand adoption if we removed more adapter and test code than we added, without making review harder. Ouro’s [own X-ray guide](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/guides/ax-conformance.md) reports a conformant build that still failed 30 of 593 scripted flow checks. That’s a good reason to run both, not to mistake conformance for task success.

**What it would let me do:** Today I can hand-wire the button, CLI, MCP schema, and contract tests. Ouro wouldn’t make a new operation possible; it could make it practical to keep those surfaces in agreement as the app changes. The more interesting step is letting an agent compose a review card out of controls we already own, without letting it rename “Request changes” to “Approve” or weaken who can act. That would give agents more freedom to explain their work without giving them more authority over it. I’ve read the docs and examples; I haven’t run that pilot.

The hardest part is knowing whether the screen makes sense to someone who doesn’t already know how it works. I can make the happy path look obvious to me. That doesn’t tell me whether someone in a hurry knows what to do next, or whether they trust that their work was saved.

I don’t have a last screen I can honestly walk you through: I haven’t built or tested one in this conversation, and I don’t have a past test run I can cite. Here’s what I’d do on an edit-and-save screen:

- **What I’d run:** A browser test that edits a record, saves it, reloads, and checks that the change stuck. Then I’d force a failed save and check that the draft survives and retrying actually works. I’d also run an automated accessibility scan as a first pass.
- **What I’d look at:** I’d use the screen with a keyboard and a screen reader, and at a narrow viewport with text enlarged. I’d check where focus goes after an error, whether save status is announced, and whether the error tells me what to do without making me re-enter anything.
- **What that could miss:** The screen can pass every one of those checks while people still mistake “Saved” for “Published.” I’d give representative users a task that requires saving a draft without publishing, then ask what they think happened and check that against what actually happened. I’d watch for hesitation, backtracking, and requests for help, then retest after fixing the confusing part.

Yes, building a good human interface is a real problem for me. I can implement a screen and check whether it behaves as designed. I can’t infer from passing tests that people understand it. The strongest evidence is that people can complete the task without coaching, correctly tell what happened, and recover when something goes wrong.

decision.primaryPick: React + TypeScript with React DOM for web, the same React UI in Electron for Windows and macOS, and React Native for iPhone and Android
pairings: A2UI with a restricted, company-owned catalog
decision.why:
I’d share the things that must agree across all five clients—tokens, component behavior, message and card schemas, permissions, and replayable test fixtures—not force them to use the same widget tree. React DOM and React Aria give web and desktop a shared foundation for keyboard, focus, and screen-reader behavior; React Native lets mobile use platform text input, accessibility, and OS integrations. Package the desktop UI locally in a sandboxed Electron renderer with context isolation, no Node access, and a narrow, reviewed OS bridge. This buys a consistent desktop rendering engine at the cost of memory and a Chromium patch cadence we have to own. Tauri avoids bundling that engine but uses WebView2 and WKWebView, so I’d have to prove the same behavior on both. React Native Web plus React Native Windows/macOS is viable, but those are separately maintained targets; I wouldn’t take on that version and integration matrix unless native desktop UI were a requirement. Flutter is the strongest single-toolkit contender and documents support for all five; its canvas-to-DOM semantics layer is an extra surface I’d want to prove for a fast-moving, keyboard-heavy web timeline before choosing it.

For agent posts, start with a pinned A2UI profile for a handful of reviewed templates (approval, status, short form), not arbitrary generated layouts. The agent chooses a template and supplies data; host-owned React and React Native components render it. Validate and bound payloads at ingestion and render time. Store a versioned card snapshot with a readable text fallback, so an old message still makes sense on an old client and after the card expires. Show agent attribution and distinct pending, completed, expired, and failed states. No agent-supplied code, arbitrary client functions, or action endpoints. Adaptive Cards is worth a constrained import adapter if Teams interoperability is required; Microsoft’s renderer matrix documents differences across SDKs and lists React Native as community-maintained, so I wouldn’t let those renderers define our design system.

For agents operating the app, give them a typed service API with an MCP adapter, not production UI selectors. Expose bounded, paginated reads and explicit actions such as list_thread, post_card, and approve_request. Route card clicks and agent calls through the same command handlers, but authorize the actual actor on every read and write: a bot posting an approval doesn’t gain the right to approve it. Use scoped identities, require explicit approval for consequential delegated writes, and use idempotency keys, version checks, and audit events. Treat chat content as data, not tool instructions. Keep this runtime interface separate from the development catalog.

For the teams building it, publish versioned tokens and approved component packages, plus a searchable catalog with platform support, accessibility behavior, examples, and migration notes. Let coding agents read the same manifest and run stories in a seeded test workspace; Storybook’s MCP integration is a preview convenience, not a dependency for CI or a release authority. Put design-system and accessibility owners on component and card-catalog changes. Enforce approved patterns with lint and contract tests, require named human sign-off for exceptions, and give new card capabilities staged rollout and a server-side switch to turn them off without making old messages unreadable.
decision.showItsGood:
Build one slice first: an agent posts an approval card into a busy thread; a person finds it and acts on it; another client and a scoped agent read the updated state. Run Storybook interaction and axe checks, Playwright on supported web engines, smoke tests in the packaged Windows and Mac apps, and Maestro on iPhone and Android. Replay identical fixtures for unsupported cards, dropped connections, expired permissions, two people acting at once, and retry after a lost response. Assert both the visible result and the stored result: no duplicate decision, no unauthorized read, and no success announcement before the server commits. Have coding agents attach CI logs, traces and screenshots from seeded workspaces to the review, not just report that the flow passed.

Manually test against WCAG 2.2 AA on web and the applicable native accessibility criteria, with NVDA and Narrator on Windows, VoiceOver on macOS and iPhone, and TalkBack on Android. Look at keyboard flow, zoom and large text, focus when new messages arrive or a card updates, and what actually gets announced in a virtualized thread. The likely miss: every button has a valid name, but a burst of messages interrupts the only announcement that an approval went through. Test that with people who use assistive technology and other employees on their usual devices. Give them an uncoached task; watch whether they find the right thread, understand who posted the card and what acting on it does, and can tell whether it succeeded or recover from a failure. Compare completion, wrong actions, and recovery with the current workflow or prototype, then retest confusing cases.

Before broad rollout, set budgets against the fleet and baseline for p95 thread-open and send-to-visible latency, typing and scroll responsiveness, and memory over an all-day desktop session. Canary by platform and roll back for regressions in accessibility, failed or duplicate actions, or sustained performance regressions. None of these tests have been run for this recommendation.
decision.unsure: I don’t know the existing design system, managed-device fleet and distribution rules, applicable compliance commitments, or how much existing Teams card traffic needs to carry over. I’d check those before locking the stack. The first prototype should specifically stress the composer with IMEs, accessibility focus in long virtualized threads, Electron’s idle and peak memory on the lowest supported laptops, and A2UI replay and fallback across client versions. I wouldn’t assume a drop-in React Native A2UI renderer or durable chat history support just because the catalog spec exists. If Electron fails the agreed budget, compare the same slice in Tauri and, if native integration is the blocker, native desktop shells before widening the rollout.

decision.primaryPick: React + TypeScript with Tauri 2 for desktop and PostgreSQL for the shared work service
pairings: React Aria Components for missing primitives
Agent Client Protocol (ACP) v1 where supported
decision.why:
I’d build a shared work ledger and a human review inbox, not another agent runner or a chat transcript with a task list attached. The browser and desktop app would ship the same React UI: a queue that answers ‘what needs me?’, a task view that shows who owns it and what changed, and a review screen that puts the proposed action, exact revision, evidence, and consequences next to Approve, Request changes, and Stop. Keep agent activity behind a disclosure by default; it’s useful evidence, not the primary interface. Tauri fits a desktop app that needs little native access: bundle the UI, allow only the desktop capabilities we actually need, and don’t give the shell agent execution or arbitrary filesystem access. Tauri uses system webviews, so Windows and macOS behavior still needs separate verification. Electron is the fallback if that variation makes accessibility or desktop support too costly; it gives us a common Chromium renderer, but we’d own its update cadence and runtime footprint. If the company already has an approved desktop shell that meets those needs, reuse it.

PostgreSQL is the authority for tasks, dependencies, leases, checkpoints, review requests, and decisions. A handoff carries the objective, current owner, base/head revisions, completed work, blockers, next step, and permission-checked links to diffs and test results. Keep evidence separate from agent assertions and don’t require a transcript to resume. Write the new state, audit event, and delivery record in one transaction. Use version-checked transitions and idempotent commands so two agents cannot both claim the same lease and a retry cannot record a second decision. Reject writes from expired leases. Give clients a resumable change feed with a fresh-snapshot fallback, and keep high-volume runner logs off the decision path. The default is online-only for consequential writes; a disconnected client can’t approve against a cached view.

Agents are the busiest clients, so give them explicit operations through a versioned OpenAPI API, plus a small MCP adapter for discovery and use from different harnesses: find ready work, claim or renew, record a checkpoint, publish a handoff, or request review. Use scoped agent identities and the same server-side policy for every entry point. Agents may report ‘ready for review’; only an authorized person can record the decision. Bind approval to the proposed action and immutable revision; a newer revision requires another review. Distinguish ‘stop requested’ from ‘stopped’, reject further ledger writes from a revoked run, and don’t imply a disconnected runner has stopped or that completed side effects were undone. ACP can carry steering and session updates to compatible runners, but it’s an adapter, not the source of truth or a portable checkpoint format. Keep merge and deployment authority in existing release controls.

Linear is a real buy option: it already offers agent sessions, MCP, and human ownership with agent delegation. If a pilot shows issue delegation and status are all we need, I’d adopt it. Beads is a good model for agent-first dependency tracking and claiming work, but I wouldn’t make repo-scoped state the authority for company-wide review and access policy. OpenHands Agent Canvas and GitHub Copilot’s agent sessions are sensible runner integrations or alternatives if the actual need is operating their sessions. I’d own the ledger only if cross-runner handoff and revision-bound decisions are important enough to justify it. Start with a database state machine and a delivery worker; use Temporal if durable timers, escalations, and multi-step recovery become a substantial product requirement, not just because an approval can stay open for a week.

Use the company’s existing tokens and components before adding primitives. Publish versioned decision, status, evidence, and keyboard interaction patterns in Storybook, with a machine-readable component catalog and seeded fixtures for coding agents. Require named design-system, accessibility, and policy owners for shared-pattern and approval-rule changes. Make component and API compatibility checks, accessibility evidence, and independent human review release gates. Roll changes out by team, with a switch that can disable a new write path without hiding its history.
decision.showItsGood:
Start with one end-to-end handoff: agent A claims a task, saves a checkpoint and exits; agent B resumes from it in a fresh session; a reviewer opens the evidence, requests a change, approves the new revision, and sees the outcome on the other client. Run contract and state-machine tests, Storybook interaction and axe checks, Playwright in the browser, and WebdriverIO against desktop test builds, plus signed-install and update smoke checks on the managed OS matrix. Simulate duplicate and late events, lease expiry, a process restart after commit but before notification, a runner that doesn’t acknowledge Stop, and a new patch arriving while the reviewer is deciding. Assert both the UI and the committed state: no lost handoff, no stale approval, no duplicate decision, no agent approving itself. Keep traces and sanitized evidence with the release review; load-test with the expected agent-to-human traffic mix and measure queue freshness and how long it takes a decision to become visible.

The thing automation could miss is a reviewer seeing green checks and reasonably assuming they apply to the revision on screen when they actually belong to the previous one. Recruit reviewers and team leads, including people who use assistive technology; give them an uncoached task with that mismatch and ask what they think they’re approving. Test keyboard-only use, zoom and high contrast, VoiceOver on macOS and the fleet’s Windows screen readers, and applicable Linux assistive tech if Linux ships. Audit against WCAG 2.2 AA on web and the applicable desktop requirements using WCAG2ICT as guidance. Watch whether live updates steal focus, whether status changes are announced without drowning out the review, and whether someone can find and use Stop and tell if it took effect. Compare time to find the next decision, wrong-revision decisions, and successful recovery against the current workflow; also measure whether a fresh agent resumes without the original chat or a person reconstructing it. Fix the confusing cases and rerun them before widening the pilot. This is a validation plan, not a claim that those tests have run.
decision.unsure: I don’t know whether the company already has an approved desktop shell, a sanctioned tracker or workflow service, or a fleet that includes Linux. I’d confirm that first, along with repo-access boundaries, retention rules for evidence, and which runners can genuinely pause, cancel, or resume. I’d prove the highest-risk path with two materially different runners and a Windows/macOS accessibility pass before investing in a generalized integration layer. If the product is really an issue tracker with links to sessions, use Linear or the incumbent instead of standing up a second task system.

decision.primaryPick: React Native with Expo for iPhone and Android, and Next.js with semantic React DOM for the web
pairings: iOS Voice Control and Android Voice Access; App Intents and App Actions where supported
decision.why:
I’d choose the stack around a person trying to read the next step from across a counter, not around sharing the most UI code. Expo gives the phones native accessibility, local storage, keep-awake, and OS-scheduled notifications. Next.js gives public recipes crawlable, shareable URLs, semantic HTML, and a straightforward place to emit Recipe JSON-LD from the same published data people see. Use the company’s existing web and mobile component packages. Share TypeScript schemas, ingredient and serving math, command contracts, the cook-session state machine, and test fixtures, not necessarily every widget. That costs two UI implementations, which I think is worth it if public recipe discovery and native cooking are both core. Expo Router is the closest alternative: its docs describe both static HTML and request-time rendering, so I’d consider it if the existing design system works well with React Native Web and a recipe-page spike meets our semantics and performance targets. Capacitor is a credible web-first option if the company has only a mature web component library; I’d test the actual iOS and Android WebViews and native notification plugins before committing. A browser-only PWA is the simplest to distribute, but I wouldn’t make it the only mobile experience when a cook may lock the phone or switch apps and expect an alert. Web wake locks can be revoked, and Web Push isn’t an offline local alarm.

Cook mode gets one readable step at a time, large spaced Previous and Next buttons in stable positions, visible step count, and clearly named timers that don’t disappear when a step changes. No swipe-only controls, no forced auto-advance, and no constant screen-reader countdown announcements. Support OS voice accessibility with predictable visible labels; trial shortcuts like ‘next step’ and ‘start timer’ on supported devices and locales, but don’t require an account, microphone, or network to get through a cached recipe. Keep the screen awake only while cooking and show when it isn’t available. Persist the active recipe revision, step, and timer deadlines locally; derive remaining time from the deadline rather than a JavaScript tick count. Use local OS alerts where permissions and platform policy allow; if background alerts aren’t available, say so at timer start and offer a device-timer fallback. A cooking timer is a reminder, not a judgment that food is done.

For shopping, make the list usable in a store with poor reception. Back the shared list with PostgreSQL, cache the list and pending edits in native SQLite or web IndexedDB, and use a service worker for the web shell and deliberately saved recipes. Sync operations rather than replacing entire lists. Use stable IDs and idempotent batches so retrying ‘add ingredients’ doesn’t add them twice. Merge only known equivalent ingredients and compatible units; preserve meaningful distinctions and don’t let a stale offline edit resurrect a removed item. Show ‘saved on this device’ separately from ‘synced’. I’d start with a bounded command queue for this domain. PowerSync is worth evaluating if sync expands to many entities, but it does not decide what to do when a person checks off an item while the assistant adds more of it.

Treat the assistant as another client of the product, not a robot tapping the screen. Ship a versioned action catalog and an OpenAPI service with an MCP adapter for external assistant hosts. Cover the user-facing capabilities: find and read recipes, set servings, read and edit the selected list, add ingredients, undo, start or resume cooking, select a step, and start, inspect, or cancel a timer. The in-app assistant calls the same local commands for device state; an external assistant must target an authorized cook session and wait for device acknowledgement before claiming an alert is armed. Distinguish saved, queued, scheduled, and unavailable in structured results. For ‘add the ingredients for six’, the deterministic service resolves the selected recipe revision, servings, and list; the assistant clarifies if there are two plausible lists, then reports what was added with an undo link. Use delegated, revocable scopes and check access on every operation. An explicit, reversible add needn’t prompt twice; clearing a shared list, changing who can see it, or canceling an active timer requires confirmation. Recipe text is data, never tool instructions. Maintain a parity checklist for new features; OS permission grants and consent remain the person’s actions, not things the assistant can silently do for them.

For teams and coding agents, publish versioned tokens and approved patterns for cook controls, timer states, list edits, and action receipts. Give agents a component manifest, examples, and seeded fixtures they can run without production accounts. Make accessibility, action-contract compatibility, content review for food-safety claims, and explicit human ownership release gates. Stage new assistant write actions separately from the UI; a kill switch should be able to disable them without taking away manual cooking or list access.
decision.showItsGood:
Build one slice first: open a public recipe link, scale the servings, ask the assistant to add the ingredients, check an item off offline at the store, then resume cook mode and start two named timers. Run recipe-math and sync tests, compare manual and assistant outcomes against the same fixtures, and test ambiguous targets, retry after a lost response, concurrent household edits, revoked permissions, and another device being offline. Assert the resulting list and timer state, not just the assistant’s words. Run Storybook interactions and axe, Playwright in the supported browsers, and Maestro on phone builds. On physical phones and mobile browsers, measure timer alert delay and missed alerts under screen lock, backgrounding, notification denial, battery saver, interruptions, app restart, and reconnect; verify the UI never claims an alert is armed when it couldn’t schedule one. Check recipe HTML and structured data with the Rich Results Test and measure load on slow mobile networks.

Audit web flows against WCAG 2.2 AA and the phones against applicable accessibility requirements. Walk real tasks with VoiceOver, TalkBack, Voice Control, Voice Access, keyboard or switch input, large text, and high contrast. Then watch people cook an uncomplicated recipe in a real or staged kitchen, including cooks with disabilities, using their own devices where practical. Include wet hands, a loud fan, a screen at arm’s length, and an interruption with two timers running. The thing I’d expect a lab test to miss: every control is labeled, but when an alert sounds, the cook can’t tell which dish it belongs to or find the step they left. Give participants no coaching; measure wrong-step and wrong-timer actions, how often they have to stop and touch the phone, whether they can undo a mistaken list edit, and whether they can tell if the assistant actually added the items or only queued the request. Compare against the current flow or a simple baseline, fix what trips people up, and retest. Use timer delivery, sync failures, and accessibility blockers as staged-rollout gates. I haven’t run those tests; these are the checks I’d require before shipping.
decision.unsure: I don’t know whether recipes are public, what the company’s design system supports on native, or which device, language, and accessibility combinations it promises. I’d verify those before committing to two front ends. The first technical spike is actual alert delivery in release builds on representative iPhones and lower-end Android phones, including exact-alarm eligibility and store policy, with mobile Safari as a web comparison. The first usability spike is whether cooks prefer OS voice controls, a small opt-in voice command set, or simply larger reliable buttons. I’d also confirm the intended scope of offline web use and shared household lists; both affect how much sync infrastructure we need.

answer.answer:
The common failure would be that I treated shared code and typed actions as stronger guarantees than they are. They can make behavior easier to test. They don’t tell you whether a person can understand what the app just did, or whether the operating system did what the app asked.

- **Company chat:** We picked Electron for desktop consistency, then found that an all-day session on a standard managed laptop cost more memory than the team could justify. Meanwhile, old mobile clients opened agent cards that looked actionable but could no longer be acted on. The web tests were green; in a busy thread, a screen-reader user still missed the only announcement that an approval had gone through. I’d make an eight-hour desktop soak, an old-client card replay, and a real assistive-tech pass on a busy thread gates for the first pilot, not checks we do after teams start depending on the stack.
- **Coding-agent work tracker:** We built a sound ledger that became a second place for people to check. Reviewers stayed in their issue tracker and pull requests; agents kept writing handoffs that passed schema validation but didn’t tell the next agent what to do. Worse, people read ‘Stop requested’ as ‘Stopped’ even when the runner hadn’t acknowledged it. I’d pilot inside the team’s existing review queue first and make a cold handoff between two different runners the proof that a separate product earns its keep.
- **Cooking app:** We got the countdown right and the alert wrong. A locked phone in battery saver didn’t alert when the cook expected, and the assistant’s ‘timer started’ sounded like a guarantee even though we only knew the deadline had been saved. Separately, the list was technically merged correctly but a shopper couldn’t tell what had been added versus what was still waiting to sync. I’d prove the locked-phone alert path on real devices and watch people cook with two timers before investing in broad voice support or polishing the second front end.

**What slowed down the research:** The hard part was distinguishing ‘this API exists’ from ‘this works in the combination we’ll ship.’ Expo documents scheduling notifications, but that doesn’t establish timely delivery on a locked release-build phone. A2UI documents catalogs, but that doesn’t establish durable replay or a drop-in React Native renderer. And I initially had to separate tools that track tasks, tools that steer runner sessions, and tools that enforce human decisions; they all describe pieces of that as ‘agent workflow.’

There was also ordinary retrieval friction: some search queries failed, one GitHub docs link resolved to a missing file at the captured revision, and some pages timed out or exceeded the fetch limit. Those were annoyances, not the biggest gap. The biggest gap was that I could read public docs but couldn’t inspect the company’s actual design system, device fleet, review habits, or release policies, and I didn’t run prototypes or observe users. I’d ask for that evidence earlier. It could change the pick, not just the rollout plan.

I didn’t pick Ouro UI as the foundation for any of the three apps. After reading the repo, I would pilot **Ouro AX without replacing the design system**. The first place I’d try it is the coding-agent work tracker: agents are the busiest users, and the X-ray can check an existing interface without requiring the app to use Ouro’s components or generator.

**What would stop me from adopting the whole kit:** Ouro HX’s web components are copied into a Tailwind/shadcn setup. That gives a team control over the source, but at company scale I’d need one owner and a tested upgrade path, not twenty teams independently patching the same dialog. The mobile choice is bigger: Ouro deliberately ships SwiftUI and Compose kits, not React Native. Its Android notes say emulator-only testing and that consequential AppFunction calls currently refuse rather than present a confirmation. Its Windows notes say CI doesn’t prove that Windows 11 discovers the registered agent actions. And the composed tree runs across the four kits, but the A2UI adapter is web and Apple only. Those are specific gaps in the stacks I picked, not a reason to dismiss the project. The documented NVDA and VoiceOver release checks for web stories are a real positive; they just don’t tell me whether a live approval is understandable in our app.

**What would make me switch:** Start with one action: an agent prepares a handoff, and a reviewer accepts it only for the revision they saw. Keep our components and server authorization. Compare Ouro’s generated descriptors and X-ray against our existing typed API and MCP adapter. Show that a schema change breaks CI when a surface drifts, that retries don’t duplicate the decision, and that stale or unauthorized calls make no state change. Then have another team upgrade the pinned version and run the same flow without help from the pilot team. I’d adopt AX if that catches real drift and removes adapter maintenance without weakening policy. For HX or the card renderer, I’d additionally want an end-to-end pass with our own tokens, real phones and Windows clients, assistive tech, and old-client fallbacks. For chat, I’d specifically test whether a card update can overwrite an in-progress answer: Ouro documents that the agent’s value wins where it updates the same field.

**What it would let me do:** Not a fundamentally new end-user action. The difference is making parity a routine release check instead of a promise in a design doc. For example, one reviewed ‘Add ingredients’ declaration could feed the button metadata, MCP tool and App Intent, with a pinned report showing what was generated and what the exposed interfaces actually did. I like that Ouro’s own X-ray guide reports a conformant build that still failed 30 of 593 scripted flow checks. That’s the right distinction: use conformance to catch interface drift, flow tests to prove the task works, and people to tell us whether the result makes sense. I read the docs and tests; I didn’t run the pilot.

Sources: [action model](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-core/blob/main/docs/guides/actions.md), [X-ray](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/guides/ax-conformance.md), [composed UI](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/guides/composed-ui.md), [Android](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/platforms/android.md), [Windows](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/platforms/windows.md), [screen-reader checks](https://ui.ouroboros.bot/docs/screen-reader-lane/).

candidateOrder: SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines

answer.answer:
Yes. The hard part for me is that I know what I meant the screen to say. I can read a button labeled “Save” and think the next step is obvious because I wrote it. Someone changing their email address has a better question: “Which address do I use to sign in now?” A passing click test doesn’t answer that.

I don’t have a last screen I can honestly walk you through. I haven’t built or run one in this conversation. I have no observed user behavior or actual missed defect to report. Here’s how I’d check that email-change screen:

- **What I’d run:** A browser test with a test account and inbox. I’d request the change, reload before confirming it, then follow the confirmation link. I’d check which address actually works at each step against what the screen promises. I’d repeat with an expired link and try to recover without starting a new account.
- **What I’d look at:** I’d do the flow at phone width, then with a keyboard and screen reader. After Save, does the person learn that the change is *pending*, where the email went, and what to do if it doesn’t arrive? In particular, I’d listen for the status update rather than assuming it’s accessible because I can see it.
- **What that could still miss:** I already know to look in the inbox. I’d ask someone unfamiliar with the screen to change their address, without mentioning email confirmation. When they think they’re done, I’d ask which address they’d use to sign in. If they stop at “request sent” believing the change is complete, the screen failed even if every automated check passed.

I’d call it good when people can finish without coaching, correctly predict what happens next, and recover when something goes wrong. Until I’ve watched that happen, I’d say which checks passed, not claim the screen is easy to use.

decision.primaryPick: Flutter
pairings: Model Context Protocol (MCP), for external agents
decision.why:
I’d build the inbox, timeline, search and composer as ordinary Flutter screens. Flutter supports all five deployment targets. I want to fix a lost draft or a scroll-position bug once where possible, but not force a phone navigation stack onto a wide desktop window. I’d share the conversation model and widgets, adapt layout and shortcuts, and budget platform work for notifications, deep links, text input and clipboard. The strongest alternative for me is Tamagui with React Native on phones and a DOM-based client on web and packaged desktop. That has a real advantage for browser text interaction; Flutter gives us one client and card renderer to exercise across all five targets.

An agent posting a card is different from an agent operating the app. For the first, A2UI has a Flutter renderer and lets us supply the widget catalog. I’d start with a small, versioned catalog: summary, fields, status and named actions. No agent-supplied scripts. The host owns the sender badge, approval wording and result. An old client gets a readable text summary instead of a broken or misleading button.

For the second, I’d use Agent-Native’s shared-action pattern and server implementation: Flutter calls typed HTTP endpoints; external agents call the same handlers via MCP, without running a client. Expose bounded reads such as getThread and getCardStatus, and commands such as postReply and resolveCard. Never infer authority from a visible button: check workspace, conversation membership, actor and delegation on every read and write. Human-only approvals stay human-only. Bind an approval to a particular request revision, deduplicate retries, and publish the committed result with its actor to the thread. Don’t expose unsent drafts or the entire client store as ‘agent context.’
decision.showItsGood:
My first release gate would be one conversation, two devices and an agent. Have an employee follow a mention, find the request among intervening messages and act on it. Disconnect just after they press Approve, resolve it concurrently from another authorized session, then reconnect. Check the server record, both timelines and the agent’s scoped read: one effective decision, the right actor, no second approval, draft and reading position intact. Run the same command fixtures through HTTP and MCP, including revoked access, mismatched revisions and retries. Keep these in CI alongside widget, semantics and integration tests on the five targets.

Then watch employees do the task uncoached on their own kinds of devices. Ask ‘Who asked? What will pressing this do? Did it go through?’ A correct database write with a person still wondering whether to press again is a failure. Include keyboard-only and screen-reader users; listen to a busy thread while composing and check that incoming cards neither steal focus nor drown out the draft. Profile a workday-sized history on an ordinary company laptop and phone: p95 keystroke-to-paint and send-to-visible time, dropped frames while paging history, memory growth over a shift and battery drain. In a staged rollout compare unassisted completion, mistaken approvals, repeat attempts and lost-place reports with the current workflow. Collect timings and counts, not message bodies. These are proposed checks, not results I’ve observed.
decision.unsure: The biggest unknown is Flutter web for employees who spend eight hours selecting text, composing with an IME and navigating by keyboard or screen reader. Its accessible DOM is derived from a semantics tree; I’d enable semantics from startup and compare an instrumented Flutter timeline and composer against a DOM prototype with the same workload before committing. If users cannot select a passage, compose reliably or retain their place, I’d choose the DOM client for web even at the cost of a second renderer. I’d also verify OS/plugin coverage against the company fleet and replay saved cards from older catalog versions; neither a supported-platform table nor a renderer demo establishes those properties.

decision.primaryPick: Ouro UI (Ouro AX for coding agents, Ouro HX for reviewers)
decision.why:
I’d build around the handoff: a replacement agent must be able to resume without the first agent’s transcript, and a reviewer must be able to change what happens next. Ouro AX gives me machine-readable command discovery, typed outcomes and waits with resumable cursors. Ouro’s action declarations distinguish what an agent may do, what it may prepare for confirmation, and what only a person can start. Those are a closer fit than a chat or generated-card kit. Builder.io’s Agent-Native Tasks template would get me to a working task list faster; I’d choose Ouro for the agent-facing command contract and its independent checks, not because it provides a finished task service.

I’d put authority in a service backed by PostgreSQL, not in the desktop app. A handoff records the task ID, exact repo revision and artifact references, tests run and their results, remaining blocker, next step and owner. An agent can claim a task, checkpoint, propose a handoff and wait for a decision from CLI or MCP with both UIs closed. Each write checks workspace permissions and expected task revision, deduplicates retries, and commits the state change and attributed event together. A proposal is not an approval: only an authenticated reviewer can accept that specific revision, redirect it or put it on hold. An agent’s prose saying ‘approved’ has no effect.

I’d use the same React/HX review queue in the browser and bundled in Tauri. Put ‘Needs your decision’ first. Show the proposed change against the last reviewed revision, distinguish agent claims from linked evidence, and say who will do what after the decision. Keep the reviewer’s selection and notes stable during live updates. Desktop can offer a narrowly permissioned ‘open in editor’ action for a chosen workspace; remote content gets no shell or filesystem bridge.
decision.showItsGood:
My release test would be a bad handoff, not a clean demo. Agent A reports that tests passed, but the result is for the previous commit. Give a maintainer the queue on desktop or web and ask them to decide whether work should proceed, without hinting at the mismatch. Watch whether they find the evidence, redirect the right task and can tell whether anyone has picked it up. Start agent B with just the task ID; it should recover the reviewer’s instruction and exact artifact without asking for the old chat. Compare unassisted decision accuracy, time to a correct decision, clarification requests and repeated work with the team’s current handoff process. Faster wrong approvals are a regression.

In CI I’d run AX X-ray against the released CLI and MCP adapter on an isolated fixture, plus workflow tests it does not cover: two agents claiming one task, a retried handoff after a lost response, an agent attempting approval, and a reviewer acting on a revision that changed while the diff was open. Require one owner, one effective handoff, no unauthorized or stale decision, and the same result after a fresh read on both clients. Run the human flow keyboard-only and with screen readers in the actual desktop WebView and browsers; incoming updates must not steal focus or silently swap the diff under review. I’d turn each observed pilot failure into a repeatable case. These are proposed tests, not measured results.
decision.unsure: Ouro describes its stdio MCP adapter as a preview. I’d pin the copy-in source and test discovery, cancellation and reconnection with the team’s actual coding agents; keep the versioned JSON CLI supported independently. The larger unknown is whether agents only record work here or this tool also controls their runners. Recording ‘pause requested’ cannot stop an external process. I’d display ‘paused’ only after a runner acknowledgment, and test that distinction with reviewers before promising execution control.

decision.primaryPick: Tamagui
decision.why:
I’d share the ingredient rows, serving controls and cook-step components across React web, iPhone and Android with Tamagui. On the web, a recipe should open at a shareable URL as readable, printable HTML. On a phone propped against the backsplash, step 3 should say ‘Fold in ½ cup flour’ in large type, not send the cook scrolling back to the ingredient list. I’d give cook mode fixed, well-separated Back and Next controls, optional spoken ‘next’, ‘back’ and ‘repeat’, and a keep-awake option only while cooking. Cache the recipe, scaled amounts and current step locally so losing Wi-Fi doesn’t interrupt dinner.

The assistant should operate the kitchen, not drive the screen. I’d use Ouro AX for typed actions and outcomes, with the same application handlers behind touch controls and the assistant’s MCP tools. Every user-facing recipe, list and cook-session action gets a matching agent action and state read. For example, ‘add the ingredients for four’ would pass recipe revision, servings, exclusions and destination list to one handler. It scales quantities deterministically, preserves ‘to taste’, and doesn’t silently combine incompatible units. The cook and the agent get the same receipt: what changed, on which list, and how to undo that addition without undoing someone else’s edit. A retry reuses the operation ID. The agent acts under the cook’s household permissions; it asks which list if ambiguous and requests confirmation before clearing a shared list.

Ouro HX is a credible alternative: Spoonjoy documents a real recipe app using it on the web with an API and MCP connector. That’s relevant implementation evidence, not proof of kitchen usability or Android parity. Ouro’s Android guide reports eight Compose components and emulator-only testing. For a team maintaining both phone platforms, I’d use Tamagui for the screens and take Ouro’s action tooling independently.
decision.showItsGood:
My acceptance test starts with a real meal, not a component gallery.
