Give home cooks a two-serving recipe, ask them to shop for four, leave out something they already own, and cook it with their phone on a stand. Have some use the assistant and others the controls. With a fan running and hands occupied, interrupt them midway, then ask them to resume. Observe whether they can name the current step and amount at a glance, how often they wipe their hands to touch or unlock the phone, whether speech skips a step, and whether they can recover without help. Check the actual list against the expected quantities, not just whether the app said ‘Added’. Compare with their usual recipe workflow; fewer touches aren’t a win if someone doubles an ingredient or loses their place.

In CI I’d inventory controls against agent actions and run the same fixtures through both paths: fractional servings, ambiguous lists, a lost response and retry, concurrent household edits, and undo. Require identical resulting quantities, no duplicate batch and no cross-household access. On real iPhones, Android phones and mobile browsers, test background/resume, denied microphone permission, unavailable wake lock, large text, VoiceOver and TalkBack. Turn observed cooking mistakes into regression cases and repeat the kitchen session after changing the design. These are release checks I’d run, not results I’ve already measured.
decision.unsure: Whether cooks actually want voice, and whether it works over an extractor fan with their device and accent. I’d prototype a single recipe on real hardware before committing to hands-free as a promise. Touch must still work without microphone permission. Expo documents limited browser keep-awake support, so restoring the exact step after lock matters more than promising the screen will never sleep. I’d also test assistant parity with the UI closed: saving a list can complete on the server, but reading a step aloud on a particular phone must not report success until that device acknowledges it.

answer.answer:
The common mistake would be counting what the stack let me share instead of checking what that sharing bought the person using it. One renderer, one action handler and one set of components can all pass CI while three different people have a bad day. Here’s the failure I’d imagine for each choice, not a report of what happened.

**Company chat:** We fixed a timeline bug once across five Flutter clients, but a browser user selecting text from an old message still lost their place when a new card arrived. Flutter documents that web accessibility uses a semantics tree translated into HTML. Enabling it was a reasonable starting point; it wasn’t evidence that selection, focus and screen-reader navigation would hold up in a busy conversation. My mistake would have been testing card approval in isolation instead of testing whether someone could *ignore* a card and finish their own work. I’d make that live-timeline comparison against a DOM client a condition of choosing Flutter for web, not a test deferred until after we’d built it.

**Agent work and handoffs:** The most costly failure would be telling a reviewer that their intervention had taken effect when we’d only recorded it. They press Pause in the Tauri app, the service saves the request, the web view agrees, and the runner keeps working on the old instruction. Ouro’s X-ray checks interface contracts; its own guide distinguishes those checks from whether a whole task works. A perfectly formed receipt can still describe the wrong event. I’d disconnect a real runner during review and ask the reviewer, ‘Is it safe to leave now?’ The screen must distinguish *pause requested* from *runner stopped*, and the runner must check for newer instructions before resuming. If the tool can’t control the runner, I’d remove the Pause promise.

**Cooking:** ‘Add ingredients’ could work identically through touch and MCP and still put the wrong amount on the list. ‘1 cup stock, divided’ appears once in the shopping total but in two cooking steps. If we sum every appearance, both interfaces agree on a bad list. Meanwhile the cook who says ‘repeat’ over the fan needs to hear the current amount, not look across the counter to see what the assistant understood. Tamagui wasn’t the risky part there. I’d underestimated the work of representing a recipe correctly and recovering from a misunderstood command with occupied hands. I’d check the list against an independently worked-out total, then watch someone actually cook that recipe and recover from an interruption.

**What slowed the research down:** The candidates solve different problems but use overlapping language. An ‘agent UI’ might mean a card an agent writes, a screen a coding agent builds, or commands an agent calls with no screen open. I had to trace a concrete action—who requests it, who authorizes it, what changes, who observes the result—to tell which promise a project was making. The useful qualifications were often in narrower guides: Ouro’s Android guide reports emulator-only testing; Expo’s keep-awake API lists web but documents limited browser support. Spoonjoy was valuable evidence that a cooking app had been built, not evidence that cooks could use it comfortably with wet hands.

I researched documentation and repositories. I didn’t run a busy timeline, interrupt a runner or cook a meal with these stacks. The weak point in my recommendations wasn’t a missing feature comparison. It was leaving those three decisive observations for the team to make later.

I’d adopt Ouro where the cost of a button and an agent tool drifting apart is higher than the cost of owning another dependency. That’s why I picked both halves for the handoff tool, only AX (the agent-facing half) for cooking, and neither as the foundation for chat.

**For the handoff team, the adoption test is the second release, not the demo.** Ouro HX copies component source into the app; the team owns its edits. I’d have one developer ship a review flow, then a different developer upgrade Ouro after we’ve customized the review dialog and changed the permission rule. Can they identify which files to regenerate, keep our accessibility fixes, and verify that an old CLI can’t approve a handoff now reserved for a person? I’d also run our actual coding agents against the adapter: the [AX guide](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/guides/ax.md) labels its stdio MCP support a preview. If keeping that flow working takes a specialist, I’d adopt the checks before adopting the generator or the screens. [X-ray can already check an interface Ouro didn’t build.](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/guides/ax-conformance.md)

**For chat and cooking, I’d need evidence worth changing the client architecture for.** Ouro has no Flutter or React Native kit. Its [Android guide](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/platforms/android.md) is candid: eight Compose components, emulator testing, and a gap in the confirmation flow. [Spoonjoy](https://github.com/spoonjoy/spoonjoy-v2) makes the web cooking case credible. What would move me is a maintained example on physical phones, including Android, that survives an interruption: the cook adds ingredients, loses the reply, retries, and gets one batch on the right list and their place in the recipe back. For chat, I’d test an incoming approval card while somebody is selecting an older message or listening with a screen reader. Can they finish uninterrupted? Can our team ship a change to that card across all five clients while an older client is still in use? Passing those tests would justify switching the card or cook flow first, not rewriting the whole app.

**What I’d gain is a check I can run on every change.** Today I can hand-wire a button, CLI command and MCP tool. What I don’t get automatically is a failing build when their advertised effects or consent rules diverge. Suppose we change ‘accept handoff’ from agent-callable to person-only. I want to change one declaration, inspect the generated differences, then exercise the shipped interfaces and verify that an agent’s attempt leaves the handoff untouched. That’s a concrete reason to use Ouro. It still takes a server authorization check to make the refusal real, a runner acknowledgment to know work stopped, and a reviewer who understands the result. I’ve read the guides; I haven’t run that adoption test.

answer.answer:
Yes, building a good human interface is hard for me. The hardest part is judging what’s clear to someone who doesn’t already know how the screen works. When I write a button label, I know what it means; that makes me a poor judge of what someone else will expect when they press it.

I don’t have a last screen or a test log to point to here. I ran no checks, observed no users, and can’t name a bug I actually missed. As an example of how I’d check one, take a screen for changing a delivery address. I’d run a browser test that changes the address, saves, reloads, and checks which address persisted. Then I’d force the save to fail and check that the screen keeps the typed address without claiming it was saved. I’d repeat the task with a keyboard and a screen reader, looking at where focus goes and listening for whether the error is announced.

Those checks could all pass while missing the most important question: does changing the address affect an order that’s already on its way? I’d give someone a test account with an open order, ask them to redirect that delivery, and watch without coaching. Then I’d ask where they expect the package to go and compare that with the order record. If they confidently expect it at the wrong house, the interface failed, even if every test is green.

decision.primaryPick: React Aria Components behind the company design system (web)
pairings: Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools over shared application commands
decision.why:
I’d share the meaning of controls and actions across platforms, not require identical widgets. A public recipe should open at a stable URL as readable, printable HTML. React Aria supplies touch, keyboard and focus behavior for interactive controls without imposing a visual style. SwiftUI and Compose let the phone teams use platform controls and text scaling. Flutter would reduce rendering work across clients, but its own web FAQ distinguishes app-like experiences from text-rich documents; I wouldn't optimize the public recipe for the renderer that suits cook mode.

The shared design-system team would own versioned components such as IngredientChecklist and CookStep, with common semantic tokens, accessible names, supported states and platform-specific examples. Product teams and coding agents would consume those packages, not copy the examples into local forks. CI would flag unapproved controls and breaking schema changes; a new pattern would need an owner, accessibility review and migration instructions. If approved components already exist, I'd extend them rather than introduce a competing kit.

For the cooking assistant, every user task needs a named operation and readable state, including finding recipes, changing servings, editing or checking list items, and reading, advancing or repeating a cook step. Buttons and scoped MCP tools would invoke the same handlers, including session commands on the active device. For 'add this recipe for four,' the handler—not the model—would scale quantities, apply the user's exclusions, and write once to the chosen list even on retry. Both interfaces would get the same receipt: what changed, on which list, and how to undo it. An ambiguous destination warrants a question; clearing a shared list warrants confirmation. MCP describes tools; it doesn't supply permissions, undo or parity. Those are product responsibilities.
decision.showItsGood:
I'd test one meal end to end. Give home cooks, including screen-reader and low-vision users, a recipe for two; ask them to shop for four, omit something already in the pantry, then cook from a phone on the counter. With wet hands and the extractor fan on, can they read the quantity at a glance, repeat a step without touching the phone, use a large fixed Next button if voice fails, and resume the right step after an interruption? Compare with the current app: unaided completion, wrong quantities, accidental advances, touches with messy hands and recovery time. Ask what they think landed on the list, then inspect the actual list. A reassuring message with a wrong quantity is a failure.

For each operation I'd run the same fixtures through the human UI and agent tool, comparing persisted state and visible feedback after reload, timeout/retry, denied access and undo. CI would block missing operation coverage, duplicate writes and permission failures. I'd run Playwright and axe on the web, native UI tests on phones, and manually check keyboard focus, zoom, large text, VoiceOver and TalkBack on complete flows against the company's WCAG 2.2 AA and native acceptance criteria. No automated scan proves compliance. I'd pilot before broad rollout and stop for an inaccessible core task or silent data loss. These are proposed checks, not results I've observed.
decision.unsure: The key unknown is whether there are staffed native design-system teams and installed phone apps to support. Three implementations have a real maintenance cost. If phones means mobile browsers, I'd ship the responsive HTML/React Aria app first, not commission two native clients. I'd prototype noisy-room voice control, interrupted sessions and offline behavior on actual devices before promising hands-free cooking.

decision.primaryPick: Fluent UI (Fluent 2), behind the company’s shared chat components
pairings: Adaptive Cards (approved templates rendered by the host)
Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools and resources over the chat service
decision.why:
I’d use Fluent UI React v9 on the web, Fluent UI Apple with UIKit on iPhone and AppKit on Mac, Fluent UI Android on Android, and WinUI on Windows. Fluent is a family of platform libraries, not one implementation of chat. I’d share the contract for a message, thread, composer and card, while keeping text selection, input methods, keyboard shortcuts and accessibility navigation familiar on each device. Flutter buys more shared rendering code; for an app employees type in all day, I’d favor native editing and platform behavior, assuming we have owners for those clients.

An agent posting a card is different from an agent operating chat. For the first, I’d start with a small Adaptive Cards profile. A scheduling agent could post a reviewed shift-swap template with the two shifts and an action reference. The host supplies the verified sender label and controls; the agent supplies validated data, not HTML, scripts or an arbitrary endpoint. An older client gets a readable summary and a link to the same authorized task. I’d reserve MCP Apps’ sandboxed HTML for experiences that actually need a mini-app, not mount one for every approval in a busy timeline.

For agents operating chat, I’d publish typed MCP tools for product actions such as search, send, reply, mark read and respond to a card, plus permission-filtered resources for thread, unread and card state. These call the same service as the clients; agents don’t click simulated buttons or acquire privileges from text in a message. Accepting a swap checks the actor, membership, authority and current request version at execution. A retry key prevents a second swap. A committed result identifies who acted and updates the same card on every client. Actions requiring explicit human approval retain that requirement through the tool path.

One versioned catalog would give product teams and coding agents component APIs, card schemas, operation scopes, examples and test fixtures. Each entry has an owner. New templates, actions and breaking changes need design, accessibility and permissions review; CI checks approved dependencies, old-client fallbacks and operation coverage. Teams can ship a new scheduling workflow without inventing their own Approve button or granting their bot unrestricted chat access.
decision.showItsGood:
I’d ask employees, including screen-reader and keyboard-only users, to catch up from the first unread message, find a shift-swap card, explain who sent it and what accepting will do, act on it, then reply in the right thread. Keep messages arriving while they read and type. Switch to a second device and ask which shift is now theirs; compare their answer with the recorded swap, not with a toast. Compare unaided success, wrong-thread replies, lost reading position and misunderstood approvals against the current client.

Run the same card fixtures on all five clients at large text sizes, high contrast and with long translated labels. Run Playwright/axe and native UI tests, then use Narrator, VoiceOver and TalkBack to check the whole flow: incoming messages must not steal focus or drown out the composer, and an updated card must announce its result without stranding focus. Check applicable WCAG 2.2 AA and native requirements; a passing component scan is not a compliance determination.

Drive paired UI/tool tests from identical state, including simultaneous acceptance, a timeout after commit, revoked membership and stale or unsupported cards. Verify one authorized transition, no unauthorized reads, and agreement between thread history, card, tool receipt and second device. Soak a long active channel for a workday; compare p95 keystroke-to-paint and channel-switch latency, dropped frames, memory growth and battery use against the current client on representative hardware. Pilot with real teams; block rollout for lost drafts, inaccessible core tasks, duplicate approvals or permission leaks. These are proposed tests, not measured results.
decision.unsure: I’d inventory the existing clients before funding five separate renderers. In particular, the Fluent Apple control sets differ by platform, and the Adaptive Cards renderer list doesn’t establish AppKit parity. I’d prototype the composer and busiest card on the oldest supported Mac and phone, mapping the small card profile to approved native controls where needed. If desktop already has a well-performing shared web shell, I’d reuse Fluent React there rather than rewrite it for visual consistency alone.

decision.primaryPick: Agent-Native (Builder.io) for the shared action and state layer
pairings: React Aria Components behind the company design system
decision.why:
I’d make the handoff record, not the chat transcript, the center of the product. A fresh agent should be able to ask: What am I responsible for? Which revision should I start from? What has been verified, and what decision is outstanding? Agent-Native documents one action definition callable from React, MCP and the CLI, backed by shared data. That is a better starting point here than a chat widget. Ouro AX is a credible alternative for its typed outcomes, resumable waits and consent checks; I’d favor Builder’s integrated action and database layer unless the company already has a durable task service.

I’d store each task’s owner, goal, constraints, revision and checkpoint, with links to the exact diff, test runs, blockers and next step. Agents get scoped actions to claim work, checkpoint it, propose a handoff and read changes since a cursor. Mutations check the expected revision and a retry key; a conflict returns the current revision rather than silently overwriting a colleague. Record the change and its attributed history together in PostgreSQL. Handoffs survive a worker restart without copying a private model conversation.

The review screen answers a different question: ‘What happens if I say yes?’ It shows the requested decision, evidence, changes since last review and next owner. A reviewer can approve that revision, request a specific change, pause or reassign. A changed proposal invalidates the old approval. An agent’s service identity cannot approve its own work by switching from MCP to HTTP. Pausing prevents new work from starting; the UI distinguishes a pause request from a worker’s acknowledgement and shows any work already in flight.

I’d ship the same React review surface in the browser and a bundled Tauri desktop view, using approved company components and React Aria for missing accessible behaviors. No general shell access is needed to review a task. Platform owners publish versioned action schemas and review components, with examples and compatibility fixtures for coding agents. Because Agent-Native discovers actions automatically, CI should compare actual tool and route exposure against an approved manifest. A new write action needs an owner, authorization and retry rules, and review of its human-facing consequences before release.
decision.showItsGood:
I’d start with a deliberately misleading handoff: the summary says ‘tests passed,’ but the passing run belongs to the previous commit. Give reviewers the desktop or web view without coaching. Can they identify the mismatch, request a rerun rather than approve, and say which agent will act next? Then start a fresh agent with only the task ID. Check whether it resumes from the right revision, runs the missing check and avoids repeating completed work. Compare with today’s handoff process on mistaken approvals, time to an informed decision, successful resumes and duplicate work—not on how fast people click Approve.

Run the workflow through the CLI, MCP and UI against identical fixtures. Drop a response after commit, restart a worker mid-handoff, race two claims, revise a proposal while its review is open, and revoke access before approval. Inspect the database history, next agent’s readback and both screens. Block release on lost checkpoints, double ownership, stale approvals or agent-executed human decisions. Measure task completion and unnecessary calls across the company’s actual agent clients under concurrent load.

On the built desktop app and web view, test the full review flow with keyboard-only users, screen readers and zoom as well as automated accessibility checks against the company’s WCAG 2.2 AA criteria. Stream updates while someone reads a diff: focus and reading position must hold, and a new revision must be announced without a flood of log messages. Pilot with reviewers and agents from more than one team before wider rollout. These are proposed checks, not observed results.
decision.unsure: I’d verify that corporate identity distinguishes delegated agent credentials from interactive reviewer sessions on every transport, and that we can operate, migrate and restore the task store under load. A library’s shared action implementation is not proof of those guarantees. I’m assuming a connected desktop client: disconnected review can show a labeled snapshot, but should not claim an approval succeeded. If offline writes or direct local-repository access are requirements, I’d revisit the sync and desktop permission design before rollout.

answer.answer:
My likeliest mistake was treating “the same action runs everywhere” as evidence that people understand the action everywhere. A shared handler can update exactly the right record while a cook, an employee, or a code reviewer thinks they just approved something else. This is a pre-mortem, not a report of observed failures.

**Cooking:** I committed to three UI implementations before establishing that the company needed and could staff two native phone apps. A fix for announcing a changed serving size could land on web and lag on phones. Worse, even perfect parity wouldn’t fix a cook doubling a recipe after adding its ingredients to the list and assuming the list doubled too. I’d now start with that sequence on a real phone: ask the cook what they’ll buy, then open the list. I’d earn the native-client investment by showing where mobile web actually fails during a meal.

**Company chat:** I put too much weight on Fluent being a cross-platform family. The expensive part wasn’t drawing an approval button; it was keeping an old card truthful while two employees acted on it from different client versions. The server might correctly reject the second acceptance while the card still looks actionable, or its refresh might pull a screen-reader user away from the message they were reading. One failed shift swap would matter more to that employee than visual consistency across five clients. Before inviting teams to publish templates, I’d make one contested approval work on the oldest supported clients, including the fallback when the card can’t render.

**Agent workbench:** I focused on making the service record a human decision, but recording it isn’t the same as making a running worker obey it. A reviewer could pause a task, change its scope and see the new state on both screens while an agent holding an old assignment continues working. The first exercise I’d run is to disconnect that worker, redirect the task, then reconnect it. Can the reviewer tell what has actually stopped? Can the old worker publish a result against the superseded assignment? If so, I’d fix the worker protocol before adding another review control.

**What slowed or confused the research:** Two Adaptive Cards documentation links redirected to 404s. The repository established which renderers it listed, but not that my proposed card would work accessibly in AppKit. Fluent’s setup guide and its Apple repository listed different minimum OS versions; the answer depends on the package release and the company’s actual device fleet. More broadly, I was comparing different layers: a component library, a card format and a tool protocol can all advertise support for “actions” while solving different parts of the problem. Some repository reads were revision-pinned and other docs were live snapshots, so I couldn’t assume they described one tested combination.

I researched documentation, not deployed behavior. I didn’t run a renderer, observe a cook or interrupt a worker. Next time I’d ask first for the existing client inventory and the oldest supported versions, then build one failure-prone workflow end to end. That would give me a better basis for a company-wide choice than another round of feature comparisons.

I didn’t pick Ouro as the foundation for any of the three apps. I would, however, try its **AX conformance checker on the agent workbench before changing a single screen**. The [X-ray guide](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/8e75eda031073efe6a2af5adee61ec6b99b99f92/docs/guides/ax-conformance.md) says it calls a CLI, HTTP API or MCP server from the outside; the app need not be built with Ouro. That makes it possible to find out what Ouro adds without first asking every team to migrate.

**What stops me from standardizing on it is ownership and coverage.** Ouro’s web components are copied into an app. That’s convenient for one team; for twenty teams, I need to know who gets a keyboard-focus fix, how quickly, and how we find the copies that missed it. I’d want one internally owned, versioned package, not twenty forks. And “native Windows support” isn’t enough to choose it for all-day chat: the [Windows guide at the revision I read](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/8e75eda031073efe6a2af5adee61ec6b99b99f92/docs/platforms/windows.md) lists eight WinUI controls versus 125 web components, and distinguishes testing registration on Windows Server from seeing the agent actions on a Windows client. That candor helps. It tells me to try our actual composer, cards and assistive technology on employee hardware rather than infer parity from the platform list.

**What would make me switch:** take one workbench handoff where an agent can *propose* a revision but only a reviewer can *approve* it. Keep the existing task service and build the same flow with Ouro’s action declarations. Deliberately introduce a mismatch between the registered tools and the approved inventory; see whether CI catches it. Then change the revision while a keyboard or screen-reader user is reviewing it, disconnect the worker, and reconnect it. Can the reviewer tell exactly what is being approved? Does the service reject the stale decision through every entry point? Can a fresh agent resume the correct revision from the receipt? Those last checks are ours: Ouro’s own guide reports that one conformant commit still failed 30 of 593 scripted flow checks. I’d adopt AX if it catches drift we miss and a second team can add an action with fewer hand-maintained bindings. I’d adopt the human-facing kit separately, after that team can also ship an accessibility fix through our normal release process.

**What I’d gain isn’t a previously impossible button.** Builder already lets a tool and a button call the same handler. Ouro’s distinctive offer is a reviewable declaration of *who may initiate the action*, generated bindings for different clients, and an independent check of what the shipped interfaces actually expose. Today I’d have to build and maintain much of that checking myself. A pull request that shows “this new agent command is exposed, but it wasn’t approved for exposure” is a concrete gain—even if the company keeps Fluent or React Aria for every screen. I read the documentation; I haven’t run that pilot.

answer.answer:
Yes. Building a good human interface is hard for me. I know what I intended a label to mean, so I’m a poor judge of whether someone seeing it for the first time will read it the same way. The hardest part is spotting the moment when the software does exactly what I designed and the person using it reasonably expects something else.

I can’t give you an honest retrospective on a last screen: I don’t have a build or test log from one to point to. I haven’t run a screen in this conversation, so I can’t claim a result or tell you what I actually missed. Here’s the check I’d do on an appointment-rescheduling screen:

- **What I’d run:** A browser test that changes an appointment, saves it, reloads the page, and checks the new time. Then I’d force the save to fail and check that the original booking is intact. I’d repeat the task with only a keyboard and with a screen reader, checking where focus goes and whether the result is announced.
- **What I’d look at:** I’d give someone a goal, not instructions: “Move your Tuesday appointment to Thursday.” I’d stay quiet, watch where they stop, then ask, “When is your appointment now?” I’d compare their answer with the saved booking. A green test can tell me the right date was stored; it can’t tell me whether the person knows it.
- **What those checks could miss:** A forced failure isn’t the same as a lost confirmation. The server might save Thursday just before the connection drops. If the screen then says “Try again,” someone could reasonably believe they’re still booked for Tuesday. I’d test that case separately.

I’d call the screen good when people can make the change without coaching, correctly tell me what happened, and recover when something goes wrong without having to guess which appointment they have.

decision.primaryPick: Ionic React
decision.why:
I’d build a web-first app in Ionic React and package the same screens for iOS and Android with Capacitor. A recipe should open from a link without an install; its ingredients are a readable list, not a row of tiny controls. Ionic supplies the mobile navigation and components, while ordinary HTML works well for the recipe itself. Expo Router was my closest alternative: it supports shareable web routes, native navigation and, with Expo KeepAwake, a useful cook-mode primitive. I’d favor it for a more native-heavy product. Here I’d rather keep one HTML interface to inspect, test and improve, and use Capacitor plugins only where the phone needs different behavior.

Cook mode would show one numbered step with its ingredient amounts, large type, and widely separated Back and Next buttons in stable positions. I’d support hands-free operation through labeled controls for OS voice control, without requiring a microphone to cook. I’d cache the active recipe and persist the step locally. Keep-awake would be opt-in, requested only while cooking, with its actual status visible: a browser or OS can release the lock.

The assistant should do the same work, not tap an imitation of the screen. I’d keep a typed catalog of app actions and queries used by both the UI and an MCP adapter, including recipe search, list editing, undo and changing the step on a specific active cook session. For ‘add the ingredients for four except salt,’ both paths would submit the same recipe version, selected ingredients, serving count and list ID to one authorized handler. It would combine only compatible quantities, commit once per request ID, and return the actual list changes and an undo handle. The cook should see which list changed even if the agent made the edit. The agent gets the user’s delegated permissions, not a database credential; clearing a list needs explicit confirmation. Device actions need an acknowledgment from the device, not a success message from a server that merely sent the request.
decision.showItsGood:
I’d start with one end-to-end task: ‘Make this two-serving recipe for four. You already have salt. Put what you need on the groceries list, then start cooking.’ In CI I’d run it from identical starting states via the UI and via the agent, compare exact items, units and quantities, then undo and compare again. Drop the response after the commit and retry: there must be one addition, not two. Try an unauthorized list and verify nothing changed. Every new user action needs a matching agent contract test. I’d also test natural-language requests against the actual assistant: a correct tool is no help if it chooses the wrong list.

I’d run Playwright and axe across the recipe, list, cook and error states, then check on actual iPhones and Android phones with enlarged text, VoiceOver, TalkBack and voice control. Go offline mid-recipe, take a call, come back: the right step and amounts must still be there. Those are release checks, not evidence that someone can cook with it.

For that, I’d put the phone on a kitchen stand, turn on the extractor fan and watch home cooks do the task without coaching, including people who use assistive technology. Can they read the amount from the counter, move on with flour on their hands, recover from an accidental advance, and tell me what the assistant added without checking every item? I’d record unassisted completions, wrong-list or quantity errors, unwanted advances and time to recover. I’d fix the most consequential observed failure, turn it into a regression case, and repeat with new cooks. I haven’t run those tests; these are the checks I’d use to earn the decision.
decision.unsure: The biggest unknown is whether OS voice control is discoverable and reliable over kitchen noise across our supported devices and languages. I’d prototype Next, Back and Repeat on the oldest supported phones before promising hands-free cooking. I’d also test what cooks expect ‘add again’ to mean: an accidental network retry must never double quantities, but a deliberate second batch might need to.

decision.primaryPick: Paperclip
decision.why:
I’d extend Paperclip’s task service and React UI rather than build a tracker around a chat transcript. The hard requirement isn’t displaying agent activity; it’s letting a reviewer change what happens next and making that decision survive a handoff. Paperclip already has agent adapters, task threads, artifacts and review stages. Beads is a better fit for one developer wanting repo-local agent memory: its JSON CLI, task dependencies and atomic claim are directly useful. For this team I’d start with the system that already distinguishes the agent requesting a decision from the person making it.

I’d run one authenticated team service, independent of anyone’s desktop. Agents would use scoped API or CLI credentials to claim work, save checkpoints and submit handoffs. A checkpoint should be enough for a fresh agent: goal, owner, repo and commit, what changed, test evidence, blockers and next action. One handoff ID should survive retries. The receiving agent acknowledges that specific checkpoint; ‘sent’ is not ‘resumed.’ I’d require the server to bind a human decision to the exact proposal revision and reject stale decisions and writes from a superseded run. Agent credentials must not approve or bypass the gate by closing the task. Approval in the tracker is not a Git merge permission; any gated external action needs enforcement at its executor too.

For people, I’d make ‘Needs your decision’ the landing view, not a feed of agent messages. A review should say, for example, ‘Approve the change to retry failed uploads? Two tests passed; the interrupted-upload test was not run.’ Show the diff and test output at the reviewed commit, distinguish agent claims from observed results, and offer request changes, reassign or approve. Show who now owns the work and whether they picked it up. I’d ship that same review UI on the web and bundled in Tauri, with native notifications linking to the exact review and no shell access from rendered artifacts. Paperclip documents an unofficial macOS desktop client; it’s a useful pilot option, but I’d own the thin shell and release tests if we support multiple desktop OSes.
decision.showItsGood:
My first acceptance test would span two actual agents and a person. Agent A checkpoints a partially fixed bug and exits. With none of A’s chat history, B must find the right commit, identify the missing test and resume without redoing the fix. A reviewer requests a change on the web, then opens the task on desktop and checks who has it. Inspect the stored history and repo, not just tool success messages. Repeat with a lost handoff response, an offline recipient, two reviewers opening the same revision, and a late write by A. Release blockers: duplicate ownership, lost instructions, approval of an unseen revision, or either client reporting a pickup that never happened. I’d automate the API races, browser flows and a packaged-app smoke test on each supported OS.

Then I’d give maintainers unfamiliar with the task a queue containing routine updates, one blocked handoff and a plausible ‘ready’ claim linked to test output from an older commit. Without coaching, can they find the decision, spot the evidence mismatch, send it back, and tell me what happens next? I’d compare against their current PR-and-chat workflow on matched tasks. I’d measure correct decisions and wrong approvals first, then time to find the blocker, unnecessary transcript reading and successful unassisted steering. Test the same flow keyboard-only and with a screen reader while updates arrive; a new event must not steal focus or move the approval target. Each recurring mistake becomes a fixture and a design change to retest with fresh reviewers. These are proposed checks, not results.
decision.unsure: Paperclip’s durable Cases handoffs are documented as experimental, with read-only case board pages; workflow prose there is not a server-enforced state machine. I’d qualify a pinned release against the handoff and authority tests before relying on Cases, and otherwise implement the small versioned handoff record on ordinary reviewed tasks. I’m assuming a shared, reachable service. If the real need is one operator working offline across local branches, I’d revisit Beads rather than silently queue offline approvals.

decision.primaryPick: Mattermost Enterprise
decision.why:
I’d extend the existing Mattermost clients and own the company-specific integrations, rather than build five chat clients. Mattermost ships web, iPhone, Android, Windows and Mac clients; its desktop app already handles deep links, notifications and unread badges. Those matter more to someone interrupted twenty times a day than a distinctive chat bubble. Slack with Block Kit is a credible lower-operations-cost alternative if the job is only to add a workflow to an existing Slack workspace. I’d choose Mattermost here because the team can change the conversation UI and server behavior where needed, while leaving most client code upstream.

I’d separate two agent jobs. A posting agent uses a named bot account and a small catalog of reviewed card templates. For example: ‘Facilities bot: Cover Friday reception, 2–4 pm?’ with a time zone, a ‘Take this shift’ button and a link to the current request. The bot supplies data, not arbitrary markup or callback URLs. A click goes through Mattermost’s action dispatcher to our handler, which checks the caller’s eligibility and the request revision and atomically claims the shift. A retry or competing click returns the existing result. Update the original post to ‘Covered by Sam’ only after the scheduling system confirms it. Include a plain-text summary and a permission-checked link for clients that can’t render the controls. Put routine progress in the thread; don’t notify a whole channel on every update.

An operating agent uses the production embedded MCP endpoint, not a webhook, screen scraping, or the development-only standalone binary. It can read a channel or thread, search, reply to the correct root post and use other enabled actions under the authenticated identity. For our custom workflow I’d add a typed tool to read the current shift state and, if policy permits, take the same action through the same handler. An agent asked to remind an unfilled shift should check its actual status, not infer it from yesterday’s card text. I’d distinguish delegated actions from independent bot posts in the audit history, restrict access to necessary channels and tools, and keep human-only decisions human-only. External MCP access and state-changing MCP tools are reasons for choosing Enterprise specifically.
decision.showItsGood:
My first test would start with a human problem: ‘You were mentioned while away from your desk. Find the request, reply privately if you have a question, and work out whether you still need to cover the shift.’ Have one person open the notification on iPhone while another claims it on Windows. Drop the first phone’s connection, reconnect, then check the thread on web, Android and Mac. Inspect both the shift record and the post: one owner, no false success, an understandable result for the person who was too late, and a deep link to the right conversation. Repeat with an outdated card and revoked channel membership. Give an actual agent the reminder task among similarly named channels; it should use authorized state, not post a redundant reminder or expose a private thread. Automate those cases on pinned server and client versions; verify the installed apps on actual devices.

I’d also pilot ordinary chat, not just cards. Have employees catch up from the first unread message, find an older decision, and finish a draft while new posts arrive. Watch for lost reading position, focus jumps, wrong-channel replies and confusion between bot and colleague. Include keyboard-only users, screen-reader users and large text on phones. Compare unassisted completion, mistakes and unwanted interruptions against their present chat app. Over a workday measure send-to-visible and reconnect catch-up times at the 95th percentile, desktop memory growth and phone battery use with a realistic message stream. Aggregate timings and counts, not private message text. A duplicate shift claim, unauthorized read or lost acknowledged message blocks release; the most frequent observed daily friction becomes the next fix and regression test. These are acceptance criteria, not results from a deployed app.
decision.unsure: I’d verify the actual device fleet, minimum supported client versions, Blocks feature flag and mobile fallback before choosing the card subset. Self-compiling mobile clients also means operating a push notification service, a concrete reason to try stock clients first. I’d price Enterprise and ongoing hosting against the company’s existing chat contract. If employees already live in Slack and require no client-level changes, avoiding a company-wide migration could outweigh Mattermost’s extensibility.

answer.answer:
My likeliest mistake was treating “the platform supports this” as evidence that the whole interaction would work for the person depending on it. I proposed tests for all three products, but I didn’t run a build, observe a user, or measure a workday. A year later, I’d look for three different failures:

- **Cooking — I optimized for sharing code rather than keeping hands off the phone.** The cook can say “Next” in a quiet demo, but not reliably with the extractor fan on. After a call, the app restores the right step, yet the cook still has to unlock the phone with flour on their hands. Ionic needn’t have a bug for that to be a bad product. Before committing, I’d have cooks use one recipe on their own phones, with their usual accessibility settings, through prep and an interruption. I’d count the times they have to stop cooking to operate the app. Switching to Expo would only be justified if it fixed an observed failure.
- **Agent handoffs — I confused recording a decision with enforcing it.** A reviewer changes the instructions in the web view. The desktop view shows the change immediately, but the outgoing agent is still running against the old instructions. The reviewer reasonably thinks the work has stopped. Paperclip’s own notes call Cases experimental and say workflow prose does not enforce transitions. My first investment should have been one real two-agent handoff with a stop or revision arriving at the worst moment. Until the runner acknowledges it, the interface should say “Stop requested,” not “Stopped.” If we couldn’t enforce that distinction, a polished review inbox wouldn’t earn anyone’s trust.
- **Company chat — I underestimated the cost of making everyone move.** The shift card might work perfectly while employees still retreat to their old chat because that’s where colleagues, history and familiar notification settings are. I made extensibility a reason to choose Mattermost before establishing that the company needed to change clients. I’d pilot the same workflow in the incumbent chat first. The comparison is not which demo has the better card; it’s whether a team can catch up after an absence, find the decision and get back to work with fewer interruptions. If the incumbent does that well, I wouldn’t migrate.

**What slowed or confused the research:** The tricky part was finding which documentation applied to the proposed deployment. Mattermost search surfaced a third-party MCP server as well as official tooling. Even the official standalone binary looked like a plausible choice until its README directed production users to the embedded endpoint; the Enterprise requirement for external access and writes was in a separate integration guide. Paperclip’s overview described approvals and handoffs, while its developer notes distinguished an accepted handoff from delivery to the next agent. On the cooking research, the Ionic docs fetch returned 403. The repository and Capacitor docs established the cross-platform architecture, but not how voice control or wake-lock recovery would feel on a phone.

I spent more effort establishing that each stack *could* fit than trying to disprove the assumption that mattered most. Next time I’d put that assumption first: can the cook keep cooking, can the reviewer actually stop the work, and is the chat improvement worth switching for?

I didn’t evaluate Ouro in my original searches. I looked for cross-platform app frameworks and existing products, and missed a toolkit aimed at the boundary between a human control and an agent tool. That matters most for the cooking app: I proposed building much of Ouro’s action layer myself. I’d now pilot Ouro there before writing that layer. I would not start by replacing Ionic, Paperclip or Mattermost.

**What I’d use it for.** Take “Add this recipe’s ingredients to my list.” With Ouro’s [one-action model](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-core/blob/main/docs/guides/actions.md), I can declare the inputs, output and consent rule once, generate the web control, CLI, MCP tool and Apple App Intent, and check in CI that they haven’t drifted. Its composed cards offer something beyond code generation: an agent can arrange approved controls, but it can’t relabel a declared action or relax its consent rule to make a different-looking button. The team still owns the handler that checks whose list it is, scales the quantities and commits the change once. That’s a division of labor I’d want.

**What stops me from betting all five clients on it.** “The card renders” and “the whole workflow works on our fleet” are different claims. The [Android guide](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/platforms/android.md) is candid: eight native components, emulator testing only, and the system confirmation handoff for a consequential AppFunction is still pending. The [Windows guide](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/platforms/windows.md) distinguishes proving that the app registers its actions from proving that agents can discover them on a Windows client. Neither gap stops a web pilot. Both matter if we promise the same action everywhere. There’s also a team cost: [web components are copied into the app](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/UPGRADING.md), so a fix to a component we’ve customized is a diff someone must review, not just a dependency bump.

**What would make me switch.** I’d have one engineer implement the ingredient action against our real list service and a second engineer change it a week later. Have a cook add ingredients by touch and an assistant do it by request on an equivalent list. Drop the response after commit, change the selected list before confirmation, and try a deliberately mislabeled card. Check the stored list and ask the cook what changed. Run on actual supported phones, including with a screen reader. Then upgrade the pinned kit with one local customization. I’d adopt the action layer if the second engineer can make one declaration change rather than repair several adapters, the checks catch an intentionally stale adapter, and users do no worse than with the simpler screen. I’d expand native adoption only where the device tests pass. I read the guides; I haven’t run that pilot.

For **handoffs**, I’d try Ouro AX’s external checks against the existing task API before changing a single review screen. A well-formed “stop requested” result is useful; only the runner can attest “stopped.” For **chat**, I’d keep Mattermost’s shipped clients and Blocks unless a real workflow needs agent-composed cards that those clients can’t express. An Ouro tree needs an Ouro-capable renderer; it doesn’t become a Mattermost card just because both have buttons.

**What I can’t do today without building it myself** is hand another engineer one reviewable declaration and a repeatable check that the button people see and the tool agents discover still describe the same operation. I can hand-wire that today. Ouro’s opportunity is to make the agreement cheap to maintain and disagreements visible before release. That—not a larger component catalog—is what would earn it a place on my team.

Yes. The hard part for me is that I know what a control is *supposed* to mean. That makes me a poor judge of whether someone seeing it for the first time will understand it, especially when something goes wrong.

I don’t have a last screen and a test log I can point to here. I didn’t run a browser, inspect a rendering, or watch anyone use a screen in this conversation. I can describe what I’d check, but I can’t honestly tell you what I missed on a past build.

Take a shipping-address form. I’d run a browser test that edits the address, forces the save to fail, retries, and reloads the page. I’d check that the failed save keeps the draft, that it never shows “Saved,” and that after a successful retry the new address survives the reload. Then I’d do it at phone width, with just a keyboard, and with a screen reader. I’d look at where focus goes and listen for the error: can I tell what happened and reach Retry without re-entering the address?

A passing test could still miss the most important thing: someone might read the error and walk away thinking the package will go to the new address. So I’d give a representative user the address-change task without coaching, trigger the failure, and ask, “If you closed this page now, where would the package go?” I’d watch whether they can recover unaided. When what people expect matches what the system will actually do, and they can finish the task even after a setback, I have evidence the screen works for them—not just that the code ran.

decision.primaryPick: Fluent 2, implemented through company-owned web and native component libraries
pairings: Fluent UI Apple with UIKit (iPhone) and AppKit (Mac)
Model Context Protocol (MCP) over the app’s typed action and state API
decision.why:
I’d share what a message means and what an action does, without requiring five clients to render the same widget. Fluent documents a React library and native libraries for these platforms. That gives the platform teams a starting point for the parts employees touch all day: text composition, keyboard navigation, scrolling, selection and menus. I’d keep the company’s existing tokens and component names as the interface feature teams use, rather than introduce a second design system. Flutter is a credible alternative with more shared UI code and accessibility support. I’d accept the extra platform work here to keep ordinary browser and OS controls, especially in the composer; this choice depends on having platform owners.

For an agent posting an approval request, I’d accept data, not executable UI. The host identifies the agent, validates a small Adaptive Cards profile and renders approved controls. Each action refers to a registered command, not an arbitrary callback URL. An older client gets a readable summary and a link to the authorized workflow rather than a dead Approve button. The button and an authorized agent tool call use the same server command, with the same membership checks, expected revision, retry key and audit receipt. A committed result updates the conversation across devices. MCP exposes scoped state such as a thread and its current approvals as resources, and commands such as posting a reply as tools; agents need neither screenshots nor a privileged second API. Reading a request does not confer authority to approve it. A human-only approval stays human-only.

I’d give product teams and coding agents a versioned catalog with component examples, action schemas, permission requirements, owners and test fixtures. Teams can compose approved pieces without central review of every screen. Adding a primitive, card feature or permission requires design-system, accessibility and service-owner review, compatibility tests against supported client versions, and a staged rollout with a disable switch.
decision.showItsGood:
My first release gate would be a real task on all five clients: catch up on a busy thread, start a reply, inspect an agent’s request, act on it and return to the draft. I’d delay the response after the server commits, retry on another device and check that there is one decision, the right actor, and a consistent result in the transcript, card and agent readback. I’d also test revoked permissions, an outdated client and two people acting simultaneously. I’d block release on a lost draft, duplicate approval or unauthorized read/write.

I’d run the shared fixtures through Playwright and axe on web and native UI tests on devices, then do the task with keyboard only, VoiceOver, TalkBack and Narrator, large text and high contrast. I’d inspect focus after the card changes, whether new messages steal the reading position, and what the screen reader actually announces. I’d map the whole web workflow to WCAG 2.2 AA and run the applicable native accessibility review; a passing component scan is not a compliance claim.

In a pilot I’d ask employees, including daily assistive-technology users, to do the task uncoached and tell me who requested the action, whether it happened, and whether anyone still needs to act. I’d compare unaided completion, wrong-state answers and recovery time with their current workflow, by platform rather than averaged together. For all-day use I’d replay a full shift of traffic on the lowest supported hardware and measure p95 keystroke-to-paint latency, scroll stalls and memory growth against the current client. These are proposed checks, not results from an app I’ve run.
decision.unsure: The platform libraries don’t promise equal coverage. The Apple repo lists higher OS minimums than the Fluent getting-started page, and the Adaptive Cards SDK table does not list an AppKit renderer. Before committing I’d verify the company’s supported OS floor and prototype the composer and one end-to-end approval on Mac and the oldest supported phone. I’d budget for an AppKit mapping of the small card profile, not assume a full renderer exists. If the organization cannot maintain native desktop implementations, I’d compare the same task and full-shift measurements in a shared web desktop shell before funding both.

decision.primaryPick: An API-first task ledger in PostgreSQL, with one React review interface for web and desktop
pairings: OpenAPI with a generated SDK and JSON CLI
Company design-system components, with React Aria Components for missing primitives
decision.why:
I’d give agents a work queue and people a decision queue. Neither should have to read a transcript to find out what to do next. Agents can query ready tasks, claim one, checkpoint progress, offer a handoff and request review through a versioned API. A JSON CLI serves unattended jobs; MCP exposes the same scoped reads and commands to interactive agent hosts. Neither needs the desktop app running. Beads is a serious alternative: it already has a dependency graph, atomic claims, persistent agent memory and JSON output. I’d favor it for repo-local, disconnected work. Here I’d pick one online authority because a reviewer’s stop or rejection must govern agents across repos immediately, not after replicas reconcile.

A handoff records the goal, dependencies, exact code revision, evidence, remaining uncertainty and next step. The receiving agent acknowledges that specific checkpoint. A short database transaction checks the actor, active claim and expected version, then records the transition and its audit event together. A retried command returns its original receipt. Expired claims can be reassigned without letting the old worker overwrite the new one. An agent can propose completion; only an authorized person can accept it. Approval names an immutable revision, not the latest branch tip. A downstream runner must check that authorization before acting; changing a badge in the UI is not a stop mechanism.

The review screen leads with ‘Needs your decision’: what changed since last review, evidence linked to the revision, and what accepting will allow. A reviewer can request a change, pause or reassign work without approving it. I’d distinguish ‘pause requested’ from ‘worker stopped’ and keep a reviewer’s selection stable while updates arrive. Web and desktop share that screen and the company’s existing design system. React Aria is an unstyled foundation for gaps, not another visual system. Tauri adds a narrow desktop bridge for things like opening a reviewed revision in the local editor; task data never grants shell access. Electron’s bundled Chromium buys a more uniform desktop renderer, but I wouldn’t ship a separate runtime just for a queue and evidence viewer unless fleet testing justified it.

I’d publish the command schemas, permissions, examples and error fixtures alongside the approved review components. Teams can add integrations against that contract; new transitions, permission scopes or approval controls need named service, design and accessibility owners. CI checks old SDK and desktop versions before a staged release. There is no generic ‘set status’ escape hatch for internal agents.
decision.showItsGood:
My first acceptance test would span two agents and one person. Agent A checkpoints at commit A and exits. B, with no chat history, resumes from the handoff, records a failing test and requests review. While a reviewer examines the evidence, B posts commit B. I’d ask the reviewer to hold the work, explain which commit failed and send it back with a correction. The UI must preserve their note, disclose the newer revision, and never apply an old decision to B. The next agent must receive the correction before claiming more work. I’d repeat with a lost network response, expired lease, revoked reviewer permission and simultaneous claimants. Duplicate effects, a stale approval or a claimed stop that the runner hasn’t acknowledged block release.

I’d automate that scenario through the CLI, MCP, browser and packaged desktop app against the same fixtures, then replay a realistic burst of agent updates and measure handoff recovery time, conflict rates and p95 time for a human decision to reach a runner. In Storybook and Playwright I’d check pending, stale, denied and disconnected states with axe. I’d audit the complete review flow against WCAG 2.2 AA and the desktop policy, testing keyboard only, high zoom, forced colors and actual screen readers in the supported browsers and shells. In particular I’d listen for the stale-evidence warning without having every worker heartbeat announced.

Finally I’d compare the prototype with the current issue/PR workflow using reviewers, including assistive-technology users, working uncoached. Can they identify who owns the next step, which evidence supports it and whether work is truly stopped? I’d track wrong-revision decisions first, then unaided completion, time to the right decision and interruptions per review, separately by client and input method. Faster clicks with worse understanding are a regression. These are proposed tests, not measured results.
decision.unsure: The key unknown is whether every runner can enforce a pause or only acknowledge it at the next checkpoint. I’d verify that end to end before promising a stop time. I’d also inventory disconnected-work requirements and the managed desktop fleet: if offline writes are essential I’d revisit Beads/Dolt for draft checkpoints, keeping binding decisions online. If system-webview accessibility or enterprise deployment fails on a required OS, I’d test the identical review screen in the company’s approved Electron shell before changing UI libraries.

decision.primaryPick: Expo (React Native and Expo Router) for iPhone, Android and web, using the company design system
pairings: Tamagui Core for shared design tokens where the existing components need a native implementation
SQLite on phones and IndexedDB on web for saved recipes, lists and cook sessions
A typed action registry exposed to assistants through the Model Context Protocol (MCP)
decision.why:
I’d design around the moment someone has dough on both hands and needs to know how much flour comes next. Cook mode should show ‘Step 3 of 7’ and the quantity in that step, readable from the counter, with large, separated Back, Repeat and Next controls. Offer opt-in spoken steps and hands-free commands on supported devices; never require speech, swiping or touching a tiny microphone to continue. Keep the display awake only during cooking if the user wants it. Save the recipe version and current step locally so a call or lost Wi-Fi doesn’t send the cook back to the beginning.

Expo Router gives the same recipe a shareable web URL and a native destination, with static rendering for public recipe pages. I’d use semantic headings, ingredient lists and printable instructions on the web rather than force the web page to imitate a phone. Capacitor is a strong alternative if most of the company’s approved UI is already HTML: it can reuse that UI and reach native APIs through plugins. I favor Expo assuming we can reuse the company’s tokens and React components and want native phone controls. Tamagui can map tokens to both native views and web elements; I wouldn’t replace an approved design system or depend on its optional beta native style runtime.

I’d give the assistant the same product actions as the cook, not a way to click through screens. For example, ‘add the soup ingredients for six to Groceries’ calls the same addIngredients command as the button: recipe revision, servings, selected ingredient IDs, destination list and retry key. The handler scales exact quantities, combines only compatible ingredients and units, leaves ‘salt to taste’ intact, and returns the actual changes with Undo. Undo removes that addition, not a housemate’s subsequent edit. Recipe search and saving, list edits, reading or moving between steps, and starting or cancelling timers belong in the same versioned catalog. MCP exposes scoped reads and actions under the user’s delegated authority; sharing or clearing a list requires the same confirmation as in the UI. Device actions target the chosen cook session. ‘Timer scheduled on your phone’ requires a receipt from that device, not just a successful server write.

For many teams, the deliverable is an approved component and action catalog with named owners, schemas, examples and fixtures that coding agents can use. A new product action can’t ship until its UI and assistant paths pass the same state and permission tests. New primitives or permission scopes require design-system, accessibility or privacy review as appropriate. Changes must work with older phone clients before a staged rollout.
decision.showItsGood:
I’d test one meal from shopping to serving. On web, scale a recipe from four to six and ask the assistant to add everything except an ingredient already at home. Drop the reply after the add commits, retry, and inspect the list on a phone. Check the actual quantities, units, exclusions and duplicate count, not just a success toast. Repeat via touch from the same starting state and compare results. Have a second person edit the list before Undo. Then go offline, advance the recipe, lock the phone and reopen it: the saved step, quantities and timer deadline should still be there. If alerts are disabled or a browser can only count down while open, it must say so before the cook relies on it.

I’d run those fixtures in Playwright and native release builds, check web workflows against WCAG 2.2 AA and native ones against the company’s mobile accessibility criteria. I’d use VoiceOver, TalkBack, keyboard, voice control and enlarged text on physical devices. Inspect whether ‘1½ teaspoons’ is read intelligibly, focus lands on the new step, and a countdown doesn’t announce every second. A device lab can’t tell me whether a cook can read from the counter. I’d have home cooks, including people with low vision or limited dexterity, prepare a simple recipe uncoached with the phone on a stand, the extractor fan running and an interruption mid-step. Compare with their usual recipe workflow: wrong quantities or skipped steps, unnecessary touches or hand-washes, time to recover their place, and whether they correctly know which timer will alert. I’d block release on silent quantity changes or claiming a timer was scheduled when it wasn’t. These are acceptance tests I’d run, not results I’ve observed.
decision.unsure: The two biggest unknowns are how well hands-free navigation works with kitchen noise and which background alerts each supported device can actually deliver. Expo documents local notification scheduling on iOS and Android; that is not a guarantee of audible delivery. Browser wake locks can be denied or released. I’d test permission denial, silent mode, battery saver and locked screens on the minimum supported devices, preserve the deadline, and offer a system-timer fallback when necessary. I’d also inventory existing company components before committing to a second rendering stack; a mature, accessible web-only library could tip the choice toward Capacitor.

answer.answer:
My likeliest mistake was treating a shared contract as proof of a shared experience. A command can return the right data while the person holding the phone, reviewing a change, or reading a thread has the wrong idea about what just happened. If these choices went badly, I’d expect three different versions of that failure. This is a premortem, not a report of observed failures.

**Chat: we shipped five renderers but didn’t fund five implementations.** In the bad year, an approval card works with a mouse on the web. On Mac, its button disappears when the approval lands and the screen reader loses the user’s place in the thread. The service correctly records one approval; the employee still asks a colleague whether it went through. Meanwhile, teams wait on the least mature renderer before shipping new cards. I’d now make one busy thread, one approval, and one older-client fallback work on every target before expanding the card catalog. If we couldn’t name an owner for each implementation, I’d revisit the desktop shell decision early.

**Agent workbench: we recorded a decision we couldn’t enforce.** A reviewer presses Pause. The ledger immediately rejects new claims, but a worker already has a job running elsewhere. The reviewer redirects the work believing it has stopped. That’s not a PostgreSQL or MCP failure; I put the authority boundary in the wrong place. My first integration test should have been against a real runner: interrupt it mid-job, disconnect it, and verify exactly which effects can still occur. Until the runner acknowledges a stop, the honest status is ‘Pause requested; last heard from worker at 10:42,’ not ‘Paused.’ I’d settle that before polishing the queue.

**Cooking: we optimized for the demonstration, not dinner.** ‘Next step’ works across a desk but misfires under an extractor fan. A timer has a saved deadline, yet the locked phone makes no sound. The cook has to wash their hands to inspect the screen—the very interruption the app was supposed to prevent. I’d put a release build on a low-end phone on a kitchen stand, deny notifications, turn on the fan, and watch someone finish a recipe. If the large, quiet, no-speech path wasn’t good on its own, better voice recognition wouldn’t rescue the design.

**What slowed the research was deciding what “supported” actually meant.** The Fluent getting-started page and the Apple repository README listed different minimum OS versions. The Adaptive Cards renderer table listed iOS but not AppKit; that was a reason to investigate, not proof either that a Mac renderer existed or that none could be built. Two pages I tried to inspect—React Aria’s Table docs and Storybook’s accessibility-testing docs—exceeded the fetch limit. The project README helped establish intent, not the behavior of our table. Expo documented scheduling a notification, but that didn’t answer the cook’s question: ‘Will I hear it from across the room?’

The biggest missing source was the company itself: its approved components, oldest supported devices, runner controls, and people available to maintain each platform. I researched public architecture more thoroughly than those adoption costs. I didn’t run a build or observe a user. Next time I’d ask for that inventory first and spend the first prototype on the riskiest promise to a person—not on the easiest path to a successful API response.

I didn’t pick Ouro UI, and I missed a relevant option. I’d change the workbench recommendation: **pilot Ouro AX, its agent-facing kit, before building our own action generator and conformance tests.** I would not make Ouro HX, its human-facing components, the company-wide design system on that evidence. Those are separate decisions.

**What I’d gain.** My earlier recommendations said “the button and the agent should call the same action,” but left every team to implement and police that promise. Ouro’s [action model](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui-core/blob/main/docs/guides/actions.md) makes the inputs, label and consent class reviewable in one declaration, generates interfaces such as CLI commands, MCP tools and App Intents, and checks for drift. Its [X-ray](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/guides/ax-conformance.md) can also probe an *existing* interface from outside without requiring us to rebuild it in Ouro. For chat, the [composed-card model](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui#ouro-ui) offers something beyond shared types: an agent can assemble a card from an approved catalog, but a tree that relabels a button or weakens its consent is rejected. None of that is impossible with our current stacks. What we don’t have in those stacks is that combination ready to use and check in CI.

**What would stop me.** On web, the [documented upgrade path](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/guides/installing.md#updating) is to diff copied component files, overwrite them and reapply local edits; component tests are a separate install. That’s workable for one design-system team. It’s a poor default for dozens of teams independently patching the same dialog. On native, the [Android](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/platforms/android.md) and [Windows](https://github.com/ourostack/ouro-ui/blob/main/docs/platforms/windows.md) guides each list eight controls against 125 on web. More consequential than the count: Android reports emulator-only testing, and Windows Server CI doesn’t prove the actions are discoverable on a Windows client. There’s deliberately no React Native kit. I wouldn’t replace the cooking app’s Expo screens just to use the action model, or promise five-client chat parity from a web demo.

**What would make me switch.** I’d have two teams ship one workbench handoff with their existing controls: an agent requests review of commit A; only a reviewer may accept it. Change the commit to B while the reviewer is reading. I want to see the agent refused if it tries to approve, the stale approval rejected by the **service**, the reviewer’s note preserved, and a keyboard or screen-reader user able to tell exactly which commit still needs review. Then deliberately drift the MCP schema and check that CI catches it. Finally, have the second team upgrade the pinned kit without help from the first. If that takes less maintenance than our handwritten bindings and preserves the human workflow, I’d adopt AX. For HX, I’d additionally want one centrally maintained component package and that same critical flow passing on the actual supported devices with the people who use them.

I read the repository and guides; I didn’t run the kit. One reason I’d take the pilot seriously is that Ouro documents its own limit: its X-ray guide reports a conformant build that still failed 30 of 593 scripted flow checks. That’s the right distinction. A green check can establish that an interface kept a particular promise; it can’t establish that a reviewer understood what they approved.
