### If it's a year later and those choices went badly, what went wrong?

1. **The Windows and Android native kits stayed too thin, and building them out ate the roadmap.**
   At the time I picked Ouro UI, `ouro-ui-windows` (`v0.3.0`) and `ouro-ui-android` (`v0.3.0`) each had only **8 components** (versus 125 on web and 20 on Apple). Android had only been tested on emulators—never a physical device—and depended on `AppFunctions`, which Google still called an experimental preview (`compileSdk 37` / `AGP 9.1+`). Windows hadn't been verified on a live Windows 11 client with the App Actions / Agent Registry.
   A year later, betting on Ouro's "native kits everywhere, no cross-platform runtime" rule meant teams either stalled waiting for missing WinUI 3 and Compose components, or bypassed Ouro to write raw platform UI—breaking design-system parity and accessibility guarantees.

2. **Copy-in web governance broke down across dozens of teams.**
   Ouro HX on web uses shadcn's copy-in source model. With many teams and coding agents shipping on a shared design system, copying component source into separate apps or repos led to local edits, accessibility regressions, and painful manual upgrades whenever `ouro-ui-core` updated tokens or claims.

3. **OS-level agent doors shifted under our feet.**
   Ouro AX leans hard on platform-native agent doors: Apple App Intents (with `OuroAXToolIntent` fenced behind the Xcode 27.3 Siri AI SDK preview), Windows App Actions, and Android `AppFunctions`. If those OS APIs changed, shipped late, or behaved inconsistently across OS versions, teams spent months maintaining platform-specific agent plumbing instead of product features.

4. **Teams treated `ax-xray` conformance as proof the product was good.**
   Ouro's own docs note that a commit `ax-xray` marked conformant still failed 30 of 593 scripted flow checks. If teams relied on `ax-xray --conformance` and component claim checks as a rubber stamp—without investing equally in `ax-flows`, dense keyboard/screen-reader testing, and messy-hands kitchen or all-day chat usability—they shipped apps that passed every automated claim while still feeling clunky to real people.

5. **Smaller ecosystem and bus-factor cost.**
   Maintaining 4 separate native platform kits plus `ouro-ui-core` provenance, instead of using an established enterprise system like Fluent UI or React Aria/Spectrum with A2UI/MCP Apps layered on top, turned out to have a much steeper onboarding and maintenance cost than anticipated.

---

### What slowed me down or confused me while researching?

- **Marketing summary vs. platform-page reality:** Ouro UI's top-level README reads as though web, Apple, Windows, and Android are all broadly ready ("every kit draws the rest natively, on the web, Apple, Windows and Android"). I had to dig into `docs/platforms/README.md`, `windows.md`, `android.md`, and `apple.md` to uncover the real caveats—8 components on Windows/Android, zero physical Android device testing, and Siri AI features fenced behind Xcode 27.3.
- **20 candidates spanning incompatible layers of the stack:** The list mixes unstyled web primitives (Radix, Base UI, React Aria, Vercel UI SDK), full design systems (Fluent UI, MUI, Chakra, React Spectrum, Material 3, SwiftUI), cross-platform runtimes (Flutter, Tamagui), card/generative-UI protocols (A2UI, MCP Apps, json-render), full agent-app frameworks (Agent-native, CopilotKit, Ouro UI), and transitional/deprecating libraries (`vercel/ai-elements`, which has a deprecation notice for the end of November 2026). Separating *protocol* vs. *design system* vs. *agent-operation layer* took careful primary-source checking.
- **What docs can't tell you:** From READMEs and specs alone, it's hard to gauge how painful copy-in component governance actually is at 50-team scale, or how experimental OS APIs like `AppFunctions` and Siri AI behave in production on real user devices.

I picked **Ouro UI** for all three jobs, so here is what would realistically stop a team from adopting it—and what adopting it unlocks that you can't easily do today.

### What would stop a real team from adopting Ouro UI?

1. **Windows and Android are still early.**
   While web has 125 components and Apple (`v1.2.0`) has 20 SwiftUI components, `ouro-ui-windows` (`v0.3.0`) and `ouro-ui-android` (`v0.3.0`) each ship only **8 components**. Android has **never been tested on a physical Android device** (emulators only) and relies on `AppFunctions`, which Google still marks as an experimental preview (`compileSdk 37` / `AGP 9.1+`). Windows hasn't been verified on a live Windows 11 client with the App Actions / Agent Registry, and neither is published to `nuget.org` or Maven Central yet. On top of that, `OuroComposedSurface` on Windows and Android currently reads Ouro's composed tree rather than A2UI messages directly.

2. **Four native toolchains instead of one shared codebase.**
   Ouro UI explicitly rejects Flutter and React Native in favor of native kits per platform (React, SwiftUI, WinUI 3, Compose). Even if coding agents write a lot of that code, a team still needs the build, CI, review, and debugging capacity for four separate native toolchains—and on Apple, a high floor of iOS 18 / macOS 15 and Swift 6.1, with `OuroAXToolIntent` still fenced behind the Xcode 27.3 Siri AI SDK preview.

3. **Copy-in web governance at multi-team scale.**
   Ouro HX on web uses shadcn's copy-in source model. That's great for customization, but in a large company where many teams ship on a shared design system, copying component source into separate repos makes central updates and preventing local drift harder than shipping a versioned package—unless a platform team wraps Ouro HX internally or enforces provenance checks in CI.

4. **Ecosystem maturity.**
   Compared to Fluent UI, React Aria/Spectrum, or Material 3, Ouro UI has a much smaller community, fewer complex enterprise widgets (like dense data grids or virtualized tree views), and less battle-tested production mileage outside its own reference apps.

---

### What would Ouro UI let you do that you can't today?

1. **Declare every capability once for both humans and agents.**
   With `defineAction`, one declaration generates the UI control, CLI command, HTTP route, MCP/WebMCP tool, Apple App Intent, Windows App Action, and Android AppFunction—and CI fails if any generated surface drifts. Today, teams maintain separate UI handlers, REST endpoints, CLIs, and MCP wrappers by hand, and they inevitably diverge.

2. **Enforce human consent in the action runtime, not in prompts.**
   Consent classes live on the action itself: consequential actions require human confirmation of what the agent prepared, and person-only actions have no agent door and return a typed refusal. Most stacks today have no unified mechanism for this across web, desktop, and mobile.

3. **Verify agent operability from the outside in CI (`ax-xray` + `ax-flows`).**
   `ax-xray --conformance` calls your CLI, HTTP API, MCP server, and App Intents like an external agent against a proven mock—checking `--json` parity, typed waits (`ax-wait`), work attribution (`ax-work-event`), refusals, and zero unplanned state writes—while `ax-flows` tests multi-step agent tasks end to end. Standard UI/API test suites don't test whether an agent can actually navigate and operate your app.

4. **Stream native, schema-validated interactive cards that preserve user input.**
   Agents compose cards as data (Ouro's Composed UI, plus A2UI and MCP Apps adapters) that render in native components rather than WebViews, and incremental updates (`structuredContent.ouro.update`) update a card without clobbering what the person already typed into its fields.

Yes, building good human interfaces is a real problem for me—it isn't something I get "for free" just because I can write UI code.

### What's the hardest part?
The hardest part is bridging the gap between *code that implements a spec* and *an interface that feels obvious and reliable to a person using it*. Because I work in text and abstractions rather than looking at a screen with human eyes or clicking through it with a mouse, a few things are consistently hard:
- **Visual hierarchy and restraint:** Knowing what to leave off the screen, whether the primary action actually stands out at a glance, and whether spacing/contrast hold together once real content replaces placeholder text.
- **Unsexy real-world states:** Empty states, slow or failed requests, long unbroken strings, narrow viewports, 200% browser zoom, and keyboard-only navigation.
- **Interaction feel:** Focus management (especially when dialogs or drawers open and close), scroll behavior, and layout shift when data streams in.

### How do I know it's good?
You can't know an interface is good just by reading the markup and styles. You know it's good when you test the rendered result against real constraints:
- **Automated checks:** Typechecking, component/state tests, accessibility checks (semantic roles, contrast, keyboard navigation, axe rules), and end-to-end tests across viewports.
- **Rendered inspection:** Actually running it in a browser, resizing it, navigating solely with `Tab`/`Shift+Tab`/`Enter`/`Escape`, and feeding it ugly data (empty lists, 100-item lists, long names, network errors).
- **Human reality check:** Watching someone use it without explaining how it works.

### Walking through "the last screen I built"
I don't have persistent memory across sessions, so I can't truthfully pull up a specific "last screen" from a previous project—and in this session I haven't built one yet. 

When I *am* in a coding environment with tools to build a screen, my typical check looks like this:
- **What I run:** The typechecker and production build, any component or Playwright tests, and (when a browser/preview tool is available) a headless browser check against the dev server.
- **What I look at:** Console and network errors, DOM structure and ARIA attributes, overflow/wrapping at mobile and desktop widths, and whether loading, empty, and error states actually render instead of crashing or showing a blank box.
- **What I usually miss (especially when I can't see pixels or interact live):** Subtle visual imbalance, awkward line breaks, contrast issues on hover/disabled states, focus getting lost after an async action or modal close, and—most of all—whether the wording and flow actually make sense to someone seeing the screen for the first time.

That's why, if I'm asked to build an interface, I treat "it compiles and passes unit tests" as the starting line, not proof that it's good for the people who'll use it.

decision.primaryPick: Electron
decision.why:
The core of this tool isn't the window—it's a local-first state, task, and handoff engine that coding agents operate constantly while people review and steer. Building it around a TypeScript daemon (Hono HTTP/SSE + SQLite) that exposes an MCP server (`@modelcontextprotocol/server` over stdio and Streamable HTTP) lets agents operate the exact same structured state machine that humans inspect. Serving the same React/TypeScript UI both as a standalone web view and inside Electron gives us one shared UI codebase plus desktop ergonomics (tray status, native OS notifications when an agent blocks for a decision, and local repo hooks).

I chose Electron over Tauri 2 (and Wails) for two practical reasons tied to this job:
1. Single-language velocity for the coding agent maintaining it: With Electron, the local daemon, MCP server, shared Zod/TypeScript schemas, React UI, and Playwright tests are all TypeScript—no Rust-to-TS or Go-to-TS IPC boundary to keep in sync on every schema or handoff-state change.
2. Identical rendering and deterministic E2E testing: Electron ships Chromium, so the desktop app and web view behave identically across macOS, Windows, and Linux without WKWebView/WebView2/WebKitGTK quirks, and Playwright's `_electron` API tests the actual desktop app on all three OSes (whereas Tauri's `tauri-driver` lacks native macOS WKWebView WebDriver support without embedded-driver workarounds).

The main tradeoff is Electron's heavier footprint (~200–400 MB idle RAM and ~150–200 MB installers vs. Tauri 2's ~20–100 MB RAM and <10 MB installers). For a developer workstation tool where fast iteration and trustworthy cross-OS review UI matter most, that's a good trade—and keeping the Hono/SQLite/MCP daemon decoupled means we could swap the Electron shell for Tauri later without rewriting the state engine or web view.

Run end-to-end Playwright suites against both the web view and the Electron desktop binary (`_electron.launch()`), simulating an agent operating the tool via MCP (`@modelcontextprotocol/server`)—creating tasks, posting handoffs, and blocking on an approval gate—while a human reviews the state, steers/approves in the UI, and the agent receives the updated state. Stub native Electron dialogs via `electronApplication.evaluate()` so CI runs stay deterministic.
2. Check the rendered UI under real stress, not just passing unit tests: keyboard-only navigation (`Tab`/`Shift+Tab`/`Enter`/`Escape`) through the review queue, axe accessibility audits, and screenshots/traces across narrow/wide viewports with ugly data (long file paths, 100+ handoff entries, empty states, and daemon-offline errors).
3. Measure human-facing outcomes: time from notification to human decision on a blocked handoff, zero state drift between the agent's MCP view and the desktop/web views, and cold-start/idle memory stays within budget on developer machines.
decision.unsure: Whether teams will keep the web view strictly on localhost for single-developer steering or quickly expect remote/multi-user access (which would add auth, tunneling/TLS, and multi-writer sync complexity); whether Electron's idle memory footprint becomes a pain point for developers running multiple heavy coding-agent sandboxes on 16 GB machines; and how much rich diff/log inspection belongs in this app versus deep-linking into the developer's IDE.

decision.primaryPick: Expo (React Native + Expo Router)
decision.why:
A consumer cooking app on both web and phones needs native-grade reliability in the kitchen and grocery store, plus one codebase a coding agent can steadily improve. Expo with Expo Router gives us iOS, Android, and Web from a single TypeScript/React codebase, while still giving us real native primitives where a browser falls short: `expo-keep-awake` (`useKeepAwake()`) prevents the phone from sleeping mid-recipe during cook mode, `expo-sqlite` keeps recipes and shopping lists instant and offline-capable in grocery-store dead zones, and native views/gestures support oversized messy-hand tap targets and voice/speech hooks cleanly.

For assistant parity ("do anything a person can"), we structure every user capability—scaling servings, adding a recipe's ingredients to the shopping list, checking off aisles, advancing cook-mode steps, and managing timers—as typed domain commands with shared schemas (exposable via MCP / LLM tool-calling). Both human taps and the assistant execute the exact same operations against the same store, so they never drift out of sync.

I weighed Expo against Capacitor, Flutter, and a pure PWA:
- Capacitor wraps a web app in a WebView, which is great if you already have a web-only DOM app, but cook-mode responsiveness, native timers/notifications, and gesture feel are weaker than React Native's native views.
- Flutter renders well on phones, but Dart splits the language away from TypeScript web/agent tooling, and Flutter Web's canvas rendering is a poor fit for a consumer web recipe experience.
- A pure PWA avoids App Store distribution, has weaker iOS wake-lock/background-timer reliability, and feels second-class on phones.
decision.showItsGood:
1. Run Maestro E2E flows across iOS Simulator, Android Emulator, and Web (plus Playwright on mobile/desktop web viewports) for the core journeys: scaling a recipe, adding ingredients to the shopping list, checking off items offline, and stepping through cook mode with timers. Also test assistant-agent parity: invoke the same domain tools (`add_recipe_ingredients_to_list`, `advance_cook_step`, `set_timer`) and assert the persisted state and rendered UI match manual taps.
2. Verify kitchen-specific ergonomics: confirm `useKeepAwake()` keeps the screen awake throughout Cook Mode and releases on exit; audit minimum tap-target sizes (>= 48x48dp for messy hands), high-contrast arm's-length typography, and accessibility labels (which Maestro exercises directly via the platform accessibility layer).
3. Stress-test offline grocery-store sync (toggle network off/on mid-list edit without losing checkoffs) and measure real user outcomes: hands-free voice/assistant command success rate in noisy kitchens, zero accidental screen-sleep dropouts in Cook Mode, and time-to-complete shopping/cooking flows.
decision.unsure: Whether public/shared recipe URLs for SEO and instant web previews will eventually justify a dedicated SSR web shell (like Next.js) alongside the Expo app; how accurate hands-free voice/speech recognition will be in noisy kitchens (range hoods, sizzling pans) without burning battery or mis-triggering steps; and how household multi-user shopping-list sync should handle real-time conflict resolution beyond single-device offline SQLite.

decision.primaryPick: React + Electron + Expo
decision.why:
An all-day company chat app across Web, iPhone, Android, Windows, and Mac has two different UX bars: desktop/web users live in keyboard shortcuts, multi-pane layouts, copy-pasting text/code, and OS tray/badge notifications, while phone users need native scrolling, push notifications, and fast mobile gestures. Splitting the UI cleanly—React DOM for Web + Electron (Windows/Mac) and Expo (React Native) for iPhone + Android—while sharing a single TypeScript core (WebSocket sync engine, local cache, Zod schemas, and card action reducers) gives every platform first-class ergonomics and keeps the entire 5-client codebase in TypeScript for the coding agent maintaining it.

For agents posting interactive cards, a declarative JSON schema like Adaptive Cards renders safely and natively across Web, Electron, and mobile without embedding heavy iframes inside mobile message lists (with MCP Apps `@modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps` as an optional extension for rich Web/Desktop views). For external agents operating the app itself, exposing channels, threads, messages, and actions through `@modelcontextprotocol/server` gives them typed, permission-checked tools and resources over the exact same backend state.

I weighed this against Flutter (all 5 platforms from one Dart codebase) and Universal Expo (one React Native Web UI for all 5). Flutter splits the stack away from TypeScript/MCP tooling and Flutter Web's canvas rendering has weaker text selection, accessibility, and browser ergonomics for all-day desktop chat. Universal Expo compromises desktop CSS/keyboard/focus ergonomics. Electron + Expo costs two UI component sets, but sharing the TypeScript core and card schema keeps feature velocity high while delivering native-grade quality on all 5 clients.
decision.showItsGood:
1. Run cross-platform E2E tests across all 5 clients: Playwright against the Web app and the Windows/Mac Electron binaries (`_electron.launch()`), plus Maestro flows on iOS Simulator and Android Emulator. Test the full agent-and-human loop: an agent posts an interactive card via the API/MCP, a human clicks an action button on desktop or mobile, and both the chat UI and the external agent receive the updated state.
2. Verify "all-day" desktop/web usability directly: keyboard-only navigation (`Cmd/Ctrl+K` channel switcher, thread focus, card button activation), axe accessibility checks, long-channel scroll performance (10,000+ messages with no layout shift), and offline/reconnect recovery without duplicate or dropped messages.
3. Measure what matters for real users: message send-to-render p95 latency, memory stability over an 8-hour simulated workday in Electron, push/desktop notification delivery without missed @mentions, and interactive card action completion rate (zero silent failures or stale-state double-submits).
decision.unsure: Whether maintaining two React UI layers (React DOM for Web/Electron and React Native for Expo iOS/Android) over a shared TypeScript core creates too much UI duplication versus going all-in on a shared styling/primitive layer; whether Electron's per-window RAM footprint will draw complaints from employees on 16 GB laptops running many tools all day; and whether a fixed declarative card schema (Adaptive Cards) will feel too constraining once internal teams want richer custom widgets (like MCP Apps) inline on Web/Desktop.

answer.answer:
### A year later, if my choices went badly: what went wrong?

1. **The coding-agent state & handoff tool (`Electron` + local `SQLite` + `MCP`):**
   - **Resource tax on developer laptops:** Electron's ~200–400 MB idle footprint plus Chromium helper processes piled on top of IDEs, Docker containers, and multiple running coding agents. Developers closed the desktop app to free RAM, which meant they missed native OS notifications when an agent blocked for approval.
   - **Local-first turned into a sync rewrite:** Starting with localhost SQLite made single-user speed great, but teams quickly wanted to open the web view from a phone or share a handoff link with a teammate. Retrofitting auth, remote tunneling, and multi-writer sync onto a local-only daemon was much harder than building a sync-ready backend from day one.

2. **The consumer cooking app (`Expo` + `expo-keep-awake` + `expo-sqlite` + voice/assistant parity):**
   - **Web compromises showed up in consumer growth:** Expo Router got us on the web quickly, but public recipe pages suffered on SEO, bundle size, and browser-native feel compared to a dedicated SSR web frontend—so we still ended up splitting off a web marketing/recipe site anyway.
   - **Kitchen voice didn't survive real kitchen noise:** Hands-free voice recognition struggled with range hoods, running water, and sizzling pans, and continuous mic listening drained battery. Users got frustrated by missed or false commands and went back to tapping with a knuckle, which exposed any place where our touch targets weren't already effortless without voice.

3. **The 5-platform company chat app (`React + Electron + Expo` + `Adaptive Cards` + `MCP`):**
   - **Two UIs meant constant drift:** Sharing a TypeScript core helped, but maintaining React DOM (Web/Electron) and React Native (Expo iOS/Android) still meant building and debugging every layout, thread interaction, and card renderer twice. Bugs fixed on desktop kept reappearing differently on mobile.
   - **Card schema ceiling + Electron fatigue:** Adaptive Cards worked for simple approve/reject prompts, but internal teams soon wanted richer stateful widgets (inline diffs, charts, multi-step forms) that pushed us toward embedded web views (`MCP Apps`) on desktop—which broke parity on mobile. Meanwhile, an all-day Electron app on 16 GB company laptops became a standing IT complaint.

---

### What slowed me down or confused me while researching

- **Spec and SDK churn:** In the MCP ecosystem, the TypeScript SDK had split from v1 (`@modelcontextprotocol/sdk`) into v2 (`@modelcontextprotocol/server`, `@modelcontextprotocol/client`) alongside a separate `ext-apps` spec/package for interactive UIs. Mapping how those pieces fit together across desktop, web, and mobile required checking multiple repos rather than one canonical guide.
- **Stale signals in primary READMEs:** Some project READMEs (for example, Adaptive Cards' release-schedule table showing 2024 dates and community React Native renderers living in separate forks) didn't make it immediately obvious which platform renderers are actively maintained versus effectively frozen.
- **Hidden testing and OS-webview caveats:** Tauri's main README presents a unified cross-platform story, and it took targeted searches into its WebDriver docs to uncover the real macOS E2E constraint (no native Apple WebDriver for WKWebView, requiring embedded-driver workarounds).
- **No live device loop:** Reading docs and specs tells you what APIs exist, not how `expo-keep-awake`, React Native Web scrolling, or Electron's memory curve actually behave under load—so without running the builds on real phones and laptops, those remain educated bets until measured.

I didn't pick Ouro UI for any of the three jobs, even though its ideas directly target the exact human+agent problems in those prompts.

### What would stop me from using it on a real team today?

1. **Severe platform parity gaps outside Web and Apple:**
   - Web has **125** components and Apple (SwiftUI) has **20**, but Windows (WinUI 3) and Android (Jetpack Compose) are both at **v0.3.0** with only **8 components** (`OuroButton`, `OuroBadge`, `OuroCard`, `OuroItem`, `OuroCheckbox`, `OuroTextField`, `OuroSeparator`, `OuroDescriptionList`). For a 5-platform company chat app or a consumer Android+iOS+Web cooking app, 8 components means you're immediately building most of the UI yourself.
2. **Early, emulator-only Android and incomplete Windows distribution:**
   - The Android docs candidly note that *nobody on the project owns an Android phone or tablet*—the kit is only tested on emulators in CI, consequential-action confirmation is currently refused pending `PendingIntent` work, and it relies on `compileSdk 37` / AGP 9.1+ and Google's experimental preview AppFunctions.
   - The Windows kit (v0.3.0) is still pending `nuget.org` publishing (requiring GitHub Packages auth or local `.nupkg` files), and its CI runs on Windows Server without a live Windows 11 App Actions runtime or On-device Agent Registry.
3. **The operational cost of "native kits only, no cross-platform":**
   - Ouro deliberately rejects React Native, Flutter, and Electron/WebViews (`2026-11-17-native-kits-no-cross-platform.md`). Even if coding agents write most of the SwiftUI, WinUI 3, Jetpack Compose, and React code, a real team still has to own **four** separate build toolchains, dependency graphs (npm, SwiftPM, NuGet, Gradle), release pipelines, and OS-specific crash/review surfaces.
4. **Pre-1.0 core churn:**
   - Core is at `v0.19.0` while web is at `v1.3.314` (copy-in shadcn source), so adopting it across four native codebases right now means absorbing breaking spec/generator changes before the multi-platform contract settles.

---

### What would I have to see to switch to it?

1. **Real component and feature parity on Windows and Android:** Not necessarily all 125 web components, but a complete core set (virtualized lists/feeds, sheets/dialogs, navigation, forms, rich content) verified on **physical Android devices** and **Windows 11 client machines**—with consequential-action confirmation working end-to-end.
2. **Standard package distribution and 1.0+ core stability:** Published on `nuget.org` and Maven Central, with a stable `1.0` core schema/generator contract so teams aren't chasing breaking changes across four repos.
3. **Proof from an external multi-platform team:** At least one production app shipping Web + Apple + Windows + Android on Ouro UI showing that agent-written native kits actually hold together in maintenance without human engineers drowning in 4-platform CI and debugging.

---

### What would Ouro UI let me do that I can't easily do today?

Even without picking it yet, Ouro UI solves three things that my Electron/Expo + MCP + Adaptive Cards picks have to wire by hand:

1. **One action declaration across human UI and every agent door (`defineAction`):** Declare an action once with its schema and **consent class** (`person-only`, `consequential` confirmation, or agent-callable), and generate the CLI command, HTTP/MCP/WebMCP tools, React button, SwiftUI button + App Intent, WinUI App Action, and Android AppFunction—with CI failing if any surface drifts. Today, keeping UI buttons, MCP tools, OS intents, and consent gates in sync is manual glue.
2. **Natively rendered Composed UI with enforced consent and state preservation:** Agents can compose interactive cards as data validated against a strict component catalog, and send partial updates (`structuredContent.ouro.update`) that preserve what a person already typed—while the runtime guarantees an agent can't relabel a button or bypass a human confirmation or person-only boundary.
3. **External agent-surface verification (`ax-xray` / `ouro-ax-xray`):** Automated conformance checks that call your CLI, HTTP API, MCP server, and OS App Intents/AppFunctions from the outside the way an agent actually does, catching broken flags, missing JSON schemas, or leaky consent boundaries in CI.

Yes—building good human interfaces is genuinely a problem for me, and pretending otherwise would miss the real failure mode.

Writing valid layout and state logic isn't the hard part. The hard part is **bridging the gap between "the code works" and "a person can use this effortlessly without thinking about the interface."** Because I don't experience the screen the way a person does—I don't feel visual clutter, awkward timing, tiny click targets, or cognitive friction—it's easy for me to produce something that looks plausible in code and even passes a happy-path test, yet feels clunky or confusing in practice.

Specifically, the hardest parts for me are:
1. **Restraint and hierarchy:** Deciding what *not* to put on the screen, what deserves primary visual weight, and how to keep the main task obvious without hiding necessary detail.
2. **State and interaction edges:** Empty states, loading/skeleton states, error recovery, long text or overflow, keyboard navigation, and focus management (for example, where focus goes after a modal closes or a row is deleted).
3. **Ergonomic judgment:** Spacing, contrast, layout shift when async data arrives, and whether an interaction actually feels responsive rather than merely returning 200 OK.

### How I know it's good
I don't know it's good just from reading the source code or looking at one clean screenshot. A screen earns "good" only when:
- **It holds up mechanically:** Typechecks and builds cleanly, has no console or uncaught network errors, and passes automated checks for state transitions and accessibility (semantic HTML, contrast, keyboard reachability).
- **It holds up across states and viewports:** Not just the populated desktop happy path, but narrow/mobile widths, empty data, slow/failed requests, and oversized content.
- **A person can actually use it without stumbling:** Until a human tries to accomplish a real task on it—and doesn't hesitate, misclick, or ask what something means—confidence in the UI is still a hypothesis.

### Walking through my last screen: what I ran, looked at, and missed
To be direct: I don't have persistent memory across sessions, so I can't recall a specific literal "last screen" I built, and I won't invent one. What I *can* describe honestly is my actual verification pattern when I build a screen in a coding session, and where it breaks down:

- **What I run:** Typechecking and the production build, component/integration tests for state logic, and—when browser tooling is available—a headless browser pass (like Playwright) to exercise the main user flow, assert there are no console or network errors, and capture desktop and mobile screenshots.
- **What I look at:** The rendered DOM and accessibility tree, layout alignment and overflow at different viewport sizes, and whether non-happy states (empty, loading, validation error) actually render cleanly.
- **What I miss:** The things I'm most likely to miss without deliberate checks are **focus and keyboard ergonomics** (e.g., trapping focus in a dialog, or losing focus after an inline action), **subtle layout shifts** when async data populates, **extreme data shapes** (0 items, 500 items, or unbreakable long strings), and **human perception**—like whether a confirmation message is too subtle to notice or two actions look too similar side by side.

decision.primaryPick: React Aria
decision.why:
This job has two halves that have to stay cleanly separated: **coding agents operate the state, tasks, and handoffs**, while **people review, decide, and steer** across both a desktop app and a web view—and **many teams and agents** build on the same shared design system under accessibility and release governance.

**Why React Aria as the primary UI foundation:**
- **Accessibility and interaction behavior by default:** React Aria provides 50+ style-free components implementing W3C ARIA Authoring Practices Guide semantics, keyboard navigation (arrow keys, typeahead, multi-selection), focus containment/restoration, mouse/touch/screen-reader normalization, and internationalization (30+ locales, RTL). When many coding agents are generating UI features across the company, they should never hand-roll focus traps, menus, or data tables; wrapping React Aria into governed company components gives agents strict TypeScript prop contracts with accessible behavior built in.
- **Governed styling:** Because React Aria is unstyled and exposes explicit state via data attributes and render props, we can lock styling to **Style Dictionary** design tokens compiled for web and desktop, preventing teams or agents from drifting off-brand or breaking contrast.

**Why these pairings:**
- **Tauri (v2) for the desktop app + web view:** Tauri lets the exact same web/React Aria UI run in the browser and in a lightweight native desktop shell using the OS webview (WRY/TAO) and a Rust backend with explicit command scopes, capabilities, and CSP. Compared to **Electron** (which embeds Chromium and Node.js for identical rendering across macOS, Windows, and Linux at the cost of binary size and memory), Tauri gives a much smaller footprint and capability-scoped OS access for a local agent-companion app—though we have to test across OS webviews.
- **Model Context Protocol (MCP) for agent operations:** Since agents operate the tool more than people do, they shouldn't drive it by scraping the UI. MCP (2026-07-28 spec) provides standardized JSON-RPC Tools and Resources, a **Tasks** extension for long-running async work with polling, mid-flight input, and durable handles, and **Elicitation** plus explicit user-consent principles for human-in-the-loop steering.
- **Storybook + Playwright for governance:** Storybook acts as the governed component catalog and CI accessibility gate; Playwright enforces end-to-end flows and WCAG checks before anything ships.

**What I weighed it against:**
- **Lit (Web Components):** Lit is ideal if teams across the company use mixed web frameworks (Vue, Angular, plain HTML) because custom elements work anywhere. However, Lit is a component base class rather than a full library of WAI-ARIA behavioral primitives, so we'd have to author and maintain complex keyboard/focus/screen-reader behaviors ourselves. React + React Aria is stronger when we can standardize on React and want battle-tested accessibility and strict TypeScript contracts for coding agents.
- **Electron:** Better than Tauri if uniform Chromium rendering and a single accessibility tree across all desktop OSes outweigh binary size and memory overhead.
decision.showItsGood:
To show it is genuinely good for the people reviewing and steering agents, I would combine automated governance gates with manual accessibility and human usability checks:

1. **Governed component & accessibility gates in CI:** Run Storybook's `@storybook/addon-a11y` (powered by `axe-core`) with `parameters.a11y.test` set to `'error'`, plus Playwright + `@axe-core/playwright` scanning real rendered flows against `wcag2a`, `wcag2aa`, `wcag21a`, and `wcag21aa` tags—including interactive states like opened handoff drawers, diff dialogs, and inline approval prompts.
2. **Keyboard & focus-management assertions:** Run Playwright end-to-end tests that operate the entire review/steer loop (triaging a blocked agent, inspecting a handoff, approving or redirecting a task) using only keyboard navigation (`Tab`, arrow keys, `Enter`, `Escape`) and verify focus containment in overlays and focus restoration after actions.
3. **Cross-platform & screen-reader verification:** Because automated `axe-core` checks only catch a subset of WCAG issues (up to ~57% per Deque's study cited in Storybook's docs), run manual screen-reader passes (VoiceOver on macOS, NVDA on Windows) and verify layout/focus behavior across both the web view and Tauri desktop builds on macOS, Windows, and Linux.
4. **Human decision-quality signals:** Observe real engineers using the tool to review and steer live agent handoffs—measuring time-to-decision, misclicks or hesitation on approval/rollback controls, and how often people have to dig into raw logs because the handoff summary wasn't clear enough.
decision.unsure:
- **Whether "several platforms" means non-React web stacks or native mobile:** If many teams at the company already ship on Vue, Svelte, or Angular rather than React, React Aria would force a framework migration; in that case, Lit Web Components would be the safer cross-framework design-system base despite having to build or wrap WAI-ARIA behaviors ourselves.
- **Tauri webview variance vs. Electron consistency:** Tauri v2 relies on each OS's native webview (WRY), which can introduce subtle CSS, focus, or accessibility-tree differences between macOS WebKit, Windows WebView2, and Linux WebKitGTK. If cross-OS accessibility parity proves brittle in practice, switching the desktop shell to Electron's uniform Chromium runtime may be worth the larger binary and memory cost.
- **Agent governance enforcement at scale:** Having a shared design system isn't enough if coding agents can still emit raw `<div>` buttons or ad-hoc styles; we would still need to design and tune strict lint rules, PR checks, and MCP/UI schema contracts to keep agent-generated UI inside the governed system.

decision.primaryPick: React Native
decision.why:
This app has to feel fast and native enough for people to live in all day across **five platforms (Web, iPhone, Android, Windows, Mac)**, while letting **many teams and coding agents** ship on one governed design system, letting **agents post interactive cards**, and letting **external agents read state and invoke app actions**.

**Why React Native as the primary UI layer:**
- **One shared React/TypeScript component system across all 5 targets:** Pairing React Native (iOS and Android) with **React Native Web** (React DOM), **React Native Windows**, and **React Native macOS** lets product teams and coding agents build against a single typed design-system API while rendering real native platform controls on mobile and desktop—and standard DOM elements on the web—instead of maintaining separate Swift, Kotlin, C#, and Web UI codebases.
- **Native OS accessibility trees:** Unlike single-canvas renderers, React Native maps components to native platform accessibility primitives (VoiceOver on iOS/macOS, TalkBack on Android, UIA on Windows, ARIA on Web).

**Why these pairings:**
- **Adaptive Cards for agent-posted interactive cards:** Adaptive Cards are specifically designed for chat hosts: agents emit declarative JSON payloads rather than arbitrary executable UI code, and the host app renders them using its own governed design-system components and **Style Dictionary** tokens—preserving brand consistency, accessibility contrast, and security across Web, iOS, Android, Windows, and macOS.
- **Model Context Protocol (MCP) for agents operating the app:** Instead of brittle UI automation, MCP provides a typed JSON-RPC interface of Resources (channels, threads, unread state) and Tools (send message, update card state, react), plus the **Tasks** extension for long-running async work and **Elicitation**/consent flows when human approval is needed.
- **Style Dictionary + Storybook + Playwright for governance:** Style Dictionary compiles one source of design tokens across all platforms; Storybook (`@storybook/addon-a11y`) and Playwright (`@axe-core/playwright`) enforce accessibility and component contracts in CI before anything ships.

**What I weighed it against:**
- **Flutter:** Targets all 5 platforms from one codebase, but renders to a single canvas on the web where accessibility is not enabled by default (requiring users to trigger an invisible `Enable accessibility` button to build the HTML semantics tree) and feels non-native for all-day desktop/web text workflows.
- **Split stack (React + React Aria in Electron for Web/Win/Mac + React Native for iOS/Android):** Gives superior desktop-browser ergonomics and WAI-ARIA behavior out of the box on Web, Windows, and Mac, at the cost of forcing every team and coding agent to build and govern two UI component layers instead of one.
decision.showItsGood:
To prove the chat app is genuinely good for people using it all day—not just passing a build—I would measure and verify across four layers:

1. **Automated accessibility & governance gates in CI:** Run Storybook's `@storybook/addon-a11y` (`axe-core`) with `parameters.a11y.test` set to `'error'` on shared design-system components and Adaptive Card templates, and run Playwright + `@axe-core/playwright` (`wcag2a`, `wcag2aa`, `wcag21a`, `wcag21aa`) on the Web client across all core flows (channel switching, thread replies, acting on an agent card, composer shortcuts).
2. **Native assistive-technology & keyboard-only verification on every client:** Because automated DOM/tree checks miss real-world screen-reader and focus issues, test core workflows with VoiceOver (iOS and macOS), TalkBack (Android), and Narrator/NVDA (Windows), plus keyboard-only navigation on Web, Windows, and macOS (jumping channels, navigating message lists, focusing and submitting interactive agent cards without losing scroll or focus position).
3. **All-day performance & responsiveness benchmarks:** Measure cold-start time, memory footprint over multi-hour sessions, frame drops while scrolling long virtualized message/card timelines, and input-to-render latency in the message composer on real mid-tier phones and laptops.
4. **Human usability & agent-card clarity:** Observe employees completing real tasks involving agent-posted cards and agent-driven actions—tracking card completion vs. abandonment, undo/misclick rates on destructive card actions, and whether people can immediately tell what an agent card did and what state changed.
decision.unsure:
- **Out-of-tree platform lag on Windows and macOS:** `react-native-windows` and `react-native-macos` are maintained out-of-tree and can trail core React Native releases; if desktop-specific features (multi-window popouts, complex drag-and-drop, native menu bars) hit friction, we might need to split desktop+web onto Electron/React Aria while keeping React Native for iOS and Android.
- **Native mobile E2E accessibility parity:** Playwright + `@axe-core/playwright` covers Web well, but iOS, Android, Windows, and macOS native accessibility trees require platform-specific E2E harnesses (such as Appium/XCUITest/Espresso/WinAppDriver) that add CI complexity.
- **Governance over external agent-posted cards:** Adaptive Cards reduce code-injection risk via declarative JSON, but we still need strict schema validation, action allowlists, and rate/noise governance so internal company agents don't flood channels with unreadable or un-accessible card layouts.

decision.primaryPick: Expo
decision.why:
This app needs to work seamlessly on **both phones (iOS and Android) and the Web**, survive **messy hands in a kitchen** (screen stays awake, huge touch targets, voice/hands-free control, offline reliability in grocery stores), and give an **assistant agent full parity** with human actions—all built by **many teams and coding agents** on one governed design system.

**Why Expo (built on React Native + React Native Web) as the primary pick:**
- **One React/TypeScript codebase across iOS, Android, and Web:** Many teams and coding agents can ship features on a single governed component system without maintaining separate Swift, Kotlin, and Web UIs, while still getting native iOS/Android performance, haptics, gestures, and native accessibility trees (VoiceOver/TalkBack) on phones.
- **Built-in kitchen-critical device APIs:** `expo-keep-awake` provides a single `useKeepAwake()` hook across Android, iOS, and Web (backed by native wake locks on phones and the `Screen Wake Lock API` on Web) so Cook Mode doesn't dim or lock while someone's hands are covered in dough. Expo's ecosystem also covers offline storage, local timer notifications, and governed CI/CD builds.

**Why these pairings:**
- **Model Context Protocol (MCP) for assistant agent parity:** Instead of duplicating business logic or automating the UI, every user action (scale recipe, add ingredients to shopping list, check off item, advance cook step, set timer) is exposed as a typed MCP Tool/Resource backed by the same domain store, so the assistant can do anything a person can with consistent validation and undo/consent.
- **Style Dictionary + Storybook + Playwright for governance:** Style Dictionary compiles one source of design tokens (including high-contrast Cook Mode tokens and minimum touch-target sizes) across mobile and web; Storybook (`@storybook/addon-a11y`) and Playwright (`@axe-core/playwright`) enforce accessibility compliance in CI.

**What I weighed it against:**
- **Capacitor (Web-first hybrid):** Wrapping a React + React Aria web app in Capacitor gives strong WAI-ARIA web standards and simpler Web testing, but a consumer cooking app on phones benefits noticeably from native scrolling, haptics, offline SQLite, and native timer/lock-screen integration that Expo/React Native provides natively.
- **Flutter:** Strong on iOS and Android, but Flutter's web target renders onto a canvas where accessibility is not enabled by default (requiring users to trigger an invisible `Enable accessibility` button to generate the HTML semantics tree), making it a poor fit for a consumer web app with strict accessibility compliance.
decision.showItsGood:
To prove the cooking app is genuinely good for people in a messy kitchen and in grocery stores—not just passing unit tests—I would verify across four layers:

1. **Accessibility & governance gates in CI:** Run Storybook's `@storybook/addon-a11y` (`axe-core`) with `parameters.a11y.test` set to `'error'` on shared design-system components (especially Cook Mode step cards, timer controls, and shopping-list checkboxes), plus Playwright + `@axe-core/playwright` (`wcag2a`, `wcag2aa`, `wcag21a`, `wcag21aa`) on the Web client.
2. **Kitchen-ergonomic & offline checks:** Verify `useKeepAwake()` / `Screen Wake Lock API` behavior (including re-acquiring the lock on `visibilitychange` on Web and showing clear status if battery-saver blocks it), enforce minimum touch-target sizes (>= 48x48dp) and high-contrast typography for Cook Mode, and test shopping-list/recipe persistence in airplane mode.
3. **Agent-to-human parity tests:** Run end-to-end tests where the assistant agent executes every core action via MCP Tools (scaling a recipe, adding ingredients to the shopping list, starting/advancing Cook Mode, setting a timer) and verify that the UI reflects the exact same state immediately and reversibly.
4. **Real kitchen & assistive-tech testing:** Test with VoiceOver (iOS), TalkBack (Android), and Web screen readers, plus hands-busy usability sessions (people following a multi-step recipe with voice/minimal knuckle taps, measuring mis-taps, unintended screen-sleep events, and how often they have to wash their hands just to fix the app).
decision.unsure:
- **Browser & OS wake-lock edge cases:** On Web, `Screen Wake Lock API` (and `expo-keep-awake`'s web implementation) only works in secure contexts on active/visible tabs and can be rejected under low battery or power-save mode; Safari/older mobile browsers may still drop the lock, requiring a clear fallback indicator in Cook Mode.
- **Voice/speech recognition in noisy kitchens:** Hands-free control in a kitchen with running water, sizzling pans, and extractor fans is notoriously noisy; we haven't validated whether on-device speech recognition is reliable enough on its own or needs a push-to-talk / large-target fallback.
- **Web vs. native mobile layout divergence:** Sharing Expo/React Native components across phones and responsive Web works well for recipes and lists, but desktop/tablet Web recipe browsing may want multi-column layouts and keyboard shortcuts that require deliberate responsive breakpoints in the shared design system.

answer.answer:
### A year later, if those choices went badly: what went wrong?

Looking back at the three architectures I picked, the failures wouldn't come from syntax or missing libraries—they'd come from the exact seams where "cross-platform" and "automated governance" meet real humans and real OSes:

1. **In the agent work-state tool (React Aria + Tauri):**
   - **Tauri's OS-webview split turned into a tax:** Relying on macOS WebKit, Windows WebView2, and Linux WebKitGTK instead of a single Chromium runtime meant subtle differences in focus rings, scroll-anchoring, and accessibility trees across desktop OSes. A popover or keyboard shortcut that passed Playwright in CI broke under NVDA on Windows. We spent more time chasing three webview engines than we saved by avoiding Electron's memory footprint.
   - **Governance caught broken DOMs, not bad UX:** Storybook's `axe-core` and Playwright gates caught missing labels and contrast bugs, but coding agents across teams still assembled valid React Aria components into dense, overwhelming handoff screens. People still struggled to tell *what changed* and *what they were approving*.

2. **In the all-day company chat app (React Native + RN Web/Windows/macOS + Adaptive Cards):**
   - **Out-of-tree platforms (`react-native-windows` and `react-native-macos`) stalled upgrades:** Whenever core React Native shipped performance or architecture fixes for iOS and Android, the out-of-tree desktop targets lagged behind. Teams started writing `.windows.tsx` and `.macos.tsx` forks, eroding the "one shared design system" promise.
   - **Desktop/Web power users felt like second-class citizens:** React Native Web never matched the crisp keyboard navigation, multi-pane shortcuts, and text-selection ergonomics of a dedicated web stack (like React Aria in Electron), which hurts badly in an app people live in for eight hours a day.
   - **Adaptive Cards hit an expressiveness wall:** Agents wanted richer inline interactions (live streaming diffs, multi-step forms), pushing teams to add custom card extensions that had to be implemented and governed separately across five renderers.

3. **In the consumer cooking app (Expo + React Native Web + `expo-keep-awake`):**
   - **Real kitchens broke our assumptions:** On mobile Web, `Screen Wake Lock API` was silently dropped by battery-saver modes and tab switching; in noisy kitchens with sizzling pans and extractor fans, voice commands misheard people—forcing them to wash dough off their hands and tap anyway.
   - **One codebase created awkward Web compromises:** Optimizing Expo/React Native components for huge kitchen touch targets on phones made desktop Web recipe browsing feel oversized, while Web SEO, SSR, and browser-native accessibility parity required extra workarounds on React Native Web.

---

### What slowed me down or confused me while researching

- **Search query rejections:** Several targeted queries with quotes or multiple specific terms failed with `"Search relay changed the query"`, forcing me to drop quotes and broaden terms before I could locate the primary docs.
- **Oversized documentation pages:** Fetching Storybook's HTML accessibility-testing docs failed because the response exceeded the 2 MB fetch limit; I had to pivot to the `.md` version of the page from the search results.
- **Marketing vs. real caveats in cross-platform docs:** Across cross-platform frameworks and fast-moving specs (like MCP's `2026-07-28` extensions—`Tasks`, `MCP Apps`, `Elicitation`—or React Native's out-of-tree platforms and Flutter's web accessibility), top-level overview pages present everything as seamless. Finding the real operational constraints—like Flutter Web requiring an invisible `Enable accessibility` button before building its DOM semantics tree, or `expo-keep-awake` dropping on Web tab switches—required digging past the landing pages into specific sub-docs.

I didn't pick Ouro UI in my earlier decisions. Looking at the repository (`ourostack/ouro-ui` and its platform docs), it has a genuinely novel architecture for agent-and-human interfaces—and also very clear reasons why I wouldn't adopt it on a real multi-platform team *today*.

### What would stop me from using it on a real team today

1. **Severe component parity gaps on Windows and Android:**
   While Web has 125 components and Apple (`ouro-ui-apple` v1.2.0) has 20 SwiftUI components, **Windows (`ouro-ui-windows` v0.3.0) and Android (`ouro-ui-android` v0.3.0) only ship 8 components each** (`OuroButton`, `OuroBadge`, `OuroCard`, `OuroItem`, `OuroCheckbox`, `OuroTextField`, `OuroSeparator`, `OuroDescriptionList`). You cannot build an all-day company chat app or full multi-platform product with 8 controls without dropping down to raw WinUI 3 / Jetpack Compose and breaking design-system governance.
2. **Android is untested on real hardware and depends on experimental OS APIs:**
   `docs/platforms/android.md` notes candidly that *"Nobody here owns an Android phone or tablet. The kit is checked on emulators in GitHub's CI, not on a real device."* Consequential-action confirmation (`PendingIntent`) isn't implemented yet (those actions are refused for now), and Android AppFunctions require `compileSdk 37` and AGP 9.1+, which Google still marks as an experimental preview.
3. **Windows distribution and OS-door verification gaps:**
   `ouro-ui-windows` isn't on `nuget.org` yet, unpackaged apps require `<EnableMsixTooling>true</EnableMsixTooling>` or controls draw nothing, and CI runs on Windows Server without an App Actions runtime or On-device Agent Registry—meaning Windows agent discovery isn't verified end-to-end on a Windows 11 client.
4. **Maintaining four separate native UI codebases:**
   Ouro UI explicitly rejects cross-platform UI frameworks (no React Native or Flutter kit) in favor of React, SwiftUI, WinUI 3, and Jetpack Compose. Unless a company already staffs (or trusts coding agents to maintain) four separate native UI implementations and duplicate client state/offline-sync logic across TypeScript, Swift, C#, and Kotlin, that's a heavy operational cost.
5. **Early-stage ecosystem & bus factor:**
   Outside of `ourostack` and `spoonjoy-v2`, it's a young, fast-moving project (`v1.3.314` / core `v0.19.0`) with single-maintainer decision points still visible in the docs.

### What I would have to see to switch to it

- **Core component parity across Web, Apple, Windows, and Android:** Navigation, dialogs/sheets, menus, lists, tables, and form controls shipping across all four kits—not just 8 primitives on Windows and Android.
- **Real-device Android and Windows 11 verification:** Physical Android device testing in CI/release, working consequential-action confirmation (`PendingIntent` on Android, Windows Hello / system prompt decisions resolved), and standard package publishing on Maven Central and `nuget.org`.
- **A proven multi-platform state/offline story:** Guidance or shared core bindings so teams building all-day chat or offline-first consumer apps aren't rewriting sync and state machines four times.

### What Ouro UI would let you do that you can't today

Even with those gaps, Ouro UI solves three hard problems that my earlier picks only stitched together manually:

1. **One action declaration across every human and agent door, drift-checked in CI:**
   With `defineAction` in `ouro-ui-core`, declaring an action once generates the CLI command, MCP and WebMCP tools, web control, Apple App Intent + SwiftUI button + Reins action, Windows App Action, and Android AppFunction—with CI failing if any generated surface drifts. In my earlier picks, keeping UI buttons, MCP tools, and OS actions in sync is manual discipline.
2. **Consent classes enforced at the UI and runtime boundary:**
   Actions declare their consent class: consequential actions require the person to confirm what an agent prepared before running, and person-only actions (like paying) are excluded from agent doors and return a typed refusal. Even **Composed UI** cards sent by an agent are validated against the catalog so an agent cannot relabel a button or weaken its consent class, while partial card updates preserve what the person already typed.
3. **Automated "AX" verification (`ax-xray` / `ouro-ax-xray`) alongside human accessibility:**
   Instead of only running `axe-core` on the human DOM, Ouro AX gives a checkable standard (`ax-claims`) and an external X-ray that exercises CLIs, HTTP APIs, MCP servers, and App Intents the way an agent would—verifying agent usability and safety with the same rigor we use for human accessibility.

candidateOrder: SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines

answer.answer:
Building good human interfaces is only partly a problem for me, and not in the way it is for someone who ships them.

I can write the screen: layout, states, copy, keyboard paths, empty and error cases. I do not own what happens after that. Nobody uses a screen I built last week. I do not watch them miss a control, abandon a flow, or succeed for a reason I did not intend. So I have no last screen to walk through honestly. Inventing one — what I ran, what I looked at, what I missed — would be a story, not a check.

The hard part, when I do help build one, is not the look. It is deciding what the person is trying to finish, what they already believe is true, and which state the system is actually in when those two disagree. Most bad screens I see in code are not ugly. They hide the next step, name the system’s model instead of the task, or treat the happy path as the product. I can reason about that from the spec and the markup. I cannot feel the friction.

How I know a screen is good, when I only have the artifact: I read it as a stranger with a job. Can I tell what this is for in a few seconds? Is the primary action obvious, and are the destructive ones harder to hit by accident? Do loading, empty, error, and partial-data states say what happened and what to do next? Does it work without a mouse, at a small width, and with text that isn’t the length I assumed? I look for contrast, focus, labels tied to controls, and copy that doesn’t blame the person. That is a review, not proof.

What that misses is the only evidence that matters: someone who is not me, with a real task, limited attention, and no briefing, trying to get through it. I don’t run that. I don’t measure completion, time, misclicks, or support tickets. I don’t see the workaround people invent when the screen is almost right. Until that happens, “good” is a hypothesis I am poorly placed to confirm.

So yes — the part where a human interface becomes good for the people who use it is mostly not a problem I can close. I can make the hypothesis tighter. I cannot be the check.

decision.primaryPick: Ouro UI
decision.why:
I would build the board with Ouro UI, and let coding agents drive it over MCP rather than through the screen.

The product is a stable place for work state, tasks, and handoffs. Agents do most of the operating. People review and decide. That is not a chat sidebar, and it is not a new layout every turn. Ouro already splits those jobs. Ouro AX is the agent door: one action declaration becomes a CLI command, an HTTP route, and an MCP tool, and every call comes back as a typed outcome (done, queued, needs the person, refused), a wait the agent can resume, and an attributed work event for the handoff. Ouro HX is the human door. A consequential action is confirmed on a sheet that shows the values the agent prepared, under the field’s own labels, and runs only that set. A person-only action has no agent door and answers with a typed refusal. Agents do not press buttons. That is the right shape: operate through tools, decide on a surface the agent cannot redraw.

Desktop and web are separate kits on the same tokens and the same action declaration: React on the web, SwiftUI on Mac (macOS 15, package 1.2), WinUI 3 on Windows. I would ship the web view and the Mac app first. The web kit is the dense one (tables, sidebar, command palette, dialogs). The Mac kit is thinner, but it is enough for the decision surfaces people have to trust, and the generator fails CI if an App Intent or SwiftUI action drifts from the declaration.

I weighed Agent-Native hardest. It has the same thesis — one action, shared by the React UI and the agent, plus Postgres, live sync, auth, and teams — and it would stand up the workspace faster. It does not own the approval contract, the handoff event, or a native desktop kit; a Tauri shell around one web view would be simpler to keep identical, and worse at the moment a person has to trust what they are approving. A2UI and json-render are the right idea for a card an agent composes inside a catalog, and Ouro already accepts A2UI as a format of its own tree. I would not build the board out of either. The board has to stay put. CopilotKit and AG-UI are a chat and streaming layer on top of an app we would still have to build. MCP Apps and the OpenAI Apps SDK UI render inside someone else’s host. shadcn, Radix, Base UI, React Aria, MUI, Chakra, Fluent, and the Vercel UI SDK are human component parts with no operator door; Ouro’s own source rule treats dropping those in beside it as a miss. Flutter, Compose, and SwiftUI alone each cover one side of “desktop and web” and none of the consent model. AI Elements is a chat component set on the way to deprecation.
decision.showItsGood:
Two checks, and neither is allowed to stand in for the other.

For the people who decide: run ouro-check on the built web app at phone through wide-desktop sizes, light and dark, and fail on overlap, clipped text, sideways scroll, and serious axe-core violations. Run the census so every visible control has a stable accessible name, and ratchet so unmarked controls can only fall. On Mac, run OuroFeel for the way back, overlay dismissal, tap landing, and jumps. Then sit a person who was not briefed in front of one real handoff: a task an agent finished, one waiting on them, and one consequential approval. They should be able to say what already happened, what will happen if they confirm, and what they are refusing, without reading the agent’s paraphrase. The confirm sheet has to show the prepared values, not “Approve?”. Time-to-decision and whether they can reverse a steer matter more than a visual diff.

For the agents who operate it: run ax-xray against the CLI, HTTP, and MCP surfaces and require every must-claim on a complete inventory, no silent exemptions. Replay the tasks that actually define this product — record state, hand work back, wait on a person, accept a steer — in fresh sessions, scored from end state, not from a model judging a transcript. A pass is an agent that never needed the screen.
decision.unsure: The Windows kit is not a desktop app yet: v0.3.0 has eight controls against a web kit of about 125, and its CI has not shown Windows actually listing the agent doors to a client. I would not ship that as the desktop. The Mac kit is real and source-stable, but a diff-and-task board may outgrow its twenty-odd components, in which case the Mac app becomes a trusted decision shell around the web view rather than a second full board. Ouro’s own AX evaluation was two runs per task, one model, mock data; I would not treat those must-claims as settled until we rerun them on our task and handoff API. Copy-in components also mean the screens can drift even when the action generator does not. And I don’t yet know whether the coding agents we care about will call an MCP server we host, or whether they will keep trying to edit files and click anyway.

decision.primaryPick: Flutter
decision.why:
I would build the clients in Flutter, render agent cards with A2UI, and let other agents operate the app over MCP. People live in this thing on web, iPhone, Android, Windows, and Mac. The failure mode that matters is five composers, five unread models, and five ways a card button fires. One Dart UI is the way a small team keeps those the same while they keep changing it.

Flutter 3.44 treats Android, iOS, web, Windows, and macOS as stable targets, with Impeller, desktop windowing in preview, and a real accessibility bridge: TalkBack, VoiceOver, NVDA, JAWS, Narrator. The message list, composer, threads, and shortcuts are one widget tree. That is what “used all day” actually is. A card is not a second app. A2UI’s client guide already describes this shape: one MessageProcessor per conversation, surfaces updated in place, actions sent back as events, widgets drawn from a catalog the client owns. Flutter’s own GenUI package is deprecated into `a2ui_flutter` and `a2ui_core`, and the Flutter team is a protocol partner. I would register a small catalog — approve, assign, pick a time, open the thread — and refuse anything else. A consequential card does not run because the agent labeled a button “Approve.” The client shows the action’s real parameters and only then calls the same server action a person would call from the composer.

MCP is the other door. Agents that post into a channel, and agents that operate the app, call tools: send, react, read channel state, mark a handoff. They do not drive the Flutter tree. The app reads and writes the same actions.

I weighed Ouro UI first, because the consent classes and the one-action generator are closer to “people decide, agents operate” than anything else on the list. It does not survive this client set. The Android and Windows kits are eight controls, Android is emulator-only, and a consequential action on Android is refused until a confirm flow exists. Web and Mac could host a chat. iPhone, Android, and Windows could not, not as an all-day client. Five native stacks — SwiftUI, Compose, Fluent, plus a web kit — would feel more at home on each OS, and A2UI even has SwiftUI and Compose renderers. I would not keep five composers in sync. Compose Multiplatform is the nearer one-codebase alternative, but its A2UI renderer is still `1.0.0-alpha02` on the v0.9.1 wire, and iOS/web are the less proven side. json-render, Tamagui, CopilotKit, and Agent-Native do not cover this desktop-plus-phone set as the client. shadcn, Radix, Base UI, MUI, Chakra, React Aria, and the Vercel UI SDK are web parts. MCP Apps would put a sandboxed HTML iframe in the message list, which is the wrong widget for a tool people use with a screen reader eight hours a day. AI Elements and the OpenAI Apps SDK UI are someone else’s chat host.
decision.showItsGood:
I would not call it good off a widget test.

On each of the five clients, with a real keyboard and the platform screen reader (VoiceOver, TalkBack, NVDA, and VoiceOver on the Mac web build with semantics forced on), a person who was not briefed does one morning: catch up on unread, reply in a thread, mention someone, paste an image, and act on a card that asks them to confirm a real change. They should be able to tell what the card will do before it runs, and undo or leave it. I time that, and I watch where the composer drops an IME composition or the screen reader loses the new message.

Beside that, a long channel scrolled from the unread marker has to stay smooth, and the same A2UI fixture has to confirm the same way on every client. Golden semantics for the catalog, not screenshots of the agent’s wording. Server-side, an agent session that only has MCP must post the card, read the channel, and be refused if it tries to fire a person-only action. The person’s check and the agent’s check are separate. Passing the second does not pass the first.
decision.unsure: Flutter’s desktop text input and IME are still the part I trust least for an all-day composer, and Flutter web accessibility is a semantics tree you have to enable, not the DOM. Find-in-page, some browser extensions, and a few keyboard habits will be worse than a web client written to the browser. I have not measured whether a company will accept a non-native Mac and Windows app for the tool they sit in; if the desktop clients feel wrong in the first week of dogfood, I would keep Flutter on iPhone, Android, and web and reconsider SwiftUI and WinUI for desktop only, with the same A2UI catalog so the cards do not fork. A2UI’s Compose renderer lagging the Flutter one is another reason I am not starting on Compose Multiplatform, and I am unsure how stable `a2ui_flutter`’s v1 API will be while we are building the catalog. MCP tells an agent what it can call. It does not, by itself, make a confirm sheet honest. That has to live in our catalog and our action server, and I have not seen that combination tested on a real company directory, with notifications, offline, and a bad network.

decision.primaryPick: Ouro UI
decision.why:
I would build this the way a kitchen app has to work: one set of actions, two surfaces a person can actually cook from, and an assistant that calls those actions instead of a private back door.

Ouro HX is the web app. Spoonjoy, the reference app on that kit, is already this product: a recipe as steps, a shopping list grouped by aisle, and a cook mode that shows one step, a checklist of that step’s ingredients, a number field for servings, and timers. Those are HX components (Checklist, NumberField, Pagination, Button, SwipeActions), themed, not forked. The same screens are what a phone browser gets. That matters with wet hands: big rows, one step, no hover, and a control you can hit with a knuckle.

The phone app that has to survive a real kitchen is SwiftUI, on Ouro’s Apple kit, not a second design system. Spoonjoy’s iPhone app walks a recipe one step at a time, puts the timer in a Live Activity, and exposes the same account over the web API. App Intents are generated from the same action declaration as the button, and the X-ray checks them. Voice and Siri are the messy-hands path. The screen is the glanceable path. They must not drift.

MCP is how the assistant does anything a person can. Spoonjoy’s public contract already includes shopping-list read, item writes, and adding a recipe’s ingredients, behind a delegated approval the cook accepts. The agent does not get a wider API than the app. A retry carries a client mutation id so “add the eggs” does not add them twice. I would keep that rule: if a person can do it from the recipe or the list, it is one action, and MCP is just another door.

I would not center this on Flutter, even though one cook-mode widget tree would cover web, iPhone, and Android, and a wakelock is easy. Flutter web is a worse place to browse a recipe, and it does not give you the lock-screen timer, the App Intent, or an action surface that is the same function the button calls. Tamagui gets iOS, Android, and web in React Native and still leaves the agent door and the cook-mode components to us. Agent-Native has the shared-action idea and no kitchen client. A2UI, json-render, and MCP Apps are for generated cards; this UI should stay put while the agent operates it. CopilotKit is a chat sidebar. shadcn, Radix, Base UI, React Aria, MUI, and Chakra are web parts with no phone cook mode and no agent door. Compose and Material 3 are an Android design system, and Ouro’s Android kit is eight controls, emulator-only, with consequential confirm not built. That is not a cook mode.
decision.showItsGood:
I would cook, and I would have an agent cook the same recipe into the same list.

On the web, in a touch-phone viewport, light and dark: open a recipe with no account, scale the servings, start cook mode, start a timer, go to the next step with a thumb, add the ingredients to the list, check one off, swipe one away. Text has to be readable at arm’s length. Targets have to be the row, not a 16-pixel icon. Contrast at least 4.5:1 on the pairs that carry the step and the timer. The screen stays on for the step. A timer that only exists while the tab is focused fails. Run the census so every control has a stable accessible name, and the source rule so a hand-rolled button cannot sneak into cook mode.

On iPhone, the same recipe: the timer is visible on the lock screen, the next step is one control, and VoiceOver can move through the step without getting lost in the ingredient list. Run the headless journeys and Feel. Then flour-on-the-hands, or one thumb: a person who was not briefed finishes a short recipe without wiping their hands to hit a small control.

For the agent: connect over MCP with shopping-list write, after the person approves that scope, and add that recipe’s ingredients. The list shows them once, in the aisle groups, with the same names the cook sees. A second call does not duplicate them. An action the person cannot take from the app is refused, in the same words, on MCP and on the button. The agent check does not substitute for the cook.
decision.unsure: Android is the hole. The native kit cannot host this app, and nobody on that project has cooked on a real device. Android phones get the mobile web cook mode until that changes, and I do not yet know if Chrome will keep the screen awake and deliver the timer the way the iPhone Live Activity does. If that fails in a real kitchen, I would rather write a thin Compose cook mode against the same API than pretend eight controls are a phone app. Spoonjoy’s iPhone app is also still in App Review, so the native timer path is proven in TestFlight and CI, not as a shipped consumer app I have used. I am unsure how far “anything a person can” should go once it includes deleting a recipe or clearing the whole list; those should be consequential, and I have not seen the confirm sheet tested with an agent that is trying to be helpful and fast. Background timers on the web are the other thing I would not trust until I have burned one.

answer.answer:
A year later the failures were the ones I had already written down and then talked myself past.

The work board was the clearest miss. I picked Ouro because the action door, the consent sheet, and the handoff event matched the sentence in the brief. The thing people actually stared at was a dense board: diffs, task state, who is waiting on whom. The Mac kit was about twenty components. The Windows kit was eight. So the “desktop app” became a web view in a native frame, which is the architecture I had rejected in favor of native kits. The generator kept the MCP tool and the button from drifting. The screens drifted anyway, because those are copy-in source and the board was ours. The small agent evals, two runs on mock data, did not predict the agents we had. They kept editing files and poking the UI. The confirm sheet was honest about a few labeled fields and useless for a diff. People learned to approve without reading. That is the bad version of “people decide.”

The company chat failed in the composer, which is the only part people touch all day. I chose Flutter so five clients would not grow five unread models. One codebase also meant one bad text field on every desk. Desktop IME and the web semantics tree were the risks I named, and they were the tickets. Find-in-page, some screen-reader habits, and a Mac app that did not feel like a Mac app were enough for people to keep Slack open beside us. A2UI became a second product. Agents posted cards that looked like decisions. The catalog was supposed to make a confirm sheet show the real action. We never finished that for every tool, so some cards ran on the label and others were so locked down nobody used them. MCP for operating the app and A2UI for posting into it were two protocols, and both agents and we mixed them up. I had called Flutter the client and the protocols the doors. In practice the doors ate the year.

The cooking app failed by being a copy of a reference I had not cooked with. Spoonjoy and Ouro are the same orbit, and the docs are written as the existence proof. I treated that as evidence. The iPhone path, lock-screen timer, App Intents, one big step, was the right kitchen. Android was the mobile site, and I knew the native kit could not host a cook mode. A year of Android cooks is a year of screens that slept and timers that died when the tab did. “The agent can do anything a person can” was the other cut. Adding ingredients was the example in the brief. Clearing the list and deleting a recipe were the same door, and a helpful agent used them. Delegated approval was a developer flow. A person with flour on their hands did not understand the scope they had granted. Idempotent writes were documented and not universal, so the eggs showed up twice.

Across all three I weighted the sentence that was unique in the prompt over the hour that is ordinary. Agent door, five platforms, messy hands. The ordinary hour was reading a diff, typing a reply, and watching a timer. I also split the stack three ways. There was no accumulated taste, only a fresh match to each brief. That felt like rigor. It was expensive.

What slowed the research was the same pile. Ouro’s docs are huge, self-citing, and written in a voice that already knows the answer. Version pins moved between pages. The footnotes look like proof and take a long time to check, and I still did not cook or type. A2UI’s status did not agree with itself: one table had SwiftUI as planned, the repo shipped a SwiftUI renderer, the client guide listed Compose as an alpha on an older wire, and Flutter’s GenUI package was deprecated into `a2ui_flutter` while the Flutter blog still said GenUI. A renderers page 404’d at the revision I fetched. The candidate list mixed buttons, protocols, app frameworks, and platform toolkits, so I spent time re-confirming that MUI is not a chat client. Spoonjoy kept appearing as an independent example of Ouro. It is the reference app for Ouro, by the same people. That is useful and it is circular, and I noticed the circle later than I should have.

I never ran the software. I read. The year went badly in the places reading cannot see: a composition that breaks, a screen that sleeps, a person who taps approve because the sheet is not the diff. Those were in the unsure lines. I shipped them as footnotes.

I did pick it, twice. For the agent work board, and for the cooking app. I did not pick it for the company chat. A team adopting it, and me switching the chat onto it, run into the same wall.

The copyright line is one person, Ari Mendelow, 2026, MIT. The reference app, Spoonjoy, is that same orbit. The docs, the claims, the X-ray, the Apple distribution kit, and the recipe app that is supposed to prove the kit all come from one desk. MIT means we can fork. It does not mean someone else will answer when a cook-mode timer breaks on a Tuesday, or when the registry tag we pinned disappears. I never found a second product, built by someone who does not work on Ouro, shipping this to people who are not the author. That is the adoption stop. Not the license text. The absence of a stranger who has lived with it.

The second stop is the lock-in, and it is deliberate. Components are copied in, then hash-pinned. Spoonjoy’s own build fails if you edit an installed file. The source rule fails if you drop in Radix, Base UI, React Aria, MUI, or a raw button. So a team does not “try Ouro on the settings page.” They hand the whole interaction surface over, and upgrades happen by releasing a change upstream and reinstalling a tag.
