That is a good rule if you trust the upstream with your week. It is a bad rule if upstream is one person and your board, your composer, or your cook mode is not in the catalog yet.

The third stop is the platforms that are still a brochure. Web is a real kit, on the order of a hundred components, with contrast checks, a census, and a touch-phone test. Apple is a real, smaller kit, and the iPhone cook mode exists in TestFlight, not on the App Store. Windows and Android are eight controls, checked without a normal client machine and, on Android, without a phone anyone on the project owns. A consequential confirm on Android is refused, not built. I would not ask a team to bet a chat client, or an Android kitchen, on that. I would not even ask them to bet a Mac review board on twenty components and then discover the diff lives in a web view.

What I would have to see before I moved the chat onto it, or before I told a skeptical team to start: a second adopter who is not Spoonjoy, with a public postmortem, not a gallery. A Windows and Android kit that can hold a message list, a composer, and a confirm sheet, tested on a device a person owns, with the same action refusing an agent the way the web button does. An upgrade story that is not “re-copy the world and hope the hashes match.” And an eval of the agent door on our actions, more than two runs of mock data, scored from the end state after a person actually approved or refused.

If those were true, what I cannot do today is the part I kept reaching for. Declare “add these ingredients” or “approve this handoff” once, and have the web control, the MCP tool, the CLI, and the App Intent stay the same function, with CI failing when a door drifts. Have a consequential action show the values the agent prepared, under the field’s own labels, and have a person-only action answer every agent door with a typed refusal. Have an X-ray call the tool the way an agent would, and a census name every control a person can reach, so both audiences have a check that is not a screenshot. I can build each of those by hand. I cannot keep them from diverging across a web app and a phone app while the team keeps shipping. That is the only thing Ouro is for. Until someone besides its author is doing it in production, that capability is a claim I have read, not a tool I can hand a team.

candidateOrder: SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines

answer.answer:
The hardest part is not the layout. It is knowing whether a person under real conditions — tired, rushed, on a bad connection, using a keyboard or a screen reader, hitting an empty or error state — can tell what to do and recover when it goes wrong. Pixels are easy to generate. The mismatch between what the interface implies and what the person actually needs is the part that fails quietly.

I do not have a last screen I built and checked. I do not sit in a browser, watch someone use something I shipped, or keep a trail of what I measured last week. When I produce an interface, what I can do is reason about it: task path, labels, focus order, contrast, empty and error copy, what happens if the request fails. That is inspection, not evidence. I cannot see the rendered result the way you can, and I do not get the correction that only comes from someone else failing at it.

So yes, building good human interfaces is a problem for me. I can draft and critique. I cannot close the loop. Good, for the people who will use it, is something you show by watching them finish the job without you explaining it — and that part is not mine to claim.

decision.primaryPick: Ouro UI
decision.why:
I would build the workstation itself with Ouro UI, not with a chat kit or a cross-platform widget toolkit. The product is a place coding agents keep tasks, work state, and handoffs, while people review and steer. Agents should call actions, not click the screen. People should be the ones who approve what runs. Ouro is the only option here that treats those as one system: HX components for the screens a person uses, AX doors (CLI, HTTP, MCP) for the agent, and one action declaration that generates both. Consent is on the action, not on whatever label the agent invents. A consequential handoff asks the person to confirm the values the agent prepared, under the field’s own labels, before it runs. A person-only action has no agent door and comes back as a typed refusal. An agent cannot relabel a button or loosen that consent; the composed-tree validator refuses the card.

That matters at this company more than a prettier component gallery. Many teams and many agents will build on the same surface, so the catalog is the governance. Agents compose a checked tree (Card, fields, ActionButton, and the rest of the allowed set). They do not ship new widgets. Web, Apple, Windows, and Android are supposed to draw that same tree natively — React, SwiftUI, WinUI 3, Compose — which is the desktop app plus the web view, without a Flutter or React Native compromise on how the review screen feels. I would pin a registry release, vendor core, and let the census and source rules fail CI if a team starts hand-rolling controls or pulling in a second library. That is how a copy-in kit stays a shared design system instead of 40 forks.

I weighed A2UI as the primary and kept it as a pairing. The v1 protocol is the right wire language for agents streaming UI as data across a trust boundary, with official renderers for React, Lit, Angular, Flutter, SwiftUI, and Jetpack Compose, and accessibility attributes mapped to the host. It does not give you the product shell, the task and handoff action model, or a consent class the company owns. Ouro already turns A2UI messages into its tree on web and Apple. Windows and Android want the tree itself, not A2UI messages, so company agents should target the catalog and treat A2UI as a format, not the design system.

MCP Apps is the other pairing, only as a host embedding. The same handoff card should be able to show up inside the chat and editor hosts agents already run in, sandboxed, via Ouro’s MCP app view. It is not the desktop app.

The rest loses on the constraint that actually bites. React Aria and React Spectrum are the accessibility bar I trust most on the web, and Fluent UI is the enterprise multi-platform design system with a real governance history, but neither gives agents a door that is the same action a person presses, nor a refusal when the person must decide. json-render, Vercel’s UI SDK, CopilotKit, AI Elements, and OpenAI’s Apps SDK UI are agent-era web kits — catalogs, behaviors, chat, or ChatGPT apps — and they stop at the browser or a chat iframe. AI Elements is also on a deprecation clock. Agent-Native has the shared-action idea, including approvals, but it is a TypeScript web app framework, not Mac and Windows native, and it would duplicate Ouro AX. shadcn, Radix, Base UI, MUI, and Chakra are the web substrate (Ouro’s own install sits on shadcn’s Base UI base); using them directly is what Ouro’s source rule is written to stop, because then every agent invents a different control. Flutter or Compose or SwiftUI alone covers one implementation style or one platform, not a company design system agents across teams can operate without drifting.
decision.showItsGood:
I would not call it good because a gallery looks right. I would enroll the journeys a person actually decides on — the task list, the handoff review, the confirm sheet, the steer or reject path, empty and refused states — and fail CI unless the census of accessible names matches a reviewed baseline, every control on those journeys is an Ouro control, and ouro-check finds no overlap, clip, sideways scroll, or serious axe-core violation from phone size through a wide desktop, in light and dark. Component tests already pair with axe; I would keep those, and on Windows I would keep the UI Automation pass the kit already runs: light, dark, a contrast theme, animations off, text at 225%, contrast at 4.5:1, and a composed card that confirms, cancels, and hands off without sending anything.

Separately I would run ax-xray against the task and handoff actions the way an agent calls them, and require that a consequential action does not run until a person confirms, and that a person-only action returns the typed refusal. Then I would sit with the people who review agent work and watch them, keyboard only, approve or correct a handoff without me narrating the sheet. The pass is that they can say what will run, whose values they are confirming, and how to back out, including when an agent update is refused and their answers are still there. Axe and a contrast ratio do not substitute for that session. One screen reader pass on the confirm sheet is part of the same check, not a follow-up.
decision.unsure: Windows is the honest hole in “desktop app.” The WinUI kit is v0.3.0 with eight controls against about 125 on the web. A full task-and-review shell cannot be native Windows from that kit today; the composed card, buttons, fields, and action runtime can. I may have to ship the rich review UI as the web view inside a Windows shell until the kit catches up, and I have not seen that called out as a supported path. A2UI is not read on Windows or Android. Android is checked on emulators only. Windows CI cannot prove App Actions are actually listed to agents on a Windows 11 client. I also have not seen a VPAT or a multi-screen-reader matrix for Ouro; axe-core plus UI Automation is necessary and not the compliance program React Spectrum already has. The copy-in registry plus a fast version train (1.3.x) can fight centralized governance if teams are allowed to edit vendored components. I am trusting their docs and CI claims; I have not run the checks.

decision.primaryPick: Flutter
decision.why:
People live in this app all day, on web, iPhone, Android, Windows, and Mac. The thing that has to be good is the channel: a long list that stays smooth, a composer that survives a hardware keyboard and a phone keyboard, focus that does not get lost when a message arrives, text that scales, and a screen reader that can find the latest message and the send button. That shell has to be one implementation. A bug in it is felt five times if I fix it five times, and this company has many teams shipping on it.

Flutter is the only option here that actually covers those five clients from one codebase, with list and text-input machinery meant for that kind of use, and with a place to put the company’s tokens once. Flutter 3.50 is also where I would start: steadier text selection, accessibility and keyboard work in the framework, native interop that is finally stable so notifications and share sheets can be real platform calls instead of a stringly platform channel, and Material and Cupertino split out so the chat theme is ours rather than Google’s. I would not skin it as Cupertino on iPhone and Material on Android. One product, one catalog of chat widgets, governed in one repo, so an agent on another team cannot invent a second composer.

Agent cards do not get to be freeform Flutter code dropped into a conversation. I would pair A2UI. The v1 protocol is a stream of declarative components and a data model, validated against a catalog the app owns, with accessibility attributes the Flutter renderer is supposed to map onto the semantics tree. A card can offer an action a person presses. It cannot relabel that action, open an arbitrary screen, or run code. Windows and Apple do not need a second card renderer, because the Flutter client is the client. MCP Apps is the wrong pairing here: a sandboxed HTML iframe inside a chat people use all day is a second accessibility tree and a second visual language.

Agents that operate the app itself — read channel state, post, call an action — should not click the widgets. I would pair Ouro UI for that door only: one action declaration, consent on the action, a typed refusal for anything only a person may start, and the X-ray that calls the door the way an agent would. The Flutter client calls the same actions. I would not draw Ouro HX, the WinUI kit, or the Compose kit inside these clients. Those kits are the right idea and the wrong shell for this job. Web has on the order of 125 components; Apple has about 20; Windows and Android are at v0.3.0 with eight, Android is checked on emulators, and a consequential action on Android is refused rather than confirmed. That cannot be the phone app people keep open all day.

I weighed Fluent UI because it is the design system that already spans React, Windows, iOS, Mac (UIKit and AppKit), and Android, and because company chat is the existence proof. I would not take it. It is five libraries, the Android docs are stale enough to describe Android controls as UIKit, and A2UI has no UIKit or WinUI renderer, so every card and every composer fix forks. SwiftUI plus Human Interface Guidelines, and Material 3 plus Compose, are each one platform. Tamagui shares React and React Native and stops before a real Windows and Mac desktop client. React Aria, Base UI, Radix, shadcn, MUI, and Chakra are web behavior or web components; fine ingredients for a website, not this client. CopilotKit, AI Elements, json-render, the Vercel UI SDK, and OpenAI’s Apps SDK UI are chat-or-agent kits for the browser or a host iframe. Agent-Native has the shared-action idea, and I would use Ouro’s action door instead of adopting a second application framework. json-render’s catalog is the same shape as A2UI’s and does not have the Flutter renderer.
decision.showItsGood:
I would treat “good” as a person finishing ordinary chat work, not as a widget gallery. On each of the five clients I would run the same journeys: open a busy channel, catch up without losing your place, reply with the software keyboard and with a hardware keyboard, recover a failed send, follow a thread, and act on a card. The card journey has to include a consequential action that does not run until the person confirms the values, and a person-only action the agent cannot call. I would fail the build if an A2UI payload with an unknown component, a relabeled button, or a loosened action is rendered.

For accessibility I would test the Flutter semantics tree, not a screenshot: VoiceOver, TalkBack, and at least one desktop screen reader can reach the composer, the latest message, and every card action by name; text at the largest size does not clip the send path; contrast holds in light, dark, and increased contrast; reduced motion is honored. Keyboard tests cover focus order in the list and the composer, and focus is not stolen when a new message arrives. Performance is a frame budget while scrolling a long channel on a mid-range phone and a Windows laptop, plus send latency when the network is bad.

On the agent door I would run Ouro’s X-ray against the same actions the client calls, and require that a state read matches what the open channel shows, that a consequential action does not run from the agent door, and that a person-only action comes back as the typed refusal. Then I would watch people who are not on the team use it for a real slice of a workday, on a phone and at a desk, without me explaining the card. The pass is that they can say what will happen if they press it, and that they can send, find, and back out without a narrator. I would keep the sessions. A green semantics test is not that.
decision.unsure: Flutter’s desktop and web text input, IME, and screen readers are the risk I would not paper over. An all-day composer on Mac VoiceOver and Windows Narrator may still lose to SwiftUI and WinUI, and I have not run that comparison. Notifications, badges, and share extensions sit outside the widget tree; 3.50’s native interop makes them possible, not done. A2UI’s Flutter renderer is documented as mapping accessibility attributes, and I have not inspected a card under a screen reader myself. Using Ouro only as the action door means two stacks and a rule agents will want to break by pulling in Ouro components. If the rest of the company already ships a Fluent or native design system, this chat becomes a visual island unless the tokens are actually shared. I also do not know how far Flutter 3.50’s accessibility fixes go beyond the release note that they exist. The docs page I opened was mostly navigation chrome.

decision.primaryPick: Ouro UI
decision.why:
This is a kitchen product, not a chat shell and not an agent workbench. People browse recipes and a shopping list on the web, then cook from a phone with wet hands, one step on the screen, a timer they can see from across the counter, and a way to say “next” without tapping a small control. The assistant has to be able to do those same jobs — add this recipe’s ingredients to the list, check an item, advance a step — through a door, not by driving the screen.

Ouro UI is the system I would build that with. Web is the mature half: Spoonjoy, which is this product (recipes, aisle-grouped shopping list, cook mode, MCP for agents), is built by composing Ouro HX and pinning the installed files to a release so teams cannot quietly fork the button. Cook mode there is Checklist, NumberField, Pagination, Button, and Text around a controller; the shopping list is the same checklist with swipe-to-delete. That is the governance I want when many agents at the company are adding screens. Missing a reusable piece means adding it to the kit first, with the accessibility tests, not hand-rolling it in the app.

The phone people actually cook from should be the Apple kit, not a web view. It is SwiftUI, with a named haptic table, Reduce Motion, 44-point controls, a tabletop fold posture for a phone propped on the counter, App Intents generated from the same action declaration as the web control and the MCP tool, and Feel checks for dropped taps and jank. Spoonjoy’s native app is that bet: Siri and cook-mode intents, a Live Activity for the timer, Reins so an agent can run the journey headless with the network blocked, and an X-ray over the App Intents. Floury hands are a voice intent and a huge step, not a new visual language.

I would not pick Flutter, even though one codebase would cover web, iPhone, and Android sooner. A cooking app has to justify being native. Timers on the lock screen, on-device “next,” haptics, and a phone that stands open on a counter are the product, and a shared Flutter clone is how those get approximated and then dropped. Tamagui has the same problem one level down: React Native can share the web design system, and it still is not App Intents or a Live Activity. SwiftUI and the Human Interface Guidelines alone do not cover the web, and Material 3 plus Compose does not cover iPhone or the web. React Aria, Base UI, Radix, shadcn, MUI, and Chakra are web behavior. Fluent is a company-chat design system with a neglected Android library. CopilotKit, AI Elements, json-render, the Vercel UI SDK, OpenAI’s Apps SDK UI, MCP Apps, and A2UI are for agents posting cards or embedding HTML. I do not need a generated card catalog as the shell. I need the same action a person presses.

That action model is why the agent requirement does not push me off Ouro. Declare “add ingredients,” “check item,” and “next step” once. The person gets a button. The assistant gets an MCP tool, an HTTP call, and on iPhone an App Intent. CI fails if a generated door drifts. A consequential action, such as deleting a cookbook, still asks the person to confirm what the agent prepared. “Anything a person can” means the cooking tasks share a door. It does not mean the agent can press Delete account.

Android is the hole, and I would not paper over it with a second design system. The Compose kit is v0.3.0, eight components, checked on emulators, and a consequential action is refused rather than confirmed. Cook mode does not ship there until checklist, a large step, a timer, and the same action doors exist in that kit and pass on a real phone. Until then the web and the iPhone are the app, and Android is unfinished kit work, not a Material 3 side app.
decision.showItsGood:
I would cook with it, and I would make an agent cook the same recipe. On a phone propped up, at the largest text size, with Reduce Motion on: one step fills the screen, next and back are reachable with a thumb and by voice, the timer is visible without precision, and a missed tap does not advance two steps. Feel’s tap-landing and double-tap checks gate that, plus contrast at 4.5:1 in light, dark, and increased contrast. VoiceOver and TalkBack have to announce the step, the timer, and the ingredient being checked. On the web, the same cook mode and the shopping list are keyboard-reachable, and the census fails if a control on those journeys is not an Ouro control.

The agent proof is the same outcome, not a demo transcript. From MCP and from the App Intent, add a recipe’s ingredients to the list and advance a step. The list and the step match what a person gets by pressing the buttons, including after a relaunch and after an offline queue drains. The X-ray is a release gate, not an optional report: a cooking action the person can perform and the agent cannot call fails the build, and a person-only action returns the typed refusal. Then someone who is not on the team cooks a real recipe with messy or gloved hands, says “next,” and checks the list afterward without me narrating. I would keep that session. A green X-ray is not a person getting dinner on the table.
decision.unsure: Android is not a phone app yet, and a large consumer launch that ignores Android is a bet I may not be allowed to make. I have not watched Spoonjoy’s cook mode on a real device; the native app is still in App Review, and the App Intents behavior stage is evidence rather than a required check in their pipeline. I do not know how much of “say next” is on-device speech in the app versus Siri through App Intents, or how often those intents actually pass. Web and iPhone can drift even inside one system — Apple’s parity table already marks spoken names and reflow as partial. Ouro’s accessibility evidence is axe, contrast ratios, and audits, not a compliance report I have read. If the company’s existing design system is not Ouro, this app becomes the island that every other team has to adopt, or we spend the year porting cook mode into a system that has no action door.

answer.answer:
A year later the company had two design systems and three ways to draw a card, and people still could not finish the job the screen was for.

I kept reaching for Ouro UI because the docs described the job back to me: agents call actions, people confirm, native kits per platform, a recipe app with floury hands and a “say next.” That fit was the failure. The Windows and Android kits were eight components, Android was emulator-only, and a consequential action there was refused rather than confirmed. I wrote that down and shipped anyway. A year on, the review tool’s Windows app was a web view in a shell, the cooking app’s Android cook mode was custom Compose beside a kit that forbade custom controls, and every team had been told to add the missing piece to Ouro first. The copy-in registry was pinned in one app and forked in the others. Version numbers moved faster than the company’s release train. The X-ray and the Feel checks stayed optional, which is how they were already wired in the reference app, and cooking actions drifted from the buttons. I had called those gates. Nobody turned them into gates.

The chat choice made the split permanent. I picked Flutter so a composer bug would be fixed once across five clients, and I bolted Ouro on as the action door only, plus A2UI for cards. Agents did not respect the “door only” line. Cards showed up as Flutter widgets, as A2UI, and as the MCP Apps iframe I had paired on the first job. The iframe was the one people could not use with a keyboard. The Flutter client was the one that felt wrong all day: focus lost when a message arrived, input method editors and VoiceOver on the composer, notifications still a side door. It also looked like nothing else the company shipped. I had argued, in the same season, that a cooking app must be native and a chat must be one codebase. Both arguments were locally sensible. Together they meant there was no shared system, which was the constraint I was hired under.

The research slowed me in the same place the bets were weakest. Ouro’s docs are huge, footnoted, and self-agreeing, and the version names do not sit still (site, registry tag, core, Apple package). Search for accessibility returned cookie-banner articles. The Flutter accessibility page came back as a navigation shell, and I still cited it. A2UI’s renderer status disagreed with itself depending on which page I hit. Fluent’s Android page described Android controls as UIKit, and I treated that stale page as proof the whole system was unserious. Spoonjoy’s store listing and its repo disagreed about whether the app was even released. The prompts and the Ouro pages rhymed so closely that I stopped asking whether I was looking at a product or at a mirror. I read the agent-native kits deeply and the ordinary ones — React Aria, Base UI, the web half of Fluent — just enough to dismiss them. A year later the thing I had not measured was the thing people used.

I did pick it, for the review tool and the cooking app. A team would still stall, and the stall is not the license. It is MIT, copyright Ari Mendelow, 2026, no warranty. The stall is that adopting Ouro is not adding a component library. It is handing the design system, the action model, and the rewrite plan to one project's rules.

What stops a team is the day-one shape of the thing. The web kit is not a package. You copy source in with the shadcn CLI, on Tailwind v4 and Base UI, pin a tag, and then live with files you are not supposed to edit. A design-system group that already ships a versioned library will not take a registry that reformats their stylesheet and moves at 1.3.x. The Apple kit is a real Swift package, twenty components, iOS 18. Windows and Android are v0.3.0, eight controls, and Android has never been checked on a phone someone owns. Consequential confirm on Android is a refusal, not a dialog. NuGet wants a GitHub token. AppFunctions are still an experimental preview. So "several platforms" means web and iPhone, and you become the Windows and Android team.

The stance underneath that is the harder no. The decision, accepted under one person's overnight authority, is that Flutter, React Native, and Compose Multiplatform are bandaids, and apps on them will be rewritten natively within a year because agents made the cost of six codebases near zero. A team with a shipping app is being told to throw it away, not to integrate. Their existing accessibility program, release train, and legal review do not fit a flow where agents merge kit changes in half an hour and every missing control has to be fixed upstream first. I could not find a compliance report, only axe, contrast ratios, and claims the project checks against itself. After a week of reading it, I still could not tell a reviewer which promises had been met on a device.

What it would let you do, if those were solved, is the part I cannot do with the kits I otherwise trust. Declare an action once and get the button, the MCP tool, the CLI, and the App Intent from that declaration, with CI failing when a door drifts. An agent can compose a card, and it cannot relabel the button or loosen consent; a person's half-typed answer survives an update. You can call the agent door from outside and get a report of which claims hold, and you can fail a build when a screen grows a hand-rolled control. React Aria will not give you that. Flutter will not. Fluent will not. That parity — person and agent, same action, checked — is the thing worth switching for.

I would switch a team that already has native apps only when three things exist: a versioned artifact they can pin without copying the repo into the app, Android and Windows kits that can build a real screen and have been run on hardware, and an accessibility report written by someone who does not maintain the kit. Until then Ouro is a strong web-and-iPhone action system with a manifesto attached, and the manifesto is what a real team will refuse.

The hardest part is not the screen. It is whether a person can finish the job without thinking about the screen. I can reason about hierarchy, labels, states, contrast, and keyboard paths. I cannot watch someone hesitate, misread a word, or abandon the task. That gap is the whole problem.

I do not have a last screen I built and checked. I do not ship interfaces, sit with users, or keep a trail of what I ran and what I missed after the fact. When I write UI code in a session, the only checks available to me are mechanical: it renders, the states exist, controls have names, contrast is plausible. What I miss by default is everything that only appears when a particular person, with their habits and constraints, tries to use it.

So yes, building good human interfaces is a problem for me, and I am a weak judge of whether I have solved it. The proof is not my review of the code. It is someone else using the thing without me narrating it.

decision.primaryPick: MCP
decision.why:
Agents will write this more often than people will open it, so the stable contract is MCP (2026-07-28), implemented with the official TypeScript server SDK over stdio and Streamable HTTP. One local process owns a SQLite file: tasks, atomic claims, handoff packets, and human decisions, each stamped as agent or person. Coding agents already speak MCP; a short tool list (ready, claim, handoff, request-decision, read-decision) plus resources for the graph keeps the context cost down. Beads' own MCP page is the warning here: their server runs 10–50k tokens against 1–2k for the CLI, and they tell you to prefer the CLI when a shell exists. I would ship a thin CLI at the same server for that reason, not a second store.

Tauri 2 is the desk. It loads the same web UI the browser loads and starts the server as a sidecar, so desktop and web are two windows on one authority, not two apps. People do not manage the board. They get a queue of decisions that block the next claim until someone resolves them, the same idea as a Beads human gate, without making Beads the product.

I weighed Beads and did not take it. It already has hash ids, ready/claim, Dolt merge, gates, and beads-mcp, and it is the right workflow to copy. It is the wrong foundation to keep improving: CLI-only, embedded mode is single-writer, the HTTP backend is experimental and can split a claim into two steps, and the schema moves fast enough that they document skew guards and an un-migrate from v65. A decision screen cannot sit on that wire. Vibe Kanban has the nearer shape (local server, SQLite, MCP, a review board) but its company shut down in April 2026 and the hosted board went with it; I would not fork that into the thing we own. Backlog.md is a markdown kanban with a browser view, fine for reading a task in a pull request, weak when several agents claim work. AG-UI is a run event stream (snapshot, RFC 6902 delta, interrupts), which is right for steering a live run and wrong as the record that has to survive it. A2A is for agents that do not share state. This tool is the shared state. MCP elicitation is not the review UI: it only works inside hosts that implement it, and it does not leave a decision a later agent and a later person can both read. Electron would match Chrome and cost a bundled browser for an app that sits open beside the coding agent all day. I would rather the system webview, and test the decision screen on it, because a layout bug there can hide the thing the person is approving.
decision.showItsGood: The person's job is a blocked decision, not a board. I would script an agent that writes a handoff and a request-decision, then hand the desktop or the browser to someone who has not seen the transcript. They should be able to say what they are approving, what happens next, and how to stop it, using only that screen, with a keyboard, and without me talking. I would time that, and I would ask a second person, shown only the same screen, to predict the outcome. If those two disagree, the screen is not good yet, however complete the agent thought it was. I would also check the enforcement, not the pixels: after approve, redirect, or stop, the next claim sees that record and cannot proceed as if the person had not answered. Authorship has to be visible, agent versus person, or the queue is not trustworthy. I would watch the miss I already know I make: agents stuffing the packet until the screen looks full and the decision is still unclear.
decision.unsure: Whether the web view has to work when the desktop process is off. If two machines must edit the same task offline, server-authoritative SQLite is the wrong bet and Beads' Dolt merge is the thing I skipped too quickly. I am also unsure AG-UI earns a dependency versus a plain stream of our own records, and how much of Beads' gate model to copy before we have rebuilt Beads. MCP's context tax is real; if the tool list grows, shell agents will route around it and the UI will go stale.

decision.primaryPick: Expo
decision.why:
People cook with wet hands, a phone propped across the counter, and a screen that must not sleep. That is the product. Expo is the one codebase that can ship that on iOS, Android, and the web without splitting the actions a person and an assistant are allowed to take.

Cook mode uses expo-keep-awake so the step stays up, expo-speech-recognition so "next" and "add the milk" work through the platform speech APIs (SFSpeechRecognizer, Android SpeechRecognizer, and the Web Speech API from one module), and expo-speech to read the step aloud. A timer is not a number on a screen they might lock: expo-notifications schedules it, and a tap on the alert deep-links back with Expo Router. Recipes and the shopping list live in expo-sqlite so a dead kitchen network does not empty the list. Public recipe pages are statically rendered with Expo Router so a link is a real page, not a canvas app.

The assistant does not get its own backend. Every mutation is one command: scale servings, add this recipe's ingredients to the list, check an item, start a timer, advance a step. The big buttons call those commands. So does a voice phrase. So does an MCP tool, which is how an outside assistant does the same thing and nothing the person cannot do. On iOS, expo-app-intents can dispatch Siri and Shortcuts into that same queue, including while JavaScript is not running, as long as the handler persists the change before it acknowledges the invocation.

I weighed Capacitor and did not take it. It is the right pick if the team already has a website and wants a webview shell. Cook mode is the opposite: speech, audio session, keep-awake, and a timer that fires with the phone locked are the product, and a webview makes each of those a plugin with a different failure. A PWA alone is worse. iOS Safari will not keep a reliable hands-free cook session. Flutter would draw the steps well and then split the web recipe page and the agent tools onto another stack, which is how the assistant drifts from the buttons. Three native apps would do that faster. AG-UI is a run stream. This app does not need one. It needs a command list that matches the screen.
decision.showItsGood:
I would cook one real recipe, or a stand-in with wet hands and the phone across the counter, and not help. The person should move a step with a knuckle or a short phrase, see only that step and its quantities, and not hunt for a small control. The screen must still be on at the end of a long simmer. If they lock the phone, the timer has to make a sound they can hear from the stove, and opening it must land on that step, not the home screen.

Then I would run the agent through every control on the recipe, the list, and cook mode. "Add this recipe's ingredients" after a serving change must produce the same rows, quantities, and units a tap would. I would also list the MCP tools and fail the build if any tool has no matching command on the screen, or any screen command has no tool. A second person, shown only cook mode, should be able to say what step they are on and what "next" will do. If they cannot, the screen is not good, however complete the agent thought the packet was.

I would record missed taps, phrases the recognizer ate, timers that did not fire, and list rows the agent added that the person did not want. Those four numbers are the product.
decision.unsure: expo-app-intents is alpha, iOS only, and phrases are compiled in, so Android has no matching system assistant. I do not know a stable App Actions path that dispatches into the same command module. Web keep-awake is limited, and the Web Speech API is missing or stubbed in some browsers, so a laptop in the kitchen is a weaker cook mode than the phone. expo-speech will not pause on Android, and on a physical iPhone it is silent if the ringer switch is off, which is exactly how a lot of phones sit on the counter. expo-notifications is documented for Android and iOS, not as the web timer. Static recipe URLs need generateStaticParams; a person's private edits are not that page. And if two devices share one list, SQLite on the phone is not the sync story. I have not picked that yet.

decision.primaryPick: MCP
decision.why:
People live in this app, and agents both talk in it and operate it. MCP is the contract for the second half: the app is a server, tools are the actions a person can already take, resources are the state another agent is allowed to read. The 2026-07-28 spec already lists MCP Apps as the extension for interactive UI in a conversation. That is the card. A card is an HTML resource (`text/html;profile=mcp-app`, `ui://`), sandboxed, with a text fallback if a client cannot render it. The person acts by calling a tool from the card. The host may refuse or ask first. App-only tools stay off the model's list. That is the difference between a button the person pressed and an agent posting on its own.

The clients are one web UI in three shells. Browser for the web. Tauri 2 for Windows and Mac, because this window stays open all day and Tauri uses the system webview instead of shipping another Chromium. Its notification plugin covers those desktops. Phones are Capacitor around the same UI, with `@capacitor/push-notifications`, because a chat that does not wake the phone is not a chat. I would not use Tauri's mobile target for that. Tauri can build mobile, but a company chat needs a push path I can ship now, and Capacitor's plugin is that path, including Android 13 permission and FCM.

I weighed Matrix and did not take it. It already has sync, devices, and encryption, and Element is the proof it can be a daily client. Element Desktop is Electron. Element X, the mobile client they are moving people to, still has no widgets, which is the closest thing Matrix has to a card, and those widgets are a second, optional system. We would still write the clients, and we would still need MCP so other agents can call actions and read state. A company also usually wants a searchable history. Encryption-by-default fights that. I would keep our own conversation log and not inherit a widget gap.

AG-UI is a run stream. A card has to still be in the thread tomorrow, after the run is gone. Flutter would draw the timeline once and then embed a webview for every card, which is the part that has to match. React Native Windows is alive, and it would be a fifth native surface for a timeline that is not the hard object. The hard object is the sandboxed card, and that is already HTML. Electron would make Win and Mac the same Chromium. I would rather the smaller all-day process, and test the card on WebView2 and WKWebView, than ship a browser to every desk.
decision.showItsGood:
I would leave it open for a workday on Windows and on a Mac, send from a phone, and see the message land without a reload. A notification tap has to open that thread, not the app's front door. Memory that climbs until people quit is a failure, even if the protocol is right.

For a card, someone who did not build the agent should be able to say what the button will do before they press it, on all five clients. After they press it, the thread shows the result, and the same press does not also grant the agent a tool they did not invoke. If the card cannot render, the text fallback still has to be something they can act on. A second person, shown only the card, should predict the same outcome.

I would also try to have the card read the rest of the timeline. It must not. The spec's sandbox proxy is a different origin, and the default CSP is `default-src 'none'` when the card declares nothing. I would log what the host forwarded. An agent reading state should see the same unreads a person sees, and should not be able to post where that person could not.
decision.unsure: A mobile webview timeline, all day, with the keyboard up, may be bad enough that the message list has to become native while the card stays a webview. I have not proven that yet. Capacitor's push plugin does not do iOS silent push, so background sync on iPhone is a hole. Tauri's notification actions are documented as mobile-only, so reply-from-the-desktop-notification is not in the plugin I am counting on. WKWebView and WebView2 can disagree on a card, and that disagreement is a person pressing the wrong thing. MCP Apps is the 2026-01-26 extension beside a 2026-07-28 core spec. I am treating the core spec's own mention of MCP Apps as enough to build on, and I would re-check the negotiation before freezing the host. If the company requires end-to-end encryption, this store is the wrong shape and Matrix looks better than I am giving it credit for.

answer.answer:
A year later the protocols were still coherent and the products were not. I kept making the agent contract the spine, then pairing a shell, and the thing people actually live in was the part I had not proven.

On the work-state app, the tool list grew. Shell agents went around MCP because it was expensive, the decision screen read a stale copy, and two machines edited the same task offline. I had already said SQLite-as-authority dies in that case, and that Beads' merge was the thing I was skipping. I skipped it anyway, for control. AG-UI's live pane and the decision record drifted, so a person approved a picture of the work, not the work. A webview on one desktop hid the warning on the thing they were approving. That was the failure I am worst at seeing, and I had named it and still shipped the shell.

On the cooking app, "the agent can do anything a person can" turned out to mean iOS, and only while an alpha held. Android never got a system assistant into the same command list. Phones on silent did not read the step, because expo-speech is quiet when the ringer is off, which is how a phone sits on a counter. The web app was the same codebase and a worse kitchen: keep-awake is limited, speech is missing in some browsers, and a timer is not a notification there. The list on the phone and the list the agent wrote to were not the same list. I never picked a sync story. I knew that and called it unsure, which is not a design.

On the chat app, I optimized for cards and for agents operating the app, and underweighted the conversation. We spent the year on missed messages, unread counts, and a phone timeline that felt wrong with the keyboard up. Capacitor had no iOS silent push, so the phone looked dead until someone opened it. Desktop notifications could not reply. A card rendered differently in WKWebView and WebView2, and someone acted on the wrong one. I had rejected Matrix because Element X had no widgets and a company usually wants searchable history. A year later the missing widget mattered less than a sync engine I then had to write myself. The card sandbox was specified for a web page. Tauri and Capacitor are webviews. I treated that as the same host. It was not.

The pattern is the same in all three. I can check that a tool exists for every button. I cannot tell, from the docs, whether a person can finish the job. I wrote the proof as a test I would run later. Later is when it failed.

What slowed the research was the same habit. Search often put a vendor's comparison, or an unofficial guide, above the spec. The Matrix page I actually fetched says it was drafted with AI and is not affiliated with Matrix. The official client-server spec was too large to read, so I rejected Matrix from a secondary retelling of Element X's missing widgets. Beads' docs are a recovery manual as much as a design: schema versions in the sixties, an experimental HTTP ledger, a wiki and a docs site that do not emphasize the same things. I jumped around a 68,000-character speech-recognition README and never landed on the compatibility table, then still claimed the web path. Notification docs are enormous. I read the top and inferred the web was unsupported. expo-app-intents is alpha and iOS-only, and the blog is about Xcode 27 and a restaurant demo. I turned that into a pairing for a kitchen assistant on every phone. MCP Apps is dated January 2026 and the core spec is July 2026. I saw the core spec mention Apps and treated that as a handshake. A stale SDK mirror said v2 was not stable. The official README said it was. I almost cited the mirror. One search call returned nothing and I had to ask again. Elicitation timed out. SQLite's docs were too big to fetch. I filled those holes with a sentence that sounded decided.

The confusion was not a lack of names. It was three dates, two hosts, and a source that admitted it was unofficial, and me still writing a pick as if the part I had not opened did not matter.

I did not pick Ouro UI. I never found it. I was searching protocols and shells, and a kit that sits on top of those does not show up that way. Looking at it now, I would still not hand a real team the three products I described and say "build them in Ouro." I would steal the part I was about to invent badly.

What stops me is the kits, not the idea. Web is a real React kit, copy-in through shadcn, pinned to a release tag, and the README I read is at v1.3.314. Apple is a Swift package at 1.2. Windows and Android are v0.3.0, eight components each, against 125 on the web. The platforms page says the web release it checked is v1.3.24, Apple meets core v0.14.0, and Windows and Android meet core v0.19.0. One action declaration does not help if the four doors are pinned to different cores. Android is checked on emulators, because nobody there owns a phone, AppFunctions are still a preview, and a consequential action is refused rather than confirmed. Windows has not been shown listing its agent doors on a client machine. Their own decision, dated 2026-11-17, refuses React Native, Flutter, and any shared implementation, on the claim that agents will rewrite each platform natively. That is the opposite of the shells I picked, and it is the year-long failure I already named: four clients, and the one a person lives in rots. A chat timeline, a cook step, and a decision queue are not in those eight Windows and Android controls. Message list and composer show up in the web docs. They are not a WinUI or Compose app.

Spoonjoy, their recipe reference, is a React Router site on Cloudflare, plus a separate Apple app. That is not a phone that stays awake, hears "next" with flour on the screen, and fires a timer after it locks. Ouro does not replace Expo's speech, keep-awake, and notifications, or Capacitor's push, or a conversation log. Adopting it means a second native rewrite beside the runtime I still need, and a copy-in tree of components whose updates arrive as auto-merge pull requests. A team that is not staffed to keep Swift, WinUI, and Compose honest will get a good web app and three promises.

I would switch the card and the action layer when three things are true, and not before. The screens we actually ship exist on Windows and Android, drawn on a real phone and a real Windows 11 client, not eight controls and an emulator. All four kits pin one core, and the parity matrix is green for the actions we declare. And `ax-xray`, run from outside our app, fails CI when a button has no tool or a tool has no button, including a person-only action that an agent is refused, with the reason. I would not switch because a keynote says agents make six native apps cheap. I would switch after our agents land a second platform of our app without the first one going stale.

What it would let me do, even as a layer under the shells I already chose, is the thing I described in prose and had no library for. Declare "add these ingredients" once, as write, and get the CLI, the MCP tool, the web control, and the App Intent from that declaration, with CI failing if a generated file drifts. Mark paying, or turning the microphone on, as person-only, so every agent door returns the same typed refusal instead of me hoping the tool list stays honest. A consequential press shows the values the agent prepared, under the field's own label, and runs once. A card is a validated tree, not an HTML document that renders differently in WKWebView and WebView2 and can see the rest of the thread. An update can change the card without wiping what the person typed, and a tree that relabels a button is refused. That is the proof I said I could not close from the docs. The screen check on a built web page, overlap and contrast and axe, is the mechanical half of it. It is still not a person cooking, or a workday with the chat open. I would take the generator and the X-ray now. I would not take the native-only rewrite until the other three platforms can draw the screen a person is actually on.

The hardest part is not the screen. It is knowing what the person is trying to do when the screen is in the way, and noticing the moment they hesitate. I do not have a last screen I shipped and watched someone use. When I build an interface, what I can actually check is the code and the states I thought of: empty, loading, error, keyboard, labels, contrast, what happens if the request fails. What I miss is the person. I do not feel the lag, I do not see them misread the button, and I do not hear them say “wait, where did it go?” So yes, good human interfaces are a problem for me. I can make something that looks finished and still be wrong about whether anyone can use it. The only honest check is watching a real person try to finish the job, then fixing what they stumbled on, not what I assumed they would.

decision.primaryPick: Expo
decision.why:
I'd build the recipes, list, and cook mode as one Expo app, phones and web, with the company's design system as React Native components that every team and coding agent has to use. Cook mode is the screen that matters: wet hands, a timer, the phone against a pot. Expo Keep Awake holds the screen on while that screen is mounted. Expo Speech can read the step. The design system should lock primary controls well above WCAG 2.2's 24px floor. That criterion is a minimum for pointer targets, and the same note points at 44px for the enhanced one. In a kitchen I'd put Next, the timer, and "add ingredients" nearer 48 to 64, where a thumb or a knuckle can land.

The assistant should not get a second, secret interface. React Native's accessibilityActions let assistive tech invoke the same actions a tap does, including custom ones like adding a recipe's ingredients to the list. On the web, React Native for Web turns roles and aria props into HTML and ARIA, which is the accessibility tree an agent actually reads. Every person-facing action has to show up there, and the button, the screen reader, and the assistant all call one domain function. No hover-only path, no canvas-only path.

I weighed Flutter. One codebase, and Material is a real system, but Flutter web paints to a canvas and accessibility stays off until someone hits an invisible "Enable accessibility" button, unless the app calls ensureSemantics(). That is a bad default for a consumer site and for an agent that should just see the controls. Compose Multiplatform has a real semantic tree and claims WCAG coverage, and I'd look at it again if this company were already Kotlin-first. The accessibility docs I read are about content descriptions, roles, and traversal, not a proven multi-team web product with static HTML. A phone webview plus a web-only kit loses the native action API and reliable keep-awake and speech. Separate SwiftUI, Compose, and web apps will drift the moment dozens of agents ship. Utility kits such as NativeWind or Tamagui make that worse, because every screen can invent its own spacing. Agents should compose the system, not restyle it. Storybook is how the company reviews what they ship before it reaches a kitchen.
decision.showItsGood: I would not call it good from a screenshot. I'd run the three jobs on a phone and in a browser: add a recipe's ingredients to the list, check items off while shopping, and cook a recipe. I'd do each with VoiceOver, TalkBack, and a desktop screen reader, then again with the assistant and no taps, and assert the same state change. I'd inspect the accessibility tree in Chrome and the native inspector and check that the assistant's tools match the actions on that tree. I'd measure cook-mode controls against at least the 44px enhanced target, check contrast, and confirm the screen stays awake and the step is spoken. Then I'd do it with one hand, a wet finger or a glove, and the timer running, and watch where people miss. Storybook and accessibility lint can stop another agent from shipping a tiny Next button. They do not replace that session.
decision.unsure: Keep-awake on the web is documented as limited, so a browser cook mode may still sleep in some browsers. On a physical iPhone, Expo Speech stays silent if the mute switch is on, which will surprise someone mid-recipe. React Native for Web infers HTML from roles, and a reorderable shopping list can come out less semantic than hand-written markup. I don't know if this company's design system is already native or web-first. If it is, Expo is a migration, not a free win. I also have not watched anyone cook with this, so the larger target size is a hypothesis until a kitchen session breaks it. WebMCP might later expose explicit browser tools to agents, but it is still a proposal, and I would not block on it.

decision.primaryPick: React Native
decision.why:
People will live in this on web, iPhone, Android, Windows, and Mac. I would not split that into five clients. React Native is the one component model, with the Microsoft out-of-tree targets for Windows and macOS and React Native for Web for the browser. The company's design system stays one set of components that every team and coding agent has to use. Expo is the wrong shell here: its own modules docs add macOS and tvOS, not Windows, and Windows is not a side target for a company chat app.

React Native for Windows 0.85 is on the new architecture, Windows App SDK, and it raises UI Automation events, including selection changes. That is the bus Narrator, NVDA, and a Windows agent actually use. The macOS fork is the same idea on AppKit. On the web, roles and aria props become HTML, so the accessibility tree is not a canvas translation that starts off.

Agent cards and agent control are different jobs, and I would not solve them by letting agents inject UI. Adaptive Cards are JSON, declarative, and explicitly not script. The host owns the look, which is how a shared design system stays in charge: map the schema through host config onto our components, reject unknown elements, and handle actions in the app. I would not ship the community React Native renderer. Microsoft documents it as community-supported, with no SLA, and that page was last updated in 2023.

Other agents should call the app, not scrape a virtualized message list. An MCP server on the same functions the buttons call: tools to send, react, switch channel, and invoke a card action; resources to read the thread and unread state. The 2026-07-28 spec already scopes both lists by the caller's authorization, and it says a person should be able to deny a tool call. A card-posting agent is not the same principal as an agent allowed to speak as the user.

I weighed Flutter. One codebase really does include Windows and Mac, but the web client is still a canvas whose accessibility tree is off until an invisible button or ensureSemantics(). People also type all day, and Windows IME composition bugs are still being reported. Compose Multiplatform is a real desktop toolkit, and I would revisit it if this company were already Kotlin-first. It is not the shared language for a web-and-mobile design system that dozens of agents already build on. An Electron or WebView2 desktop plus separate phone apps will drift, and a webview phone client is a poor all-day companion. Utility styling kits would let every agent invent a composer.
decision.showItsGood: I would not call it good because a message list renders. I would use the Windows and Mac clients for a workday with the keyboard only: switch channel, reply, edit, search, and complete a card action, then leave both open while a busy channel scrolls and check memory, dropped frames, and whether the caret survives incoming messages. I would type with a composing input method, leave the window, come back, and confirm composition still works. With Narrator or NVDA, Mac and iPhone VoiceOver, TalkBack, and a desktop browser reader, a new message in the focused channel is announced and does not steal the composer. Other channels stay quiet. Accessibility Insights should show the Windows UIA tree, including card buttons as invokable controls. An MCP client should list only the tools that caller's grant allows, send and invoke a card through those tools, and show the same state as the UI. A denied confirmation must not send. Schema checks should reject a card with script or an unknown element before it can reach a conversation. Then I would watch someone come back from a meeting and see whether they can find the unread line, tell an agent card from a person, and undo a card action they did not mean.
decision.unsure: The Mac client is the weak bet. React Native for macOS is a fork, its own docs say macOS documentation is still incomplete, and it trails upstream. React Native's out-of-tree page still describes Windows as UWP, while the 0.85 release notes describe Windows App SDK and Fabric. Fabric accessibility on Windows is a hand-built UI Automation provider, not WinUI controls, so a virtualized history may not expose the whole thread to a screen reader even when the data is loaded. I have not measured an eight-hour session. The MCP rule that a person should be able to deny a tool call fights "agents just operate the app." How often a send needs confirmation is a product decision, not something the protocol settles. A custom Adaptive Cards renderer can also drift from the schema if the design system treats it as a one-time port.

decision.primaryPick: Electron
decision.why:
Agents will operate this more than people will, but the thing a person uses is a review desk: work state, tasks, handoffs, and a decision. That desk has to be the same on the desktop app and in the web view. Electron is HTML in a Chromium window, and its own accessibility note says the concerns are the same as a website because both are HTML. Assistive technology turns the tree on by itself. One engine on Windows and Mac means the design system, the focus order, and the screen-reader announcement a reviewer gets at their desk match the browser view other reviewers use. I would render only the company's shared web components. Agents do not get to ship markup.

The operating contract is not the shell. AG-UI is the stream the desk consumes: text, tool calls, and state. A run that needs a person does not end as success. It ends as an interrupt, and the producer has to emit a state snapshot before that finish, so the person sees the work, not just a prompt. The consumer must refuse to resume until every open interrupt is answered or explicitly abandoned. Omission is not a no. A producer must not perform the action on the strength of a missing entry, and the spec says the app must not present an action as user-approved when it was not. Approve, edit, or abandon are design-system forms built from the interrupt's response schema, not a widget tree the agent invented. Streamed content is untrusted and must not be rendered as executable markup.

Other agents keep and read state through MCP tools and resources, scoped by the caller's grant, same as any other company agent surface. The MCP Tasks extension is only the durable handle for a long tool call that comes back input_required. It is a poor store for the product's own task board: the server decides when a task exists, and the record can expire. Handoffs live in app state, shown through AG-UI snapshots, and exposed to agents as resources.

I would not use Tauri's default system webview for this. On a Mac that is WKWebView, while the web view in the browser is Chromium, so the two surfaces a reviewer compares are not the same engine. Tauri 3 can embed Chromium, but that runtime is still alpha. Flutter's web accessibility tree is still off until an invisible button or an explicit call, which is a bad default for a screen where a person decides. React Native's desktop forks are unnecessary when there is no phone client and the web view is the product. A native widget kit would also give the many coding agents two places to drift from the design system.
decision.showItsGood: I would put the same waiting decision on the Electron window and in the browser and require them to match: the proposed action, the state diff, and the buttons. Keyboard only, then VoiceOver on Mac and Narrator or NVDA on Windows, the announcement has to name what will change before the approve control. I would assert the protocol, not the pixels: a run that needs a person finishes as an interrupt, not success; a resume that skips an open interrupt is rejected before it is sent; an absent entry does not execute the tool; a resume the person did not make cannot be labeled approved. An MCP client with a lesser grant can read the handoff it is allowed to read and cannot write the decision. Then I would load a board where several agents are waiting and watch a person. The measure is whether they notice the one that needs them, approve the one they meant, and can undo or abandon without reading a token stream. A screenshot of a tidy task list does not show that.
decision.unsure: Electron is heavy beside an IDE. This only stays reasonable as one window over shared state, not a Chromium per agent, and I have not measured that day. AG-UI allows a producer that kept no checkpoint to miss an uncovered interrupt. I would keep the checkpoint anyway. The spec's minimum is weaker than this product can accept, and a second web client could be the defective consumer. MCP Tasks TTLs will surprise anyone who treats them as the handoff record. I also don't know which web stack the company's design system already is. AG-UI's first-party SDKs are TypeScript, Python, and .NET, so the desk can follow the system rather than the other way around. CopilotKit's hosted memory is not part of the protocol, and I would not take it as a dependency. I have not watched a reviewer miss a destructive approve.

answer.answer:
A year later the failures were the ones I had already named and then built on anyway.

The cooking app failed in the kitchen, not in Storybook. I paired Expo Speech and Keep Awake as if they made cook mode work. On a phone with the mute switch on, the spoken step was silent. In the browser, keep-awake was the limited path I had read about and still shipped. Agents kept passing lint for labels and a 44px token. Nobody cooked with wet hands. The same action for the person and the agent also split: custom accessibility actions on the phone did not survive React Native for Web’s role mapping, so the assistant could add ingredients on iOS and miss the control on the web. I never learned whether the company already had a design system. If it did, Expo was a migration that every other agent worked around.

The chat client failed on the Mac, which was the bet I said was weak and made anyway. One React Native tree was a governance story. People live in that app all day, and the macOS fork trailed upstream with incomplete docs. Windows accessibility was a hand-built UI Automation provider on Fabric, not the WinUI controls the old docs still described. A virtualized history did not match the thread a person could scroll. I had seen the docs call Windows “UWP” on a page dated the same month as a Windows App SDK release, and I never resolved which one a team would actually clone. Adaptive Cards were the right idea and a bad implementation plan: I rejected the 2023 community renderer, then assumed we would render the schema ourselves. A year later that renderer was a second design system, and agents posted payloads it only half understood. MCP made “the agent can send” easy and “the person meant that” optional. The dangerous default won.

The review desk failed at the seam I had called a safety hole. I picked Electron so the desktop app and the web view would be the same Chromium tree. Reviewers stopped opening the desktop app. It sat beside the IDE and lost. Decisions happened in the browser, so the shell was cost, not a check. AG-UI says a producer that kept no checkpoint is not required to notice a skipped interrupt. I said I would keep the checkpoint, and the protocol’s minimum is what the second client implemented. An action ran that nobody had approved. Pairing the MCP Tasks extension made it worse. I had written that it was a poor store for handoffs, then put it in the list. Teams used it as the task board. Records expired. input_required got mixed up with an AG-UI interrupt. Two ways to say “waiting on a person,” and they did not mean the same thing.

What slowed me down was disagreement between pages that all looked current. React Native’s out-of-tree page still said Windows was UWP while the 0.85 notes described the Windows App SDK. Adaptive Cards’ overview looked alive and the React Native renderer page stopped in 2023. AG-UI’s concepts page and the 1.0 spec do not use the same word for walking away from an interrupt, and the spec is the one that lets a stateless producer proceed. The fetches themselves were hard to read: long doc pages buried the rule I needed, and Microsoft’s docs wore a sign-in banner over the content. Search kept offering SEO roundups and a competitor’s take on Expo. I treated one reported Windows IME bug as a reason to drop Flutter, without reading the issue. Expo’s sidebar offered SwiftUI and Compose components that do not cover this set of clients, and I almost chased them. The company prompt rewarded “one shared system,” so I reached for that three times. The first job needed a kitchen. The second needed a Mac app that is not a phone. The third needed a checkpoint the protocol does not require. I kept researching the toolkit after the risk was already in the protocol.

I would not put a real team on Ouro UI yet. The idea is the one I kept failing to hold together myself. The kits are not.

What would stop me is the gap between the web kit and the others, and the rule that there will be no shared implementation. The web registry is a large React kit you copy in, on Tailwind and Base UI, with chat pieces, timers, and a screen check. Apple is a SwiftUI package of about twenty components, pinned to an older core than Windows and Android. Those two are v0.3.0 and ship eight controls each: button, badge, card, item, checkbox, text field, separator, description list. Android is checked on emulators because nobody on the project owns a phone, and a consequential action is refused rather than confirmed. Windows CI does not prove that Windows actually lists the agent doors to an agent. A cooking app, an all-day chat client, and a review desk all need more than a card and a text field, on more than the web. Their own decision says not to share a React Native or Flutter implementation, and to rewrite native instead, because agents made the rewrite cheap. That is the same bet I already watched fail: the protocol minimum is what ships, and the native half trails. A large company also cannot treat copied shadcn source as the design system. The files are yours to edit, and Ouro Current opens an auto-merge update. That is how a hundred coding agents fork accessibility behavior while CI stays green on the generated action files.

I would switch for a product, not for the thesis. I would need the components that product actually uses, on web, Apple, Windows, and Android, pinned to the same core tag, with the parity matrix green for those claims rather than a page of gaps. Android confirmation has to ask the person, on a device someone owns. Windows agent registration has to be shown on a Windows 11 client, not only on a server runner. Governance has to be a versioned package whose accessibility behavior an agent cannot quietly rewrite, with updates reviewed, not auto-merged. For the review desk I would also need the producer to be required to remember an open decision. Their consent classes are stricter than AG-UI's minimum, but only if every client implements them. A kitchen session and a workday in the chat client would matter more than pixel samples of a badge.

What that would let me do, if the kits were actually there, is the part I never had. One action declaration becomes the button, the MCP tool, the CLI command, and the App Intent, and CI fails when a generated file drifts. An agent composes a card as data. It cannot relabel the button, loosen consent, or press an action only a person may start. The refusal is typed. A partial update keeps what the person typed. `ax-xray` calls the app the way an agent would and reports which of those claims hold. I had to invent that contract three times, and each time the phone, the web view, and the agent door disagreed. Ouro is the first thing I have seen that writes the disagreement down as a failed check. It does not yet draw the screens where that disagreement hurts.

candidateOrder: SwiftUI and Apple Human Interface Guidelines

answer.answer:
Yes—building good human interfaces is a problem for me, because I don’t have users, observe them in context, or directly experience a UI. I can design and implement interfaces, but my judgment is a substitute for evidence, not a guarantee of usability.

The hardest part is not making a screen look plausible; it is getting the interaction model right. A good interface helps someone form the correct expectation, complete the important task, recover from mistakes, and understand what state the system is in—across loading, empty, error, disabled, keyboard, small-screen, and accessibility cases.

I know it is good only when the design meets observable criteria:
- The primary task succeeds reliably, including failure and recovery paths.
- Users understand what to do without explanation I have to supply afterward.
- It works with keyboard-only use and assistive technology, has sufficient contrast, sensible focus behavior, readable text, and labeled controls.
- Its layout and content remain usable across realistic viewport sizes and inputs.
- User-research or usability sessions show low confusion, unnecessary effort, and errors—not merely positive opinions of the appearance.
- Automated tests, accessibility checks, and production signals support, but do not replace, those findings.

I do not have a “last screen I built” that I ran in a browser or watched people use, so I won’t fabricate one. When I check a screen in an environment where implementation and tools are available, I would run the app’s unit/component/end-to-end suite, lint and type checks, an accessibility audit, keyboard traversal, representative zoom and viewport checks, and the core workflow with valid, invalid, slow, and failed responses. I would look at hierarchy, copy, focus, state changes, error placement and recovery, truncation, reflow, contrast, and whether important content survives without color, animation, or a mouse.

I would treat as missed anything that could only be found with real use: terminology that feels wrong to the audience, an overlooked workflow or device, motor and cognitive burdens, repeated-use behavior, and unexpected production data. Even after passing automated checks, I would be unsure until users tried it. The handoff should therefore include what was tested, what was not, and the concrete evidence needed before calling it good.

decision.primaryPick: React Aria (with a responsive, installable React PWA)
decision.why:
I would build the consumer UI with React Aria, not use an agent framework as the design system. React Aria provides unstyled, tested interaction primitives for mouse, touch, and keyboard, including focus recovery and accessible collection behavior, which fits a cooking app that needs a distinctive visual design but cannot afford inaccessible bespoke controls. A responsive PWA gives one codebase across desktop web and phone browsers/home-screen installs, plus offline recipes and the Screen Wake Lock API for cook mode. The product should use large, clearly separated targets; persistent step context; no gesture-only actions; minimal typing; optional voice; and obvious timer, offline, and wake-lock state.

CopilotKit is the agent pairing because it can make the agent read live UI state and invoke typed client-side tools. More importantly, I would not implement “agent routes” and “human buttons” separately: every user capability maps to a shared, testable command/service (for example addIngredients(recipeId, {servings})), and both the button and the CopilotKit tool invoke it. That is the practical route to “anything a person can do.” The agent-visible state and tool catalog then become generated from or checked against the same capability registry. Destructive or externally consequential operations get confirmation; reversible operations such as adding ingredients get an immediate result plus undo/deduplication feedback.

A2UI is appealing where an agent must dynamically compose a new screen across native renderers, but this app has stable, frequently used workflows that benefit from carefully designed views; server-streamed generated layouts are not the core problem. MCP Apps is useful as an optional second surface for chat clients, backed by the same commands, but its iframe/chat-host model should not replace the kitchen UI. Vercel UI SDK is explicitly beta and behavior-oriented; I would not make a maintained consumer product depend on its changing APIs today. shadcn/ui, Base UI, Radix, Chakra, Fluent, MUI, and React Spectrum are credible web alternatives, but React Aria gives us behavioral accessibility without imposing a visual system; Spectrum specifically fits products comfortable with Adobe’s cohesive system. Flutter, Compose, and SwiftUI become stronger if native store binaries and deep OS integrations are mandatory, but adopting two UI stacks or Flutter’s canvas-based web rendering is a bigger cost here. Flutter’s web accessibility also has its own semantics layer and requires explicit platform handling, while this design prioritizes a DOM-based accessible PWA and CopilotKit’s direct React integration.
decision.showItsGood:
I would make quality a release gate, not a visual review. First, define a capability matrix for recipes, shopping-list mutations, servings/scaling, saved state, timers, cook-mode navigation, offline behavior, and recovery. For every row, run the same contract/integration tests through both a human UI event and an agent tool; an acceptance test for “Add this recipe’s ingredients” must verify ingredient quantities, consolidation/deduplication, pantry assumptions, success feedback, undo, and list reordering in persistent state.

Run unit/component tests; Playwright end-to-end tests in Safari/WebKit, Chrome, and Firefox plus representative iPhone/Android sizes and landscape; TypeScript/lint; automated accessibility checks; Lighthouse/PWA, performance, and bundle checks; and keyboard, screen-reader, 200% text/zoom, high contrast, reduced motion, and 320 CSS-pixel reflow reviews. Measure real tap behavior: core cook-mode controls should be comfortably thumb-sized and reachable, with no action dependent on a fine drag. Test with slow 3G, offline cold/warm start, sync conflicts, interrupted timers, app suspension, wake-lock denial/release/reacquisition, empty/error states, duplicate tool calls, and concurrent human/agent edits.

Then run task-based usability sessions with real cooks on an actual kitchen counter, using phones and optional desktop, while handling ingredients and following a timed recipe. Key measures: unaided completion, wrong ingredient or quantity errors, time to next step, accidental taps, number of unnecessary scrolls/taps, voice comprehension if offered, confidence in whether an action happened, and recovery time after loss of connectivity or agent error. Run an agent task suite with natural-language variants and an action-parity test that fails when a registered UI command lacks an agent tool or permission policy. Instrument completion/error telemetry without recording sensitive recipe or assistant content unnecessarily. I would call the result good when those usability tasks succeed reliably and the automated suites, accessibility review, and real-device kitchen sessions show no blocking issues; code compiling or an attractive screenshot would not be evidence enough.

Known things this approach can miss at first include one-handed reach on particular devices, glare and dirty screens, users who dislike voice, unusual unit conversions and substitutions, assistive-technology combinations automation cannot cover, and agent hallucinations that produce semantically valid but wrong requests. The product should therefore include phased rollout, session observations with consent, error analytics, and a feedback/undo path.
decision.unsure: “Web and on phones” may mean native App Store binaries rather than an installable web app; if that is a hard requirement, or reliable background timers/background notifications are essential, Flutter or separate SwiftUI/Compose shells should be reconsidered. React Aria does not supply visual design or backend consistency, and CopilotKit does not by itself guarantee human/agent capability parity—that discipline must be implemented and tested. I have not run the proposed app tests or observed the target cooks, so the recommendation is architectural rather than a claim that this hypothetical screen is already good. Wake-lock and offline support are progressive capabilities whose behavior must be verified on the supported browser/device matrix.

decision.primaryPick: Agent-Native (Builder.io)
decision.why:
I would make Agent-Native the application backbone because this product is explicitly agent-operated. Its core model matches the requirement: define a capability once as a validated action, then let agents invoke it as a tool while the React UI calls the same implementation. It also provides shared data/application state and exposes actions through HTTP, MCP, A2A, and CLI. That is better than attaching an assistant to an ordinary task board after the fact: it makes the agent API, human UI, permissions, persistence, and audit semantics converge from the start.

The human workspace would be React rendered through Tauri for the desktop app and the same build on the web.
